articles.title: Nio devait arrêter ses stations d'échange de batteries en Europe, il en ouvre une nouvelle
articles.text:
Sur l’A7, entre Francfort et Hanovre, les conducteurs de Nio ne trouvaient aucune station pour changer de batterie. Le constructeur chinois vient d’ouvrir une station près de Kassel, alors qu’il avait assuré à ses clients européens qu’il ne construirait plus aucune station.
C'est un sacré ascenseur émotionnel pour les propriétaires européens de Nio, après avoir appris au printemps que la marque ne construirait plus « ni stations ni bornes en Europe », nous explique Numerama. Chez Nio, le client achète sa voiture sans batterie et loue celle-ci au mois. En Europe, Nio achète seul ces batteries et les garde dans ses comptes, faute de partenaire financier, et chaque station de troisième génération est conçue pour stocker jusqu’à 21 batteries pleines. Plus Nio ouvre de stations, plus il doit donc acheter de batteries. En ouvrant la station de Kassel, il continue de les payer seul, et les conducteurs de sa citadine Firefly ne pourront pas l’utiliser.
Faute de partenaire, Nio paie seul ses batteries européennes
William Li, fondateur et P.-D.G de Nio, avait posé le problème devant des clients norvégiens. « En Europe, nous n’avons ni partenaire ni société de ce type, ce qui veut dire que tous les actifs de batteries fournis via le BaaS seront détenus par nous, dans notre bilan », expliquait-il. Ce partenaire, Nio l’a trouvé en Chine, mais pas en Europe.
Le constructeur a malgré tout ouvert une station sur l’A7, là où ses clients manquaient le plus de solutions. Les conducteurs qui quittaient la station de Reiskirchen, au nord de Francfort, devaient jusqu’ici rouler 290 kilomètres avant la suivante, près de Hanovre. Les propriétaires qui partent du sud de l’Europe vers la Scandinavie sont les premiers concernés. « Ce site comble un vide important sur les axes de circulation nord-sud de l’Europe », a fait valoir l’entreprise.
Geely pourrait apporter à Nio le partenaire qui lui manque. Le groupe chinois s’est engagé à prendre 30 % de NIO Power, qui gère l’échange et la recharge des voitures de Nio, en apportant sa filiale Yiyi Power et 640 millions de yuans. Des responsables de Geely ont ensuite interrogé William Li sur l’Europe. « Tout à l’heure, des collègues de Geely me demandaient aussi si nous devions, l’an prochain, lancer notre plan de réseau d’échange de batteries en Europe et l’annoncer ensemble », a raconté le patron de Nio dans un entretien vidéo diffusé en Chine. Il n’a dit ni quels pays seraient couverts, ni si Geely financerait ce réseau.
Aucune station pour la Firefly, la citadine conçue pour l’Europe
L’obstacle de la Firefly est technique. Nio a dessiné cette petite citadine en priorité pour l’Europe, avec une batterie de 42,1 kWh incompatible avec les stations de troisième génération installées sur le continent, dont celle de Kassel. En Chine, le constructeur a réglé le problème avec des stations de cinquième génération ouvertes aux trois marques du groupe. Devant les propriétaires réunis aux Pays-Bas, la direction européenne avait en revanche exclu ces nouvelles stations du continent, d’après le participant.
Les premières Firefly livrées en Europe ont donc été vendues avec leur batterie, sans abonnement, faute de stations adaptées, et leurs conducteurs rechargent sur une borne. Un conducteur français a encore moins de choix. Nio a installé ses stations en Allemagne, aux Pays-Bas, en Suède, en Belgique et en Norvège, mais aucune en France. Si vous partez de France au volant d’une Nio, vous devrez passer la frontière belge ou allemande avant de pouvoir changer de batterie.
Le BaaS est un modèle où la voiture est vendue sans batterie : l’utilisateur loue la batterie via un abonnement et peut l’échanger en station. Ce système implique que quelqu’un finance et possède le stock de batteries nécessaires aux échanges. En Europe, faute de partenaire financier, Nio doit acheter et détenir lui-même ces batteries comme des actifs dans son bilan, ce qui immobilise beaucoup de capital. Plus le réseau de stations s’étend, plus le besoin en batteries « en réserve » augmente mécaniquement.
Une station d’échange automatise le retrait de la batterie vide et l’installation d’une batterie chargée, puis recharge la batterie retirée en interne. Pour garantir un échange rapide, la station doit disposer d’un stock de batteries pleines, dimensionné selon la fréquentation. Une station de troisième génération peut stocker jusqu’à 21 batteries, ce qui représente un inventaire coûteux à financer et à maintenir. Ce stock est aussi un point critique opérationnel : s’il est insuffisant ou mal adapté aux modèles compatibles, l’échange perd son intérêt face à la recharge sur borne.
L’échange de batterie exige une standardisation stricte : dimensions du pack, points de fixation, connectique haute tension, interfaces de communication et procédures de sécurité doivent correspondre exactement à ce que la station sait manipuler. La Firefly utilise une batterie (42,1 kWh) conçue avec des caractéristiques physiques et/ou d’interface différentes de celles gérées par les stations de troisième génération déployées en Europe. Résultat : même si la station est sur le trajet, elle ne peut pas effectuer l’échange pour ce modèle. En attendant un réseau compatible, les propriétaires de Firefly se reposent sur la recharge classique sur borne, avec batterie achetée plutôt que louée.

articles.title: Russian gasoline-powered drone spotted on the front lines
articles.text:
Ukraine spots Russia deploying a mystery new petrol-powered drone that could fly further than ever before
Russian loitering drone swaps electric motor for a gasoline engine
- Ukraine identifies a mysterious Russian drone powered by gasoline
- Red-starred wings distinguish the unfamiliar aircraft in photographs
- Russia's new drone resembles the Lancet with different propulsion
Ukrainian defense specialists have identified a previously unknown Russian aircraft powered by gasoline, which adds to Moscow's growing range of unmanned weapons.
The drone reportedly resembles Russia's Lancet loitering munition, although its combustion engine sets it apart from the electrically powered weapon.
“A new enemy drone has been spotted on the front. It resembles the Lancet in shape but has a gasoline engine. We are waiting for captured examples to study. Get in touch,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technologies.
Gasoline engine distinguishes the aircraft from Lancet
Images show red stars painted on the wings, but nothing visible in the photographs identifies the aircraft or what it is designed to do.
According to Beskrestnov, the name, manufacturer, and specifications have emerged, yet he has declined to release them until they are confirmed.
The propulsion system is the clearest reported difference from the Lancet, a Russian loitering munition developed by ZALA Aero Group that uses an electric motor.
Burning gasoline could allow longer missions without reliance on battery capacity, since combustion engines can offer greater endurance depending on fuel use and design.

However, the drone's flight duration, operational range and payload capacity have not been disclosed, which prevents any comparison with existing Russian unmanned aircraft.
Russia continues developing battlefield drone capabilities
The Lancet is designed to strike artillery systems, armored vehicles, and radar installations, launches from a catapult, and comes in versions with varying warheads.
Russia has modified the Lancet family before, and the Ukrainian defense has identified an updated version with a redesigned antenna system.
That change potentially affected the drone’s communications, though Ukrainian defense reporting says its forces kept intercepting the upgraded systems, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.
The new drone could give Russian forces another propulsion option for missions where extended endurance is an advantage, though its deployment extent is unknown.
At a defense forum in Kyiv last month, Ukrainian military officials and industry representatives warned that battlefield technologies were evolving rapidly.
Participants urged faster innovation and wider use of AI tools, along with autonomous systems, and asked engineers to forecast Russian developments six months to one year ahead.
Ukraine has also expanded its domestic drone manufacturing, with locally produced systems accounting for 95% of unmanned aerial vehicles procured for its armed forces.
Similarly, Russia has expanded its drone manufacturing, with satellite imagery showing that the Alabuga zone in Tatarstan grew by 340 hectares in a year.
Ukraine’s military intelligence said Russia produces about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month and that Moscow seeks more capacity at Alabuga.
Bloomberg reported plans for more than 7 million FPV drones, while Beskrestnov estimates Russia’s yearly strike drone capacity at 36,000 to 40,000 units.
With both sides expanding their drone factories, the gasoline-powered aircraft is an indication of what may follow as manufacturers keep testing new engines and designs.

articles.title: Samsung W27 : les images du smartphone pliable de luxe en fuite
articles.text:
Samsung aura fait de 2026 une année pleine de smartphones. Car un quatrième modèle de luxe est sur le point de sortir !
Quel sera le smartphone pliable de l'année ? L'iPhone Duo, ou alors le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 ? Dans tous les cas, Apple va être loin de son rival historique dans le domaine, au niveau du nombre de modèles qui sont lancés cette année. Car après le Galaxy Z Fold 8, le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, le Galaxy Z Flip 8, c'est un nouvel appareil dit W27 qui va arriver sur le marché. Et aujourd'hui, on le découvre en image !
Le Samsung W27 se révèle en images
Il y a quelques jours, on découvrait une première image publicitaire du quatrième smartphone pliable de Samsung, le W27. Il s'agit d'un smartphone plutôt de luxe, que Samsung va lancer ce 29 octobre, et que vous pouvez dorénavant découvrir dans des images fuitées sur X par Evan Blass, ci-dessous.
La version ici proposée est dite Aura Blue. Le smartphone affiche un design bleu et doré sur les bords qui réussit très bien esthétiquement parlant. Pour ce qui est à l'intérieur, la fiche technique devrait être la même que le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.
Un smartphone qui sera exclusif à la Chine
Pour la version mise en vente, on s'attend à ce qu'une seule version avec 16 Go de RAM et 1 To de stockage soit mise en vente. Niveau prix, il faudra évidemment s'attendre à une étiquette avec un très gros chiffre dessus, sachant que le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra est déjà cher (à partir de 2 199€) et que cet appareil le sera plus encore.
Enfin, pour ceux qui auraient eu le coup de coeur, il faut quand même que l'on vous précise que ce smartphone ne sera vendu qu'en Chine ! Alors, si jamais vous vouliez tout de même vous le procurer, il sera nécessaire d'aller le chercher directement à la source, avec une petite importation à la clé.
Source : GSMArena, Evan Blass sur X

articles.title: Yes, it’s cheaper to buy the iPhone 18 Pro and new iPad mini than a single iPhone Duo — but the money misses the point
articles.text:
It’s been an exceptionally busy few months for Apple. In just seven weeks, the Cupertino giant has refreshed its store shelves with the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Duo, HomePod mini 2, HomeView, OLED iPad mini, iMac M6, and MacBook Pro M6.
That’s eight new products designed to tempt you to reach for your wallet, but by offering more choice than ever, Apple has also thrown up some unique new buying conundrums.
For instance, if it’s cheaper to buy an iPhone 18 Pro and Apple’s new iPad mini than it is to buy the iPhone Duo (spoiler: it is), should you? That’s the argument currently doing the rounds on Reddit and TechRadar sister site Tom’s Guide, where my colleague says the iPhone 18 Pro/iPad mini combo is “cheaper and better” than Apple’s first foldable.
I can absolutely see the logic in this position. The iPhone 18 Pro costs $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099. The new OLED iPad mini costs $699 / £699 / AU$1,099. Together, they cost $1,898 / £1,898 / AU$3,198, while a single iPhone Duo costs $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499. You’d be getting two great products instead of one, and saving $101 / £101 / AU$301 in the process.
The iPhone 18 Pro is also a better phone in many ways than the iPhone Duo. It’s thinner, lighter, has better cameras, and doesn’t rely on Touch ID. The OLED iPad mini, meanwhile, offers a Duo-comparable entertainment experience, and can even be equipped with the same Nano-Texture display technology as Apple’s first foldable. No brainer, right?
But the fundamental difference between these two purchase decisions is that one involves two devices, and the other only one. These are not like-for-like experiences. Owning and using an iPhone 18 Pro alongside an iPad mini is not comparable to the experience of owning and using a single iPhone Duo. But the reverse is true.
The Duo is a compromise, yes, but it still offers an undeniably iPad-like experience in pocketable form. You’re paying a premium for its versatility and portability. The whole point of the Duo (and foldables generally) is that it lets you experience a tablet whenever and wherever you are. It’s like using a spork while camping to save you packing a spoon and a fork. Or buying a Range Rover Sport instead of a Ferrari and a family-sized minivan.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The new iPad mini is small, sure — but are you really going to walk around with an 8.5-inch tablet in your pocket? Tom’s Guide’s assertion that “Apple has inadvertently priced its own foldable out of the market for anyone willing to carry a small bag” makes a rather big assumption about the number of people willing to carry a small bag on their person at all times. I am not one of those people, and I don’t know many of them.
All this being said, I am no great iPhone Duo defender. For me, the compromises of getting an iPad-like experience in an iPhone-sized device are, at the time of writing, too great, and I would personally rather stick with my iPhone 18 Pro (and, yes, maybe even buy an iPad mini for watching movies in bed or on the plane).
But that does not mean I think I can recreate the experience of owning the iPhone Duo by buying two separate Apple products — watching movies in bed or on the plane is not the same as watching movies wherever I please.
Buying the iPhone 18 Pro and the new iPad mini might be better value for money than buying a single iPhone Duo, but value and compatibility are two different things. There’s definitely something to be said for owning one device that offers the best of both worlds, and anyone considering the iPhone Duo should remember that before being swayed one way or the other.

articles.title: PrivacyHawk data removal service review
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
PrivacyHawk is a decent data removal service, but more could be improved, like its customer support channels and data broker coverage. However, it provides a broad feature set outside data removal, like dark web monitoring, spam call blocking, and more.
Reasons to buy
- + User-friendly interface
- + Deep scanning
- + iOS & Android mobile apps
Reasons to avoid
- - No live chat support
- - U.S.-centric data broker coverage
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Any personal information posted online could be harvested by data broker sites and remain in their databases for a long time. These sites pose privacy risks that need to be mitigated. A data removal service like PrivacyHawk is an effective mitigation strategy: it scans data broker sites for your data and sends deletion requests where it’s discovered.
PrivacyHawk is one of many data removal services and identity theft protection tools out there. And you’re probably wondering, “Why should I choose it over other options?” I reviewed the platform to answer this question. Read on to learn about its features, pros, cons, and other factors to help decide whether it’s your ideal choice.
PrivacyHawk: Plans and pricing
You can check out the PrivacyHawk platform by clicking here.
It has a simple pricing system. Individuals can choose either the Premium or higher-priced Platinum plan. The former offers mostly data removal, while the latter offers extra features like dark web monitoring, identity theft protection, and priority support.
The Premium plan costs $20 per month, and the Platinum plan goes for $30 per month. However, PrivacyHawk offers steep discounts for users who choose to pay annually. An annual Premium subscription goes for $74, compared to $240 if paid month-to-month, and an annual Platinum subscription costs $125, compared with $360 if paid month-to-month. These steep discounts make an annual payment the best option.
PrivacyHawk also offers family discounts for both the Premium and Platinum plans. For Premium, a Family package (covering 4 people) goes for $200 annually, and the Platinum Family package costs $300 annually.
If paid month-to-month, the Premium Family plan costs $40, while the Platinum Family plan costs $50. This sums up to $480 over 12 months for the Premium plan, and $600 for the Platinum plan, which are overly high prices. I wouldn't advise paying month-to-month for the Family package—choose it only if you can afford the annual payment.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
PrivacyHawk doesn’t offer a standard free trial, which is a drawback, but there’s a 30-day window to request a refund if you're unsatisfied with what you get. After downloading PrivacyHawk, I discovered that I could run some free scans (as part of a so-so, unofficial free tier package), but this isn’t a substitute for a standard free trial.
PrivacyHawk: Setup
Setting up PrivacyHawk doesn’t take much effort. It has designated iOS and Android apps, a feature that sets it apart from most data removal platforms I’ve tested. Setting up PrivacyHawk starts with downloading the app from the Play Store (Android) or App Store (iOS).
After downloading the app, you can sign in with an existing Google or Apple account. Provide the necessary sign-in permissions, and you’ll enter your PrivacyHawk dashboard.
PrivacyHawk welcomes new users with a free scan, as I noted when discussing the lack of a standard free trial. To begin the scan, you’re prompted to enter your name, last name, and age. PrivacyHawk then runs this data against a network of 100+ people-finder sites to discover where your personal data may be present.
Notably, this scanning is geared towards U.S.-centric data broker sites. Non-U.S. residents can run a digital footprint scan, but can’t scan or send deletion requests to data broker sites.
I wasn’t comfortable with the fact that I needed to sign into my email again to run a digital footprint scan (although I did eventually). For most platforms I’ve reviewed, typing the email address is what’s needed to run the scan.
However, PrivacyHawk claims it works by analyzing email inboxes to see which companies could expose personal data. It also compiles a list of junk email senders that you can quickly unsubscribe from. If you’re comfortable with signing into your email address for a deep digital footprint scan, you can do it.
PrivacyHawk covers a network of 100+ data broker sites. This figure isn’t large compared to several competitors, but PrivacyHawk only focuses on U.S.-centric data broker sites, rather than providing global coverage. A scan can take anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours, after which you’ll see a list of the data broker sites hosting your data. You can quickly initiate deletion requests, and this is where the real work begins.
PrivacyHawk sends automated deletion requests to data broker sites, asking them to remove your personal information from their database. If an automated request isn’t sufficient, PrivacyHawk’s team can send a manually drafted legal request to the data broker sites. Processing removal requests can take a long time, maybe 30 to 90 days, depending on the data broker site. Fortunately, I could monitor the progress of each request from the smartphone app.
You may have discovered your data present on a data broker site that isn’t covered by PrivacyHawk. In that case, you can initiate a manual removal request for that site from your dashboard. PrivacyHawk’s team will send a deletion request on your behalf and follow up on it.
After the initial scan and deletion requests, PrivacyHawk runs monthly rescans of your personal data and sends email alerts if your data is found on any site. You can then initiate new deletion requests. Overall, I found PrivacyHawk to be a reliable data removal platform, although with limited U.S.-centric coverage.
PrivacyHawk: Ease of use
PrivacyHawk scores high when it comes to user-friendliness. The mobile app felt very smooth to navigate, with features neatly arranged and an uncluttered dashboard for scanning, initiating, and monitoring deletion requests.
The interface features a white background with brightly-red-colored icons & buttons that are easy to find. From signing up to scanning and managing deletion requests, I have no complaints about PrivacyHawk’s ease of use.
PrivacyHawk: Security and privacy
PrivacyHawk may not be the best data removal platform, but its complementary features make it practically a full-fledged security suite. With a single app, you can check if your data was discovered in data breaches, identify and block robocall numbers, and counter spam emails. A PrivacyHawk subscription significantly boosts your online privacy and security.
PrivacyHawk: Support
PrivacyHawk users have access to a detailed Help Center with user guides and manuals related to all its features. This Help Center proved very valuable as a new user navigating through data broker and digital footprint scans.
When I needed direct help, I contacted PrivacyHawk’s team via email. I saw what looked like live chat support, only to discover it was an AI chatbot, and I couldn’t chat with human support staff. Given the price of a PrivacyHawk subscription, I think live chat or telephone support should be provided, but they aren’t available.
PrivacyHawk: Competition
I’ll highlight OneRep as the main competitor to PrivacyHawk. It offers broader coverage, with a network of 300+ public data broker sites and 500+ non-public ones, compared to PrivacyHawk’s 100+ coverage. Its plans are more affordable than PrivacyHawk’s.
However, PrivacyHawk offers complementary features like dark web monitoring, identity theft protection, and robocall blocking, while OneRep offers email breach monitoring and little else. I think PrivacyHawk is a more complete security suite, but OneRep is a better option for data removal.
PrivacyHawk: Final verdict
PrivacyHawk has its pros and cons. Its data broker coverage is limited, but for the covered sites, it offers deep scans and effective deletion requests.
For sites not covered, you can still initiate manual deletion requests, although success rates may be lower. PrivacyHawk offers advanced complementary features that make it feel like an enterprise security suite.
The most notable drawbacks are the limited customer support, the lack of a standard free trial, and the limited broker coverage. However, PrivacyHawk remains a decent data removal platform.

articles.title: CyberStrikeAI Uses 44 AI Agents to Automate Hacking Operations Against Japan Targets
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of three cyber attacks targeting organizations in Japan in which artificial intelligence (AI) was a key element, either in the driving seat or to assist a human operator.
TrendAI, which analyzed three exposed server environments used by threat actors to conduct the malicious cyber operations, described them as distinct from previously published attacks that have leveraged ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration testing framework, to single out entities in South Korea and Japan.
"These environments held reconnaissance and attack tools, scripts, target lists, results, logs, and command histories," security researchers Bakuei Matsukawa and Joseph C Chen said. "They ranged from workspaces used largely by hand by skilled operators to AI-agent platforms that automated the entire workflow, including command and control."
The first of the three attacks has been found to abuse CyberStrikeAI, another open-source penetration testing tool that was previously put to use in an attack campaign targeting Fortinet FortiGate appliances. The activity was concentrated in a short period in October 2026.
The AI-driven activity leverages the offensive security tool to automate various aspects of the attack lifecycle into a repeatable workflow, beginning with reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery and validation, and exploitation, to command-and-control (C2), persistence, data exfiltration, and automated reporting.
This involves delegating the work among 44 agents to handle various aspects of the attack, while also enabling the generation of forms and fake login pages in the Japanese language.
"In a short period, at least 19 identifiable organizations, including at least 16 in Japan, were subjected to validation activity," Trend Micro's enterprise security division said. "Each had a report in the same format and an index of evidence. These were outputs of a structured process run by the platform, rather than ad hoc notes left by an operator."
The second case has been characterized as a human-led attack with assistance from a large language model (LLM) to accelerate planning and tool development. Analysis of the infrastructure and artifacts indicates that the campaign is also designed to target AI workflow platforms and inference services with an aim to obtain large amounts of inference capacity at low cost.
One of the intrusions is said to have targeted a geographic information system (GIS) server exposed with default credentials, resulting in the theft of cadastral and commercial records, Windows credentials, and email data. The entire campaign lasted for 24 days in August and September 2026.
The third instance is where the AI's role has been found to be confined to developing the operator's tools and scripts, suggesting a limited role played by the technology in a series of campaigns designed to target edge devices from Cisco, Citrix, F5, and Yamaha using published vulnerabilities, management functions, or credentials present in configuration files.
The threat actor is estimated to have run at least six campaigns from January to October 2026, opportunistically striking exposed VPN devices and WebLogic servers. "The operator was experienced, with established practices for automation and evidence management," the researchers said.
There is currently no evidence at this stage that suggests these three incidents share an operator. It's also unknown if the attacks have targeted other regions and what AI models are being used to pull off the attacks.
That said, the attacks involving these threat actors are not restricted to Japan and neighboring countries like South Korea. The operator behind the first case has targeted organizations in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while the third case featured organizations in the U.K., France, Italy, Qatar, and Colombia in its WebLogic discovery lists.
"AI has increased the attackers' workforce, but the work still consists of looking for unlocked doors," TrendAI said. "The types of doors and the weaknesses that leave them open have not changed. What has changed is the ability to try thousands at once, adapt to the target country's language, and continue without fatigue."
The development coincides with the discovery of multiple campaigns in which threat actors of varied motivations have integrated agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows, allowing them to speed up research, malware development, social engineering, and other parts of an attack.
To make matters worse, AI is being increasingly used to accelerate reconnaissance, automate decision-making, and industrialize social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation of security flaws. According to Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, AI has collapsed the median time from vulnerability discovery to weaponization to well below 24 hours.
The adoption of AI by bad actors is reducing the time, expertise, and cost required to discover and exploit weaknesses, at the same allowing attackers and defenders alike to operate with greater speed, scale, and autonomy, the Windows maker added.
"The key issue is not simply whether an actor has frontier AI," Trend Micro said. "Access to capable models can already produce meaningful operational gains. Ecosystem depth, however, determines how reliably, independently, and at what scale those capabilities can be sustained."
"AI is no longer an experimental capability for APT groups; it is an operational component embedded directly into campaigns."
The growing demand for AI tools by threat actors has also opened up a new monetization avenue that peddles stolen AI provider session tokens and offensive AI tools APEX AI, MessiahGPT, and DarkGPT, further commoditizing cybercrime and lowering the barrier to entry for carrying out advanced, persistent, and evasive attacks.
Last week, Microsoft revealed that a China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used ARTEX to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. The activity has been attributed to Storm-0940, which it said has used the framework since as early as September 2026 to automate password-spraying attacks on hundreds of organizations.
"While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," Microsoft said. "Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations."
According to local media reports from South Korea, authorities have identified seven suspects linked to a cybercrime operation that broke into more than 90 organizations in the country, most of which involved ARTEX. The 32-year-old mastermind behind the activity is alleged to have worked at a cybersecurity company between 2019 and 2022, gaining expertise in penetration testing.
In 38 of the incidents, the threat actors demanded ransom payments of 360 million won ($270,000) in exchange for not leaking the stolen data. More than 8.2 million records are believed to have been siphoned from compromised organizations.
Some of the other AI-oriented campaigns that have been documented in recent weeks are listed below -
- 
    A financially-motivated threat actor operating under the handle
    
      BUGSTER
    
    configured the
    
      Hermes Agent framework
    
    with
    
      DeepSeek V4
    
    as its reasoning engine and Cursor as a secondary tool (both with safety controls disabled) to run a WordPress brute-force campaign against an Indian university's website and generate a REST API enumeration report.
    
  - The attacker also breached a second Indian public university, exfiltrating a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students. A third attack enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform to extract a storefront API token, admin email addresses, phone numbers, and payment merchant IDs.
  - "The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders)," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations."
- An e-crime group named CyberCartel has been observed using a multi-agent system called CARLIY0S to coordinate attacks against banks and payment providers across Latin America. The framework employs a cognitive swarm comprising four role-specialized Claude models that "debate each target and defer to one arbiter" before the main orchestrator acts. "The group assigned different roles to commercial AI models to analyze targets, develop attacks, and coordinate operations," Straiker said.
- Threat actors have developed an offensive AI agent designed to hijack exposed AI endpoints to run autonomous attacks, with instructions allowing it to carry out up to 100,000 steps without human approval while the legitimate owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. The system features a malicious loop called Skynet mode that employs a set of 74 tools to scan for targets, infect them, deploy cryptocurrency miners, and reinfect compromised hosts.
- An affiliate for the The Gentlemen ransomware operation has used Anthropic Claude Code during intrusions into at least six organizations in late June 2026, including to generate and execute reconnaissance and exploitation commands, write malicious scripts, modify firewall policies, and identify high-value business systems.
- A credential-harvesting operation codenamed Zerofot built a scanner named "auto_scan" that integrated OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to harvest thousands of API keys and tokens from thousands of exposed hosts across the internet.
- An AI-generated Python framework called RAGE has been used to scan internet-facing services (e.g., Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, Apache Tomcat, Jenkins, Hadoop YARN, Confluence, and Supervisord), exploit vulnerable deployments, capture credentials, and deploy cryptocurrency miners.
- A human operator employed frontier AI models to breach an enterprise network autonomously over a 10-hour period. "The actor breached a publicly accessible web service to tunnel into the network, deploying an automated recon agent to map internal microservices," Unit 42 said. "Sub-agents combed enterprise code repositories, extracting hard-coded tokens and service passwords." The attacker then harvested master administrative credentials and hijacked an enterprise code application to exfiltrate cloud access keys. The stolen cloud keys were then used to turn the victim's AI endpoints into post-compromise infrastructure.
- A suspected Russian-speaking cyber actor used an AI-assisted workflow to exploit PaperCut NG/MF servers and compromise hundreds of instances. "The campaign extended beyond initial exploitation into a structured post-exploitation pipeline covering Windows credential collection, service-credential harvesting, internal network pivoting, Metasploit automation, and victim packaging," Hunt.io said.
- A Chinese-speaking threat actor has breached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, using an autonomous penetration testing engine called Cairn, tasking it to probe targets, search for security weaknesses that could lead to code execution or account takeover, attempt to break in, and steal sensitive data.
"AI is serving as a force multiplier and an expanding attack surface at the same time," Rapid7 said. "Generative AI is accelerating established attack methods by reducing the time, skill, and coordination previously required to execute them at scale."
"Rather than introducing entirely new categories of exploitation, threat actors are integrating AI into existing workflows to industrialize phishing, automate reconnaissance, and refine malicious scripts with greater speed and precision."

articles.title: iPhone Duo chez Orange, Bouygues, SFR et Free : voici quand vous pourrez vraiment le recevoir
articles.text:
L’iPhone Duo d'Apple est en vente depuis le 23 octobre, mais sa disponibilité chez les opérateurs français reste très inégale, entre une livraison sous quelques jours, une attente jusqu’en décembre ou une rupture de stock. Clubic fait le point.
La disponibilité de l’iPhone Duo varie fortement d’un opérateur à l’autre, quatre jours après la sortie du premier smartphone pliant d’Apple. Selon nos relevés du mardi 27 octobre, Orange, Bouygues Telecom et SFR affichent des délais de livraison allant de quelques jours à plus d’un mois, tandis que Free est tout simplement en rupture de stock. Ce démarrage intervient alors qu’Apple vient de reconnaître des fissures sur l’écran intérieur d’un petit nombre d’appareils, qui font forcément tâche.
Commander l’iPhone Duo chez un opérateur ? Préparez-vous à patienter jusqu’en décembre
Commençons par l'opérateur historique, Orange, qui mise sur la régularité. Quelle que soit la capacité (on rappelle que le téléphone existe en 256 Go, 512 Go, 1 To et 2 To), l'iPhone Duo est annoncé livré à partir du samedi 14 novembre sur son site. Avec un forfait, il coûte de 1 619 euros pour le 256 Go à 2 999 euros pour le 2 To, et la facture peut s'étaler sur 24 mois sans intérêts. Orange prévient toutefois que ce délai reste indicatif, suspendu aux approvisionnements d'Apple.
Chez Bouygues Telecom, il y a du stock également et les dates varient selon la capacité de l'iPhone Duo. La version en 256 Go, affichée dès 1 891,90 euros avec forfait, et celle en 1 To sont promises à partir du 16 novembre. La 512 Go, elle, peut être livrée à partir du 20 novembre. Ironie du calendrier, la version la plus onéreuse est aussi la plus rapide. L'iPhone Duo 2 To est livré dès ce vendredi 30 octobre, mais contre 3 211,90 euros réglés en une seule fois. Et pour ce dernier, malgré un prix tout simplement exorbitant, son stock est signalé comme étant « faible ».
SFR réclame davantage de patience à ses clients, comme l'a remarqué Univers Freebox. La version 256 Go est disponible en précommande à 1 941 euros avec un forfait engageant sur 24 mois, puis 100 euros remboursés, mais son expédition n'est prévue qu'à partir du 7 décembre. Les versions 512 Go et 1 To sont indisponibles, et seul l'iPhone Duo en 2 To semble en stock. Contacté par Clubic, Free nous confirme une rupture de stock sur ses modèles 256 et 512 Go, les deux en vente chez l'opérateur de Xavier Niel, sans avancer de date de retour.
Le premier iPhone pliant, entre prouesses et premières fissures
L'iPhone Duo, présenté le 9 septembre, ouvert aux précommandes le 16 octobre et en vente depuis le 23, est le premier smartphone pliant d'Apple. La rareté s'est fait sentir dès le lancement, puisqu'en Apple Store, il fallait avoir réservé un créneau de retrait, et chaque client était limité à deux exemplaires. Le téléphone existe en Ciel nocturne et en Blanc stellaire.
Une fois fermé, il se manie comme un iPhone compact, avec un écran de 5,4 pouces. Ouvert comme un livre, il déploie une dalle de 7,6 pouces, 50 % plus grande que celle de l'iPhone 18 Pro Max. Il pèse 254 grammes, pour 5,2 mm d'épaisseur déplié et 11,3 mm plié. Il embarque la puce A20 Pro des iPhone 18 Pro, deux capteurs de 48 mégapixels et Touch ID, un lecteur d'empreintes logé dans le bouton latéral qui remplace Face ID. Il fonctionne uniquement en eSIM, une carte SIM dématérialisée, et la compatibilité avec l'Apple Pencil est promise pour plus tard. Son prix public varie, selon l'espace de stockage, entre 2 339 à 3 839 euros.
Ce lancement historique pour Apple ne se fait pas sans polémique. Plusieurs propriétaires ont en effet signalé des fissures sur l'écran intérieur, généralement le long de la pliure, parfois au bout de quelques dépliages seulement et accompagnées d'un craquement. Apple a reconnu qu'un petit nombre d'appareils est concerné, sans en préciser la cause. Le démontage d'iFixit, publié le 25 octobre, ne l’a pas identifiée avec certitude non plus. Le spécialiste de la réparation accorde tout de même au Duo une note provisoire de 5/10, la meilleure qu’il ait jamais donnée à un smartphone pliant. Il faut tout de même relativiser, car ce score mesure la facilité à réparer l’appareil, pas sa résistance aux chocs ni à l’usure.

articles.title: GoAhead TLS Flaws Allow Revoked Client Certificates and Enable Session Decryption
articles.text:
The GoAhead embedded web server loaded a certificate revocation list into its default TLS backend but never turned revocation checking on, so a revoked client certificate could still pass login on affected setups.
The flaw is in builds that use the OpenSSL backend with mutual-TLS, where the server checks a client certificate and vice versa, and a revocation list is configured to block revoked certificates.
That is a setup an operator turns on deliberately; a default build does not. GoAhead 6.1.1, released to device makers on August 2, 2026, and publicly published on October 12, fixes it.
GoAhead is a small web server that device makers build into firmware to run management pages on routers, printers, gateways and industrial controllers. Its maker, EmbedThis, says it runs in hundreds of millions of devices.
The flaw was found by Sébastien Féry of FoxIO, who described it and two other TLS problems in a write-up on October 26.
On an affected build, the server loads the revocation list file at startup and reports no error, so an operator who configured it has every reason to think revocation is working. It is not. A client whose certificate was revoked, for example a stolen or retired device, completes the handshake as if the certificate were still valid and gets whatever access that identity allows.
In FoxIO's test against GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2, a revoked certificate was accepted with issuer checking switched on.
The OpenSSL advisory describes revoked client certificates as silently accepted. To be exploited, the build must use the OpenSSL backend with client certificates required, a trusted certificate authority bundle and issuer checking enabled, and a revocation list configured; the attacker must hold a certificate signed by a trusted authority and listed as revoked. Builds that use the Mbed TLS backend are unaffected; that backend checks revocation via a separate code path.
The identifier on the advisory is CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1 by EmbedThis. As of October 27, that identifier and the others below were not yet live in the public CVE and NVD databases; EmbedThis says it has requested them. The severity ratings are the vendor's own.
Researchers cover two further problems, each tied to a specific TLS build. The versions and fixes differ, so the table below maps each by backend.
| TLS build | What goes wrong | Affected versions | Fix or interim option | 
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenSSL (default) | Revocation list loaded but never enforced; revoked client certificates accepted. CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1. | 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 | Upgrade to 6.1.1. No interim option in the advisory. | 
| LibreSSL legacy verifier (3.2.x, 3.3.2–3.3.6) | A client certificate chain longer than the limit is accepted when client certificates are required but issuer checking is off. CVE-2026-115884, rated 7.4. | 6.1.0 and earlier on those LibreSSL versions | Upgrade to 6.1.1, or turn issuer checking on with a trusted CA bundle, or use OpenSSL or LibreSSL 4.x. | 
| Mbed TLS | A length typo sends a 1-byte Diffie-Hellman value instead of the full 2048-bit one, so a passive observer can decrypt the session. Rated 5.9. No CVE assigned. | 4.0.2 through 6.1.0 | Upgrade to 6.1.1, turn off finite-field DHE suites, or use the OpenSSL backend. | 
The Mbed TLS problem only reaches a session if the client accepts the broken setup. OpenSSL, current Go, current Java, and mainstream browsers refuse a value that small and fall back to a stronger key exchange, so the session never completes.
Clients without a minimum-size check, such as some embedded or custom ones, accept it, and then anyone who recorded the traffic can work out the key and read the session. TLS 1.3 and ECDHE sessions are unaffected, and Mbed TLS 4.x removed the key exchange they rely on.
The LibreSSL problem allows an attacker to present a certificate chain longer than GoAhead's 10-certificate limit and still complete the handshake as an authenticated client, without any trusted key.
It appears only on builds linked against the older LibreSSL versions listed above and only where client certificates are required with issuer checking off. OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC and LibreSSL 4.x reject the over-long chain.
Which backend and settings a build uses are chosen when the firmware is compiled, so a device owner cannot tell from the outside which apply. That is also why the fix is slow to arrive: GoAhead 6.1.1 is a drop-in replacement that device makers rebuild and ship as a firmware update, and an owner gets it only when their manufacturer does so. Whether any manufacturer has shipped it is not known.
As of October 27, no source reported any of these problems being used in attacks. EmbedThis's policy is to end a disclosure embargo and publish early if a flaw is being exploited or disclosed by someone else, so the coordinated October 12 release is consistent with no known attacks.
However, it does not prove there are none. EmbedThis notifies customers of security updates through its Builder portal. FoxIO has published proof-of-concept code and offers fingerprints through its JA4Scan tool to find GoAhead servers by backend. The tool is free, but its source is available only on request, and a fingerprint identifies a build, not a confirmed-vulnerable server.
None of the device makers EmbedThis lists as GoAhead users, which include HP, Oracle, Siemens, Canon, Rockwell, D-Link and Comcast, has been shown to run an affected backend and setting. The affected population is not established.
The same 6.1.1 release closes 11 advisories in all, three of them rated critical. One is a login bypass: on a build using HTTP Basic or form login, an attacker who knows a valid username can sign in with any password if that user's stored password is in the newer Blowfish format, which GoAhead added in version 6.1.0. EmbedThis says form login is the default for its built-in administration pages.
After upgrading, EmbedThis recommends ending active sessions, restarting the server, and changing Blowfish-stored passwords.

articles.title: The US Navy is turning to a portable nuclear microreactor to power a key military base even if the lights go out
articles.text:
The US Navy is turning to a portable nuclear microreactor to power a key military base even if the lights go out
Truck-mounted nuclear microreactor should keep the lights on
- The US Navy has picked Radiant's 1MW Kaleidos microreactor for a prototype plant at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana
- The Pentagon wants it running by September 2028 to keep critical systems powered through potential grid outages
- Kaleidos has not publicly gone critical yet, and one unit will back critical loads, not the whole base
The US Navy wants one of its most important weapons installations to keep running if the commercial grid goes down, so it chose a nuclear reactor that can be trucked in to do the job.
The Navy said it had selected Radiant Industries to design, build, and deliver a prototype microreactor power plant for Naval Weapons Station Crane in southern Indiana, a day after the California startup announced the win.
Brendan Rogers, Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Energy, Installations and Environment, said dedicated reactor power means "our critical naval support systems will never go dark."
A 'portable' nuclear reactor for critical infrastructure
Radiant's reaction to being picked has been jubilant: President and COO Tori Shivanandan said there is "no organization in the world with more experience in nuclear power" than the Navy, and the company now bills itself as the only nuclear firm selected by the Army, Navy, and Air Force.
It has multiple reasons to be proud; Kaleidos is a factory-built, helium-cooled, TRISO-fueled reactor rated at 1MW of electricity. Radiant says it can travel by road, sea, or air; needs no cooling water, major excavation, or extensive on-site construction; and runs for up to five years per fuel load over a 20-year life.
It will not roam around Crane; the whole unit travels in tandem. Radiant handles its own fueling, refueling, and spent-fuel storage, so host sites never keep spent fuel and can be returned to greenfield within two years of removing a unit, per the company.
The US Army's Janus program (which procured this) requires all radiological material to leave a host site within two years of shutdown, meaning either enlisting the US Department of Energy to help with any potential disposals or shuttling it elsewhere, often on public roads. Critics see the flip side: anti-nuclear group Beyond Nuclear argues the model puts reactors loaded with irradiated fuel on public highways on their way back to the factory.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The Navy's announcement gives no output, cost, or schedule; the 1MW figure is Radiant's. That is modest for a sprawling installation, and Army officials have been clear that Janus reactors are not meant to run whole bases. They will stay tied to the grid, and Jeff Waksman, the Army's principal deputy assistant secretary for installations, said they are "not going to provide 100% of the power on any of these installations."
The chosen deployment location is no ordinary one; Crane hosts the Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane Division and the Crane Army Ammunition Activity, which, together, handle weapons development, electromagnetic warfare, strategic missions, advanced manufacturing, and conventional munitions production, according to the Navy.
This isn't the Navy's first onshore reactor play; in March 1962, a portable 1.75MW pressurized water reactor known as PM-3A went critical at McMurdo Station in Antarctica, and a Navy team ran it for a decade.
It suffered a hydrogen fire in its first year, shut down for good in 1972 amid cost and corrosion concerns, and removing it meant shipping thousands of tons of contaminated gravel and soil back to the US, according to the Naval Historical Society of Australia. Waksman has cited Janus' two-year cleanup rule as a key break from how the military ran reactors in the 1950s and 1960s.
None of this means Crane won't get its reactor, but it does create red tape and a cautious environment. On the other side of the equation, the Pentagon has a hard deadline and an eager host state; the Navy's reactor program is lending its expertise; and Radiant has a $750 million Army contract in tow.
However, for now, the Navy has picked a reactor that has never publicly run at power to keep a weapons base lit when the grid fails, and testing at Idaho National Laboratory will decide whether "never go dark" is a plan or a hope once it happens.

articles.title: IA : des travailleurs de l'ombre portent plainte pour violation des règles sur les données
articles.text:
Des personnes travaillant dans l'entraînement des modèles IA portent plainte dans plusieurs pays. Et cette action nous fait découvrir des coulisses peu reluisantes pour l'industrie.
On le sait, derrière l'entraînement des modèles IA, il y a de nombreuses « petites mains », que l'on redécouvre périodiquement à l'occasion de scandales. Il y avait ainsi au mois de mars dernier celui des annoteurs au Kenya qui visionneraient les vidéos, même les plus intimes, captées par les Ray-Ban de Meta. Et aujourd'hui, une plainte d'ampleur vient d'être déposée, cette fois contre Scale AI.
Une plainte contre Scale AI déposée dans plusieurs pays, dont la France
La société Scale AI est sur la sellette. La firme américaine spécialisée dans la préparation de données est en effet attaquée en justice dans quatre pays de l'Union européenne : les Pays-bas, l'Italie, l'Autriche et la France.
L'association autrichienne Noyb, qui est bien connue pour son combat pour la protection de la vie privée, est ici à la baguette, avec d'autres partenaires. Elle soutient dans cette action en justice cinq travailleurs indépendants qui officient sur la plateforme numérique de Scale AI, Outlier. Ce sont ici à la fois les conditions de travail, mais aussi les infractions présumées au RGPD, qui sont mises en causes.
Des employés surveillés et tracés
Ces travailleurs sont employés pour effectuer des tâches complexes, comme la rédaction de prompts, ainsi que le classement de réponses ou l'annotation de données. Quand ils reçoivent la notification de leur tâche, ils ont alors 20 minutes pour l'exécuter, et voient leur rémunération (de 20 dollars de l'heure) divisée par deux s'ils dépassent ce délai.
Au-delà de cette cadence infernale, c'est l'absence de respect de la vie privée qui est pointée du doigt par les plaignants. Car en travaillant avec Scale AI, ils intègrent de nombreux traceurs sur leurs appareils électroniques, traceurs qui collectent des données très personnelles telles que l'adresses IP, l'activité sur des réseaux comme Facebook ou TikTok, les types de clics ou les mouvements de souris. Scale AI irait même jusqu'à user de la reconnaissance faciale.
Source : Le Monde

articles.title: A 989g laptop with a built-in stylus promises exceptional endurance
articles.text:
This Japanese brand solves the 2-in-1 laptop dilemma with a 989g frame — offering 28.5 hours of battery life and a stylus charging inside the body
Dynabook’s V83/PA convertible laptop stores and charges its stylus
- Dynabook V83/PA packs a rechargeable stylus inside a convertible laptop weighing 989g
- The 13.3-inch touchscreen delivers WUXGA resolution in a lightweight convertible design
- Battery estimates reach 28.5 idle hours and 16 hours during video playback
Dynabook has introduced the V83/PA, a 989g convertible laptop which offers the portability of conventional notebooks.
The device incorporates a stylus that fits into a dedicated compartment within its chassis, allowing users to store and recharge it internally.
Its 13.3-inch LCD touchscreen offers 1920 × 1200 resolution, and its convertible design allows users to switch between regular business laptop and tablet use.
Lightweight construction with extensive connectivity
Measuring approximately 298.8 × 212 × 18.8mm, the laptop features rounded rear edges, a Dark Tech Blue finish and an enlarged touchpad.
The laptop includes two Thunderbolt 4 connections, with one installed on either side to accommodate peripherals without restricting cable placement.
Two additional USB 3.2 Gen 1 connections accompany HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet and a 3.2mm audio socket for attaching conventional computer accessories.
Its wireless connection uses Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4, while optional mobile broadband configurations provide access to either 4G or 5G networks.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The keyboard incorporates spill protection against approximately 30cc of liquid, but for protection, users have to shut down the computer after accidental spillage.
Dynabook has not published the battery capacity, but it estimates 28.5 hours idle and 16 hours of video playback.
Intel processors, AI capabilities, and enterprise security
Under the hood, these laptops offer different Intel chips, including the Core Ultra 7 365, Ultra 7 355, Ultra 5 335 and Ultra 5 325 chips.
The Dynabooks come with a memory capacity of 16GB or 32GB of RAM, accompanied by 512GB or 1TB of SSD storage and Windows 11 Pro.
The V83/PA includes a proprietary AI tool that translates and summarizes onscreen content when users circle the relevant information with a finger or stylus.
Processing takes place locally rather than through external servers, allowing the software to handle selected content without transmitting it for cloud analysis.
For video conferencing, the laptop also supports AI noise cancellation and Windows Studio Effects, which provide additional software capabilities for online meetings.
Its proprietary Empower Technology sustains processor performance during demanding workloads.
Dynabook offers the V83/PA with either a 5MP front sensor that supports facial recognition or a 0.92MP alternative, and the rear camera is rated at about 8MP.
Users can also unlock the device with a fingerprint reader, which sits alongside the face recognition option on the higher-resolution camera.
Business protections include Secured-Core PC conformity, NIST SP800-171 support, and a proprietary security manager that guards the BIOS.
The V83/PA starts at ¥1,057,320, roughly $6,740, and that figure covers only the base configuration, so the 32GB RAM and 1TB SSD version will likely cost considerably more.
Its 989g weight and battery endurance remain manufacturer estimates that no independent test has verified.
Many premium convertibles and ultralight laptops from other brands offer comparable processors and memory for less, although few of them store a charging stylus inside the body.
The V83/PA therefore depends on its low weight and built-in pen to justify a price that is hard to defend for specifications that are otherwise fairly typical.
