articles.title: Microsoft Authenticator Flaw Let Permissionless Android Apps Steal Work Account Tokens
articles.text:
Microsoft has fixed a flaw in its Authenticator app for Android that let a malicious app with no permissions pose as a trusted Microsoft app, such as Teams, and collect sign-in tokens for a victim's work account.
Microsoft tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-80097 and fixed it in Authenticator for Android version 6.2606.4246, so anyone using the app should update.
In the researchers' tests, the tokens gave full access to the account's email, files, and calendar. Microsoft says exploitation also needs the victim to complete a sign-in step in Authenticator, and that the flaw has not been used in attacks.
The research comes from Ofek Levin, working through a fellowship program at the security firm Enclave, which published the technical details on October 23, 2026. Microsoft assigned the CVE on September 8 and rated it 8.6 on the CVSS scale, which it labels "Important."
On Android, Authenticator does more than show six-digit codes. It also acts as a broker: when Teams, Outlook, or another Microsoft app needs to sign a user in, it asks Authenticator, and Authenticator hands back a token, a digital pass that proves the user is logged in. Because the broker controls access to the entire account, it should be careful about which app it grants a token to.
The flaw let the wrong app get one. Authenticator exposes a component, an activity named AccountChooserActivity, that any app on the device can start. When the attacker's app started it, Authenticator built its token request from values the attacker's app supplied, including the name of the app it claimed to be. The app said it was Teams, and the broker believed it.
A signature check was supposed to stop this, but it did not. The check looked up the real signature of the app being impersonated and confirmed the request matched it. Because Teams was genuinely installed on the device, its real signature was there to read, so the check passed.
Authenticator could also see which app had actually made the request, Enclave found, but it did not use that to decide whether to hand over a token.
In Enclave's tests, posing as Teams and requesting Microsoft Graph tokens returned permissions to read and send mail, read and write files, and read and write calendars, among others.
Microsoft describes the result more generally: a successful attacker could authenticate as the signed-in user and reach that user's resources. The tokens apply to the work account signed into Authenticator on that device, not to other accounts.
The two accounts disagree on one point a reader should weigh. Enclave reported that its proof of concept returned tokens without any user interaction, other than the presence of a signed-in account.
Microsoft's advisory says exploitation requires installing a malicious app on the device and convincing the user to complete an authentication flow in Authenticator. Its CVSS score also indicates that the flaw requires user interaction.
Microsoft says the flaw has not been exploited and was not publicly disclosed before the fix, and rates exploitation as "less likely." It was part of the company's September 2026 Patch Tuesday and was not one of the two Windows flaws flagged that month as already under attack. The vulnerability is not listed in the U.S. CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 26, 2026.
The fix is to update Microsoft Authenticator for Android to version 6.2606.4246 or later, as linked in Microsoft's advisory. Organizations that manage Android devices can require that minimum version through their device management. Microsoft's advisory gives the fix but does not say whether updating cancels any token a malicious app may already have obtained, so that remains unclear from the available sources.

articles.title: Un juge croit reconnaître un texte rédigé avec Claude dans un recours, une étudiante condamnée
articles.text:
Le tribunal administratif de Rennes a condamné une étudiante à 750 euros d’amende, coupable d'un recours abusif. Sa requête contre un refus d’admission en master portait, selon le juge, les marques d’une intelligence artificielle de type Claude, d'Anthropic.
Le 22 octobre 2026, le tribunal administratif de Rennes a infligé une amende de 750 euros pour recours abusif à une étudiante ayant été refusée en master de psychologie à l’université Rennes 2, vient d'apprendre Clubic. Saisi plus de quatre mois après ce refus, le juge des référés a rejeté sa demande d’inscription provisoire. Il a aussi relevé, dans la requête, différents marqueurs typographiques qu’il attribue à l’intelligence artificielle générative.
Ni urgence ni doute sérieux pour le tribunal administratif
L'affaire a démarré avec un refus d'admission en première année de master de psychologie, opposé par l'université Rennes 2 à Delphine*, une étudiante qui ne voulait pas en rester là. La décision était datée du 3 juin 2026, mais le juge des référés n'a été saisi qu'il y a quelques jours, le 18 octobre. L'étudiante a notamment demandé la suspension de la décision et une inscription provisoire sous huit jours.
Elle a expliqué ce délai entre la décision et le recours par un été chargé, avec la phase complémentaire de la procédure nationale, la gestion des désistements, une saisine du recteur le 20 juillet, puis une demande d'aide juridictionnelle le 17 août. Sur le fond, elle conteste le refus sur quatre points. Le chef d'établissement se serait cru tenu de suivre l'avis de la commission. L'acte fixant les capacités d'accueil et les critères de sélection serait introuvable sur le site de l'université. Les membres de la commission n'auraient pas été régulièrement désignés. Et enfin, la signature électronique du refus serait irrégulière, car l'homologation du téléservice Mon Master ne couvrirait plus ses conditions d'utilisation.
Forte de ces arguments et pour obtenir gain de cause, la jeune femme est passée par un référé-suspension, une procédure d'urgence qui permet de geler une décision en attendant que le tribunal la juge sur le fond. Encore faut-il réunir deux conditions : une véritable urgence et un doute sérieux sur la légalité du refus. Le juge n'en a retenu aucune et a rejeté la demande sans même organiser d'audience. Concernant l'urgence, il a estimé que les démarches faires durant l'été n'empêchaient pas d'agir plus tôt, que les cours ont sans doute commencé depuis plusieurs semaines et qu'une nouvelle candidature reste possible pour 2027-2028. Côté légalité, aucun argument ne le convainc, et l'absence de documents sur le site de l'université, par exemple, ne prouve pas qu'ils n'existent pas. Le dossier de la candidate ne plaide pas non plus pour elle. Quatorze autres masters de psychologie l'avaient refusée sans même l'inscrire en liste d'attente, et six autres l'avaient classée, à une exception près, entre la 152e et la 357e place.
Un recours jugé abusif et marqué par l'usage de l'intelligence artificielle générative
Le juge aurait pu s'arrêter là, mais il a pourtant choisi d'utiliser l'article R. 741-12 du code de justice administrative, qui permet de sanctionner une requête abusive jusqu'à 10 000 euros. Selon lui, la demande de Delphine ne remplissait aucune des conditions du référé. Elle visait de plus une formation dont la candidate n'avait manifestement pas le niveau. Le texte comporte en outre des erreurs révélatrices. Une « Madame B. » apparaît plusieurs fois dans les arguments, une « Mme C. » surgit dans la partie sur les frais, et une autre requête à l'objet analogue a été enregistrée. Le juge s'est posé des questions sur des recours considérés comme stéréotypés, produits en masse, et pas même entièrement mis à jour. Vous nous voyez venir ?
L'intelligence artificielle a alors fait son entrée dans la discussion. Le magistrat a fait état d'un mélange d'apostrophes courbes et droites, de nombreux tirets cadratins, des puces en ronds noirs et une argumentation très ordonnée, pédagogique, mais bien trop répétitive, ce qui peut être caractéristique d'un recours à l'IA. Le juge cite même Claude.ai, le chatbot d'Anthropic, comme potentiel outil d'« intelligence artificielle générale » utilisé. Ces indices restent discutables, car un simple copier-coller depuis un traitement de texte peut laisser les mêmes traces. La sanction est tombée malgré tout, et elle est de 750 euros, à la charge de l'étudiante elle-même.
*nous avons modifié son prénom

articles.title: Ajman Chamber prepares to launch Thara initiative for entrepreneurs and investors
articles.text: Ajman Chamber will launch the Thara Investment and Entrepreneurship Ecosystem on October 29, 2026, during the inaugural Thara Connect Forum at the Thara Entrepreneurship Centre in Ajman. The initiative aims to develop an integrated ecosystem supporting entrepreneurs and startups at different stages of growth, while facilitating investment opportunities and partnerships between emerging businesses and investors. Held under the patronage of Sheikh Humaid bin Rashid Al Nuaimi, Ruler of Ajman, the forum will bring together investors, business leaders, entrepreneurs and industry experts from the UAE and international markets. The event will feature panel discussions, networking sessions and a startup exhibition, alongside the unveiling of Thara's initiatives and services designed to support entrepreneurship and investment in Ajman. Press release: Ajman Chamber is preparing to launch the Thara Investment and Entrepreneurship Ecosystem during the inaugural Thara Connect Forum, scheduled for Thursday, 29 October 2026, at the Thara Entrepreneurship Centre in Ajman. The event will be held under the patronage of His Highness Sheikh Humaid bin Rashid Al Nuaimi, Supreme Council Member and Ruler of Ajman, and in the presence of His Highness Sheikh Ammar bin Humaid Al Nuaimi, Crown Prince of Ajman and Chairman of the Executive Council. The forum will bring together leading investors, business leaders, entrepreneurs, and industry experts from the UAE and abroad, providing a platform for exchanging knowledge, strengthening connections, and exploring investment and partnership opportunities. H.E. Eng. Abdullah bin Mohammed Al Muwaiji, Chairman of Ajman Chamber, emphasised that the launch of Thara reflects the UAE leadership's vision of building a diversified and competitive economy in which entrepreneurs and startups play a key role in driving economic growth. H.E. Maryam Khalifa Al Nuaimi, Chairperson of the Thara Investment and Entrepreneurship Ecosystem, highlighted that Thara represents a significant step forward in Ajman's approach to the new economy through the development of an integrated environment designed to support entrepreneurs at different stages of their business growth. The forum will feature a series of panel discussions and specialised networking sessions, alongside a startup exhibition showcasing innovative solutions and providing opportunities for entrepreneurs to connect directly with investors and business leaders. The event is also expected to unveil further details about the Thara Investment and Entrepreneurship Ecosystem, including its components, initiatives, and opportunities for supporting investment and entrepreneurship, reinforcing Ajman's position as an attractive destination for innovative businesses and emerging ventures.

articles.title: ‘The open-ear market has a strong new contender’: Sennheiser’s first clip-style open earbuds are a surprisingly solid first attempt, but they're not perfect
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Sennheiser’s Accentum Clip have their quirks — some connectivity issues I hadn’t expected, oddly-placed touch controls, and a slightly more noticeable fit than some other cuff-style buds — but they’re a great clip-on debut from the brand and one I’d recommend for a few key reasons. Firstly, they deliver when it comes to Sennheiser’s natural sound profile, especially at moderate volume, where there’s a good amount of bass and clarity. They’ve also got a neat battery protection feature, LDAC support, and a great value price. There’s so much competition in this area that there are still cheaper options I’d suggest over them, but they’re a highly impressive entrant into the open-ear category for Sennheiser.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent natural sound signature
- + Useful battery protection feature
- + Great for situational awareness
Reasons to avoid
- - A couple of wireless connectivity and multipoint issues
- - Touch controls are easy to accidentally activate
- - Cheaper alternatives available in a crowded market
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Sennhesier Accentum Clip: two-minute review
Clip-on (or cuff-style) examples in our best open earbuds guide once felt like a niche trend alongside the more sensible shape — the one that arcs behind your ear. But these ear cuff-esque offerings may now be the next major personal audio craze.
The first ones to hit were Huawei’s FreeClip, and they were followed soon after by the premium Bose Ultra Open Earbuds. That was in early 2024, and they’re still among the best options you can buy today.
These days, everyone from Soundcore and Shokz to Earfun and Sony offers a clip-on set of buds, made to attach to the back of your ears and direct audio with tiny speakers pointing to your ear canals. They’re good for hearing everything around you at the same time as your music, and Sennheiser has just got in on the action with its Accentum Clip, available in Black and Cream colors.
The naming of Accentum (as opposed to Momentum) means they’re part of Sennheiser’s more affordable range, but they still promise the brand’s well-known rich and natural sound. The press release for the new buds says that “the growing demand for truly open earbuds has come with sonic compromises” and that these buck that trend by offering “brilliant Sennheiser sound in every situation”.
But we’ve also been here before with the cheap and slightly disappointing Sennheiser Accentum Open. I was keen to try the Accentum Clip and hoped they improved upon the previous attempt.
The good news is that these offer great performance in most of the areas that matter. Once you get a comfortable fit (which I found a tiny bit more challenging than usual), they deliver a clean and accurate sound. You have to be careful with volume levels, as too much volume introduces distortion, but they’re overall pretty delightful-sounding for this category.
And they’ve got excellent battery life, although I did encounter a couple of connection and multipoint quirks. Rivals from Shokz beat these on comfort and weight, while Soundcore undercuts them in the price department. That said, I still reckon they’re some of the best-sounding clip-ons I’ve heard, and that is important in a congested market.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The bad news? If you’re in the US, you seemingly can’t buy these at launch. They could be coming at a later date, but for now, US buyers will have to look at other clip-on contenders. As to why, Sennheiser told prospective buyers that it’s a "strategic decision based on the legal environment”, in a comment on Reddit. But decisions can be rethought, can't they…
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Specifications
| Component | Value | 
| Water resistance | IP54 | 
| Battery life | 9 hours; 36 hours with case | 
| Bluetooth type | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Weight | 6.8g per earbud | 
| Driver | 12mm dynamic | 
Sennheiser Accentum Clip: Price and release date
- Launched on July 23, 2026
- Sells for £149 / AU$289 (around $180, although not officially available yet)
- Sennheiser’s first-ever clip-on buds
The Sennheiser Accentum Clip went on sale on July 23, 2026, after being announced almost a month earlier, on June 18. While they’re Sennheiser's first-ever challenger in the clip format, the brand previously tried its hand at a “semi-open” AirPods-style with the Accentum Open, which lacked app support and had flimsy build quality.
You can buy the Accentum Clip for £149 / AU$289. That puts them firmly in the middle of the pack for this style of earbuds. You can get the Soundcore AeroClip or new Shokz OpenDots Air for a competitive $129 / £129.99 / AU$219, or increase your budget to get the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds for $299 / £299 / AU$449.95.
Another top pick, the Shokz OpenDots 2, costs $199.95 / £179.99 / AU$339, while budget contenders like the EarFun Clip 2 set you back as little as $79.99 / £69.99 (about AU$120).
So, stiff competition — and Sennheiser's come in at a busy time.
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Features
- 9 hours of playback on a charge; 36 hours with the charging case
- 5-band graphic equaliser in the Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app
- LDAC support and a battery protection mode to enhance longevity
The Sennheiser Accentum Clip are easy to set up and customise, and they support the Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app, which is one of the best companion apps in the business.
Right after adding them to the app, I was able to do a firmware update, turn on battery protection (more on that in a moment), Bluetooth multipoint, and customise the default touch controls. Here, you can also enable “advanced sound quality”, which turns on the buds’ LDAC capabilities.
As they’re open earbuds, you’re not getting any noise-cancellation (very few buds like this offer it, although the Shokz Openfit Pro and Honor Earbuds Open are two that do), which would draw more battery, so the promised battery life is 9 hours of listening, which extends to up to 36 hours when you factor in recharging via the case.
I checked battery life after three hours of continuous playback and they'd dropped by 40%, indicating a respectable 7.5 to 8 hours of total playtime at 50% volume. That's not quite Sennheiser's official figure, but still a solid real-world showing for open-ear buds — matching rivals like the Bose Ultra Open and Huawei FreeClip.
There’s not a long list of features here, although I do think they nail the basics. The battery protection mode, which makes them charge more slowly and prevents them from charging to 100%, is a fantastic feature to increase the longevity of your earphones. It reduces stress on battery cells and means you could vastly improve their lifespan.
There’s a 5-band EQ for tinkering with the sound, the ability to turn on the high-res LDAC codec and connection management. I’ll talk more about sound in a separate section, but it’s worth saying that one of my few disappointments here was with connectivity. Multipoint just didn’t really work effectively.
It connected to two devices, but audio would restart on the wrong device when pausing and playing again, or sound wouldn’t come out when watching some Instagram Reels. With multipoint off, you also can’t “pull” the connection from one device to another like you can on others. You have to manually disconnect and reconnect. These were all unexpected flaws for buds running Bluetooth 6.0, and hopefully will be fixed via firmware.
- Features score: 4 / 5
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: design
- Comfort takes a little getting used to
- As do the touch controls…
- IP54 dust- and splash-resistant
Most cuff-style buds look pretty similar, but there are some notable deviations from the formula in Sennheiser’s design. They’re a little heavier than some rivals, at 6.8g per bud, and a little more of that mass is at the back, where the battery is held in the part that clips behind your ear.
In use, this makes them “pinch” ever so slightly more than some comparable rivals, and it’s essential to find the right position to angle the driver to fire audio into your ears. Get it slightly wrong, and you’ll have a less-engaging sound.
The stretchy part is a little chunkier than on some rivals, too, which may also affect how they feel to wear. I was able to get them sitting comfortably, but it takes a little trial-and-error.
Once they were on, the other big difference I noticed is that they use touch controls at the front of the buds (on the speaker part) rather than at the back on the battery container. This, unfortunately, does mean several more accidental taps. But, luckily, you can tweak and turn off capacitive control in the app.
They’re IP54-rated, so they can survive dust and light splashes, and they go in a fairly compact and discreet charging case with the Sennheiser logo on the top. I like that the case stands upright on a tabletop, and it’s small enough to be pocketable.
They’re just in white or black shades, and the plastic of the buds and case doesn’t feel quite as premium as Sennheiser’s flagship true wireless pair; but this is the Accentum line, so that isn’t a huge shock.
- Design score: 3.5 / 5
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Sound quality
- Natural, warm Sennheiser sound
- Best suited for indoor listening
- They have LDAC support, but it doesn’t make a difference
Open earbuds always have to make a couple of compromises to bring you audio while maintaining your awareness of the outside world. Keeping your ear canals unplugged means you don’t have the acoustic seal required for deep low frequencies, for example.
That said, Sennheiser has managed to bring much of its natural and balanced sound signature across to the Accentum Clip, and these offer a pleasant, warm listen. Vocals and instrumentation sound as I expected, and there’s none of the harshness or hollowness I’ve heard on some cheaper clip-ons.
Across a wide range of listening (including ambient focus playlists, the new Myles Smith album, summer pop playlists, and Michael Giacchino’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day soundtrack), I found the 12mm drivers deliver impressive clarity and refinement. At moderate listening levels (up to about 70%) I felt they had a good bass presence with a bit of weight to kick drums.
But, crank the volume up and it does change things a bit. I’d definitely prefer to use these in quieter indoor environments over the busy outdoors, because increasing the volume introduces distortion, takes some of the texture out of the bass, while fine details end up getting a bit lost.
Audiophiles will be happy to see that the Accentum Clip support the high-res LDAC codec, alongside standard AAC and SBC. In use, though, I couldn't detect any meaningful audible difference when switching between streaming via LDAC on a Google Pixel 10 Pro and AAC on an iPhone 17 Pro. High-res support is great, but it doesn’t make an obvious difference in this product and using LDAC will probably just burn through your battery life a little quicker.
- Sound score: 4 / 5
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Value
- Great value compared to Sennheiser’s last 'open' pair
- But they’re undercut by quite a few other cuff buds
While the Sennheiser Accentum Clip are a good pair of clip-on buds, you’re paying mid-range money for a pair that feels ever so slightly below-mid-range, given how many elements are evidently a “first try” at this form factor.
I like them for sound quality, but because I found comfort, control and connectivity a little less convincing, I think there are cheaper rivals with better features.
When compared to Sennheiser’s last open earbuds attempt, the Accentum Open, these are a far better value proposition because they include app support and features like battery protection, control customisation, and LDAC.
But if compared to the rest of the open bud market, there are serious challengers available at lower prices from the likes of Shokz, Earfun, Soundcore, CMF by Nothing and Soundpeats.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Sennheiser Accentum Clip?
Score card
| Features | Solid battery performance, useful battery protection, and extensive app controls (including EQ and customizable touch gestures) make for a strong feature set. | 4 | 
| Design | Cuff-style clip with an IP54 build, though the touch controls are prone to accidental taps. The fit does also feel slightly heavier than some rivals. | 3.5 | 
| Sound quality | Impressively warm and natural at moderate volumes, though bass and detail fall off when pushed louder. | 4 | 
| Value | More affordable than flagships like the Bose Ultra Open, offering great audio and features for the price despite having several cheaper rivals. | 4 | 
Buy them if…
You need Sennheiser sound in the clip-style
At moderate volume, I loved the sound on offer from the Sennheiser Accentum Clip — they’re detailed, warm, and engaging.
You need LDAC support
LDAC is extremely rare for the open clip-on category; even the major players stick to the basic codecs, and while I can’t say it made the biggest difference in sound, some high-res purists will appreciate its presence.
You want to hold onto them for a very long time
That battery preservation feature is a big deal — controlling how fast they charge and setting a charge limit could double or triple how long they last compared to others.
Don’t buy them if…
You need a fuss-free fit
An ever-so-slightly chunkier build (for this category) meant I needed a few attempts to get the right fit, and that can be frustrating with the oddly-placed touch control panel.
You’re on a tight budget
This may be a lower price for Sennheiser, but there’s healthy competition among open buds, and these aren’t quite among the best budget options.
You’d like to use multipoint
While it may be fixed in a firmware update, I can’t pretend the multipoint issues aren’t a strange issue and one I wouldn’t have expected in 2026 from buds at this price — especially a pair with Bluetooth 6.0.
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Also consider
EarFun Clip 2
These prove you don’t need to spend loads of money to get comfortable, secure clip-on open earbuds that actually sound good. While the cheap build reflects the budget price tag, the inclusion of LDAC, an impressive 11-hour battery life, and IP55 water resistance make them a great entry point for those new to open earbuds.
Read our full EarFun Clip 2 review
Bose Ultra Open Earbuds
It's been two years since they launched, and the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds are still a benchmark for open-ears, delivering rich sound and Bose’s immersive audio while keeping your spatial awareness intact. They're undeniably expensive, but the featherlight cuff design is so comfortable and surprisingly secure that I often forget I'm wearing them.
Read our full Bose Ultra Open Earbuds review 
How I tested the Sennheiser Accentum Clip
- Tested for two weeks
- Paired with Android, iOS and macOS devices
- Used during multiple activities
I tested the Sennheiser Accentum Clip over two weeks, pairing them with my iPhone 17 Pro, MacBook Air, and Google Pixel 10 Pro, which allowed me to thoroughly test multipoint connectivity and LDAC support.
I wore them mostly at home while working, cooking, and during full-day listening sessions, as well as outside on walks in the park. I used them to play a wide variety of media, including music of several genres, podcasts, and YouTube videos.
I also ran a battery test on these to see if the real-world performance lived up to the claims.
I've been testing gadgets since 2020, and I've reviewed countless headphones and earbuds, including dozens of open-style models from brands like Shokz, Nothing, Soundcore, Bose and Huawei.
Read more about how we test at TechRadar
- First reviewed: October 2026
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Simon Cocks is a freelance tech journalist and the former Technology Editor for Good Housekeeping UK. With over a decade of experience, Simon has written for several major titles, including Esquire, Digital Spy, Shortlist, and Men’s Health. He specializes in testing out the latest gadgets, and has reviewed smartphones, headphones, speakers, e-readers, and much more.

articles.title: Madica secures $6 million to invest in up to 30 African startups
articles.text: Africa-focused pre-seed investment programme Madica has secured an additional $6 million commitment from Flourish Ventures to extend its investment pilot by three years, targeting 25–30 more early-stage startups across the continent. Launched in 2022 and led by Emmanuel Adegboye, Madica is a sector-agnostic investment programme affiliated with Flourish Ventures, providing early-stage funding and hands-on company-building support to African founders underserved by traditional venture capital networks. Madica has invested in 18 startups across 10 African countries and 12 sectors, including AI, climate technology, semiconductors and biotechnology. Its portfolio companies have subsequently attracted additional funding averaging twice Madica's initial investment, while more than half have at least one female co-founder. The additional capital will support new pre-seed investments, expanded company-building assistance and a longer evaluation period to assess portfolio growth and investment returns. Eligible startups must be headquartered in Africa, have a minimum viable product with paying customers and have received little or no institutional funding. Press release: Madica, a structured pre-seed investment programme for African startups, today announced $6M in additional capital from Flourish Ventures to extend its investment pilot by three years. Building on lessons learned and early signs of traction across its portfolio, Madica will back 25-30 additional companies and deepen its company-building support for exceptional founders who are underserved by established venture capital networks. The extended pilot will build further evidence for Madica’s founding conviction: that these founders can build world-class businesses capable of generating venture returns when equipped with the right capital and support. Launched in 2022, Madica set out to demonstrate that exceptional founders in Africa’s overlooked markets, sectors and networks can build globally competitive businesses with the right capital and support. The sector-agnostic programme has since backed 18 startups across 10 countries and 12 sectors, combining patient pre-seed capital with structured, hands-on company-building support. These companies have attracted, on average, twice Madica’s investment in additional funding, an early signal of investor confidence as they work towards the commercial outcomes needed to challenge prevailing assumptions about where venture-scale businesses can emerge in Africa. The extended pilot will allow Madica to track how companies across a broader portfolio translate early traction into sustained business growth, examining the role of its investment and support model in that progress and assessing the potential to generate venture returns through exits. This continues the pilot’s original purpose: to build tangible evidence that can challenge assumptions about which founders and markets offer venture-scale opportunities in Africa. The findings will help refine Madica’s approach and provide practical lessons that other investors can adapt and apply. “Madica was launched as an experiment to test whether pairing capital with hands-on company-building support could help overlooked founders building world-class businesses generate venture outcomes, and in many ways, our work sits at the intersection of the very many questions that underpin the state of early-stage venture investing in Africa. From the outset, we knew that gathering meaningful evidence would require years of investment, support and learning," said Emmanuel Adegboye, Head of Madica. “Three years have given us valuable lessons and encouraging early signals, but building enduring companies and assessing venture outcomes takes longer. Flourish Ventures’ continued commitment gives us the capital to build on those lessons and test our conviction across a broader portfolio while deepening our company-building support. We want the resulting evidence to give other investors a model they can apply, shaping where funding goes and how founders are backed across Africa, well beyond Madica”, he continued. Today, Madica’s portfolio spans over a dozen sectors, including climate-tech, semiconductors, AI, HR, biotech, mobility and more, reflecting the breadth of innovation emerging across the continent. The diversity is also evident in the volume and reach of applications, which span 28 sectors and 78 countries, with 40% coming from outside Africa’s four largest venture capital markets. This signals both the depth of untapped entrepreneurial potential across Africa and the urgent need for more inclusive funding pathways. Every company in Madica’s portfolio is majority African-owned, more than 50% have at least one female co-founder, and 39% are led by female CEOs, demonstrating a deliberate approach to identifying and backing talent that established investment networks have often overlooked. “We retain our conviction that with the right capital and support, exceptional talent across Africa can build world-class businesses. Madica’s first three years have strengthened that belief, and we are excited to continue backing the team as they help more entrepreneurs achieve that mission,” said Efayomi Carr, Investment Partner at Flourish Ventures and Co-founder of Madica. Madica continues to seek exceptional founders building early-stage startups across Africa. To pitch your startup, visit the Madica website. Eligible startups must have a minimum viable product (MVP) with proven traction from a few paying customers, founder(s) engaged full-time, little or no institutional funding, and be headquartered in Africa.

articles.title: Keystone to Destroy 18,835 Hardware Wallets After Hackers Steal Device Verification Key
articles.text:
An attacker who gained access to Keystone's website obtained the key that its hardware wallets use to prove they are genuine, the company said in a statement on October 26.
Someone with that key could build counterfeit devices that pass the online check owners use to verify a Keystone. A buyer who trusted a counterfeit could have their crypto stolen, but the incident did not involve owners' recovery phrases or wallet private keys.
Keystone will destroy 18,835 unsold devices that carry the key, and all new devices will get a new one.
Keystone found the unauthorized access on October 20, and its advice to owners depends on when a device arrived. For a device received after that date with the old key, the company said: "Even if such a device passes authentication, we cannot completely rule out the possibility that it is counterfeit."
Owners of such a device should contact Keystone support and use it only after the company confirms it is genuine.
A device delivered before October 20 that passes the check can be considered genuine and used normally, according to Keystone. The company has not said when the attacker first got in.
The attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool used by Keystone's website to escalate privileges, according to the company. That let the attacker obtain customer data and the key.
Keystone blocked the attacker's access on October 20 and has since fixed the vulnerability. It has not said where the key was stored.
How the Device Check Works
The owner scans a QR code on Keystone's verification page with the device, then enters the code the device displays on the page.
In Keystone's open-source firmware, the QR code carries that code in encrypted form, and the device decrypts it with its stored key. So a correct code shows that the device holds the key.
The key is used only for this check. It plays no part in creating recovery phrases, deriving private keys, or signing transactions.
Anyone with a copy of the key could produce the right codes, so a counterfeit device carrying it could pass the check. Such devices could be sold or shipped to customers, leading to the theft of their crypto, Keystone said. The company has not reported any counterfeit devices or thefts.
The key is written into each device during manufacturing and cannot be erased or rewritten. The firmware keeps it in memory, which can be written only once, and refuses to accept a second key. So devices already made cannot be switched to the new key.
Customer Records
Keystone first disclosed the breach on October 24, saying a third party had obtained customers' shipping information.
The incident affected 25,964 buyer records from purchases on Keystone's website between 2024 and 2026, the company said on October 26. The records hold names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order details. Keystone's online store runs on Shopify, which stored and managed the records.
Payment card and bank details and government ID numbers were not involved, Keystone said. Purchase records from Amazon and Keystone's other sales channels were not affected.
Keystone has also included 12,873 unpaid checkout records in its response as a precaution. These hold names, contact details, and shipping information from purchases that were never completed.
Some of the affected data should already have been deleted. Keystone had promised to delete shipping information 180 days after each order.
An automated tool Keystone built to erase records in bulk did not work reliably. Some deletions failed, and Keystone did not catch the failures in time.
Keystone is shortening the period it retains customers' personal data from 180 days to 90 days, effective immediately. It has asked Shopify to delete buyers' personal data older than 90 days and expects that to be done on November 3. As of October 27, its privacy policy still listed 180 days.
Keystone is emailing affected customers and plans a page where people can check whether their information was affected.
What Keystone Owners Should Do
Keystone's guidance covers these situations:
- Delivered before October 20: A device that passes the check can be used normally.
- Received after October 20 with the old key: Do not use the device until Keystone support, at support@keyst.one, confirms it is genuine. Keystone told these owners to follow instructions on its device verification page, but the page showed no such instructions as of October 27. Keystone has not said how to tell which key a device carries, or what owners who have already sent crypto to such a device should do.
- Waiting on an order from Keystone's website: Shipping is paused until devices with the new key are ready. As of October 27, the store listed the Keystone 3 Pro as a pre-order expected to ship within 4 to 6 weeks.
- Bought through Amazon or a reseller: The same guidance applies, because it is based on when a device arrived, not where it was bought. Keystone sells through Amazon official stores and authorized resellers. Keystone has not said whether devices with the old key are still on sale there.
- Already holding crypto with a Keystone: Owners do not need to move their crypto just because of the incident, Keystone said. Those with a device received after October 20 with the old key should still follow the steps above.
- Scam messages: Treat any call, text, email, or letter offering a refund, a replacement device, a recall, wallet verification, or help moving crypto as a scam. Keystone will not ask anyone to return a device. Never enter a recovery phrase into a device you did not order, and type keyst.one into your browser instead of following links.

articles.title: La demande d'iPhone Duo s'effondre : les scalpers pourraient bien perdre leur pari, et leur argent
articles.text:
Les scalpers qui comptaient fermement sur les pénuries d'iPhone Duo pour se faire une marge confortable se prennent un retour de bâton. Ces derniers voient ainsi leurs espoirs d'argent facile réduits à peau de chagrin, au gré des problèmes matériels de ce dernier.
En sumérien, ça se prononce "cheh". Les revendeurs qui avaient précommandé en grand nombre l'iPhone Duo, le premier smartphone pliable d'Apple, se retrouvent aujourd'hui contraints de brader leurs stocks. En cause : une série de problèmes matériels qui ont terni le lancement de l'appareil et dissuadé de nombreux acheteurs potentiels.
Des prix de revente revus à la baisse en Chine
Selon des informations en provenance de Chine, plusieurs revendeurs (scalpers) ont dû réduire significativement leurs tarifs. Le modèle 1 To de l'iPhone Duo a ainsi vu son prix chuter de plus de 400 dollars depuis vendredi 23 octobre, date de lancement officiel de l'appareil.
Cette baisse de prix a toutefois eu un effet : certains consommateurs, jusqu'alors hésitants, ont profité de la chute des tarifs pour finaliser leur achat, entraînant un léger regain d'intérêt pour le produit.
Des précommandes tendues, des mois d'attente
Le 16 octobre, jour d'ouverture des précommandes pour l'iPhone Duo, la demande avait été particulièrement forte. De nombreux revendeurs avaient alors acheté d'importantes quantités de l'appareil dans l'optique de les revendre ensuite à des prix bien plus élevés, jouant sur les pénuries.
Mais voilà, tout ne s'est pas passé comme prévu. Quatre jours après son lancement, l'iPhone Duo a fait l'objet de multiples signalements concernant des écrans fissurés et des charnières défaillantes.
Apple reconnaît un problème sur certains appareils
Interrogée par Mark Gurman, correspondant en chef d'Apple pour Bloomberg, la firme de Cupertino a confirmé être au courant de problèmes affectant l'écran interne "d'un nombre limité d'unités de l'iPhone Duo". Apple recommande aux clients concernés de contacter le service AppleCare afin d'obtenir gratuitement le remplacement de leur appareil.
L'entreprise a précisé que la majorité des unités commercialisées ne présentaient pas ce défaut. Ce souci, s'il doit se produire, arrive assez rapidement après l'acquisition du smartphone selon la marque à la pomme. C'est toutefois un peu facile à dire au bout de seulement quelques jours de commercialisation. Le nombre exact d'appareils concernés par ce problème matériel n'a pas été communiqué par Apple.
Lors de ses premiers smartphones pliables en 2019 et 2020, Samsung avait été victime de problèmes similaires. Si ces défauts pouvaient être tolérés à une époque primitive pour les smartphones pliables, leur réapparition sur un appareil de 2026 pose question.
Source : PhoneArena

articles.title: Forget Rolls-Royce — BYD's imminent rival could be the new luxury sedan king and the first EV with solid-state battery tech
articles.text:
BYD’s Rolls-Royce rival is almost ready to go — and it could be the world's first to use solid-state battery tech
New flagship sedan eyes up the world's leading luxury brands
- High-end electric sedan aims to rival Rolls-Royce, Mercedes-Benz and BMW
- Quad-motor platform and solid-state battery tech rumored
- Flagship model is due to be unveiled in Dubai in November
Chinese EV maker BYD has been teasing a number of photos in the lead up to the launch of one of its most luxurious and technologically accomplished model to date.
It is understood that BYD’s luxury sub-brand, Yangwang, will be the badge on the hood of the upcoming vehicle, codenamed “Project Hu” that, even in its extensive camouflage, can easily be recognized as a Rolls-Royce or BMW i7 rival.
Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing revealed photos of the vehicle earlier this month, while China's ThinkerCar X account also posted videos suggesting it's undergoing final testing.
The long, luxurious electric sedan is tipped to feature massive coach doors, which are rear-hinged to make it much easier to clamber in and out, while the predicted 5.5m length is large enough to see it go toe-to-toe with the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class and the Huawei/JAC-built Maextro S800, according to CarNewsChina.
There is no confirmation on the powertrain that will underpin the model, but speculation suggests it will pack Yangwang’s quad-motor architecture and DiSus active suspension.
It is also hotly-tipped to be one of the first production models to be released with the BYD Group’s solid-state battery technology, while teaser images show it next to BYD's Flash Charge technology, suggesting top-ups could take a matter of minutes.
During a recent interview, BYD’s executive vice president Stella Li revealed that the company’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027, which coincides with a suggested launch date for the Project Hu vehicle.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It also makes sense given that prices for the Hu are rumored to start in the two million yuan range, or about $300,000 / £225,000 / AU$430,000, according to Electrek, which would help cover the cost the expensive, non-mass produced solid-state battery tech.
Analysis: Even the luxury market isn't safe
The fact that BYD is choosing to unveil Project Hu in Dubai next month suggests that it is confident that its products can rival some of the most luxurious and globally-recognized automotive badges on sale in the world today.
CarNewsChina states that YangWang already offers a U8 (the marque’s enormous premium SUV) in the Middle East for 659,900 AED — or around $180,000 / £134,860 / AU$256,420 — which greatly undercuts things like the Bentley Bentayga and Rolls-Royce Cullinan.
If BYD’s products genuinely stand up to the industry benchmarks, prestige western brands could soon have to fend off the same sort of competition that is causing headaches for manufacturers in the fiercely ruthless mass markets.

Currently, EVs are the focus of his attentions, but give it a few years and it will be electric vertical take-off and landing craft. Outside of work hours, he can be found tinkering with distinctly analogue motorcycles, because electric motors are no replacement for an old Honda inline four.

articles.title: AI-Generated Fake Login Pages Are Making Account Takeovers Easier
articles.text:
Fake login pages are nothing new, but generative AI is making them easier to build and more convincing. Attackers can recreate familiar login screens, impersonate trusted brands and tailor phishing attempts to specific employees or organizations.
Some fake login pages go beyond stealing passwords. They can also capture MFA codes or hijack authenticated sessions, allowing attackers to gain access to corporate accounts even when additional security measures are in place.
How AI is making fake login pages more convincing
Attackers have long used fake login pages to steal credentials, but generative AI makes it easier to create convincing replicas of legitimate authentication portals. From company logos and page layouts to login prompts, these fraudulent pages can closely resemble the websites employees regularly access.
AI also makes it easier to tailor phishing campaigns to specific organizations or employees. For example, attackers can create personalized IT notifications that direct employees to a fraudulent login page using the company's branding and familiar authentication prompts.
These attacks often rely on lookalike domains that closely resemble legitimate web addresses, with subtle spelling changes or additional characters. Combined with realistic login pages and targeted messaging, these tactics make phishing attempts harder to recognize.
While these techniques aren't new, generative AI lets attackers create, customize and adapt phishing campaigns more quickly and at a larger scale. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report found that phishing accounted for 44% of the AI-assisted initial-access techniques examined.
How fake login pages lead to account takeovers
Fake login pages can capture more than usernames and passwords. Some replicate multi-step authentication processes to collect MFA codes, which attackers can attempt to use before they expire to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts and applications.
More sophisticated attacks use Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) techniques to intercept authentication sessions. In these attacks, a fraudulent website acts as a proxy between the user and the legitimate service, relaying authentication requests in real time. After the user successfully authenticates, the attacker may capture a session cookie or authentication token and use it to access the account without completing another MFA challenge.
This makes session hijacking particularly dangerous. Even with MFA enabled, attackers can potentially access accounts by stealing active session tokens. This lets them hijack an authenticated session without entering a password or completing another MFA challenge.
Why traditional phishing defenses aren't always enough
Security awareness training helps employees recognize phishing attempts, but convincing login page replicas can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate websites. Even experienced users can overlook subtle warning signs, particularly when a fraudulent page uses familiar branding and authentication prompts.
Email filters, URL blocklists and website reputation services can stop many known phishing threats, but newly registered domains and short-lived phishing sites may evade detection. Attackers also distribute malicious links through text messages, collaboration platforms and search ads, letting phishing attempts bypass email-based defenses.
URL inspection provides another layer of protection, but lookalike domains can be difficult to identify. A valid HTTPS connection also doesn't guarantee that a website is legitimate.
These gaps highlight the need for security controls that can evaluate suspicious websites and detect potential credential-harvesting attempts before users enter their login information.
How organizations can protect against credential theft
Organizations can reduce the risk of credential theft by strengthening authentication, detecting suspicious login pages and limiting what attackers can access if an account is compromised.
- Use phishing-resistant MFA and passkeys: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys use cryptographic authentication tied to legitimate website domains, reducing the risk of credential theft through fraudulent login pages.
- Implement browser-level phishing protection: Browser-based security tools can detect look-alike domains, brand impersonation and suspicious URL patterns. AI-powered detection can help identify credential-harvesting sites and warn users before they enter sensitive information.
- Monitor authentication and session activity: Unusual sign-in locations, unfamiliar devices and suspicious session behavior can indicate account compromise. Continuous monitoring helps security teams identify and respond to potential account takeovers.
- Limit privileged access: Enforcing least-privilege policies and removing unnecessary standing privileges limits what attackers can access through compromised accounts. Just-in-time access further reduces the window of opportunity for abusing elevated permissions.
- Establish phishing response procedures: Organizations should have clear processes for reporting suspected phishing attempts, revoking compromised sessions, resetting credentials and investigating unauthorized access.
Protecting credentials before they're exposed
Phishing protection needs to extend beyond email filters and traditional detection methods to the point where users enter their credentials.
Keeper's AI-powered Phishing Protection uses on-device AI to identify suspicious websites, including look-alike domains and spoofed login pages, warning users before they enter their credentials.
By identifying suspicious websites earlier, organizations can reduce opportunities for credential harvesting and prevent stolen credentials from leading to account takeovers.
Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

articles.title: Singapore's Rently secures $12 million credit facility to expand into UAE
articles.text: Singapore-based proptech startup Rently has secured a $12 million growth credit facility from January Capital to expand its rental payment solutions across Singapore, Hong Kong and the UAE, as well as new markets. Founded by Dominic Schacher, Tarik Stafford, Siebren Khamphorst and Emeric Martin, Rently offers a rental payments platform that allows tenants to pay rent in flexible instalments, earn rewards and manage payment schedules. In the UAE, its Rent Now Pay Later service enables monthly rent payments while landlords receive scheduled payouts. Rently claims to have processed more than AED 100 million in rental contracts in the UAE, where transaction volume has increased more than fivefold year-on-year. Across its three markets, the company reports over $50 million in annualised rental volume and more than 2,400 tenants using its platform. The facility will support rental transaction financing, customer acquisition and geographic expansion. Rently is also preparing to raise $10 million to $15 million in Series A equity funding to develop new products and enter additional markets from 2027. Press release: Rently, the platform that lets tenants choose how and when they pay rent, has secured a $12 million growth credit facility from January Capital, a leading technology investment firm backing high-growth companies across Asia Pacific and beyond. The facility allows Rently to fund more deals, extending Rent Now Pay Later and its broader rent flexibility offering across its existing markets, Singapore, Hong Kong and the UAE, and into new ones, helping the next thousands of tenants on their housing journey. The big picture: one platform, three markets Rent is the largest recurring expense for most households, reaching up to 40% of monthly household income in Rently’s markets¹, yet it is still paid in rigid, upfront and unrewarding ways. Rently is now running at over USD 50 million in annualised rental volume. Year to date, volume is nearly three times the same period of 2025, with more than 2,400 tenants paying rent through Rently. The same platform adapts to how each market rents: monthly payments instead of upfront cheques in the UAE; rewards on rent and flexible payment dates in Singapore and Hong Kong. Zoom in: the UAE Dubai alone registered almost 1.2 million tenancy contracts in 2025. Yet many residents still pay up to a full year of rent upfront in one to four cheques, while earning a monthly salary. Easing that upfront burden has become a policy priority: in June 2026, the Dubai Land Department launched Flexi Rent to let tenants pay rent monthly. Rently’s Rent Now Pay Later (RNPL) closes that gap: tenants pay rent monthly, while landlords continue to receive structured, timely payouts. Rently has already handled more than AED 100 million worth of rental contracts in the UAE. Its rental transaction volume has grown more than fivefold year on year, and growth has kept accelerating quarter after quarter, right through a year of regional conflict. Rently works with real estate agencies like White & Co as well as Co-living firms and property managers in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Taimur Khan, Managing Director, Middle East, said, "People in the UAE earn monthly, but most still pay rent upfront in a handful of cheques. That is the gap we are closing. We now bring on more tenants in a single quarter than we did in the whole of 2025, and this facility means we can say yes to many more tenants and to the agencies and landlords we work with, as demand keeps climbing.” Jason Edwards, Partner, Growth Credit, January Capital, added: “Rently addresses a real financing constraint for tenants across different rental markets. This investment underscores January Capital's commitment to supporting fast-growing companies in the Asia-Pacific region with flexible, non-dilutive credit solutions and we are pleased to partner with Rently through this next phase of growth.” Shiv Mahajan, CEO of Rently, commented, "Rent is the biggest payment most people make and still the least flexible. Our ambition is to triple the number of tenants we serve over the next 12 months and become the leading rental payments platform in every market we operate in. This facility gives us the capital to serve more tenants as we scale, while keeping our equity focused on building new products, investing in technology and expanding into new markets.” The facility strengthens Rently’s capital stack as the company prepares for a $10-15 million Series A equity raise to double down on its core offerings and expand into new markets in 2027 and beyond. Rently is leveraging AI to accelerate its growth and automate much of how it operates, so it can keep scaling efficiently as volumes grow. Rently previously raised $3 million in Pre-Series A funding from investors including Hustle Fund, 5I Ventures, Woh Hup, Orvel, Orange Bloom and Feedback Ventures.

articles.title: Alibaba obtient gain de cause contre une décision du Pentagone : une petite victoire dans une longue affaire
articles.text:
Entre la Chine et les États-Unis, c'est une guerre commerciale sans fil qui s'opère depuis des années. Le Pentagone, armée américaine, avait indiqué que les entreprises du secteur de la défense avaient interdiction de travailler avec l'IA chinoise, mais un juge opère un retournement de situation.
Un juge fédéral américain a temporairement bloqué une règle du Pentagone qui menaçait de priver certaines entreprises de leurs contrats de défense si elles employaient des lobbyistes également au service d'Alibaba. Le tribunal californien a accordé lundi la demande d'injonction formulée par Alibaba, dans l'attente de l'issue de son recours juridique plus large contre le ministère américain de la Défense.
Un litige qui date de plusieurs mois
L'affaire remonte à juin dernier, lorsque le Pentagone a inscrit Alibaba sur une liste d'entreprises qu'il considère comme apportant un soutien à l'armée chinoise. Cette décision est le fruit de décisions globales de durcissement des restrictions américaines visant les technologies chinoises. Le département du Trésor a par ailleurs mis en place des limitations concernant les investissements américains dans l'intelligence artificielle et les biotechnologies chinoises.
L'inscription sur cette liste du Pentagone ne déclenche pas de sanctions formelles. Cependant, elle limite les partenariats du ministère de la Défense américain avec les entreprises qui exploiteraient des solutions du géant chinois. À partir de 2027, ces restrictions devraient également s'appliquer aux achats de leurs produits effectués via des fournisseurs tiers.
Une loi distincte sur les lobbyistes
Une loi américaine séparée interdit aux prestataires du Pentagone d'employer des lobbyistes qui représentent également des entreprises figurant sur cette liste. Ainsi, les cabinets partageant des lobbyistes avec Alibaba feraient face au risque de perdre leurs contrats avec le ministère de la Défense.
Après l'inscription d'Alibaba sur la liste en juin, l'entreprise aurait mis fin aux missions de plusieurs dizaines de ses lobbyistes à Washington.
Une décision judiciaire renverse une partie des sanctions
La décision rendue lundi empêche temporairement le gouvernement d'appliquer la restriction relative aux lobbyistes à l'encontre d'Alibaba. Elle ne retire en revanche pas l'entreprise de la liste du Pentagone, cette question faisant l'objet d'un volet distinct de la procédure judiciaire engagée par l'entreprise.
Alibaba avait saisi la justice américaine en juin, estimant que son inscription sur cette liste n'avait « aucun fondement factuel ou juridique ». L'entreprise affirme servir des consommateurs, des entreprises de livraison et des clients professionnels, et dément bien évidemment tout lien avec l'armée chinoise.
Pour l'heure, ni Alibaba ni le département de la Défense n'ont commenté cette décision.
Un contentieux qui dépasse Alibaba
La contestation envers la liste du Pentagone dépasse la seule cause d'Alibaba. Le laboratoire pharmaceutique chinois WuXi AppTec avait obtenu en août une décision de justice lui permettant de ne pas y figurer.
En septembre, deux filiales du constructeur automobile BYD ont également engagé une action en justice contre la restriction sur les lobbyistes, estimant qu'elle porte atteinte à leur liberté d'expression. Le fabricant de drones DJI conteste par ailleurs son inscription sur cette liste, après qu'une cour d'appel a ordonné au gouvernement de revoir sa décision.
Source : TheNextWeb

articles.title: "AI threats are real - it's not some kind of urban myth": Microsoft UK security head on why your business should be prepared for a new generation of AI cyber threats
articles.text:
"AI threats are real - it's not some kind of urban myth": Microsoft UK security head on why your business should be prepared for a new generation of AI cyber threats
Security is everyone’s problem now, Microsoft warns
As AI becomes an increasingly important part of our everyday lives, the role it plays in cybersecurity for both attackers and defenders is coming under rising scrutiny.
Microsoft recently released its Digital Defense Report (DDR) highlighting the role that AI is playing in crafting new and more devious cyberattacks, with businesses being hit with more threats than ever before.
But Microsoft is also using its own AI tools such a Copilot to help support its digital crimes unit, showing that the attackers won’t have all the advantages.
At the recent Microsoft Frontier Tour London event, I spoke to Dr Jon Davies, Chief Security Adviser, Microsoft UK, to find out more.
AI threats are here
“Frontier AI is transforming the threat landscape,” Davies tells me. “Right now, AI threats are real, it's not an urban myth, or something we're going to see in 2030.”
The DDR found that as AI becomes more widely available, the barrier of entry into cybercrime is being lowered, allowing hackers to launch a record number of campaigns against consumers and businesses alike.
The UK was particularly affected, becoming the most targeted country for nation-state and geopolitical cyber activity in Europe, facing 76 observed events in the past year, and ranking fifth in the world for countries where customers are most frequently impacted by cyber threats.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Davies notes that the AI threat has been building for a while, as attackers turn to automation to carry out more advanced attacks - with so-called “swarm attacks" becoming particularly more common as attackers get agents to do their dirty work
“We're getting to the point where the technology, compute, and storage is catching up with the ambition of the attacker,” he says, pointing out that defenders are embracing AI too.
“We've been solving one problem at a time as (threats) have evolved,” he adds, “the opportunity with agentic AI is to elevate the human up into the orchestration.”
But despite all the AI intelligence being funneled into creating new and more complicated attacks, more “basic” forms of scam like phishing are still proving incredibly effective, showing that the human will always remain the weakest link when it comes to cybersecurity.
The DDR found phishing attacks jumped globally from 7% to 23% of incident-response intrusions year-over-year, with attacks using fake meeting invites and calendar markers among the scams on the rise, and Davies highlights how criminals are taking information gathering on specific C-suite individuals to a new high in order to get them to click on a link.
“An attacker has no ethical line,” he points out, “phishing…is still the front door for any organization…(and) I don't think it's going to go away - with AI on its side, it's only going to get more real and harder to detect.”
So where does the responsibility lie when it comes to awareness? Davies says it should be a combination of individual and collective culpability - which means those annoying phishing tests your employer sends you are probably here to stay.
“The whole point of those training exercises is to help educate us, show us what the attackers are doing…I don’t think we should be embarrassed if we’ve clicked a link in one of those exercises, as the point is to educate and train.”
“It’s everyone’s responsibility to put a seat belt on, you are accountable to it, and regardless of who you are in your personal life, you are responsible for cybersecurity. We’re at that step change now where it’s not just the cybersecurity teams responsible for security - it is everyone within the organization.”
Davies notes that “security can be the seatbelt for AI transformation,” likening it to the introduction of the seatbelt in cars - as although they worked from day one, it still took some time to catch on.
“Security is the same way for enterprises - we can buckle up,” he adds, noting that the seatbelt doesn’t slow the car down, and eventually the change happened, making seatbelts (and safety overall) a key reason why we might buy a specific car.
So with the huge amount of threats facing cybersecurity defenders on a daily basis, how can security professionals stay positive?
“It’s really tough,” Davies says, “the threat landscape is evolving extremely, extremely fast at the moment. It has to be embedded from top to bottom - from the board level downwards through the C-suite and down to the employees - but it also then needs to be trained up from frontline staff.”
He adds that given the number of widespread cybersecurity stories hitting the headlines these days, more and more C-suite executives are becoming aware of the need to stay protected - and challenging their CISO about what they plan to do about it, and how they can recover if the worst happens.
“We’re having these conversations quite regularly,” he says, “as a member of the security profession, we’ve asked for a seat at the table for a number of years - and we’ve finally got that.”
Davies points out that the DDR isn’t just a commercial or PR exercise - it is Microsoft’s view from the front lines of the battle against the latest cybersecurity threats.
“We’ve got skin in the game,” he says, “there is no other organization on the planet that can do this at that level, it’s giving back what we’re able to share to help organizations measure their risk and threat.”
“The physics of cyber are changing,” he concludes, “we’ve got variables that we can change - but they (attackers) also have variables they can change on their side…it's a scary place out there...the world that we're living in right now is very dynamic.”
