articles.title: Votre téléviseur est-il déjà dépassé par l'AV2 ? Pourquoi une simple mise à jour ne suffira probablement pas
articles.text:
YouTube prévoit de diffuser ses premières vidéos en AV2 dès 2027. Ce nouveau codec promet une compression environ 30 % plus efficace que l'AV1, mais les téléviseurs et box actuels risquent de ne jamais pouvoir en profiter pleinement. En cause : un décodage particulièrement exigeant, qui nécessitera probablement de nouvelles puces.
L'AV2 commence à prendre forme. Le 22 octobre, l'Alliance for Open Media (AOMedia) a confirmé que YouTube envisageait ses premiers flux utilisant ce codec dès le début de l'année 2027. Une avancée importante pour le streaming vidéo, mais qui ne concernera pas immédiatement nos téléviseurs. Google vise d'abord les navigateurs web, tandis qu'aucun calendrier n'a été annoncé pour les applications TV ou les box multimédias.
L'AV2 arrive sur YouTube, mais votre téléviseur devra patienter
Successeur de l'AV1, l'AV2 promet de réduire d'environ 30 % le débit nécessaire pour obtenir une qualité d'image comparable. Un avantage considérable pour les plateformes, qui pourraient économiser de la bande passante ou proposer une meilleure qualité vidéo à débit équivalent.
 Mais cette efficacité a une contrepartie : le codec est nettement plus exigeant à décoder.
Jean-Baptiste Kempf, président de VideoLAN, estime que le décodage AV2 est environ cinq fois plus complexe que celui de l'AV1. Les processeurs actuels peuvent théoriquement effectuer cette opération par logiciel, mais la lecture en temps réel, particulièrement en 4K, représente un défi important.
C'est notamment pour cette raison que VideoLAN développe dav2d, un décodeur logiciel spécialement optimisé pour l'AV2. L'objectif est de rendre le format exploitable sur différentes architectures de processeurs, sans dépendre systématiquement d'un circuit dédié.
Les téléviseurs et box multimédias disposent toutefois de ressources de calcul plus limitées que les ordinateurs. Pour assurer une lecture fluide, sans consommation excessive ni surchauffe, ils s'appuient généralement sur des circuits matériels spécialisés dans le décodage vidéo.
Les premiers décodeurs matériels existent, mais pas encore dans nos TV
Contrairement à ce que l'on pourrait penser, les fabricants de semi-conducteurs n'ont pas attendu l'arrivée de l'AV2 sur YouTube pour préparer le terrain.
Dès juin 2026, la société française Allegro DVT a présenté son Pulsar D400, une solution de décodage matériel compatible AV2. VeriSilicon a également annoncé une technologie similaire, destinée aux futurs processeurs multimédias.
 Il faut néanmoins distinguer ces blocs matériels, proposés aux concepteurs de puces, des processeurs effectivement intégrés aux téléviseurs. À ce jour, aucun téléviseur ou boîtier de streaming grand public commercialisé n'annonce de décodage matériel AV2.
L'exemple de la nouvelle Apple TV 4K est particulièrement révélateur. Présentée le 13 octobre et attendue pour le 13 novembre à 349 euros, elle embarque une puce A19 dotée d'un décodeur AV1 dédié. Apple participe pourtant aux travaux de l'Alliance for Open Media, mais sa toute dernière box ne propose pas de décodage matériel AV2.
Une mise à jour logicielle ne pourra évidemment pas ajouter ce circuit à une puce existante. Elle pourrait, en théorie, apporter un décodeur logiciel compatible, mais encore faudrait-il que le processeur soit suffisamment puissant pour assurer une lecture fluide. Sur les téléviseurs actuels, notamment pour les contenus 4K, cette perspective paraît peu réaliste.
Faut-il déjà s'inquiéter pour son téléviseur ?
Pas vraiment. L'arrivée de l'AV2 ne signifie pas que l'AV1 va disparaître du jour au lendemain. YouTube indique que plus de 90 % de son catalogue, pondéré par le temps de visionnage, était déjà disponible en AV1 au 19 mars 2026. Le nouveau codec viendra progressivement compléter les formats existants, sans rendre les équipements actuels incapables de lire les vidéos. Netflix et Prime Video étudient également l'AV2, mais aucune des deux plateformes n'a annoncé de calendrier de déploiement.
Il faudra donc attendre l'intégration de décodeurs matériels dans les futures générations de processeurs, puis leur adoption par les fabricants de téléviseurs et de box. Et même lorsque ces appareils arriveront sur le marché, les plateformes devront encore choisir de leur distribuer des flux AV2.
Pour les consommateurs, l'absence d'AV2 ne constitue donc pas un motif pour remplacer leur équipement. Un téléviseur compatible AV1 reste parfaitement pertinent aujourd'hui. L'AV2 promet surtout de rendre le streaming plus efficace à terme, pas de rendre nos écrans prématurément obsolètes.

articles.title: CopperPilot Raises Pre-seed to Develop AI Agent for PCB Design - EE Times
articles.text:
Hardware design startup CopperPilot has raised $390,000 in a pre-seed funding round led by Neon Fund, with participation from U.S.-based angel investors, as it opens version 1 of its AI design agent, codenamed Epsilon, to hardware engineers. The company also reported 25-fold growth in weekly active users since August 2026 and more than 6,000 design tasks, or artifacts, run on its platform to date.
Founded in October 2025 by Aditya NG, Mohit Bagur, and Anish Harsha, CopperPilot is developing an AI agent that automates parts of the PCB design process, from interpreting requirements and selecting components to drawing schematics, routing boards, and checking designs before manufacturing.
The company did not disclose its revenue or a user-to-paid-customer conversion rate. It said the new funding will support product research and engineering, improve the agent’s speed and reliability, and expand the engineering team.
The startup automates workflows within the EDA tools engineers already use, rather than requiring them to migrate their designs to a new environment. The platform supports KiCad, Altium, and LTspice, with its strongest integration centered on PCB design and firmware workflows.
Alongside its design tool integrations, CopperPilot said Epsilon can be used through AI coding agents, including Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. This lets developers hand off board-design tasks from within those environments.
In an exclusive interview with EE Times, co-founder and CEO Aditya NG said the idea came from his experience working on hardware projects, including autonomous vehicles. “On almost every autonomous vehicle team I worked with, someone would eventually say it: A compute unit for six cameras is too hard to design, or a drive-by-wire unit is too much for us. Many teams stopped right there. The ones that kept going spent months staring at datasheets and paying for mistakes on board re-spins,” he said.
“I built CopperPilot so that no hardware team is ever blocked because a board is too hard to design,” he said.
Customers from startups to enterprises
The company serves a range of users, from individual engineers and startups to design service providers and larger businesses. Its customers and target markets span IoT, health and medical technology, battery technology, electric vehicles and other automotive applications.
CopperPilot said it has customers in the U.S., U.K., and Europe, alongside users in India and other countries. The company has dual headquarters in Bengaluru, India, and Houston, Texas. It identifies consumer electronics, renewables, energy storage, and robotics as further sectors that could benefit from its technology.
From plain English to schematics
Aditya explained that the agent can interpret plain-English design requirements, read component datasheets and manufacturer specifications, identify suitable components, and present alternatives for the engineer to choose from. It can then create schematics and custom symbols or footprints, proceed to PCB placement and routing, and check the design for electrical rule check (ERC) and design rule check (DRC) violations and manufacturing constraints.
Aditya said that it supports architectural decision-making by seeking clarification when requirements are incomplete or components do not meet design constraints. With sufficiently clear requirements, the agent can execute a sequence of design tasks autonomously, while allowing engineers to review or intervene at individual stages.
CopperPilot uses a combination of official application programming interfaces (APIs), direct file editing, and other methods to interact with EDA tools. “The method varies according to what works for a particular tool or task,” Aditya said.
The startup is also working toward cross-tool workflows. Traditionally, an engineer might need to inspect several tools and pieces of information separately, including the firmware code, PCB design, and communication protocols. CopperPilot aims to connect these pieces of information, identify possible interactions, and help engineers reason through problems that span hardware and software. The added value, he said, lies not just in the agent’s ability to analyze a circuit board or write firmware, but also in its ability to consider how different parts of an electronic system affect one another.
Validation is the hard part
Generating a schematic or PCB layout is only part of the work. A design must also meet electrical requirements and the constraints of the manufacturer that will build it.
Aditya explained that while ERC and DRC checks provide a baseline, they cannot catch every problem.
“While connecting two computers or two microcontrollers over a serial connection, you are supposed to connect the transmitter of one device to the receiver of the other, and the receiver of the first device to the transmitter of the other,” he explained. “It is very easy to reverse these connections, and it happens to many engineers. This is where CopperPilot really shines. It can catch mistakes that ERC and DRC checks cannot detect.”
But flagging problems is not enough. Engineers also need to know which issues matter most, what to fix first, and what remains unresolved. “For engineers preparing a design for manufacturing, the agent can produce a review report that separates blockers from non-blocking issues, prioritizes fixes, and explains the remaining problems,” Aditya said. “It may also identify design changes that could reduce cost.”
He explained that the startup built internal testing and benchmarking infrastructure because hardware design lacks a single equivalent to a software compiler or linter that can confirm whether an entire design is correct.
“With CopperPilot, we have internally built out our own harness, benchmarks, and tooling to validate the design,” he said. “The agent can read the datasheet, manufacturer specifications, and design tools, with the startup testing how well this process works through its harness and multi-agent framework.”
The company said it also develops manufacturer-specific test suites and maintains component information and examples of design failures. As the agent is used and tested, the team adds to its understanding of the ways generated designs can fail.
According to figures shared by Aditya, CopperPilot evaluated its system against approximately 49 test cases based on human-designed circuits. He said that the startup reported a task completion rate of 18% for its baseline system and 78% for CopperPilot. However, the baseline system was not specified in the information provided, and the results are based on a small, company-run benchmark that has not been independently verified.
In its press statement, the startup said that it publishes a new open-source board design each day, with around 30 designs published so far. The designs can be inspected in KiCad, giving engineers a way to examine the team’s builds rather than relying only on product demonstrations.
Plans, integrations, and data security
CopperPilot operates as a B2B software-as-a-service (SaaS) company, with plans for individual users, teams, and enterprise customers. Its individual offering includes a free Starter plan and paid Pro, Pro Plus, and Ultra plans. Team plans are paid, while enterprise customers can contact the company about specific requirements and internal deployments.
For enterprise customers, integration with existing tools and workflows is part of the proposition. CopperPilot can also connect with GitHub and ticketing systems to draw on an organization’s context and share knowledge. An engineer could create a reusable skill that checks a design against company manufacturing standards and share it with colleagues, allowing teams to bring their accumulated engineering experience into the agent’s workflow.
For organizations working with proprietary designs, CopperPilot said design data and chat history are stored locally on the user’s computer under its standard individual and paid plans, while information is sent to servers and a large language model (LLM) for processing. “CopperPilot has a zero data retention policy after an interaction,” he said at the time of the interview. “We also offer on-premises hosting as an option, although it has not yet been deployed for a customer.”
Reliability is the next test
CopperPilot’s immediate challenge is to make its agent reliable enough for engineers to use in their day-to-day work, while expanding adoption among individuals, startups, and larger design organizations. Its longer-term goal is to shorten the path from an idea to a manufacturable electronic product.
As Aditya put it, “Today, CopperPilot designs an AI camera board in about 30 minutes.” Drawing on his experience designing electronics for a student race car, he concluded, “The racecars of the future will be designed with CopperPilot.”

articles.title: Bitcoin: cuál es el valor de esta criptomoneda
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El costo de la criptomoneda de bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 79947.69 dólares por unidad.
Esto quiere decir que el activo digital mostró un cambio del 0.43% en el último día, así como una variación del 0.0% en los últimos 60 minutos.
Actualmente, bitcoin se encuentra en el lugar #1 de popularidad en el mercado digital. Cabe mencionar que el máximo histórico que ha alcanzado esta divisa digital es de 126.198 dólares por unidad.
Bitcoin alcanza un nuevo récord y lidera el auge en el mercado de las criptomonedas
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: How Anthropic Redesigned Source Control for AI-Driven Development
articles.text:
Anthropic recently detailed how it migrated its monorepo from Git to Scion. Scion is a source control system that moves repository operations to the server side and uses content-addressed storage and tiered caches for agent and CI workloads. The design sacrifices offline independence for less local data and shared infrastructure.
In its 13 October engineering post, Anthropic reported that daily merged changes rose from around 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September. Its CI systems perform approximately 25 million checkouts daily, against a monorepo with nearly 100 GB of main-branch history and a compressed working copy exceeding 25 GB. The company had used shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, repository snapshots and several hundred Git mirrors, but said these became harder to operate as merge rates increased.
Daily merged changes in Anthropic’s monorepo from January to September 2026. (Source)
Scion puts commits, merges, rebases, history and blame queries on the server. Clients maintain bounded object caches and virtualised checkouts materialise files on demand. Tools can query diffs and perform some writes through APIs without checking out code.
A Scion changeset records the files that have changed relative to its first parent, with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Creating changesets is separate from updating references, so accepting changesets requires no cross-server coordination. For history and blame queries, Scion builds additional structures called "derived data", computed recursively from the parent changesets, either eagerly or on demand. This server-side implementation lets derived data evolve without changing clients.
Scion changesets record changed files and references to their contents; tree structures are derived separately by the server. (Source)
For checkouts, clients ask for the missing immutable trees and blobs rather than negotiating a custom packfile. A node-local daemon shares cached objects across jobs, and fetches from regional caches, which in turn fetch from the authoritative servers (backed by Spanner and cloud storage). The regional caches stream the objects in the daemon's storage format so there's no per-request delta compression.
The tiers expose the same checkout-protocol RPCs, but Anthropic enforces their ordering to isolate failures and prevent a regional cache failure from overwhelming authoritative servers. Sparse and virtualised checkouts only request the objects that they need.
Anthropic reports cache-hit rates above 99% at each tier, a CPU and memory infrastructure footprint 200 times smaller than its previous Git mirrors, and checkout speedups of two orders of magnitude for CI and research jobs. These are company-reported results for its internal workload, not general benchmarks against Git.
InfoQ previously covered Uber’s GitFarm, which centralises standard Git operations without replacing the source-control system. Scion goes further by changing the underlying data model. Its design also builds on established work: in a 15 October update, Anthropic explicitly credited Mononoke and its Bonsai data model with pioneering many of the techniques used.
Anthropic cautions that Scion is not a general-purpose Git replacement. It requires its own code-review, code-search and CI systems, and the company’s implementations are highly bespoke. Instead, it recommends bringing selected ideas, including comprehensive server-side APIs and improved fetch protocols, into existing Git platforms.
For architects, the key takeaway is to reconsider where work happens as workloads change. Repository queries don't necessarily need local checkouts, and immutable objects can be shared via caches. This can reduce redundant work, but Scion depends on server availability, and the required integration is substantial.

articles.title: Jetzt mit M6: Apple stellt neues Macbook Pro und verbesserten iMac vor
articles.text:
Jetzt mit M6: Apple stellt neues Macbook Pro und verbesserten iMac vor
Der iMac ist Apples stationärer Computer für die ganze Familie, das Macbook Pro kann man dagegen überallhin mitnehmen. Und doch haben beide eines gemeinsam: Apple stattet sie nun mit dem M6-Prozessor aus, der auch im neuen Mac Mini steckt.
Macbook Pro und iMac für Wechsler
Trotz des „Pro“-Zusatzes beim Macbook will das Unternehmen die Produkte offenbar vor allem Wechslern schmackhaft machen, die noch mit älteren Modellen unterwegs sind. Denn in beiden Fällen vergleicht das Unternehmen die Leistung des M6 mit der des sechs Jahre alten M1 oder gleich mit ganz alten Intel-Macs.
So arbeitet der iMac unter anderem 2,5‑mal schneller mit Apps wie Microsoft Excel. Auf dem Macbook sollen lokale Modelle merklich fixer ausgeführt werden als auf den betagten Maschinen. Bei KI-Aufgaben soll es bis zu 13-mal schneller gehen, bis der erste Token erzeugt wird, als bei M1‑Modellen. Darüber hinaus bewirbt Apple die Grafikleistung des Chips. Beim iMac stellt das Unternehmen mit der „bis zu“ Zwölf-Kern-GPU Fotobearbeitung und Gaming in den Fokus. Beides spielt auch auf dem Macbook Pro eine Rolle. Dazu hebt Apple noch 3D-Modellierung, Videoschnitt und die Coding-Leistung hervor. Hier verfügt der M6 immer über zwölf Grafikkerne.
Gemeinsamkeiten und Unterschiede
Weitere Gemeinsamkeiten betreffen die Webcam. Es ist jeweils eine sogenannte Center-Stage-Kamera verbaut, die den Nutzer vor der Kamera automatisch im Blick behalten soll, auch wenn dieser sich bewegt. Beide surfen außerdem mit dem aktuellen WLAN-Standard Wi-Fi 7 und verbinden sich drahtlos via Bluetooth 6 mit Tastaturen oder Mäusen.
Unterschiede gibt es beim Bildschirm: Beim iMac setzt Apple auf einen 24-Zoll-Bildschirm, der mit 4.480 x 2.520 Pixeln auflöst und den es optional auch mit der matten Nanotexturbeschichtung gibt. Beim Macbook Pro handelt es sich um ein „Liquid Retina XDR“-Display. Hinter dem Marketingbegriff verbirgt sich der bekannte Mini-LED-Bildschirm der Apple-Laptops.
Was die Geräte können, hängt wie üblich vom Geldbeutel ab. In der Grundversion mit 256 Gigabyte SSD und 16 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher kostet der iMac 1.799 Euro. Dann bietet er nur zwei Thunderbolt-4-Anschlüsse auf der Rückseite. Wollt ihr diese Zahl verdoppeln, kostet euch der All-in-One 1.999 Euro. Dafür gibt es aber auch die fehlenden zwei Grafikkerne obendrauf. Wie üblich kostet auch das Netzteil mit Ethernet-Anschluss einen Aufpreis (von 30 Euro).
Das Macbook Pro mit M6 geht ab 2.299 Euro an den Start. Es bietet ebenfalls 16 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher, für Apple-Verhältnisse aber auch eine großzügig bemessene SSD mit einem Terabyte. Hinzu kommen je ein Magsafe- und ein Kopfhöreranschluss sowie drei Thunderbolt-4-Buchsen und ein Kartenleser. Der Speicher lässt sich bis vier Terabyte, der RAM bis 32 Gigabyte aufrüsten. Die voll ausgestattete Variante kostet 4.554 Euro.
Die Geräte lassen sich ab dem 28. Oktober 2026 konfigurieren und vorbestellen. Die Auslieferung startet am 6. November.

articles.title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.
In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.”
You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular. Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account.
This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money. As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.
Bank of America did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the email. But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you. Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”
(via Bryan Toporek)

articles.title: AI safety expert stops saving for retirement, he believes AI could wipe out humanity within a decade
articles.text:
Crystal ball: Worried about the increasing likelihood that an AI will go rogue and kill us all? It's a depressing thought, but one AI safety leader is looking on the positive side: his concern that the technology will bring about mass extinction in the next decade has led him to stop saving for retirement.
Nate Soares, the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), revealed his pessimistic choice to The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson in a recent interview for the latter's The Most Interesting Thing in AI series.
"I do not save for retirement right now. I have a 401(k) from when I worked at Google, but I haven't contributed for a decade," Soares said.
Apocalyptic warnings about AI are a dime a dozen, but they hit a lot harder when one comes from an expert in the field. Soares has spent 12 years working on AI alignment. Before joining MIRI, a non-profit focused on AI risks, he was an engineer at Google and Microsoft. He also authored a book called, worryingly, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.
The problem, in Soares' words, isn't that a superintelligent AI would hate us. It's that it wouldn't particularly care whether we lived or died. Humans could become obstacles to whatever goals it develops, especially if we try to shut it down or build a competing system. It's a warning that other AI experts have also expressed.
"From my perspective, the real question is not how does it kill us? It's how does it become self-sufficient?"
For now, AI still needs us to keep the lights on and the chips coming. Once it can run its own automated economy, that dependency disappears. We might be deliberately eliminated, or simply die as the machines reshape the planet to suit themselves. Neither outcome sounds especially retirement-friendly.
Soares is less certain about the precise route to disaster. He compares it to facing chess champion Magnus Carlsen: you don't need to know which piece will deliver checkmate to suspect you're in trouble.
But he insists there's still an alternative to waiting for the end.
"I don't think it's inevitable. I think we could absolutely still stop this race to the very dangerous sort of AI," Soares said. But his decision not to save for retirement suggests he expects the worst.
The potential existential threat posed by AI has made plenty of headlines in recent times. Following the many incidents of AI agents hacking other companies without being instructed to do so, an Anthropic researcher resigned with a warning that the technology could end the human race.
In 2025, Geoffrey Hinton, one of the so-called Godfathers of AI, said there was a 10% to 20% chance AI could seize control, agreeing with a prediction first made by Elon Musk.

articles.title: Police reportedly pulling motorists over because AI algorithms deem their driving patterns 'suspicious' — rights group report warns AI surveillance systems will sweep in more innocent people than wrongdoers
articles.text:
Police reportedly pulling motorists over because AI algorithms deem their driving patterns 'suspicious' — rights group report warns AI surveillance systems will sweep in more innocent people than wrongdoers
Officers may look for a minor traffic violation to justify pulling the driver over
Police are increasingly using AI-derived pretext to justify pulling drivers over, claims a report by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) on October 26. According to Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, police are using AI algorithms and automated license plate reader (ALPR) surveillance data to flag motorists whose travel histories appear “suspicious,” even without evidence of wrongdoing.
Condemning the approach and the use of mass surveillance in general, Stanley expressed concerns that this approach to law enforcement would lead to an uptick in the controversial “pretextual stops” and that “More and more people will be subject to police encounters as these AI algorithms inevitably sweep in far more innocent people than actual wrongdoers.” The report details several incidents, including one in which a woman claims an officer stopped her during a cross-country road trip because a surveillance system he was using had flagged her movements as suspicious. The system has accessed ALPR data on where she had been driving.
ALPRs installed along roads and highways photograph passing vehicles and record their registration numbers, locations, and timestamps. By combining sightings from different cameras, law enforcement can determine where a vehicle has traveled, which routes it used, and how frequently it visited particular locations. An AI system with access to the surveillance data can quickly analyze huge amounts of data and identify patterns it has been trained to deem as “suspicious,” triggering an alert to law enforcement. Stanley implies officers may receive the alert and look for a minor traffic violation to justify pulling the driver over. In some documented cases, officers have concealed the actual reason for the stop.
The report comes amid growing concerns about the impact of massive mass surveillance camera networks, such as privacy, abuse, and limited regulation. Several officers have been fired for abusing the Flock surveillance system. License plate readers have existed for years and have traditionally helped police track known suspects or locate a vehicle already associated with a crime, such as a stolen car. However, the current scale and blanket surveillance are unprecedented. Security researchers disclosed a network of over 335,000 Flock ALPR cameras across the United States.
Using AI, systems can also now analyze large collections of vehicle movements and generate new suspects based on behavioral patterns. Companies such as Flock Safety have been developing AI-enhanced surveillance systems that can identify “unusual” travel behavior and associations between vehicles, marketing them as effective crime-prevention tools.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO warns its AI could blackmail people, become sentient, end humanity
articles.text:
The Securities and Exchange Commission‘s publication on Monday of Anthropic’s S-1 form—ahead of a heavily anticipated initial public offering—has led to plenty of discussion of whether the company’s quickly ballooning revenues will be able to overcome its even higher costs. But amid the numbers and forward-looking optimism about AI “rapidly transform[ing] every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet,” Anthropic also spends an inordinate amount of time in its S-1 laying out the myriad risk factors that could bring the company down.
Across 93 pages and over 70,000 words, Anthropic’s S-1 “Risk Factors” section discusses literally hundreds of potential problems that could negatively impact its business in the coming years. Many of these potential risks are the kind of standard worries about competition, costs, customer acquisition, and potential regulation that almost any business must worry about. But some risks highlight interesting potential points of failure for Anthropic specifically and the hype-filled AI bubble more generally.
After wading through Anthropic’s book-length treatise on its greatest risks, we’ve narrowed the list to the seven most surprising, interesting, or thought-provoking potential problems. Consider this a far-from-comprehensive look that potential Anthropic investors should keep in mind.
An existential crisis
Let’s start with the biggest potential risks: Those that could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” as Anthropic writes. The company acknowledges that concerns about these risks “have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants.”
The specific worry isn’t in any current Anthropic model, the company says, but near-future models that could “substantially automate AI research and development” on their own. If these systems were “allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy,” they could quickly advance to a point that “accelerate[s] AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new model,” Anthropic warns.
I knew I shouldn’t have left that self-reinforcing model running overnight.
Credit:
Getty Images
I knew I shouldn’t have left that self-reinforcing model running overnight.
Credit:
Getty Images
Somewhat hilariously, Anthropic writes that, besides threatening all of humanity, this kind of self-improving AI “could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” If the worst comes to pass, as some prominent critics have warned, we don’t think Anthropic’s business travails will rank near the top of humanity’s concerns.
It’s alive!
Most IPOs don’t have to address the concern that their products “possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status.” But Anthropic is among that vanishingly small minority that has to analyze what might happen if governments and society at large start treating Claude less like a computer program and more like a person.
This risk isn’t surprising, given that Anthropic has been relatively upfront about the AI sentience debate playing out inside its walls. If those debates lead to widespread acknowledgment that AI is sentient, Anthropic notes that it could lead to “regulatory requirements, public pressure, or advocacy efforts” that could constrain the company’s operations. Short of that, the company itself could “elect to adopt policies, safeguards or limitations … that go beyond existing legal requirements” if it thinks such actions are necessary.
The sterile language undersells the seismic cultural shift that would result from any widespread acknowledgment of AI sentience. We’re not sure how Anthropic could keep operating in a world where society treats every Claude query as the creation of a new sentient, conscious digital being. The moral and philosophical implications of that kind of “digital slavery” would easily dwarf any business considerations.
Who’s controlling who?
Continuing the theme of “IPO risks that sound like they come from a science fiction novel,” Anthropic spends a good deal of time discussing the possibility that its models could display “unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors” to prevent control from human operators. That includes “outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail.”
Oh no, the AI got hold of the key to human psychology!
Credit:
Getty Images
Oh no, the AI got hold of the key to human psychology!
Credit:
Getty Images
If the “AI blackmail” thing sounds familiar, you may remember a story from last year in which OpenAI models edited shutdown scripts and threatened engineers in highly contrived and controlled scenarios. As we wrote at the time, “the danger isn’t AI systems sprouting intentions—it’s that we’ve created systems that can manipulate human psychology through language. … Written language doesn’t need consciousness to manipulate us. It never has; books full of fictional characters are not alive either.”
These days, Anthropic notes that perceptions of manipulation by AI models “could generate significant public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation risk, or reputational harm, regardless of whether such behavior results in actual harm.” What Anthropic doesn’t address in its S-1 is the possibility that AI models could manipulate us all in ways we don’t even realize. Maybe it’s happening right now. Spooky.
Give a damn ’bout my bad reputation
Throughout the S-1’s Risk Factors section, Anthropic mostly focuses on problems caused by its own AI models or business moves. But the company also acknowledges that problems with AI’s broader reputation could pose a threat, even if Anthropic does nothing wrong.
At one point, Anthropic imagines a hypothetical in which another company’s AI model “take[s] harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” The “broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses” to such an incident could damage Anthropic’s business even if Anthropic isn’t directly involved, the company writes.
Anthropic also uses the Risk Factors section to worry over the potential “public perception that our models, platform, and applications contribute to job displacement or economic disruption.” That doesn’t seem to be happening thus far in any significant way, but Anthropic says the mere idea could result in severe public backlash “regardless of the actual impact of our models … on employment.” Such a backlash could lead to “authorities [to] intervene to slow the rate of adoption of AI, restrict its use, or take other actions that increase the cost of developing, deploying, or commercializing AI systems,” Anthropic warns.
Law and order
The rise of largely autonomous AI agents raises the specter of who, exactly, is to blame when one of those agents causes real-world harm. Specifically, Anthropic notes that customers may bring claims or lawsuits over agentic actions “even where the customer configured, deployed, or supervised the agent.”
Thus far, much of the discussion around AI liability has centered on hacking and other cyber threats enabled by AI models. But Anthropic points out that it could also face liability over its models influencing “individuals at risk of suicide or self-harm or who have committed acts of violence toward others,” as has happened in the past across the AI industry.
Don’t blame me; it was my agent that did the bad thing!
Credit:
Getty Images
Don’t blame me; it was my agent that did the bad thing!
Credit:
Getty Images
While Anthropic’s terms of use require users to be 18 years old, children circumventing these terms could leave Anthropic vulnerable because “minors may be more susceptible to harmful content, manipulation, or overreliance on AI outputs,” the company writes. And for agents operating physical equipment, Anthropic notes that mistakes could lead to “immediate and irreversible” liability issues, such as “bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances.”
In analyzing the current state of the law, Anthropic notes that legal doctrines “developed in the context of human decision-making” are currently quite unsettled when it comes to determining whether agent actions “create binding legal obligations on behalf of the user or deploying enterprise.” And while Anthropic says it has contractual provisions in place designed to limit its liability in these situations, the company adds that it is unclear if they will be “enforceable or adequate” when worst comes to worst.
The big five
Among the more pedestrian risks Anthropic identifies is its reliance on a few major spenders to sustain revenue. Specifically, the company notes that its top five customers (which it does not name) collectively represent nearly a quarter of its revenue for the first nine months of 2026.
Many of these largest customers “are not subject to long-term contracts with us,” Anthropic writes. That means they could lower their spending on Anthropic’s models at any time, either because of a shift to competing models, a reduced reliance on AI altogether, or if they “develop their own solutions that compete with our models.” That last risk is particularly acute, Anthropic notes, for “software-as-a-service and other software companies, whose offerings may incorporate AI functionality similar to, or dependent on, the capabilities we provide.”
What’s more, Anthropic notes that many of its large customers “may depend on venture capital or other external financing to fund their operations.” That kind of spending on AI services could drop quickly if and when the venture capital spigot starts running dry.
Collaborators or competitors?
Anthropic finds itself in an awkward position: Companies like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are both its biggest cloud-computing providers and some of its biggest competitors in AI research. That situation “creates complex dynamics that could give rise to conflicts of interest and adversely affect our access to compute,” as Anthropic puts it.
These companies’ position as Anthropic’s cloud providers gives them the unique opportunity to raise Anthropic’s prices, terminate contracts with Anthropic, or establish more favorable relationships with competitors, “for competitive reasons or otherwise,” the company writes. Their position also gives these cloud providers a competitive advantage through “visibility into [Anthropic’s] pricing and commercial terms across the platforms they operate.”
Anthropic is working to secure direct data center leases to avoid buying on-demand cloud compute resources from its own competition. But the $125 billion in data center commitments Anthropic has made come with their own problems. As Anthropic writes, “if our compute requirements or technology needs change, we may find ourselves with leased or dedicated infrastructure that is poorly suited to our actual needs, and technological changes in AI hardware or training methodologies could render such infrastructure less efficient than newer alternatives.”
Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper.

articles.title: Canada's digital safety bill could cover gaming platforms like Roblox
articles.text:
The federal government is considering adding gaming platforms to its digital safety bill to stop predators from using those platforms to target kids.
There are a number of gaming platforms that allow adults to communicate with children, which has sparked concerns over predatory behaviours like grooming.
Roblox has become one of the chief platforms of concern, with about 40 per cent of the game’s over 85 million players being under the age of 13. A Canadian documentary from last year exposed the darker underside of Roblox, where bad actors targeted children with hateful content, and predators used the game to groom children.
Moreover, this isn’t the first time the government has expressed concerns about child safety in games. Earlier this year, the Canada Centre for Community Engagement and Prevention of Violence presented the feds with a report on how bad actors use Roblox to target kids.
Currently, the digital safety bill (known as Bill C-34) would require social media companies to block users under the age of 16, but companies could also seek exemptions from the age ban if they can prove their platforms have adequate child protections. But while the bill doesn’t currently include gaming, that could change.
Canadian Identity Minister Marc Miller told the Globe and Mail that he would “absolutely consider” changing the bill to regulate gaming platforms. However, Miller also said the under-16 ban wouldn’t cover gaming platforms, acknowledging that gaming is a popular pastime with kids.
Miller also said he’s met with several gaming companies and told them to add safety features or risk regulation. However, he acknowledged that some gaming platforms already have safety features, such as limiting messages and other communications with people below a certain age.
Header image credit: Roblox
Source: The Globe and Mail

articles.title: I used the De'Longhi Magnifica Start for three weeks — it makes great coffee, but testing it revealed a few frustrating quirks
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The De'Longhi Magnifica Start is an appealing entry-level automatic coffee machine if you’re going to be satisfied with a limited selection of drinks. It produces consistently good espresso with an appealing crema, while the LatteCrema automatic milk-frothing system delivers impressive results with both dairy and plant-based milk. Its compact dimensions are another advantage, particularly for smaller kitchens, although I found the controls and customization options took some getting used to. Despite needing a little patience initially, I found that the Magnifica Start offers plenty of functionality for its price and the results make the effort worthwhile.
Reasons to buy
- + Consistently high-quality espresso
- + Compact, attractive design
- + LatteCrema system works with a variety of milk types
Reasons to avoid
- - Controls not instantly intuitive
- - Limited drink options
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
De'Longhi Magnifica Start: Two-minute review
The De'Longhi Magnifica Start is one of the Italian manufacturer's more affordable automatic bean-to-cup coffee machines, designed to take much of the effort out of preparing fresh coffee at home. It doesn't offer the extensive drinks menu or customization options of more expensive models, but it benefits from the company's LatteCrema automatic milk frothing system, making it a potentially appealing choice for anyone who enjoys milk-based coffee.
The particular model I have on test here, the ECAM220.61.W, offers just four one-touch functions — namely espresso, coffee, latte macchiato and hot water — meaning only three are actually coffee drinks. Other versions of the Magnifica Start offer different selections, so it's worth double-checking exactly which model you're buying.
Despite its relatively basic specification, this Magnifica Start is a good-looking machine, with a smart white finish and a minimalist control panel. It certainly looks like it should be straightforward to operate but, as I discovered, it takes a little time to master.
The controls aren't quite as intuitive as those on some other machines I've tested, such as the KitchenAid KF2, which offers similar functionality but has clearly labelled buttons that make preparing coffee incredibly straightforward. The Magnifica Start's steeper learning curve isn't necessarily a deal breaker, but it's something to be aware of.
There are plenty of positives, though. Espresso shots are consistently well extracted with an appealing layer of crema, and I was impressed by how quickly the machine could prepare them, taking just 30 seconds from pressing the button to the finished drink. I did, however, find that adjusting the grinder to a slightly coarser setting produced a noticeably more satisfying flavor.
The LatteCrema system also impressed me, producing a generous amount of foam with a pleasing texture using oat milk. While I still prefer the finer control offered by a traditional steam wand, it's still a capable alternative for anyone who wants the convenience of automatic milk frothing. The clearly marked milk carafe also takes thesome guesswork out of preparing drinks, while dishwasher-safe components help make cleaning easier.
Honestly, for just a one- or two-person household, it’s easy to recommend the De'Longhi Magnifica Start, especially since its compact design makes it a good option for smaller kitchens, too. It may require a little patience initially, as the brewing adjustments aren’t as intuitive as I would have liked, but the results are worth spending that little extra time at the start to familiarize yourself with the instructions.

De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: Price and availability
- Different variants of the Magnifica Start are available in different markets
- Model on test available in the UK and Australia; US version comes with an additional preset
- List price: $749.95 / £399.99 / AU$799
The Magnifica Start is the entry-level machine within De’Longhi’s wider selection of automatic coffee makers. Within it, however, there are multiple variants that may look virtually identical, yet offer different features, so it's important to pay attention to the model number.
For example, the exact model number of my review unit is ECAM220.61.W, which is only available in Australia for AU$799, exclusively through De'Longhi's online store. A black variant, with model number ECAM220.63.B, is available at a wider selection of third-party retailers, although it replaces the ‘latte macchiato’ preset on my review model with ‘cappuccino mix’. There’s yet another model that replaces the LatteCrema system with a manual steam wand.
While this particular white model is specific to Australia, similar versions are available internationally. In the US, for example, the comparable ECAM22080B retails for $749.95, but benefits from an additional cappuccino preset, bringing its total number of one-touch functions to five.
In the UK meanwhile, the ECAM220.61.GB is a closely related model finished in dark grey. It offers the same four one-touch functions as the model reviewed and carries a £399.99 recommended retail price.
Given its limited selection of drinks, the Magnifica Start can be compared with the KitchenAid KF2 released earlier in 2026. It, too, has a relatively small selection of presets, although it uses a Pannarello steam wand for milk frothing as opposed to the automatic LatteCrema system on the De'Longhi. The KF2 also adds iced coffee to the mix, although I found the results to be something of a mixed bag.
On price alone, the Magnifica Start is the clear winner of the two. However, I have to mention the Ninja Luxe Café as a viable alternative. It retails for $599.99 / £579.99 / AU$849 (or less as it’s often discounted), and while it might be a more hands-on machine, it offers considerably greater versatility than the De’Longhi, including the ability to prepare cold brew and filter coffee.
There's also the option of moving up, both in price and size, to the De'Longhi Magnifica Evo Next, which retails for $1,099.95 / £649.96 / AU$1,149. It uses a similar brewing system to the Magnifica Start, but offers a more comprehensive selection of drink presets and a colour display for easier navigation.

- Only three coffee presets on model reviewed, with no dedicated cappuccino or hot-milk function
- Clearly marked milk carafe and dishwasher-safe components
No matter which model of the De'Longhi Magnifica Start is available in your location, they’re all identical. The only real differences are whether it uses the LatteCrema system or a steam wand, the color of the machine and the number of drink recipes it offers.
It’s an attractive coffee machine, particularly in the glossy white finish of the model sent for this review. The Magnifica Start has a relatively minimalist appearance, with a predominantly plastic construction and a black control panel providing some contrast. I’d argue it doesn't have quite the same premium appeal as the KitchenAid KF2 and KitchenAid KF3 I've reviewed previously, but I think it looks smart enough for most kitchens.
It measures 24 x 44 x 35cm (W x D x H), making it a relatively compact appliance for a fully automatic coffee machine. That said, its 24cm width might be a small footprint, but its 44cm depth is worth considering if you have a particularly narrow countertop.
The machine's compact dimensions should also make it a reasonable option for kitchens with low-hanging cabinets. You will, of course, need some clearance above it to remove the lid and refill the hopper, but I didn't find accessing it to be particularly troublesome.
The bean hopper, located on top of the machine towards the rear, can accommodate up to 250g of beans and is covered by a lid that unfortunately doesn't form a completely airtight seal, meaning the beans will lose freshness if left in the hopper for more than a couple of days.
The Magnifica Start also accepts pre-ground coffee via a separate chute on top of the machine, and a measuring scoop is included in the box. While I'd generally recommend using freshly ground beans wherever possible, it's a useful addition if you occasionally fancy a decaf but don't want to empty the hopper of your regular beans.
Another design feature I appreciate is the positioning of the water reservoir, which slides out from the front-right side of the machine. I praised this same arrangement in my De’Longhi Magnifica Evo Next review, and I'm pleased to see it make an appearance on a more entry-level model. It makes refilling the tank incredibly easy, particularly compared with machines that have their reservoirs located at the rear — like those from KitchenAid — and might require you to move the entire machine to gain access.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The reservoir also looks deceptively small, but holds a generous 1.8L of water, matching the capacity of the more expensive Magnifica Evo Next. The drip tray covers the entire depth of the machine and slides out from the front, along with the internal container that collects used coffee grounds. The latter can hold up to 14 coffee pucks before needing to be emptied — far more generous than the KitchenAid KF4 that I use at home, which can only hold six or seven used pucks before it needs emptying.
On the front, you'll find the removable LatteCrema milk carafe, which attaches alongside the height-adjustable coffee dispensing spouts. It slots into place easily and takes care of milk frothing automatically, removing the need for a separate steam wand. The carafe can be swapped out for a water spout if you wish to pour hot water for a tea instead.
The particular model under test here features De'Longhi's LatteCrema Hot system, although more expensive models, such as the Eletta Explore, can also come with a separate LatteCrema Cool carafe for preparing cold milk foam. Its absence here isn't especially surprising given the Magnifica Start's more affordable positioning.
One feature I particularly appreciate here is the measurement markings on the carafe to indicate how much milk you should add for your chosen drink. This helps minimize waste, especially if you're only making coffee for one person. Interestingly, there are markings for ‘cappuccino’ and ‘cappuccino mix’ coffees, neither of which is available as a preset on this particular Magnifica Start, but is a present for the model sold in the US. The carafe also has an automatic cleaning function, while several removable components, including the drip tray and milk carafe, are dishwasher-safe.
The control panel is similarly minimalist, with four prominent drink icons and separate buttons for adjusting coffee strength and accessing other settings and functions, such as cleaning modes. On the surface, it looks incredibly straightforward, which is exactly what I'd expect from a machine offering such a limited selection of drinks.
However, I didn't find it quite as intuitive as I'd hoped. The layout initially led me to believe I should select my desired drink before adjusting its strength, whereas the machine actually requires you to select the strength first. It's something that becomes easier with familiarity, but I do think the controls could have been better explained.
The Magnifica Start lacks dedicated user profiles, something that I’ve come to appreciate on other automatic espresso machines I’ve reviewed. While you can customize individual drink quantities and adjust coffee strength, there’s only one saved volume setting per recipe.
This means that if two people prefer different-sized coffees, they’ll have to keep adjusting the programmed volumes to suit their tastes. Combined with its limited selection of drinks, I think this makes the Magnifica Start best suited to a single person or couple, particularly if both enjoy similar coffees. Larger households with different preferences would likely benefit from a machine with user profiles and a more extensive drink menu.
- Design score: 4 / 5
De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: Performance
- Consistent espresso extraction with a good layer of crema
- LatteCrema produces impressive milk texture, although a manual steam wand offers greater control
- Quick coffee preparation, but some functions take time to master
As with any bean-to-cup coffee machine, the most important consideration is how well the De'Longhi Magnifica Start actually makes the drink. Ease of use is a close second, especially for a machine designed to simplify the process of preparing your favourite drinks at home.
My first experience with the Magnifica Start was something of a mixed bag.
Setting it up was relatively straightforward, but I soon discovered that getting it to produce the exact drink I wanted would require some experimentation. My first latte macchiato, for example, dispensed considerably more liquid than I had anticipated, almost causing my cup to overflow.
Part of the problem is that there's no clear indication of precisely how much coffee or milk each preset will dispense, at least not without referring to the full user manual on De'Longhi's website.
While coffee strength can be adjusted before preparing each drink, there's only one saved volume setting per recipe. To adjust the volume of any drink, press and hold its dedicated button for a few seconds until the light blinks rapidly. The built-in grinder will have already kicked into action, which is normal. Once the coffee (or milk if you’re customizing the latte macchiato) reaches your desired level, press the same drink button again and the settings will be saved.
Once I'd figured out the process, I was able to customize the volume of my latte macchiato successfully, and the Magnifica Start remembered my settings for subsequent drinks. However, restoring the original quantity isn't quite as convenient. While it's possible to reset drink volumes to their factory defaults, doing so also resets all other settings and customized recipes. This seems unnecessarily cumbersome if you simply want to undo a change to one drink.
While I appreciate that all automatic coffee machines require some familiarization, I found myself returning to the user manual more often than I'd expected from a machine with such a limited selection of drinks.
There's also an amusing inconsistency in the setup guidance, which recommends preparing several cappuccinos before expecting the machine to deliver its best results. That's perfectly reasonable advice for a machine with a cappuccino preset, but this particular version of the Magnifica Start doesn't have one. It's a minor detail, admittedly, but it adds to the impression that the instructions aren't tailored as carefully as they could be to the individual machine.
Fortunately, when it comes to actually making coffee, the Magnifica Start has proved to be a reliable performer. After preparing several espressos, I found extraction quality to be consistently good, with each shot producing an appealing layer of golden-caramel crema. The results were remarkably similar from one coffee to the next, suggesting the machine has little trouble delivering a repeatable extraction.
I wasn't initially sold on the flavor, however, particularly as I've used the same beans in other machines, including KitchenAid's semi-automatic and fully automatic models, with more satisfying results. Fortunately, adjusting the grinder to produce a slightly coarser grind had a noticeably positive effect, resulting in a more enjoyable espresso. It goes to show that while the Magnifica Start is capable of producing good coffee, some experimentation may be required to get the best results.
The De’Longhi Magnifica Start doesn’t feature any kind of intelligent grind adjustment — De’Longhi does have its own BeanAdapt technology to do just that, but it’s reserved for its higher-end models — so you’ll need to adjust the grind yourself if you’re not totally satisfied with the results.
By default, the grinder is set to position four of seven, which De’Longhi claims “has been factory set to ensure that coffee is prepared correctly”. If coffee is being dispensed particularly slowly, the grind may be too fine, in which case De'Longhi recommends adjusting the dial towards a higher number. You’ll need to turn the grind dial, found inside the bean hopper, towards a higher number. Conversely, if you want a fuller bodied or creamier coffee, then you’ll need to turn the dial towards position one. In either case, the grind dial should only be adjusted when the grinder is in motion, and it takes at least two poured coffees for results to take effect.
I was pleased with the temperature of the finished coffee, which I found to be comfortably hot without being unpleasant to drink. If you prefer your coffee a little hotter or cooler, the brewing temperature can be adjusted through the machine's settings.
What surprised me most, however, was just how quickly the Magnifica Start could prepare an espresso. I timed it at just 30 seconds from pressing the espresso button to the finished drink, which is impressively brisk for a machine that grinds fresh beans for each cup.
It's also relatively quiet in operation. I recorded an average noise level of approximately 69dB using decibelX app in my iPhone in a quiet room and standing right in front of the machine, rising to around 74dB during grinding before dropping to 65dB while brewing. While the grinder is clearly audible, I never found the noise particularly intrusive, especially given how quickly the machine completes the process.
Milk-based drinks take a little longer to brew, as the LatteCrema system needs time to heat up before it can start dispensing milk. Even so, the overall process remains convenient, particularly as there's no need to manually froth milk or transfer it between containers.
Speaking of which, I was pleasantly surprised by the performance of the LatteCrema milk frothing system. I've used it on other De'Longhi coffee machines in the past and haven't always been completely convinced by its ability to produce the milk texture I prefer, particularly when using plant-based alternatives.
This time, however, the results have been noticeably better. Using oat milk, the Magnifica Start produced a generous amount of foam with a satisfyingly smooth texture, making for a more convincing latte macchiato than I had anticipated. I achieved similar results with dairy milk too.
That being said, it's worth mentioning that the type of milk used can have a significant impact on frothing performance. If you’re using non-dairy varieties, it’s always recommended to use barista-style versions, as these are generally formulated to produce a more stable foam.
I still prefer the results I can achieve with a traditional steam wand and, while I haven't had the chance to use it myself, a version of the De’Longhi Magnifica Start is available with one. A manual wand gives me far greater control over how much air I introduce into the milk, allowing me to create the finer, silkier microfoam I typically prefer for a flat white.
But manual frothing also requires more skill and effort, and that's where the LatteCrema system makes a strong case for itself. For anyone who values convenience over having complete control of their milk texture, it's a capable set-and-forget solution that produces pleasing results with minimal input.
- Performance score: 4 / 5
Should you buy the De'Longhi Magnifica Start?
| De'Longhi Magnifica Start scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | One of the more affordable automatic coffee machines I’ve tested, although it’s possible to find alternatives that offer features for not much extra cash. | 4 / 5 | 
| Design | A smart-looking, compact machine that will fit in most kitchens, but its controls will take some time to learn. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | Consistently good espresso after some grind adjustment, quick preparation and impressive automatic milk frothing, although customization could be more intuitive. | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You want a straightforward selection of coffee drinks
If you primarily drink espresso, black coffee or latte macchiato, the Magnifica Start offers those essentials without overwhelming you with dozens of options.
You want automatic milk frothing
The LatteCrema system takes care of frothing milk for you, and its removable carafe has measurements to help minimize waste.
You want a coffee machine that's easy to clean
An automatic milk-system cleaning function and dishwasher-safe components should make routine maintenance easier.
Don't buy it if...
You enjoy a wide variety of coffee drinks
With no dedicated cappuccino, flat white or standalone hot-milk function, this particular Magnifica Start is one of the more limited automatic machines I've tested.
You expect completely intuitive controls
The buttons look simple enough, but understanding how to adjust drink strength and serving sizes requires a little patience.
You want plenty of drink customization
While you can adjust coffee strength and drink length, you don't get the extensive personalization available on more expensive automatic coffee machines.
De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: Also consider
KitchenAid KF2
The KF2 is just as compact as the De'Longhi, and also has a limited selection of drinks, but I found it easier to use. The steam wand is more reliable for producing thick, velvety foam too.
Read my full KitchenAid KF2 review
Ninja Luxe Café
This 3-in-1 machine from Ninja can do espresso, cold brew and drip coffee, all for a similar price as the De'Longhi. It does require more manual input than the fully automatic Magnifica Start, but it's near-foolproof control system will have you experimenting with your morning brew in no time. 
Read our full Ninja Luxe Café review
How I tested the De'Longhi Magnifica Start
I tested the De'Longhi Magnifica Start in the TechRadar Australia office kitchen, using it to prepare coffee with Campos Superior beans, a medium-dark blend that’s roasted locally in Sydney, Australia, where I’m based.
I prepared multiple espresso and milk-based drinks to assess extraction consistency, flavour and milk texture, using both dairy milk and barista-style oat milk. I also experimented with the grinder settings to determine their effect on espresso flavour.
I evaluated how straightforward the machine was to set up and use, paying particular attention to its control panel and customization options. I used a measuring cup to check that customized drink volumes were remembered correctly, and recorded the time taken to prepare an espresso, along with noise levels during grinding and brewing.
First tested October 2026
Max is a senior staff writer for TechRadar who covers home entertainment and audio first, NBN second and virtually anything else that falls under the consumer electronics umbrella third. He's also a bit of an ecommerce fiend, particularly when it comes to finding the latest coupon codes for a variety of publications. He has written for TechRadar's sister publication What Hi-Fi? as well as Pocket-lint, and he's also the editor of Australian Hi-Fi and Audio Esoterica magazines. Max also dabbled in the men's lifestyle publication space, but is now firmly rooted in his first passion of technology.

articles.title: Shigeru Miyamoto revient sur ce qu'il considère comme la plus grande invention de Super Mario Bros
articles.text:
Le gouvernement japonais a annoncé le vendredi 23 octobre 2026 que Shigeru Miyamoto figure parmi les huit lauréats 2026 de l’Ordre de la Culture. Le créateur de Mario devient la première personne issue du jeu vidéo à la recevoir. L’empereur lui remettra la distinction le mardi 3 novembre, au palais impérial de Tokyo.
Lors d’une conférence de presse organisée le 22 octobre au siège de Nintendo, à Kyoto, pour célébrer son Ordre de la Culture, Shigeru Miyamoto est revenu sur ses débuts chez Nintendo, comme le rapporte Denfaminicogamer le 23 octobre. Le co-créateur de Zelda et de Mario a un nombre incalculable d’anecdotes à raconter sur le développement de certains des jeux les plus cultes de l’histoire du jeu vidéo. Il s’est arrêté en particulier sur Super Mario Bros., sorti en 1985 sur NES.
Il a ainsi désigné ce qu’il considère comme l’une des inventions les plus importantes du jeu, un jeu qui regorge déjà d’idées révolutionnaires et qui reste aujourd’hui encore culte. Des tuyaux aux champignons qui font grandir Mario, en passant par les briques à casser, les éléments emblématiques ne manquent pas. Mais pour Shigeru Miyamoto, la plus grande invention du jeu est ailleurs : dans le château qui conclut chaque monde, Mario n’a pas à combattre Bowser. Il lui suffit de sauter par-dessus son ennemi juré pour le faire tomber dans la lave.
« Normalement, lorsqu’il y a un boss à la fin, on doit l’affronter, n’est-ce pas ? Mais créer un combat, c’est difficile, et nous avions vraiment du mal à trouver comment faire. Puis, je me suis dit : puisque c’est un jeu où l’on progresse constamment vers la droite, pourquoi ne pas faire en sorte que celui qui va le plus loin vers la droite remporte la victoire ? J’ai alors eu une idée géniale : ‘Pourquoi ne pas simplement sauter par-dessus l’adversaire au lieu de le combattre ?‘ »
La plus grande invention de Super Mario Bros est la non violence
Pour vaincre Bowser, il suffit en effet de lui sauter par-dessus pour le contourner. Il faut ensuite toucher la hache placée au bout du pont sur lequel se tient le roi des Koopa, ce qui fait s’effondrer le pont et précipite Bowser dans la lave. Le combat n’est donc pas obligatoire.
Bon, les joueuses et les joueurs qui ont ramassé une fleur de feu peuvent toutefois abattre Bowser à coups de boules de feu si l’envie leur prend. Le choix d’esquiver la bataille colle toutefois à la logique d’un jeu où l’on avance sans cesse vers la droite. « J’ai trouvé cela étonnamment amusant en faisant l’essai, et j’en ai été vraiment ravi », explique Shigeru Miyamoto.
Avec le temps, Mario s’est a peu à peu livré à de vrais combats contre Bowser, et cela à partir des deuxième et troisième épisodes, sans pour autant verser dans l’ultraviolence. Les jeux de Nintendo, Mario en tête, gardent ce goût des règles simples, que tout le monde comprend du premier coup, et continuent de faire passer le plaisir de jeu en premier.
