articles.title: Russian boats spotted loitering over undersea cables connecting Europe and US
articles.text:
Russian boats spotted loitering over undersea cables connecting Europe and US
Economic activity depends on subsea communications cables
- Russia appears to be using civilian vessels to spy on critical undersea cables between the US and Europe
- The UK relies on the cables for around economic activity that amounts to £65 billion a year
- Maritime law severely limits engagement with civilian vessels in international waters
Russian civilian vessels are being used to map undersea cables linking the UK and Europe with the United States, according to an investigation by The Telegraph, which adds that fishing trawlers are performing espionage in the waters around Britain.
Analysis by the publication has found evidence of over 500 incidents carried out by what are described as “commercial proxies”, the use of which appears to sit within a 2022 maritime doctrine approved by Russian President Vladimir Putin aimed at mobilizing fishing and other civilian vessels.
If the information was used aggressively, undersea cables could be targeted and disrupt banking, transport, and even trans-continental mobile phone data.
Commercial proxies
In response to the investigation, the British government has announced a security crackdown, with sentencing and fines for anyone proven to have sabotaged undersea cables.
Fishing vessels conducting undercover undersea operations may seem like something straight out of a Tom Clancy book or a James Bond movie, but with over 500 recorded incidents, it appears to be happening.
The Telegraph’s analysis found several repeated actions in the movement of civilian vessels around undersea cables, and while their general path is publicly available, is is believed that the surveillance sought to establish specific routes. With this information, the undersea cables could be more accurately targeted by saboteurs.
“We’ve been pretty clear, and the head of MI5 has been pretty clear, that Russia is starting to use commercial proxies in order to do some of their work for them in that space", noted Britain’s telecoms minister Ian Murray, adding the publication of the investigation may “deter some of those commercial proxies that might be doing the work for hostile state actors.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Active monitoring
Some 17 vessels were identified by the investigation, with one spending 113 hours apparently surveying nine cables, and another repeatedly crossing over cables. Photography of the vessels concerned raised eyebrows, with a senior naval officer observing of one: “The hold could be easily used for other activities to store an uncrewed surface vehicle (USV) or remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).”
Tethered ROVs could potentially map the precise location of undersea cables, according to naval experts. Additionally, vessels travelling at slow sped could use sonar to map the seabed. One civilian craft spent 42 minutes around the trans-Atlantic Hibernia Express cable, moving at under two knots.
The British government has introduced proposals that will replace its outdated Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, with intentional damage of undersea cables carrying a maximum 14 prison sentence. Unlimited fines are also planned.
The Royal Navy has sought to reassure the British public, with a source telling The Telegraph that “We’re clearly watching Russia, watching what they’re doing for the security of the nation. We are actively monitoring them at sea.”
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Christian Cawley has extensive experience as a writer and editor in consumer electronics, IT and entertainment media. He has contributed to TechRadar since 2017 and has been published in Computer Weekly, Linux Format, ComputerActive, and other publications.
He currently heads up the team at smart home website Matter Alpha, and writes about retro gaming at Gaming Retro.

articles.title: Modders unlock hidden AI power on Nvidia RTX 20, 30, and 40 series GPUs, nearly doubling some benchmarks
articles.text:
Sounding off: A used RTX 3090 has become the go-to card for running AI models at home, mostly because 24GB of memory costs far less on a gaming card than on a workstation one. That bargain comes with a catch Nvidia prints in its own spec sheets, though. On GeForce cards, one of the most common kinds of AI math runs at exactly half speed. A few open-source projects now claim to remove that limitation on RTX 20-, 30-, and 40-series cards.
The limit lives in the tensor cores. When they multiply FP16 or BF16 numbers and add up the results in higher-precision FP32, GeForce cards issue those instructions at half the rate of the FP16-accumulate mode. That FP32 mode is the one most training and plenty of inference actually rely on. The workstation cards Nvidia builds on the same chips – the RTX A6000, for example – run it at full speed.
The first fix came from GitHub user Zagitta, who published "gpu-unlock" for RTX 30-series cards. It's a Linux kernel module that kicks in before Nvidia's driver loads. That's when it rewrites two speed-select registers on the GPU and resets the card. Nvidia's regular driver then takes over as usual, so nobody has to flash a VBIOS or patch a driver.
On an RTX 3090 Ti capped at 450W, the developer's matrix-multiply tests show BF16 throughput climbing from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS. TF32 nearly doubled, too. FP16 saw a smaller gain of 35%.
Other developers have since adapted the module for the remaining two generations. A version called gpu-unlock-ada doubled an RTX 4090's FP16 instruction rate from 165.6 to 331.6 TFLOPS. That's a raw issue rate, though – the README is upfront about it – so real matrix workloads on a card tested by an independent owner saw smaller gains of 12% to 34%.
On the older side, turing-unlock targets the RTX 2080 Ti and was tested on one of the 22GB memory-modded cards popular with budget AI builders. Its developer measured 36% to 64% faster FP16 matrix math, depending on matrix size. BF16 doesn't apply here, since Turing never had hardware for it.
Unfortunately, gamers won't really notice any difference, since games barely touch this kind of math. Chatbot token speeds hardly move either, mostly because generating text is limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw compute. Prompt processing reportedly runs 14% to 36% faster, though. Image generation and fine-tuning should benefit the most, since both lean heavily on FP32-accumulate tensor math.
For now, support is largely limited to Linux, apart from a couple of experimental Windows ports validated on specific hardware.
Zagitta considers hardware damage very unlikely, pointing out that the card's usual throttling and power management stay in place. The turing-unlock README is more cautious, warning that tensor cores draw a lot of power and that running them flat out may damage hardware.

Motorola Edge 70 Pro com autonomia prolongada tem oferta com cupom
Motorola Edge 70 Pro (256 GB) com bateria que dura até 49 horas e câmeras de 50 MP sai 30% mais em conta que o preço original, em oferta do Mercado Livre no Pix com cupom
O Edge 70 Pro de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 3.129 no Pix com cupom HOJETECH no Mercado Livre. O celular intermediário premium da Motorola, que traz bateria de longa duração e câmeras de 50 MP, recebe desconto de 30% sobre o preço original de R$ 4.499.
A bateria de 6.500 mAh do Edge 70 Pro, um dos lançamentos recentes da Motorola, possui autonomia de até 49 horas de uso, segundo a fabricante. O suporte a carregamento ultrarrápido de 90 W permite receber uma carga para um dia inteiro em apenas 9 minutos, um recurso excelente para usuários com agendas corridas.
Outro destaque são suas câmeras, todas de 50 MP: a dupla wide com OIS e ultrawide com ângulo de 122º captam belas cenas ao ar livre, a telefoto periscópica com zoom óptico de 3,5x entrega boas aproximações, e a frontal tira ótimas selfies. Todas gravam vídeos em 4K, com as traseiras suportando 120 fps.
Seu chip Mediatek Dimensity 8500 Extreme e os 12 GB de RAM física suportam a execução de apps em multitarefa e soluções da suíte Moto AI. Já os 256 GB de armazenamento disponibilizam espaço interno adequado para guardar fotos e vídeos.
A tela Extreme AMOLED de 6,78″ do Edge 70 Pro apresenta uma alta taxa de 144 Hz, brilho de até 5.200 nits e suporte a HDR10+. Tal combinação a permite reproduzir imagens com cores vibrantes e alta fluidez nas transições em apps e games, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer lugar.
O corpo do gadget traz o vidro Gorilla Glass 7i, que protege a tela contra pancadas e arranhões. As certificações IP68/IP69 e militar MIL-STD-810H conferem proteção em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais, e situações mais extremas como altas temperaturas.
O Motorola Edge 70 Pro de 256 GB (R$ 3.129 no Pix com cupom HOJETECH) será atualizado até o Android 19 e conversa com redes 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.

articles.title: Discord is making its public communities more searchable, and people have concerns | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Discord announced on Tuesday it will make some conversations in its public servers searchable and easier to find on the internet. The new update targets conversations in “Discoverable Servers,” public Discord servers that administrators have made eligible to appear in the platform’s Server Discovery feature.
The aim is to help people find useful information that might otherwise remain buried in Discord conversations to a wider audience.
According to Discord, more than 63,000 Discoverable Servers host discussions on everything from gaming strategies and fandoms to language learning and niche interests. By making some of these conversations searchable, Discord hopes to extend the reach of its communities beyond the platform itself.
The move also taps into the appeal of traditional internet forums, where users can find answers by searching through publicly accessible discussions. Gaming communities could draw attention to walkthroughs, developers could reach more people with technical advice, and content creators could attract new audiences without relying solely on Discord’s internal discovery tools.
Starting November 16, every Discoverable Server will have its own web page, which may feature automated summaries of discussions in active public channels. Beginning in mid-December, selected messages from public channels may also appear in search engine results.
Server administrators will be able to choose which channels are included, while individual members can opt out of having their messages made publicly searchable. Published messages will not display usernames or avatars. Private servers, direct messages, and group direct messages are excluded.
The announcement has sparked backlash over privacy. Some users are concerned about exposing conversations to audiences far beyond their original context, arguing that posting in a public Discord server does not necessarily mean users want their messages to be discoverable across the wider internet.
Others have raised concerns about whether these conversations could be used to train AI models. Similar arguments emerged during controversies surrounding Reddit’s data-sharing practices and AI training, when users questioned whether their posts and comments should be used to train AI without their explicit consent or compensation.
Discord says users can manage their preferences in settings, while server administrators retain control over which channels participate. Notably, the option to make messages discoverable is turned off by default in the EU, U.K., Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea because of legal restrictions. Teen users are also excluded from the feature.

articles.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
articles.text:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.
The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.
The cat has left the bag
The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.
With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.
“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”
CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.
As the official advisory puts it:
During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode.IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle): for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field, and it advances the destination pointer by the cumulative rather than the per-fragment length, so an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path restricts the message length.
The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.
Yet another forever day
CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail, stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiplefuzzingprojects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.
Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include:
PKFail, a supply-chain failure resulting from non-production test platform keys, public for more than a decade before they were discovered, used in hundreds of device models
Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.
There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.
“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars. “Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”
CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).
In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code, however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation… for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well.
Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2.
While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them.
Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond.
Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting.
Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts.
Dan Goodin is Senior Security Editor at Ars Technica, where he oversees coverage of malware, computer espionage, botnets, hardware hacking, encryption, and passwords. In his spare time, he enjoys gardening, cooking, and following the independent music scene. Dan is based in San Francisco. Follow him at here on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. Contact him on Signal at DanArs.82.
1. The system is in PXE boot. That requires both that PXE boot is enabled for the system and that the attacker hits a window of seconds when the computer is watching its network adapter for PXE traffic.
2. The attacker can reach the computer with ICMP traffic in this window. A great proportion of Internet facing resources are sitting behind some sort of front-end service, be that CloudFlare or various sorts of load balancers. If you ping the address for such a system, it's the front-end that answers those ICMP messages without delivering them to the back-end server.
The PHP thing was a vulnerability in a system that's intentionally exposed directly to Internet traffic and that's available 100% of the time, which made it far more exploitable.
The other thing that will really help with fixing this is that there need not be any extra service downtime. The fix is in the firmware, so patching needs only to set the firmware up to perform a capsule update on rebooted. The reboot itself can be delayed until one next happens normally.

articles.title: Keybytes ‘truly modular keyboard’ starts with one key and is assembled like Lego — each magnetic key module has its own RISC-V microcontroller for the ultimate in customizability
articles.text:
Keybytes ‘truly modular keyboard’ starts with one key and is assembled like Lego — each magnetic key module has its own RISC-V microcontroller for the ultimate in customizability
Connect as many or as few keys as you like to the Keyword hub in any arrangement you like. But it might end up costly.
Developer notaroomba (AKA Nathan Alspaugh) has published details of his Keybytes project on GitHub. In essence, this is a modular project where a Keyword hub is magnetically connected to Keybit keys, and each key has its own microcontroller. Hence the number of keys and their layout are entirely up to the user, with a modular design akin to building Lego.
We’ve seen oodles of imaginative and truly excellent mechanical keyboards over recent years, but Keybytes probably offers the greatest flexibility with regard to layout and key selection we’ve ever seen.
It starts with a Keyword, which is the main board that the Keybits connect to. This central component houses a stacked pair of PCBs. The top board packs an Arm Cortex M4-powered microcontroller, Bluetooth antenna, and flash memory. The lower board offers USB-C, charging, and a buck-boost converter.
Adding keys seems like a cinch. Every Keybit, one of the modular keys, contains a CH32V003 RISC-V microcontroller. Moreover, it features pogo pins on all 4 sides of every key for power and I2C. The case is magnetic so you can connect it to any aspect of the Keyword and other Keybits. Atop the Keybit, a Cherry MX switch is installed. We guess you can follow the GitHub MIT-licensed plans for this project and use your preferred variety of mechanical switches.
On the GitHub project page, there are no more than two Keybits together with a Keyword, so you don’t get to see what crazy layout plans he’s hoping to conjure up. However, it is still early days. Per the project journal, Keybytes only became a thing back in March this year, and it was only over the weekend that the developer got to finally boast “it finally works!!”
Both the Keyword and the Keybit modules are 1U sized (19.05 x 19.05mm).
Alspaugh, a student at MIT, has shared all the assets, files, and details you might need to make your own Keybytes keyboard. The GitHub repository says that everything is released under the permissive MIT license.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
It might quickly become expensive for individuals to put together a usable layout with, say, 60 keys. Getting the PCBs made, buying and soldering all the components, and 3D printing all the custom bits and pieces is also a considerable task when your proposed keyboard layout is more than a handful of shortcut keys. In the aforementioned journal, Alspaugh actually mentions that he priced up a “full sized keyboard (2 keywords and like 110 keybits) and it's around $900 assembled.”
Keyword has a status light, but the Keybits lack any kind of lighting. My wishlist for Keybytes 2.0 includes customizable RGB lighting, and I would also like to propose Dialbits, a Fingerprintbit, and a matching Touchpadbit.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

articles.title: Android Auto vuelve a la pantalla del móvil gracias a esta app gratuita
articles.text:
Hubo un tiempo en el que Android Auto se utilizaba desde la pantalla del móvil. Años antes de que Google centrara la experiencia en la pantalla del coche, solo bastaba con abrir la aplicación para acceder a una interfaz adaptada a la conducción, con navegación, controles multimedia y más. Si bien Google puso fin a esa función en 2022, alguien ha conseguido llevar de vuelta la experiencia de Android Auto al teléfono y sin pagar un céntimo.
PhoneAuto es una nueva app que permite ejecutar la interfaz completa de Android Auto en el teléfono. De acuerdo con su creador, el objetivo es ofrecer una experiencia pensada para la conducción, sin necesidad de contar con una pantalla compatible integrada en el vehículo.
Esto es posible gracias a que la app reproduce la interfaz real de Android Auto, incluyendo los enormes botones que permiten moverse entre las distintas secciones. Los usuarios tendrán acceso a Google Maps, reproducción de música, llamadas, mensajes y compatibilidad con el Asistente de Google. Phone Auto adapta automáticamente el diseño a las dimensiones de tu móvil, de forma similar a lo que vemos en la versión actual de Android Auto que se ajusta al tamaño de la pantalla del coche.
Android Auto ya se puede usar de nuevo en el móvil
De acuerdo con el repositorio de GitHub, Phone Auto se vale de una característica para desarrolladores conocida como head unit server. Esta función de Android Auto se utiliza normalmente para pruebas y ejecutar la interfaz del sistema directamente en el móvil. El usuario solo necesita activar el modo desarrollador y poner en marcha el servidor correspondiente, aunque existe una opción para automatizar el proceso a través de permisos de accesibilidad.
PhoneAuto se encuentra en una fase beta y, según las primeras pruebas, el rendimiento es sólido. 9to5Google reporta que la interfaz responde bien en modo horizontal, aunque si se usa en modo vertical existe un retraso al interactuar con ella. Es probable que ese lag se elimine en las próximas semanas antes de que se lance una versión final que estará disponible para instalarse desde la Google Play Store.
Cómo instalar PhoneAuto paso a paso
Si te interesa instalarla, puedes hacerlo a través de sideloading usando el APK que se distribuye en el repositorio de GitHub. La app es es gratuita y no incluye anuncios ni es necesario crearse una cuenta de usuario. Solo considera que esta versión beta dejará de funcionar el 19 de enero de 2027, por lo que deberás actualizarla a una beta más nueva o instalar la versión definitiva desde Google Play.
- Descarga el archivo APK más reciente de PhoneAuto desde su repositorio oficial.
- Permite la instalación de aplicaciones desde el navegador o gestor de archivos cuando Android lo solicite.
- Instala Android Auto desde Google Play si tu móvil no lo incluye.
- Abre los ajustes de Android Auto, desplázate hasta la sección Versión y tócala diez veces para activar el modo desarrollador.
- Pulsa el menú de tres puntos y selecciona Start head unit server.
- Abre PhoneAuto y pulsa Start Android Auto para iniciar la interfaz. Aquí puedes activar el modo vertical si deseas utilizar esa orientación.
- Cuando termines de usarla, cierra la sesión desde la aplicación.

articles.title: La liste des constructeurs chinois qui assemblent en Europe s’allonge encore
articles.text:
C’est un nouveau rebondissement pour la marque Great Wall Motor, qui avait brutalement freiné ses ambitions européennes avant de changer une nouvelle fois d’avis à la mi-2026. Selon Autonews Europe, le constructeur chinois vient de sceller un partenariat avec un industriel bulgare pour assembler ses premiers véhicules en Europe. La décision est un nouveau virage dans sa stratégie européenne, à tel point que GWM donne le tournis à force de jouer les girouettes.
Produire en Bulgarie, donc dans l’Union européenne, devrait permettre au constructeur d’échapper aux surtaxes douanières européennes sur les voitures électriques importées de Chine (20,7 % de droits antisubventions pour GWM, en plus des 10 % prélevés sur toute voiture importée). Après BYD en Hongrie, Xpeng chez Magna en Autriche ou encore Leapmotor et Chery en Espagne, c’est au tour de GWM d’annoncer une production européenne, lors de son « Tech Day » à Milan du 27 octobre 2026.
Great Wall Motor : un parcours en dents de scie en Europe
La marque a indiqué que le premier modèle à être assemblé en Europe sera le SUV Ora 5, dans sa version électrique. D’autres modèles hybrides rechargeables devraient ultérieurement sortir de ce site de production bulgare. L’usine pourra produire jusqu’à 50 000 véhicules par an. Un objectif de capacité ambitieux pour GWM, dont les ventes européennes ont chuté à environ 3 500 voitures en 2025.
L’histoire de GWM en Europe ressemble, pour l’heure, à des montagnes russes. Après une arrivée remarquée en Allemagne avec l’Ora Funky Cat, devenue depuis l’Ora 03, la marque avait soudainement levé le pied au printemps dernier, allant jusqu’à fermer son siège européen de Munich (tout en conservant son centre de recherche et développement opérationnel depuis 2021).
L’annonce d’une ligne d’assemblage en Bulgarie marque donc une nouvelle tentative de relance en Europe, après plusieurs revers stratégiques. Le constructeur dit vouloir, à terme, des « parcs industriels intégrés » en Europe pour ses voitures et leurs composants, sans préciser de pays. L’an dernier, un de ses dirigeants évoquait auprès de Reuters un objectif de 300 000 véhicules produits en Europe d’ici à 2029, soit six fois la capacité annoncée en Bulgarie.
La France de nouveau dans le viseur
Avec la France, Great Wall Motor entretient une relation tout aussi floue. Si le constructeur avait profité du Mondial de Paris 2022 pour lancer en grande pompe sa conquête de l’Europe, la marque a toujours consciencieusement évité de se lancer sur le marché français. De temps à autre, la France apparaissait dans les projets de la marque avant de disparaître à nouveau de sa stratégie quelques mois plus tard.
Si GWM concentre actuellement ses forces de vente sur l’Italie, l’Espagne et les Pays-Bas, le groupe confirme préparer activement son implantation en France. Le marché français avait d’abord été ciblé, avant que le projet ne soit mis en suspens lors du gel de la stratégie européenne de la marque. Si vous arrivez à suivre, bravo !
Les intentions sont bonnes, mais la discrétion et les changements d’avis réguliers de Great Wall Motor interrogent. En boudant le Mondial de l’Auto, organisé à Paris du 12 au 18 octobre, pour annoncer son retour européen une dizaine de jours plus tard lors d’un événement maison à Milan, GWM s’est privé d’une vitrine. Cette communication en catimini traduit peut-être une prudence nouvelle, Mais cela ne révèle-t-il pas plutôt les fragilités de ce plan ?

articles.title: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
articles.text:
Engineers from Amazon Web Services (AWS) have described how the team that maintains the Linux kernel for EC2 infrastructure handles kernel CVEs. The process combines an automated filter, an AI agent and human review. The team also argues that it needs to move to newer long-term-support (LTS) kernels, as older branches collect fixes that are never backported.
Dylan Johnson and Justinien Bouron gave the talk at the Linux Plumbers Conference in Prague earlier this month. At the start of the recording, Johnson explains that the team maintains the kernel used within EC2 infrastructure. This is separate from Amazon Linux and from the kernels that customers run in their virtual machines.
After the kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority in February 2024, the team saw about two kernel CVEs a week before 2024 and about 16 a day afterwards, with 848 published on 15 August 2026. The kernel CVE documentation states that the project cannot know how a given system uses the kernel, so users must decide which CVEs apply to them.
The first stage of AWS's process does not use AI. Bouron explained that kernel CVE records are published in JSON and list the affected versions and source files. A script discards a CVE if the kernel version is outside the affected range, or if none of the listed files are built into the image. In AWS's environment this removes about 70% of CVEs, although Bouron said the figure depends heavily on kernel configuration.
The remaining CVEs go to an AI agent. It receives AWS's kernel source tree, the configuration for each platform, a description of the environment and threat model, and a severity rubric. The agent produces a table that records the affected subsystem, the vulnerability type and the attack vector. Bouron said the team ignores CVSS scores, because they are not specific to its environment.
"We're really using it as a very fancy classifier."
Dylan Johnson
Two engineers usually review the table. According to the slides, the agent needs about 3.4 seconds per CVE, compared with minutes for a person. Bouron said review is now the slowest step in the process, and that the team does not intend to remove it.
"We don't want to hinge our entire security posture on the output of an LLM agent."
Justinien Bouron
When asked about accuracy, Bouron estimated that between 5% and 10% of the agent's decisions were problematic. This was an informal estimate, and the talk did not describe a formal evaluation.
The team also disabled kernel features it did not need, to reduce the number of applicable CVEs. Bouron called this approach "deceptively difficult". The slides list more than 32,000 configuration options, and removing the wrong one can cause bugs or performance regressions that appear months later.
The team's data also shows that older LTS branches receive fixes later and carry more unfixed CVEs. For CVEs affecting all six branches studied, the median time from a mainline fix to an LTS release was 31.8 days for Linux 5.10 and 18.1 days for 6.18. On 16 September, 1,709 known CVEs were unfixed in 5.10, compared with 229 in 6.18. These are counts for each branch, and they do not show how many affect AWS's own kernel.
Backporting fixes in-house brings its own risks. Bouron pointed out that CVE records often name only the final fixing commit. A team that misses the prerequisite commits may still be vulnerable after applying the listed fix.
AWS has shortened its own upgrades. Johnson said the move from 4.19 to 5.10 took about two years, measured from the start of porting work to full production deployment. The next upgrade took about a year, and the move to 6.18 took about six months. During the 5.10-to-6.12 upgrade, 43% of tracked issues were fixed in userspace, where workloads depended on older kernel behaviour. Johnson said the team will now run stable kernels in testing through the year, and move the fleet when each new LTS release appears.
Microsoft's Azure Linux team described a similar pipeline at the same conference. Its triage verdicts come from a rule table, and AI only suggests inputs to it. The team uses agents for backporting, and reported that a build-and-test feedback loop raised its success rate from about 50% to 80%. Google DeepMind's CodeMender, which InfoQ covered in October 2025, focuses on writing fixes. Its announcement stated that human researchers review every patch before it is submitted upstream.
Berend de Boer, CTO of Process Focus, commented on LinkedIn about the work involved in running cloud infrastructure. He listed host patching and Linux CVEs among the work that organisations take on when they build their own cloud. "Focus on what makes your business valuable to your customers," he wrote.
AWS has not released the tools. Asked about open-sourcing them, Johnson said the team would like to explore sharing the filtering tool. He also acknowledged that AWS's internal users make it easier to disable features than it would be for a general-purpose distribution.

articles.title: Instax mini Evo 2 : Fujifilm ajoute un grand écran tactile et une touche de vidéo à son appareil instantané
articles.text:
Instax mini Evo 2 : Fujifilm ajoute un grand écran tactile et une touche de vidéo à son appareil instantané
Fujifilm renouvelle son appareil photo instantané hybride avec l’Instax mini Evo 2. Au programme : un écran tactile de 4,5 pouces, une aide au cadrage et de courtes vidéos pour accompagner les photos.
Instax est décidément sur une rampe de lancement à tout-va en ce moment avec pas moins de trois modèles annoncés depuis août 2026 ! Fujifilm a commencé par le petit Pal 2, puis l’imprimante Link Wide 2, et enfin le classique Square 2. Le fabricant nippon vient d’ajouter un quatrième petit nouveau à son catalogue avec un savant mélange de photographie numérique et d’impression instantanée : l’Instax mini Evo 2.
Fujifilm Instax mini Evo 2
- 
                    
                        Fujifilm instax mini 12 Meilleur prix : 79 €Voir le test
- 
                    
                        Fujifilm Instax mini 41 Meilleur prix : 94.85 €Voir le test
- 
                    
                        Fujifilm Instax Square 2 Meilleur prix : 109.9 €Voir le produit
- 
                    
                        Fujifilm Instax Mini LiPlay+ Meilleur prix : 179 €Voir le test
Après un premier mini Evo sorti en 2022, le concept reste similaire et s’adresse à ceux qui aiment les petits tirages papier, mais préfèrent sélectionner leurs images avant de consommer une cartouche de films. On peut ainsi prendre plusieurs photos, regarder le résultat à l’écran et imprimer uniquement celles qui nous plaisent.
Cette nouvelle version conserve les commandes d’inspiration argentique et les effets créatifs inhérents à la gamme, tout en apportant quelques nouveautés à la prise de vue.
Écran tactile de 4,5 pouces et aide au cadrage : les nouveautés de l'Instax mini Evo 2
La principale évolution concerne l’écran LCD, qui passe à une diagonale de 4,5 pouces et devient tactile. De quoi faciliter le cadrage, la prévisualisation des photos et les réglages de l’appareil.
Fujifilm introduit aussi une fonction baptisée Instax Expanded View. Derrière ce nom se cache un affichage qui montre une scène plus large que la zone effectivement photographiée, délimitée par un guide à l’écran. L’idée est de pouvoir observer ce qui se trouve autour du cadre pour ajuster sa composition avant de déclencher.
L’exposition, la balance des blancs et le flash sont réglables, tandis qu’un mode macro permet de photographier des sujets de près. Un petit miroir intégré aide par ailleurs à se cadrer pour les selfies.
Instax Immersive Movie : la vidéo s'invite sur le mini Evo 2
Autre nouveauté, la fonction Instax Immersive Movie enregistre les quatre secondes précédant la prise d’une photo. Elle permet donc de conserver un court souvenir animé en complément de l’image fixe. Une carte microSD, vendue séparément, est toutefois nécessaire pour en profiter.
Pour modifier le rendu des images, le mini Evo 2 propose toujours 10 effets d’optique et 10 effets de film, soit 100 combinaisons possibles, à la manière de ce que proposent les autres Instax de la gamme Evo, comme le mini Evo Cinema, ou le Wide Evo.
L’Instax mini Evo 2 fait aussi office d'imprimante pour smartphone
Comme son prédécesseur, le mini Evo 2 peut également servir à imprimer des photos prises avec un smartphone grâce à l’app Instax mini Evo, que Fujifilm annonce avoir repensée. Celle-ci permet aussi de commander l’appareil à distance, ce qui peut notamment servir pour les photos de groupe.
L’appareil utilise les films Instax mini, à acheter séparément, et se recharge en USB-C. Sa disponibilité est prévue à partir de fin novembre 2026 au prix conseillé d’environ 270 €. Une augmentation importante par rapport au mini Evo de 2022 (200 €), mais qui peut s’expliquer en partie par la présence d’un écran tactile à l’arrière.

articles.title: London’s Querio launches with €4.48 million to help companies tackle conflicting answers across AI tools | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Querio, a London-based analytics platform for data teams and their AI agents, has launched today with €4.48 million ($5 million) in total funding.
Its investors include BMW i Ventures, which led the company’s Seed financing, alongside LAUNCH, the fund run by Jason Calacanis, Haatch Ventures, Araya, Forum Ventures, and Secways.
“Companies want to use AI with their data, but they need to trust the answer. Querio lets data teams hand more of the work to AI agents while a person stays in charge of every change that reaches the business,” said Javier Bonilla, co-founder and CTO at Querio.
Founded in 2024 by Rami Abi Habib (CEO) and Bonilla (CTO), Querio is an AI analytics platform that helps data teams give the whole company consistent answers in the AI tools it already uses. It keeps a company’s reports, definitions, and analysis in the data team’s GitHub and claims to give business users consistent answers in Claude, ChatGPT, and Slack, with the data team reviewing every change.
According to the company, it was launched to address the growing challenge of keeping answers consistent across tools as employees turn to AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT for business questions.
It says that when each tool uses a different version of the company’s numbers, people get conflicting answers, and data teams spend their time reconciling them instead of doing new work.
Querio claims to give data teams one place to define what the company’s numbers mean, and keeps that work in the team’s own GitHub rather than locked inside a vendor’s product.
“For thirty years, analytics tools have kept a company’s logic inside the vendor’s product, where it’s hard to move and hard for AI to work with. Now everyone is asking data questions in Claude, Slack and wherever else they work, and they get three different revenue numbers. We built Querio so the data team owns that logic, and every AI tool in the company answers from it,” said Abi Habib, co-founder and CEO of Querio.
The UK startup highlighted that business users can ask questions in Claude, ChatGPT or Slack and get the same answer each time. It further notes that when the business changes, Querio’s AI agent updates the affected reports and definitions, and the data team approves each change before anyone sees it.
“Say sales renames a field in the CRM. The revenue dashboard breaks, the Slack bot says no deals closed last week and Claude gives a third number. With Querio, the agent spots the change, fixes everything that depends on it and sends the data team one update to approve. After that, every tool gives the same answer,” Abi Habib added.
Querio is SOC 2 Type II certified and HIPAA- and GDPR-compliant. It also said it does not train on customer data and maintains no-training and no-storage agreements with its AI model providers. It works with companies including OpenVPN and agree.com.

articles.title: Apple adds M6 to 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac — starts at $1,999 for the new clamshell notebook
articles.text:
Apple adds M6 to 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac — starts at $1,999 for the new clamshell notebook
Apple's latest chip is in two more machines
Apple is updating two more computers to its M6 system-on-chip. The base 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac lineup are getting the company's latest processor ahead of tomorrow's "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles.
These devices are retaining the same designs that they've had for years. The computers will be available for pre-order on Wednesday at 10:10 a.m. PT (1:10 p.m. ET) and will ship on Nov. 6. The M6 in the MacBook Pro will be configured with 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores, alongside dual neural engines for certain on-device AI workloads. On the iMac, there will also be a cut-down option with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU.
The MacBook Pro will be configurable with up to 32GB of RAM and is being updated with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 using Apple's N1 networking chip. The iMac is also getting those networking benefits, as well as a 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port. Like previous iMacs, the number of ports you get is tied to the chip, with two Thunderbolt 4 ports with the base chip or four with the option with more cores.
It's no surprise that Apple is pushing both of these as AI-forward machines, both with the new chips and the recently released Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features in macOS 27 Golden Gate.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 will start at $1,999 ($1,899 with education discount), while the iMac will begin at $1,499 ($1,449 with education discount) for the 10-core CPU/GPU configuration and $1,699 ($1,599 with education discount) for the full chip.
Both of these new systems are being announced the day before Apple is expected to release a MacBook with an OLED touchscreen. Yesterday, in a week of announcements, Apple debuted a redesign of the iPad Mini with a thinner body and an OLED display.

articles.title: Lo que Carl Jung puede enseñarnos sobre envejecer bien: "Deberíamos saber que hay un proceso interno e implacable que fuerza a restringir su vida"
articles.text:
Desde hace tiempo, hay una frase de Carl Gustav Jung sobre la vejez que no deja de aparecer una y otra vez: que quien envejece debería saber que su vida ya no crece ni se ensancha, que hay "un proceso interno e implacable que fuerza a restringir su vida". Suena a taza de desayuno (si los fabricantes de tazas de desayuno tuvieran cierta tirria a la tercera edad) y a frase de autoayuda falsa que circula bajo firma ilustre. Pero no. Por una vez, es suya.
Paradójicamente, que sea de Jung no es garantía de nada. Por mucho cariño que le tengamos al viejo suizo, sigue siendo verdad que fue a casi todos los efectos un charlatán de intuición prodigiosa; pero charlatán al fin y al cabo. Un erudito esotérico cuyas teorías extienden cheques que la evidencia empírica no suele ser capaz de pagar.
Y esto es un buen ejemplo de sus limitaciones: durante décadas la psicología ha vuelto obsesivamente a esa idea (que, con los años, la vida social se encoge) y ha acabado dándole la razón en todo, menos en lo importante: y es que no es la edad lo que estrecha la vida, es el tiempo que creemos que nos queda.
¿Qué dijo exactamente Jung? La frase sale de 'Die Lebenswende', un ensayo que Jung presentó en 1930 y que, tras revisarlo a conciencia, acabó publicando en 'Seelenprobleme der Gegenwart' en 1931. Tenía 54 años y, desde hace tiempo, había una imagen que le obsesionaba: que la vida era como el arco que marca el sol en el firmamento.
Es decir, entre los 35 y los 40 años, la vida humana llegaría a su cénit, al mediodía. A partir de ahí, empezaba la tarde y es inútil vivir como si fuera aún por la mañana. Según lo veía, lo que ocurría era que el sol (perdonadme por seguir alargando la metáfora) dejaba de "derramar su luz" en el mundo y recogía sus rayos para iluminarse a sí mismo. Tiene su enjundia: no puede entenderse como un decaimiento, sino como un momento de encontrarse con quien realmente somos.
Lo interesante es que Jung no hablaba solo de viejos y jubilados. Hablaba de cuarentones. Con 54 años, es posible que ni siquiera hubiera salido de la crisis de la mediana edad.
El problema es que la idea envejeció mal (je). En 1961, mientras estudiaban con datos de adultos de 50 a 90 años en Kansas City, Elaine Cumming y William Henry desarrollaron la llamada 'teoría del desenganche'. A partir de entonces 'envejecer' sería entendido como una retirada mutua e inevitable entre la persona y la sociedad. Algunos lo han llamado "ensayo general de la muerte".
O sea, en Cumming y Henry sí que hay un decaimiento. Y lo cierto es que la teoría ha sido muy criticada. Hoy, a efectos prácticos, se considera desacreditada. Sobre todo, porque nos dimos cuenta de que los mayores no estaban más tristes que los jóvenes.
Lo explicó Laura Carstensen. Esta psicóloga de Stanford se dio cuenta de que el mundo estaba lleno de gente que había tenido pérdidas muy reales que, contra el estereotipo, mostraba un bienestar emocional relativamente alto.
Para ella la clave (que llamó selectividad socioemocional) está en otro sitio: en que todos llevamos, de una forma u otra, la cuenta de lo que nos queda. Cuando creemos que es mucho, priorizamos explorar, crecer e invertir; cuando creemos que nos queda poco priorizamos sentirnos bien, cuidarnos y protegernos.
¿Pero eso no es, sencillamente, hacerse mayor? Pues no. El ejemplo clásico que se suele poner es que si a un joven de 20 años le preguntas con quién pasaría los siguientes veinte minutos, sus respuestas son muy amplias (y suelen ser en torno a "explorar"). Si le pides que imagine que se va a mudar, sus respuestas se van rápidamente al segundo modo.
Así que sí, Jung acertó con lo que pasa, peor no en el por qué pasa. Y eso, a la hora de enfrentarnos a ello, es fundamental.

articles.title: 8 500 éoliennes et panneaux solaires en accès libre : la boulette européenne — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une étude néerlandaise menée par l’entreprise Modat et le Centre national de cybersécurité des Pays-Bas (NCSC-NL), présentée le 6 octobre, a identifié plus de 8 500 systèmes informatiques de parcs solaires et éoliens accessibles depuis Internet, alors qu’ils ne devraient pas l’être. Une exposition qui pourrait faciliter les cyberattaques en permettant de mieux repérer les équipements et rechercher les vulnérabilités exploitables.
Ces systèmes sont répartis dans 35 pays européens. L’Allemagne en compte 884 (solaire et éolien), dont 212 dans l’éolien, le chiffre le plus élevé d’Europe pour cette filière ; côté solaire, l’Espagne arrive loin devant avec 2 766 systèmes exposés.
Le 13 octobre, une semaine après la présentation de cette étude, l’Office fédéral allemand de la sécurité informatique (BSI) a alerté sur les risques de cyberattaques visant différents types d’installations, dont les unités de production d’énergie (centrales hydroélectriques, parcs éoliens, installations d’incinération de déchets, installations solaires de toute taille, unités de cogénération et installations de biogaz).
L’organisme a publié une série de recommandations destinées en priorité aux exploitants de petites et très petites installations pour les aider à repérer les failles de sécurité et à prévenir les intrusions susceptibles de perturber le fonctionnement de leurs équipements.
Cette alerte suit de près une attaque qui a touché la France. Dans la nuit du 11 au 12 octobre, des pirates ont pris la main à distance sur les systèmes de réfrigération de centaines de supermarchés, dont des Intermarché, des Super U et des E.Leclerc, en les basculant en mode dégivrage. Le ministre de l’Économie, Roland Lescure, parle d’environ 700 magasins touchés, et une partie des denrées a dû être jetée. Claudia Plattner, présidente du BSI, estime qu’une telle attaque aurait pu viser n’importe quel pays et redoute des imitateurs.
Des failles informatiques qui exposent les centrales aux cyberattaques
Mal protégées, les centrales peuvent devenir des cibles de cyberattaques dans le cadre d’une guerre hybride. Or, selon le BSI, des failles de sécurité élémentaires continuent d’exposer de nombreuses installations à ce type de menace.
Le BSI vise d’abord les petites installations. En Allemagne, les centrales de moins de 100 MW ne relèvent pas des règles imposées aux infrastructures critiques, et ne sont donc soumises en principe à aucune obligation de cybersécurité particulière. L’office précise que ses consignes valent quelle que soit la taille de l’installation ou le statut de son exploitant, solaire domestique compris : un particulier dont l’onduleur est accessible depuis Internet est concerné au même titre qu’un exploitant de parc éolien.
Les vulnérabilités les plus courantes sont les mots de passe par défaut qui n’ont jamais été modifiés, ou qui sont réutilisés sur plusieurs équipements. Exposer directement les systèmes de commande à Internet est aussi très risqué. Pour surveiller leurs installations à distance, certains opérateurs rendent en effet accessibles des interfaces de supervision ou des automates industriels depuis le réseau public. Certains opérateurs font aussi trop confiance aux réseaux privés. Un réseau mobile privé ne garantit pas à lui seul que les appareils qui y sont connectés soient suffisamment protégés les uns des autres.
L’IA peut aussi faciliter le travail des attaquants. Elle permet, entre autres, de rédiger des scripts, d’analyser des informations techniques ou d’adapter des outils existants pour repérer des systèmes vulnérables. Associée à des mécanismes d’automatisation, elle peut aussi accélérer les recherches et multiplier les tentatives d’intrusion.
Dans son document, le BSI cite notamment l’attaque survenue en Pologne le 29 décembre 2025 contre plus d’une trentaine de parcs éoliens et solaires, ainsi qu’une centrale de cogénération qui chauffe près d’un demi-million de clients. Sur les parcs éoliens, les attaquants ont coupé les communications avec les gestionnaires de réseau et bloqué les équipements de commande et de protection, sans toutefois perturber la production ni la distribution d’électricité.
Autre précédent cité par le BSI, aux États-Unis cette fois. En août 2026, des attaquants ont accédé à des automates et à des systèmes de supervision laissés ouverts sur Internet chez plus de 30 gestionnaires d’eau municipaux. Ils ont pu modifier des valeurs de fonctionnement et bloquer l’accès aux équipements pour compliquer le retour à la normale.
Les recommandations du BSI pour mieux protéger les installations
Pour limiter les risques, le BSI recommande en priorité de supprimer tout accès direct à Internet aux systèmes de commande industriels. Les automates programmables, les interfaces de supervision et les interfaces homme-machine ne doivent pas être directement accessibles depuis le réseau public.
Lorsque l’accès à distance est indispensable, les connexions doivent être sécurisées au moyen d’un VPN. Les exploitants doivent également remplacer les identifiants par défaut, choisir des mots de passe robustes et activer l’authentification multifacteur. Le BSI conseille par ailleurs de vérifier si la connexion au cloud du fabricant est vraiment indispensable, l’idéal étant de faire fonctionner l’installation uniquement en local. Il insiste enfin sur la mise à jour des logiciels et des micrologiciels, en particulier ceux des routeurs et des dispositifs d’accès à distance.
Le BSI prévient toutefois qu’un mot de passe ne suffit pas toujours, car certaines failles peuvent être exploitées sans aucune authentification. Il demande donc d’activer aussi les protections déjà présentes dans les équipements, comme les listes de blocage et le filtrage des protocoles. Il conseille enfin de vérifier régulièrement, idéalement de façon automatique, si de nouvelles mises à jour sont disponibles.

articles.title: Pour Halloween, la Maison-Blanche veut vous faire peur avec un jeu vidéo sur le socialisme
articles.text:
Pour Halloween, certains jeux vous proposent d’échapper à des zombies. Celui de la Maison-Blanche vous invite à fuir le collectivisme. Baptisé Red Scare: Midnight Run, il figure désormais dans la rubrique Arcade du site présidentiel américain. Le programme est annoncé sans détour : « Vaincre le socialisme et le communisme. »
Dans un message publié sur X ce 26 octobre, le compte officiel de la Maison-Blanche invite les internautes à remplacer le doomscrolling, cette habitude de faire défiler les mauvaises nouvelles, par une partie de jeu vidéo. À condition, donc, de trouver la menace communiste plus reposante.
Ce nouveau titre rejoint une collection dont les autres occupations consistent notamment à capturer des migrants à la frontière ou à remplir un compte d’épargne Trump. Accessible depuis Arcade.gov, cette salle d’arcade lancée le 3 septembre 2026 rassemble aujourd’hui six jeux. Vous l’aurez compris : tous participent à la promotion des idées et des politiques de l’administration américaine.
Un « bouclier MAGA » contre le collectivisme
Dans Red Scare, il faut courir, sauter, glisser et éviter les obstacles pour distancer ses poursuivants. Le parcours comprend quatre étapes et 12 000 mètres à franchir, à travers des décors évoquant le rationnement, une fonderie saisie et un cimetière plongé dans le noir. La course s’accélère progressivement, tandis qu’un « bouclier MAGA » figure parmi les protections affichées.
L’habillage d’Halloween laisse peu de place au doute sur le propos : le collectivisme vous poursuit, la prospérité se compte en points et Donald Trump est associé à votre protection. En cas d’échec, le jeu annonce que le collectif vous a rattrapé.
Un autre titre, Escape from Socialism, adopte une approche différente : un jeu de mémoire où l’on retourne des cartes pour retrouver des paires. Les associations révèlent des chiffres issus d’une analyse du Council of Economic Advisers, l’organe de conseil économique de la présidence, consacrée au programme des Democratic Socialists of America. Il s’agit donc de projections produites par l’administration sur un programme politique adverse (et non de coûts déjà constatés).
Des classiques du jeu vidéo au service de Trump
Les autres jeux déclinent les priorités présidentielles. Rio Run reprend le principe de Snake pour faire capturer des migrants à la frontière. Supply Line demande de trier des aliments dans l’esprit du slogan « Make America Healthy Again ». Flappy Bill fait voler un aigle au-dessus de Washington, tandis que Trump Savings Tycoon invite à remplir les comptes d’épargne pour enfants promus par l’administration.
La vocation politique de cette salle d’arcade est d’ailleurs assumée. Au lancement, un responsable de la Maison-Blanche expliquait à ABC News vouloir opposer une « culture du plaisir et de la victoire » à la vision « socialiste » attribuée aux démocrates. Soit.

articles.title: Meta gets $3 billion from Nvidia, team up to make Muse AI faster and cheaper to run
articles.text:
What just happened? One day after Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion to fuel its AI spending, Nvidia has confirmed it will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering. Team Green calls the move a strengthening of the companies' AI partnership, one that will deepen their collaboration on the Muse AI models.
When Meta announced its stock offering yesterday, it was reported that Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom had indicated interest in buying up to $5 billion worth of the company's shares collectively. The world's largest company by market cap has now confirmed its contribution.
The original fundraising plans comprised roughly $35 billion in initial offerings and a separate $60 billion share-sale program, expected after Meta's new nonvoting Class C shares begin trading in early 2027. That later program remains subject to final terms. Reuters reports that Meta increased the overall fundraising figure to $97.5 billion on Tuesday.
Nvidia says the expanded partnership will focus on improving training and inference performance across Muse and its family of models, while reducing the cost of running them. The companies claim Muse has delivered strong benchmark results and surging downloads since launch, though there are no included figures.
There is, unsurprisingly, more Nvidia hardware involved. Meta plans to expand its deployment of Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs, alongside Spectrum-X Ethernet networking and BlueField-4 technology. The aim is to squeeze more performance from each watt and improve the movement of data across its infrastructure.
The pair are also considering further work on Nvidia's OpenShell framework for deploying agents safely and Sentry for monitoring their behavior.
Muse sits at the center of Mark Zuckerberg's push for personal superintelligence. Meta describes it as an agent that can take action across everyday services, from sending emails to booking travel, with users deciding how much access to grant it.
Meta expects capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion this year, nearly all of which is fueling its AI infrastructure buildout. The tech giant's latest quarterly results showed revenue rising 26% to $64.6 billion.
For Nvidia, investing in a customer that plans to deploy more of its hardware adds to more questions about circular financing across the AI industry, which comes down to chip suppliers backing the companies that buy their products.

articles.text:
Lancés en Chine le 21 septembre, en même temps que la série X500 et la Watch 6, les Vivo Buds Clip sont les premiers écouteurs à clip de la marque lancés en Europe, et notamment en France. Au lieu de s’insérer dans le conduit auditif, ils se fixent autour de l’oreille grâce à un arceau flexible en alliage de titane à mémoire de forme. Les bruits extérieurs restent ainsi audibles. C’est le même principe que les Sony LinkBuds Clip, Huawei FreeClip 2, Shokz OpenDots 2, Bose Ultra Open Earbuds, Motorola Moto Buds Loop, JBL SoundGear Clips, Oppo Enco Clip 2, Anker AeroClip 2, CMF Clip Pro ou les récents Samsung Galaxy Buds On.
    Pour aller plus loin
Meilleurs écouteurs ouverts en 2026, le comparatif des open ear
            
Chaque écouteur pèse 5,2 grammes. Les deux sont symétriques, et le système adapte automatiquement les canaux stéréo selon l’oreille choisie. Les transducteurs mesurent 12 mm, et un dispositif limite les fuites sonores. Selon Vivo, l’autonomie atteint 10 heures par charge et 42 heures avec le boîtier. Les écouteurs peuvent aussi se connecter à trois appareils en même temps.
Les Buds Clip proposent aussi de la traduction en temps réel et des notifications de transport générées par intelligence artificielle. Ces fonctions exigent toutefois un smartphone Vivo ou iQOO compatible. Ils sont déclinés en noir, blanc ou violet.
    Pour aller plus loin
Écouteurs à clip d’oreille : quand le confort prend le pas sur le son
            
Vivo Buds Ultra : réduction de bruit jusqu’à 60 dB
Les Buds Ultra sont des écouteurs true wireless à système hybride, qui associe un transducteur dynamique et une armature équilibrée développée avec Knowles. Ce sont les écouteurs les plus haut de gamme de la marque.
Ils embarquent quatre microphones et la fonction Intelligent Noise Cancellation 2.0, qui réduit le bruit de 60 dB au maximum selon la marque, mais de 28 dB en moyenne sur une bande passante de 5 500 Hz.
L’autonomie annoncée est de 11 heures par charge et de 50 heures avec le boîtier, deux valeurs mesurées par Vivo avec l’ANC désactivée (codec AAC, volume à 50 %).
Une charge de 5 minutes procure 2 heures d’écoute, et le boîtier accepte la recharge sans fil. Les écouteurs prennent en charge le LDAC, l’audio Hi-Res sans fil et la connexion à trois appareils. Ils sont proposés en blanc Glacier et en noir Cosmic.
Vivo Headphones Studio : un casque de 238 grammes
Le Headphones Studio est le premier casque circum-auriculaire de Vivo pour l’Europe. Il pèse 238 grammes, et ses coussinets sont conçus pour exercer moins de pression sur les branches de lunettes. Il embarque des transducteurs de 40 mm et une fonction de réduction de bruit adaptative atteignant 58 dB. Selon Vivo, cet ANC compense même un léger décalage des oreillettes lorsque l’on tourne la tête.
L’autonomie grimpe à 75 heures sans ANC et à 35 heures avec. Dix minutes de charge fournissent neuf heures d’écoute. Le casque gère le LDAC, le Hi-Res Audio Wireless et la connexion à trois appareils. Il est décliné en noir et en violet.
Disponibilité et prix des écouteurs et casque Vivo
Les écouteurs Vivo Buds Ultra sont disponibles pour 199 euros en France en noir ou en blanc. Comptez 179 euros pour les Vivo Buds Clip. Le casque Vivo Headphones Studio, de son côté, est proposé à 169 euros.
