articles.title: How technology is driving manufacturing's next leap
articles.text:
Technology has become part of how modern businesses operate. The more difficult question for business leaders is deciding where they can create meaningful value.
Every year brings new tools, platforms and applications that promise to make businesses faster, more efficient and more competitive. Keeping up with all of them is neither practical nor necessary. What matters is understanding the problems within the business that technology can genuinely help solve and having a clear way to measure whether it has made a difference.
That means technology decisions belong directly in executive and strategic discussions. They dictate how work gets done, how choices are framed, how capital and human resources are deployed, and how rapidly an organisation can pivot. While technical teams lead implementation, deployment decisions must remain tightly aligned with overall business priorities.
The most pragmatic starting point is operational diagnosis: Where is time being lost? Where are decisions constrained by limited data? Which processes introduce unnecessary friction or cost? Addressing these concrete pain points provides a far stronger foundation than selecting a technology and searching for a problem to solve.
This problem-first philosophy guides our digital strategy at UAC of Nigeria PLC and the 1879 Tech Hub. For instance, our deployment of SAP S/4HANA strengthens operational controls, enhances efficiency, and provides real-time visibility across the end-to-end supply chain. In 2025, we executed an upgrade and cloud migration that significantly reduced infrastructure costs and laid the groundwork to integrate CHI Limited’s enterprise platforms into our unified architecture.
At 1879 Tech Hub, that approach can mean building a solution when a specific business need calls for it, or harnessing existing technologies when they can address the problem effectively. We have developed tools including Legal Compass for legal operations, SalesUp for route-to-market visibility, Ops Shield for safety and compliance, and Proc360 for procurement. We also harness technologies such as computer vision and machine learning through Factory AI to give teams greater visibility across the production floor, helping them identify safety violations, quality defects and operational inefficiencies earlier and respond more quickly.
Successful adoption depends on more than the technology itself. Leadership needs to be clear about the business outcome, teams need to understand how a new system affects their work, and the organisation needs the skills and processes to sustain it. This becomes particularly important as AI and other advanced technologies become more widely used. A highly capable system has limited value if the people expected to use its output cannot understand it or apply it appropriately to the business context.
For organisations beginning their technology journey, this means resisting the pressure to do everything at once. A focused use case, a clear business objective and a way to measure the outcome provide a stronger foundation for scale. Once a solution has demonstrated value, the business has something tangible to build on, whether that means extending it to another production line, applying the learning to another function or addressing a different problem.
For African enterprises, this disciplined methodology is particularly urgent. Companies across the continent navigate unique operating environments characterised by fragmented supply networks, diverse consumer segments, and infrastructure variability—demanding targeted, highly scalable technology investments.
The pace of technological change will continue to increase. Business leaders will have to make decisions about AI, automation, data and other emerging technologies while balancing competing priorities and assessing which solutions are genuinely relevant to their businesses. The opportunity lies in building the discipline to first understand the problem, test technology against it, measure the outcome, and use what works to make the next decision. That is how technology moves from being another business investment to becoming a practical driver of better performance.
David Asama Dogeni is a technology executive and innovation leader with over 15 years of experience driving enterprise-wide digital transformation across diverse industries. He currently serves as Senior Vice President of Technology and Head of the 1879 Tech Hub at UAC of Nigeria PLC, where he leads strategic initiatives that embed technology at the core of business operations, enabling sustainable growth and long-term competitive advantage.

articles.title: Exclusive: Meta director Rohit Patel departs after 8 years to take on Microsoft Office Suite
articles.text:
After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc, a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.
Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan, AI researcher Andrew Tulloch, and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith.
Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc.
Ndoc brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers. The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed.
The design reflects Patel’s background. During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work. For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents.
“Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.”
In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said.
Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models. Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models.
“I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.”
Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years.
His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone. At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.”
Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.”
Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space.
OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, SpaceXAI, and Google have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools. And last month, OpenAI launched Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools.
Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea.
“Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.”
There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though. It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows. Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use.
“My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do. If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.”
Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said.
As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list. It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens. He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year.
For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go.
“Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.”

articles.title: Ford simplifies using your EV as a home battery with the $30K Fathom
articles.text:
This morning, Ford revealed that buyers of the forthcoming Fathom—the company’s sub-$30,000 electric pickup truck due next year—will get more than just a truck. Until now, vehicle-to-home technology—like the setup Ford developed for the now-discontinued F-150 Lightning—takes DC power from the electric vehicle and runs it through an inverter built into the wallbox to turn it into AC the house can use. But with the Fathom, that inverter is built into the truck from the start. So every Fathom will be able to act as a backup battery for your home.
It’s typical: You wait a decade for a cheap electric truck, and then two come along almost at once. And they’re two radically different products from two radically different automakers that I think will reveal a few preferences from the EV-buying public. One is the Blank Slate, from a brand new startup offering a bare-bones two-door that capitalizes on features the Internet says it wants, like no onboard modem, no touchscreens, and no infotainment system.
The other is the result of one of Detroit’s big three taking a long, hard look at Chinese EVs and asking itself, “How do we make a car that cheap?” Although the Ford Fathom will cost $5,000 more than a Slate, that money does buy an extra pair of doors, modern conveniences like an infotainment system, CarPlay, electric windows, and a vast dealership network to service the car. That may be helpful given how many recalls Ford issues each year.

articles.title: Loon clears key regulatory hurdle to offer Canadian dollar-backed stablecoin | BetaKit
articles.text:
Calgary-based FinTech startup Loon has secured the green light from domestic securities regulators to issue its Canadian dollar-backed CADC stablecoin in Canada.
Loon announced on Tuesday that its newly established CADC Reserve Trust has received receipt for its final prospectus from the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), giving it exemptive relief to offer the blockchain-based token. Paytrie, the Calgary company that originally created CADC—and from which Loon spun out of last year—has also been granted exemptive relief to distribute CADC.
Though Loon still has more work to do to ensure compliance, including migrating legacy CADC over to this new contract, this marks the completion of one of the key and final regulatory steps required for Loon to issue CADC, and for Paytrie to deliver it, Paytrie co-founder and Loon co-founder and CEO Kevin Zhang told BetaKit in an interview. He claimed that the two firms have carved out a new framework around stablecoin distribution in the process.
“If you’re a new stablecoin company in Canada and you wanted to issue a Canadian dollar stablecoin, you should be doing it exactly the same way we just did it.”
Kevin Zhang, Loon
“If you’re a new stablecoin company in Canada and you wanted to issue a Canadian dollar stablecoin, you should be doing it exactly the same way we just did it, because this will allow Canadians full access the same way that you expect a stablecoin to work, like USDC,” he said.
The value of stablecoins is pegged to another reserve asset beyond crypto. In the case of fiat-backed stablecoins, that asset is typically a currency like the US dollar. Stablecoins are usually, though not always, less volatile than other digital currencies. For each CADC token purchased, $1 CAD will be deposited into a reserve trust account with ATB Financial.
Loon is one of several Canadian firms that have been working to deliver a regulated, CAD-backed stablecoin to alleviate friction for domestic users and reduce the value exported by using US dollar-backed alternatives. Toronto-based Stablecorp secured similar approval to Loon last year for its QCAD offering, while Calgary’s Tetra Trust is pursuing a slightly different path for its own CADD stablecoin.
This appears to make Paytrie the second non-cryptocurrency trading platform to secure the relief necessary to offer stablecoins in Canada, after US-based ZeroHash, as an “authorized participant.”
RELATED: Government of Canada unveils proposed stablecoin regulations
These milestones come days after the Government of Canada released its proposed stablecoin regulations, which Zhang described as “a positive step forward” with no big surprises, noting that it follows many of the same principles as the United States GENIUS Act.
Led by Zhang and other former Paytrie staff, Loon launched last year with $3 million CAD to focus exclusively on CADC, which the startup acquired from Paytrie in 2025. Paytrie built CADC as an experiment as it set up its core stablecoin on- and off-ramp business, and since its launch in 2021, the stablecoin has facilitated over $1 billion CAD in transactions.
Zhang and his team began working with regulators while they were still at Paytrie, beginning with the Alberta Securities Commission before they were redirected to the OSC. He claimed that Tuesday’s announcement required “18 to 24 months of intense back-and-forth,” and “significant” legal investment on both companies’ behalf.
The biggest issue Loon faced, Zhang said, was how long it has taken Canada’s Stablecoin Act to become law, adding that delay “created a huge gap in the market.” Were it in effect earlier, Loon’s path would have looked a lot different: the company would have simply sought approval directly from the Bank of Canada, the CEO said.
RELATED: Paytrie spinout Loon raises $3 million to oversee Canadian dollar-backed stablecoin
With stablecoins increasingly used for payments, accessing them through a crypto exchange for this application “can be quite limiting,” Zhang argued. He claimed Paytrie’s capacity to deliver CADC will enable a wider array of cross-border and decentralized finance use-cases.
Zhang said the feds’ draft stablecoin regulation rules contained “nothing too out of the box, which could be a good thing or bad thing.” It also appears to signal that the federal government intends to soften its ban on stablecoin yield.
One thing it does not do, however, is create a regulatory advantage for CAD-backed stablecoins compared to their US-dollar counterparts; rather, it establishes a level playing field, he said. Zhang was hoping that policymakers would push the legislation “a little bit further” to help CAD-backed stablecoins compete domestically and abroad.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy Loon.

articles.title: African startups invited to apply for Yamaha’s TRANSPOSE Innovation Challenge 2026 - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African startups are invited to apply for the second edition of Yamaha’s TRANSPOSE Innovation Challenge, a Yamaha-backed programme that will see winning founders receive funding and support to build the future of sound and entertainment.
The Japanese music and audio giant is looking for startups that can help it reimagine how people experience music, live events and entertainment, with selected companies offered project funding, technical resources and mentorship to test, validate and scale their products.
The inaugural edition of the challenge last year attracted 314 applications from startups across 63 countries.
This year’s edition is structured around four challenge tracks. The Venue track seeks solutions that elevate live events, sports and concerts through immersive technology, visuals and crowd interaction, while the Senior track focuses on harnessing music and entertainment to support active ageing, cognitive health and intergenerational connection.
The Game track is looking for startups combining gaming mechanics, audio and intellectual property (IP) to add playfulness to everyday life, while the Timeless track targets solutions that turn temporary live entertainment experiences into lasting digital or physical assets.
Successful startups will have the opportunity to co-create with Yamaha using its proprietary technologies, domain expertise and assets, and will also gain access to exclusive fundraising discussions with the company’s corporate venture capital (CVC) team.
The Grand Prix Award winner will receive up to JPY5 million (US$32,000) in proof-of-concept (PoC) funding, as well as the chance to collaborate with Yamaha and its partners. The Yamaha Award comes with up to JPY2 million (US$13,000) in PoC funding and a collaboration with Yamaha, while the YMI Fund Award offers direct fundraising discussions with members of the Yamaha Music Innovations Fund.
Applications are open here until October 31.

articles.title: Nebius cut rollout collection time by 66.9% — here’s what changed
articles.text:
Nebius cut rollout collection time by 66.9% — here’s what changed
In AI agent training, you can pay for powerful GPUs and still spend much of your time waiting. Agents need to attempt tasks and produce results before the model can learn from them. A few slow attempts can hold up the next training update, making the systems that run those tasks a major factor in training speed and cost.
Di Jin, VP of AI Training at Amsterdam-headquartered Nebius, says teams coming from pretraining or supervised fine-tuning can underestimate the work these systems do.
“If you staff and design it as a training project, inference becomes the bottleneck nobody owns.”
Rollout generation often takes most of a training step’s wall-clock time, making batching, cache management and scheduling central to how fast the model can learn. “If you staff and design it as a training project, inference becomes the bottleneck nobody owns,” Jin says.
Time to a trainable batch
He adds that engineers should measure time to a trainable batch alongside throughput. Average tokens per second can hide the long tail: in a synchronous batch, the step cannot finish until the final trajectory is completed.
Agent trajectories do not all have the same length. Many finish quickly, while others take longer, leaving training GPUs waiting on a handful of stragglers. For this reason, Jin advises engineers to treat the inference engine as part of the post-training reinforcement learning optimizer.
Data misunderstood
Learning from data generated by an older model version involves a tradeoff. Some policy lag can improve GPU efficiency by letting generation and training overlap, Jin says, but its safety depends on how much the policy has changed and how the training algorithm handles the difference.
Jin tells The New Stack, “In fully synchronous RL, inference GPUs wait while training runs, and training GPUs wait while generation runs. Letting generation use weights that are one or a few updates old allows both to run in parallel. That overlap is how most large-scale systems reach reasonable utilization.” When success on a hard task is rare, he adds, an already successful trajectory can be valuable to reuse even if it is slightly stale.
Staleness becomes harmful when the policy that generated a trajectory has drifted too far from the policy being trained. The useful measure is divergence, not a universal limit on how many training steps old the data can be.
“Staleness isn’t the enemy. Unmeasured staleness is.”
Rather than seeking to eradicate old data, engineers and organizations should measure and manage staleness. They can apply importance-sampling corrections, usually truncated to limit variance; drop or down-weight samples beyond a staleness threshold; and track divergence between the generating policy and the current policy. Jin says: “Staleness isn’t the enemy. Unmeasured staleness is.”
Environments are the new data
In Jin’s experience, data and environments take up most of the work in successful RL post-training. Algorithm design is the smallest slice, while infrastructure enables fast iteration. “Infrastructure determines how fast you can iterate. But what the model actually learns is decided by the tasks, environments, and rewards you give it,” he says.
For agents, that means focusing on the environments that generate training experience. Supervised fine-tuning uses a collected dataset; in agentic RL, the model generates trajectories by interacting with an environment.
Reproducible containers, codebases, websites, and APIs with realistic states help the model’s learning transfer to real use. Engineers also need reliable verifiers and tasks at a useful difficulty level. As the model improves, the task set needs refreshing so tasks don’t saturate and stop producing a learning signal. Jin says: “Building environments is the new data curation.”
As with previous technologies, problems occur where systems hand over to one another. The trainer, inference engine, sandbox, and verifier may each work on their own, yet failures emerge at the interfaces. A model can exploit verifier loopholes and receive rewards for behavior that doesn’t accomplish the intended task. Sandboxes can also fail or misbehave, corrupting the training data.
Engineers should record whether an episode ended in model success, model failure, infrastructure failure, or an unknown outcome. Exclude failures attributable to infrastructure from policy-gradient updates. Failures caused by the model’s own actions should still be scored as model failures, so triggering a timeout or another error doesn’t become a way to avoid a penalty.
Long-horizon agentic RL combines trajectories, tool calls, and external latencies, creating bursts of GPU demand and periods of waiting. For GRPO-style training, where sibling attempts at a task are scored against one another, engineers should schedule around group completion rather than launch order. A group enters a ready bank once all sibling attempts finish; the trainer then takes eligible complete groups regardless of when they were launched. Time to a trainable batch is the governing measure, while tokens per second remains useful for diagnosing inference. Routing matters because keeping a conversation close to its cached history can avoid repeated prefill work.
In a Nebius experiment on a Terminal-Bench-based workload, changes to routing, sandbox execution, and batch assembly reduced fixed-weight collection time for a 256-trajectory batch by 66.9%. That measured batch collection, excluding the trainer’s forward, backward, and optimizer work; it did not measure complete training speed.
For agentic AI rollouts, an infrastructure goal is to reduce the time expensive GPUs spend waiting on sandboxes, browsers, code execution, and other non-GPU dependencies.
“Your most expensive GPU is often waiting on your cheapest container.”
Jin recommends scaling CPU and sandbox capacity independently of GPUs and provisioning it generously, because idle containers are comparatively inexpensive. “Your most expensive GPU is often waiting on your cheapest container,” he says.
Keeping sandboxes ready, using snapshot and fork methods, can take environment startup off the critical path. It doesn’t remove the time needed to run tools. Jin recommends putting sandboxes on the same network fabric as the GPUs where possible to minimize the cumulative latency of the hundreds of tool calls an agent may make. Per-step timeouts and budgets can limit the disruption from a hung browser or process. Engineers should track GPU-hours spent waiting on environments, alongside utilization and time to a trainable batch, to identify where additional investment would help.
When the maths does not match
During RL post-training, the rollout engine and the trainer can assign different probabilities to the same tokens, even when they start from the same weights. Quantization, kernels, batching, and, in mixture-of-experts models, expert routing can all contribute. Those differences can introduce systematic bias into training updates.
Jin recommends aligning the numerics first, then measuring and correcting the remaining mismatch. That can mean matching the quantization scheme and computation used in the trainer’s forward pass to the rollout engine, while retaining higher-precision weights for optimization. Importance-sampling corrections can help manage residual differences, but clipping alone should not be assumed to solve every form of mismatch.
Evaluation should use the precision, inference engine, and version that will serve the model. Changing quantization or kernels calls for another evaluation.
Keeping the weights in step
As training updates the policy, rollout workers need a reliable way to receive new weights while keeping policy lag within acceptable limits. Jin describes three broad patterns: resharding weights in memory when training and inference share GPUs; transferring weights directly to separate inference workers; and publishing checkpoints that inference engines hot-load through storage. The best choice depends on the model, hardware topology, and freshness requirements.
A full service restart can introduce avoidable downtime, but storage-based publication does not have to require one. Asynchronous transfer and compact updates can move much of the work off the critical path. Teams should measure end-to-end publication latency separately from the pause needed to apply the weights.
Weight publication also needs an explicit plan for active requests and cached state. Depending on the engine, teams can finish, abort, or pause requests before applying an update, and clear or recompute cached context as needed. If a trajectory spans policy versions, record which version generated its tokens so the training system can handle that mixture deliberately. Coordinate transfers with rollout traffic where they share resources, and monitor publication delays alongside policy age.
Designing these components together helps teams improve iteration speed while keeping training data and policy updates reliable. Jin advises smaller teams to start with a simple setup and add asynchronous complexity when measured bottlenecks justify it.
Before scaling, check:
- Batch readiness: How long does it take to assemble a complete, usable batch, including the straggler tail?
- Policy freshness: Can every rollout be traced to the policy version that generated it, and what drift makes it too stale to use?
- Numerical alignment: How different are the trainer’s and rollout engine’s probabilities, and what correction handles the remaining gap?
- Environment reliability: Can you distinguish infrastructure failures from model failures and reproduce an affected episode?
- Weight publication: What happens to active requests and KV caches during an update, and how long does publication actually take?
- Evaluation: Are you testing the model in the precision and serving stack users will encounter?

articles.title: He probado el vivo X500 Pro Max y lo tengo claro: hay vida (y muy buena) más allá del iPhone
articles.text:
Se presentó hace un mes en China, pero ahora llega al mercado europeo para demostrar que hay vida más allá del iPhone, del Samsung de gama alta de turno y de los cientos de móviles Xiaomi. El nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max es uno de los móviles más prometedores del año. Llega con un apartado fotográfico muy interesante, un conjunto de especificaciones que no decepciona. Pero también, con la misma pregunta de siempre: ¿realmente merece la pena frente a toda su competencia?
Porque admitámoslo: a estas alturas ya no es suficiente que un móvil tenga una buena pantalla, un procesador potente o una batería capaz de aguantar todo el día. Los móviles de gama alta han alcanzado un nivel tan alto elevado que las diferencias entre un modelo y otro son casi imperceptibles. Por eso, lo importante ahora está no solo en los detalles, sino en esos extras que hacen especial a un móvil: accesorios que suman y aportan mas experiencia, un software que va más allá de animaciones bonitas y fluidez, etc. Aquí es, precisamente, donde este vivo X500 Pro Max quiere hacerse un hueco.
Llevo un mes probando este móvil a fondo. Incluso viajé a Shanghái hace un mes para asistir a su presentación oficia, donde pude probar en profundidad aspectos como su cámara, su batería, su pantalla o su rendimiento. Un mes es tiempo más que suficiente para ir más allá de unas primeras impresiones y comprobar si lo que ofrece este dispositivo realmente merece la pena o no.
Ahora, toca responder a la pregunta: ¿es este vivo X500 Pro Max una alternativa real a los grandes referentes de la gama alta? ¿O estamos entre otro móvil que promete mucho, pero que termina en nada?
Sin sorpresas ni decepciones
El vivo X500 Pro Max es uno de esos móviles que no decepcionan; ni por su diseño, ni por su construcción. Es un móvil elegante, muy resistente y con detalles muy bien pensados para mejorar su ergonomía, como ese doble acabado con una parte mucho más gomosa, que evita que el móvil se te resbale de las manos y por ejemplo no se te caiga al agua (aunque también cuenta con certificación IP69).
El vivo X500 Pro Max también es muy bonito. Destaca por su gran cámara circular, por sus marcos en un acabado mate o su gran pantalla, que en este caso es de 6,85 pulgadas. Es un panel AMOLED con una resolución de 1400 x 3168 píxeles, un brillo de 2.000 nits (con picos de hasta 4.000 nits) y una tasa de refresco de 144 Hz. Es una pantalla muy brillante, con una nitidez excelente y con una interpretación de los colores muy buena: el panel OLED los satura ligeramente, pero sin pasarse, y presenta unos muy buenos ángulos de visión.
El rendimiento del vivo X500 Pro Max tampoco desentona con su diseño o su pantalla. En este caso, nos encontramos un procesador Dimensity 9600 Pro, un SoC de gama alta que está acompañado con 12 o 16 GB de memoria RAM. Dicho procesador ofrece un rendimiento excelente para el día a día y una potencia más que suficiente para ejecutar tareas de IA, tanto de edición como de productividad.
Respecto a la autonomía, este vivo X500 Pro Max tiene una de 6.750 mAh. Se trata de una batería de sicilio-carbono que ofrece una autonomía más que decente para el día a día, aunque un poco justa en condiciones de uso más intensivo. Cuenta, además, con carga rápida de 90W y una carga rápida inalámbrica de 40W.
Así son las cámaras del vivo X500 Pro Max
Hablemos del que, sin duda, es el apartado más importante de este Vivo X500 Pro Max: sus cámaras. Este modelo cuenta con un sensor principal de 50 megapíxeles y una apertura f/1.6, así como una cámara ultra gran angular de la misma resolución (aunque con una apertura f/2.0). Le acompaña, además, un teleobjetivo periscopio de 200 megapíxeles, que permite tomar fotografías con un zoom de 3.5X. Todas estas cámaras se han desarrollado con Zeiss, como fruto de una colaboración entre ambas compañías consolidada ya durante varios años.
La cámara es: impresionante. Hacia tiempo que no disfrutaba tanto haciendo fotos con un móvil. Ofrece un detalle excelente en la mayoría de situaciones, incluso en condiciones de baja luminosidad.
Tiene una interpretación de los colores muy buena, cuida mucho las sombras y consigue una exposición más que correcta en todos los escenarios. Lo fuerte es que estos resultados se consiguen incluso con el modo automático. Además (y algo que me encanta) es que puedes escoger entre diferentes filtros desarrollados por Zeiss, que le dan un toque artístico a las imágenes y consigue, incluso, imitar a las cámaras tradicionales.
Eso sí, no es oro todo lo que reluce. La cámara del vivo X500 Pro Max tiene un pequeño inconveniente relacionado con el procesado a la hora de hacer fotos a personas. En muchas ocasiones la cámara tiende a "deformar" los rostros de las personas. Es algo que se nota solo al hacer zoom, y que es claramente un "error" del procesado con IA que realiza la cámara.
El vivo X500 Pro Max también es compatible con el kit fotográfico que incluyen los otros modelos. Aunque, ojo, necesitas comprar uno específico para este modelo, pues el kit incluye una funda y un anillo adaptado a este tamaño. Dicho kit incluye también dos objetivos: Uno de 200 mm y otro de 400 mm. Es un añadido muy bienvenido si quieres tomar fotografías con más zoom o centrarte aún más en los detalles. Eso sí, colocar el objetivo es un proceso bastante engorroso. Por no hablar de que tienes que quitarlo si quieres utilizar el resto de cámaras.
¿Merece la pena el nuevo móvil de vivo?
He de reconocer que este vivo X500 Pro Max es uno de los mejores móviles del mercado. Es bonito, tiene una muy buena pantalla, su rendimiento es excelente, también su batería, su apartado fotográfico es increíble y sus extras hacen que sea un móvil mucho mas versátil y atractivo que cualquier otro modelo de gama alta.
Ahora bien, hablemos del precio. El vivo X500 Pro Max sale a la venta por 1.599 euros (1.499 euros con la promoción de lanzamiento) o 2.199 euros si quieres el kit fotográfico con los dos objetivos. Sin el kit, el terminal prácticamente iguala el precio de los mejores móviles del mercado. Además, el smartphone tiene argumentos suficientes para competir de tu a tu frente a los mejores móviles del mercado. La cuestión es si esos argumentos son suficientes para justificar un desembolso tan elevado.
Si buscas un móvil que destaque especialmente por sus cámaras y que ofrezca una experiencia sobresaliente a la hora de tomar fotografías, este es tu móvil. El vivo X500 Pro tiene una de las cámaras más versátiles que he probado nunca, y uno de los puntos más positivos es que, a diferencia de otros modelos con características similares, no necesitas ser un experto en fotografía. El modo automático, reitero, consigue unos resultados excelentes, y con un poco de aprendizaje puedes conseguir auténticas maravillas con el modo pro.
El Kit fotográfico, por su parte, es una propuesta muy particular y que puede resultar muy atractiva para aquellos que buscan experimentar más con la fotografía móvil. No obstante, no es para mi. Salvo que esté disponible a través de alguna oferta o promoción, no veo necesario gastarse 700 euros en este añadido. Sobre todo teniendo en cuenta que la cámara ya hace fotografías muy buenas.
En definitiva, el vivo X500 Pro Max es un móvil sobresaliente que tiene argumentos de sobra para plantar cara a los grandes del mercado. No es barato, precisamente, pero si el presupuesto no es un problema, estamos ante uno de esos teléfonos que conviene tener en cuenta antes de decidir qué móvil comprar. No obstante, también es importante tener en cuenta que el Vivo X500 Pro Max es muy parecido al Vivo X300 Ultra (el modelo anterior), por lo que si estás pensando en comprar este modelo y no te importa tener lo último de lo último, tal vez te interese optar por la generación anterior a cambio de un precio más reducido; apenas vas a notar diferencia.

articles.title: Google Photos 7.97 permet enfin de personnaliser l'onglet « Collections » : voici comment faire
articles.text:
Quelques mois après l’arrivée d’une barre de navigation flottante, l’application Google Photos continue d’évoluer pour offrir plus de personnalisation dans l’affichage de vos Collections. On vous montre à quoi cela ressemble et comment l’utiliser.
Une nouvelle façon d’épingler et de personnaliser les carrousels
L’ancienne interface de l’onglet « Collections » de Google Photos. – © 01net
La version 7.97 de Google Photos affiche désormais une zone en haut de l’onglet Collections baptisée « Épinglés ». Ce carrousel affiche par défaut les favoris, les captures d’écran et la corbeille, tout en vous laissant la liberté de retirer ces catégories en faisant un appui long dessus, ou d’en ajouter en utilisant le bouton « + » sur la droite. Lorsque vous cliquez sur ce dernier, vous pouvez choisir les dossiers à épingler et réorganiser l’ordre de ces derniers.
La nouvelle interface de l’onglet « Collections » de Google Photos 7.97. – © 01net
Juste en dessous, les différents thèmes se présentent aussi sous forme de carrousels : « Sur cet appareil », « Albums », « Personnes et animaux », « Lieux » et « Documents ». Pour chaque collection, un bouton « Tout afficher » placé dans le coin supérieur droit permet de basculer vers une vue globale en grille ou en liste.
Les autres collections regroupées en bas de page
Le bas de la page accueille désormais une grille dédiée aux « Autres collections », regroupant les moments, les vidéos, les ajouts récents, les autocollants, les créations, les archives, les éléments verrouillés ainsi que la corbeille. Le bouton pour réorganiser l’ensemble des carrousels se trouve tout en bas de l’écran. Il est baptisé « Commander de nouveau » (étrange nom).
Les autres collections se changent aussi d’affichage sur la dernière version de Google Photos. – © 01net
La mise à jour de la version 7.97 de Google Photos est en cours de déploiement côté serveur, ce qui veut dire qu’il vous suffit de redémarrer votre smartphone et/ou de fermer l’application et de la rouvrir pour voir apparaître cette nouvelle interface.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: The Huntress Tragic Quadrant: Ranking Threats Hitting Businesses Hardest
articles.text:
Cyber headlines often focus on the flashy attacks, but the ones that actually cause OH $#!T moments are the tactics that abuse the tools and workflows you already trust. If you run a small or mid-sized organization, whether you handle IT yourself or outsource it, it’s a constant race to keep up with attackers and their evolving tactics.
The bottom line is that you need to know which attacks are landing in environments like yours, and how to prioritize your defenses against them.
The Tragic Quadrant at a Glance
That’s why Huntress created the Tragic Quadrant, a ranked list of the cyber tactics putting businesses at risk, built to show you where to focus regardless of what’s trending week to week.
Fix These Threats First: The OH $#!T Corner
Each of these tactics hides inside something your team uses every day, like a remote access tool or a Microsoft 365 login.
RMM Abuse Is Steady and Holding
Remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools are a staple for IT teams, which is exactly why attackers abuse them. One rogue RMM install gives an attacker persistent access that looks like ordinary admin work.
In Q1 2026, 45% of endpoint-related incidents Huntress investigated involved RMM abuse. Attackers are also using AI to build convincing fake document shares and service agreement lures that trick users into installing unwanted RMMs.
Mailbox Manipulation Is an Entry Point to BEC
So far in 2026, 24.6% of Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) signals point to mailbox manipulation and persistence. With mailbox access, an attacker can change inbox rules and send vendor replies to folders nobody is watching, like RSS Feeds or Archive.
From there, they can tweak invoice details and redirect payments to their own accounts, all without any malware for detection tools to flag.
Account Takeover That Sidesteps MFA
Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks made up 18.9% of all identity-based threats Huntress tracked in 2025. The attacker sits between the victim and the real Microsoft 365 login page, steals the session token in transit, and forwards everything along so nothing looks off to the user.
As long as that session is valid, the attacker can access the account without a password or a fresh MFA prompt.
If you were hit with ransomware, what would you do?
Your files are encrypted, your operations are down, an attacker has named their price, and they're waiting for you to respond. Do you pay? Do you negotiate? Do you even engage at all?
Choose your next move in a simulated ransomware incident, built from tactics Huntress has seen used against real businesses. You'll see how ransomware operators behave when they think they're in control, and what steps you can take for catching an attack before it becomes a negotiation.
Try the Simulator →
Your Next Stop: The Other Three Corners
Once you’ve covered the top-right tactics, the others still deserve a plan. Each one is evolving fast, potentially moving toward the OH $#!T corner at any time.
Device Code Phishing Turns Low-Key Deadly
Device code phishing is less common, but it rides on Microsoft’s real device code login flow, so “check the URL” advice doesn’t help. A convincing prompt nudges someone to enter a short code on a genuine Microsoft page, and the attacker walks away with an access token that can outlive a password reset.
In one 16-day window, a phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit called EvilTokens hit 344 organizations across five countries. Defenders should be suspicious of unusual device code prompts and odd token activity.
ClickFix Is a Daily Intrusion Pest
ClickFix leans on the copy-paste muscle memory people use to get past everyday friction. A fake CAPTCHA or “verification failed” prompt tricks someone into pasting a malicious command into their terminal. The paste itself triggers the malicious code, so no exploit chain is involved, and it can lead to infostealer malware or ransomware.
ClickFix accounts for about 2.2% of Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) detection signals so far in 2026, but nearly 99% of those detections are high severity.
AI Platform Abuse Is Overhyped, for Now
This one sits in the overhyped corner because it’s still an emerging pattern. Attackers hide malicious content behind real AI tools and workflows people trust.
A fake “desktop client” or “productivity helper” might live inside a shared conversation or a hosted artifact on a trusted AI domain like Claude or ChatGPT, which makes it tricky to tell what’s malicious.
In one case, FakeAgent used a malicious Claude Artifact on the real claude.ai domain to send people looking for Claude Desktop to SectopRAT, reaching 29 organizations in two days.
Make the Tragic Quadrant Your Starting Point
The Tragic Quadrant helps you pick what to fix first when everything feels urgent.
Start in the top right corner and ask a few simple questions: Which remote tools are approved, and how do we catch mailbox rule changes and odd session behavior before they turn into something worse?
Grab your copy of the Huntress Tragic Quadrant to work through every corner on your own timeline and decide which gaps to close next

articles.title: OPINON: Europe’s legal work is awash with AI slop, but there is a way to fix it | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe’s startups have been riding a wave of innovation, creating numerous applications of generative and agentic AI. This innovation has explored the art of the possible, but it has also flooded the world with slop. Content is awash with it, whether it is LinkedIn posts or quotidian corporate drivel.
The slop extends to legal work
AI was supposed to make work easier, but now many are grappling with what Jamie Bartlett, author and BBC journalist, describes as “the burden of AI clog“. Cleaning up this mess means that AI is not saving time, but is actually creating more work.
The slop extends to the legal domain, with contract negotiations and other legal work now being absorbed by a lengthy review process because of AI. Even the bodies that are supposed to be drafting the laws are swimming in slop. In the US, for example, the Office of the Legislative Counsel, is reportedly overwhelmed by the error-riddled drafts that AI has generated.
The problem isn’t AI per se
Advances in LegalTech in Europe, and beyond, means there are many tools to assist with legal work. Despite this, however, their output is of varying quality. And some law firms still don’t have a proper policy in place for how employees use AI, which means some teams are relying on general LLMs (like ChatGPT or Claude) for their drafting and reviewing.
As contracts are amended in negotiations, much of the document is struck through and sent back saturated with red lines. AI editors are ripping and replacing much of the content, and the changes usually lack insight and relevance.
This is hardly the way to engage in a negotiation, and the trigger-happy nature of the tools is likely to aggravate the other party. Judgement and discretion have been lost in the process. Many tools don’t know the difference between dogmatically applying the letter of the law and letting things go for the sake of progressing a negotiation.
Unnecessary redlining can be stopped
This, however, is a problem that Europe’s startups can solve. There are ways to ensure that legal work doesn’t descend into slop, and to prevent the revisions turning into an infinite ping pong match between AI agents.
The focus instead needs to be on judicious editing, where the tool knows when to leave something alone. The amendments should be minimal, and these should be aligned to a well-defined playbook.
This playbook sets out a firm’s position, policies and approach and sets parameters for what is, and isn’t, acceptable. The tool scans for compliance issues, conflicts and highlights areas of difference. It can then make suggested edits that align with this well-defined playbook and offer a best-case scenario for the company, or firm.
This approach is more likely to bridge the gap between the parties and get to a consensus quicker, without the need for human intervention.
AI should be a blessing, not a burden
When used correctly, legal AI can be a blessing for companies and means more work can be done in-house before calling in outside counsel. Such tools can be used as mediation portals, where differences of position are highlighted and evaluated first instead of text being ruthlessly red-lined.
The excessive redlining needs to stop, as does the AI slop and the AI clog burden it creates. At the moment, users are putting up with it albeit complaining about the extra work that AI creates. Soon, however, the slop won’t be tolerated. 
We expect the bar to be raised of what AI-enabled work should look like. Expectations will shift and users will soon demand AI tools that edit in a way that is precise, relevant and insightful.

articles.title: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
articles.text:
On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to The Verge are growing increasingly tired of the company’s antics.
Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
Expert ‘shepherds’ will decide how best to share the latest breakthroughs in computer science and physics.
It has been a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still grappling with the hundreds of preprints unceremoniously dumped on them at the start of October. This time, OpenAI says it is working with expert “shepherds” to decide how best to share its latest breakthroughs.
All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Some extend OpenAI’s previous work and others break new ground. Following advice from OpenAI’s “shepherds,” each has a different release strategy. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated output, “leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.” For its computer science finding, OpenAI will also assemble an external group of researchers “to explain the result.” Physics, meanwhile, has not been released at all, and OpenAI said it will “defer” to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.
- The mathematics result appears striking. It purports to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. Roughly speaking, the problem asks how little space is needed to rotate a needle or pencil in every direction. A proof of the three-dimensional version was among the achievements for which NYU mathematician Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal earlier this year. Brown University mathematics professor Brendan Hassett told The Verge OpenAI’s claim “looks well supported,” though he stressed he had not yet checked the Lean formalization, a means of computationally verifying results.
- The physics result explores the Standard Model, the most successful and complete theoretical framework in physics. It concerns quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong nuclear force, one of nature’s four fundamental forces (alongside gravitational force, electromagnetic force, and weak nuclear force) and its relationship to Yang-Mills theory, a cornerstone of modern particle physics. Yang-Mills theory is also at the heart of one of the seven Millennium Prize problems in mathematics, though OpenAI’s work does not address the unresolved “mass gap.”
- The final result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption in theoretical computer science that certain problems cannot be solved substantially faster than brute-force approaches. It is closely related to P versus NP, another Millennium Prize problem and one of the field’s biggest unsolved problems, which asks whether problems whose solutions can be easily checked are also easy to solve.
Given the varying levels of disclosure and the complexity of evaluating such work, it is difficult for researchers to fully judge the company’s findings. Even with all of the information, doing so would take time. But experts who spoke to The Verge said there are good reasons to take the results seriously, variously describing them as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”
“It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them.”
But researchers’ excitement about the science was tempered by exasperation with OpenAI’s conduct, a familiar feeling after months of what they describe as an exhausting barrage of AI-generated findings. Many were eager for the wider community to get on with the arduous task of scrutinizing the AI lab’s findings and questioned why OpenAI was putting up additional barriers by handpicking experts to oversee the process.
Most experts The Verge spoke to welcomed OpenAI’s decision to consult outside researchers, but argued that publicly announcing results should also mean making that work available for anyone to scrutinize. “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” said Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, welcoming the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds released previously. But he questioned the decision to restrict access to experts of OpenAI’s choosing. “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them,” he said.
“The fact that they handpick the group is a disaster,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Verge. “The large labs have enough power as it is. They should not be picking winners and losers.” Karch initially suggested selecting researchers through a “competitive process,” though he acknowledged it would likely produce a similar group, which he described as “first rate.” Later, he questioned why OpenAI “can’t release the proof now,” in addition to appointing its team of experts. “This would democratize access while still showing that they care about making the results meaningful and understandable,” he said.
“My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset.”
It is exactly the kind of gatekeeping the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), a group of experts OpenAI had previously pledged to consult on how to share its findings, warned against just a day before the announcement. “We recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice,” they said, arguing that selecting certain people to receive the output first is “unnecessary,” borrows the reputation of selected researchers, and risks unequal access, biased selection, and delays, among other issues. Instead, they recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with formalized proofs and information on how the problems were chosen, and provide funding and other support for people working on understanding the results.
Following the publication of the latest results, AGMAI urged OpenAI to “make public without delay the natural-language and Lean outputs behind its announced” results in physics:
”While these are central questions in physics, they are also important questions in mathematics. The existence of quantum Yang–Mills theory is part of a Millennium Prize problem and the construction of interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions has been a goal of mathematical physics for decades.
We have great respect for the scientists asked by OpenAI to lead this work. But as we explained in our recent statement, understanding should develop in the open, with everyone given the same access. OpenAI have said they delayed release until the Lean formalization was complete. By their own account this is now complete, so there is no scientific reason for delaying the release any further.”
Making the findings openly available could also lead to better science and encourage wider adoption of new tools like AI, Hassett said. “Having many groups around the world wrestle with these results supports rapid adoption of new tools by those that would like to use them,” he said.
”Fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution ... the papers are difficult to read and verify.”
Finding a way to communicate with researchers in the fields OpenAI is increasingly encroaching on that satisfies everyone may be impossible. The company says it is experimenting with different approaches and acknowledges that each has tradeoffs. “My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset,” said Stanford mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman. “So it’s just a question of finding the least offensive option.”
Xiaoyu He, a mathematics professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology, thinks the problem is deeper than how OpenAI chooses to announce its findings. ”The results are very impressive,” he said, “but I think they are making a show of trying to be responsible and thoughtful about how they release results while not being able to change the main issues: that fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution, and that the papers are difficult to read and verify.”

articles.title: Tailscale Rushes Patches After Uncoordinated Disclosure of ‘Tailworm’ Flaws
articles.text:
Tailscale is getting ready to ship a client update that addresses privilege escalation weaknesses in Tailscale SSH. Details of the bugs went public over the weekend.
Tailscale provides a mesh VPN service that uses the WireGuard protocol to connect an organization’s devices and services over a private, peer-to-peer network.
The Tailscale vulnerabilities, dubbed Tailworm, are described in a report from Cyberdione Labs. It lists 11 findings affecting version 1.104.2 of the Tailscale client and version 0.29.5 of headscale, an open source control server that organizations can host themselves.
Cyberdione Labs published the report before any patches were available, drawing criticism on social media, though the researchers argued that rapid awareness would speed up remediation.
Six of the findings are rated high severity, and four of them concern Tailscale SSH, which grants access based on device identity and network policy instead of passwords or keys.
According to the Tailworm report, Tailscale SSH performs some forwarding operations with root privileges, and the safeguards meant to restrict them can be bypassed.
An attacker who has compromised one device could exploit this against any server that device is permitted to reach over Tailscale SSH, as long as the access rule allows forwarding. In lab tests, this resulted in root access on target servers and the theft of keys that can be used to add rogue devices to the network.
That initial foothold could come from common methods such as phishing, a vulnerable web application or a malicious software package.
Researchers showed that these SSH flaws are wormable. Since no user credentials are involved, an automated attack chaining these bugs moved from machine to machine across every server the policy granted SSH access to, at under a second per hop and with no user interaction.
The report also describes flaws in an experimental app connector feature, the Serve feature, headscale and the client’s relay component that could be exploited to reach cloud metadata services and internal networks while bypassing access rules, expose a node’s administrative interface to remote peers, or cause denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.
Tailscale says fixes are close
Responding on Reddit, Tailscale VP of Engineering Mike Shaver said the company was already running its own investigation, with input from outside security specialists, when the report came in.
“Most of the issues we’ve identified so far concern what happens after someone has been authorized to connect, particularly how Unix privileges and SSH forwarding are handled. In some cases, a session may be able to do more than the configured local user should be allowed to do,” Shaver said.
“While it’s a serious concern, it isn’t the same as an unauthenticated attacker being able to connect to arbitrary machines, but the potential impact depends on how SSH access is configured,” he added.
In an update shared on Monday, Tailscale said fixes were in place for most of the issues and that it was aiming to release a patched client by the end of Tuesday, October 27, pending testing. A security advisory and a technical write-up will follow once the update is out.
The Tailworm report, updated on Tuesday, says fixes for several findings have landed in Tailscale’s public code repositories. None had made it into a numbered release at that point.
“Based on our current assessment, we’re not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH,” the vendor said.
Until the patch arrives, Tailscale advises organizations to review their SSH access policies and disable SSH forwarding where it isn’t needed, which it says mitigates several of the more serious findings.
Neither Tailscale nor the Tailworm report mentions in-the-wild exploitation.

articles.title: OpenAI frappe fort avec GPT-6.1 Terra, une IA aussi redoutable qu’économique pour automatiser vos tâches
articles.text:
OpenAI frappe fort avec GPT-6.1 Terra, une IA aussi redoutable qu’économique pour automatiser vos tâches
OpenAI a lancé GPT-6.1 Terra, son nouveau modèle intermédiaire capable de piloter votre ordinateur trois fois plus vite qu’Astra tout en divisant son coût par deux.
Après avoir lancé les versions GPT-6 Astra, Sol et Luna en septembre dernier, OpenAI met enfin à jour son modèle d’IA de milieu de gamme. Baptisé GPT-6.1 Terra, il succède directement à la version 5.6 sortie cet été, avec pour objectif de démocratiser l’automatisation des tâches sur ordinateur et le raisonnement visuel. En prime, les performances sont clairement revues à la hausse, quitte à titiller celles des modèles plus avancés, tout en abaissant le coût de 50 %.
GPT-6.1 Terra : l'IA agentique d'OpenAI pour piloter votre ordinateur
Positionné dans la gamme d’OpenAI entre le modèle économique Luna et le plus avancé Sol, le nouveau Terra mise avant tout sur le “computer use”. L’IA est donc optimisée pour utiliser votre ordinateur à votre place. Lire et comprendre ce qui s’affiche à l’écran, déplacer le curseur, cliquer et passer d’une application à l’autre pour effectuer une tâche devient ainsi un jeu d’enfant.
Sur le volet des performances, GPT-6.1 Terra exécute les tâches sur ordinateur plus de trois fois plus vite que ses grands frères GPT-6 Astra et GPT-6.1 Sol. Sur le test Agents’ Last Exam, qui évalue la capacité d’une IA à réaliser de vraies missions de bureau complexes, il devance son prédécesseur de 15 points pour un tiers du coût, tout en se montrant trois fois plus efficient que Claude Opus 5.5 en raisonnement maximal. En programmation, son score sur le test Terminal-Bench 4.0 passe quant à lui de 21,5 % à 50,3 %.
La fiabilité progresse dans les mêmes proportions. Sur un test interne avec un effort de raisonnement faible, le taux d’erreurs factuelles chute de 53,6 % à 16,7 %, et descend jusqu’à 4,3 % lorsque le modèle mobilise le maximum de sa réflexion avant de répondre. Le cabinet indépendant Artificial Analysis souligne de son côté que le taux d’hallucinations recule de 88 % à 38 % par rapport à GPT-5.6 Terra, pour un coût moyen ramené de 1,40 à 0,40 $ par tâche.
Prix et disponibilité de GPT-6.1 Terra sur ChatGPT Work et Codex
Du côté de la grille tarifaire, l’accès via l’API est désormais facturé aux développeurs 1 $ (environ 0,89 € HT) par million de tokens en entrée et 5 $ (environ 4,45 € HT) en sortie. C’est tout simplement deux fois moins cher que GPT-6.1 Sol et l’ancienne génération GPT-5.6 Terra, mais 10 fois plus onéreux que le modèle d’entrée de gamme Luna.
Pour le grand public et les professionnels, GPT-6.1 Terra est déployé dès à présent dans ChatGPT Work et Codex. Si les formules gratuite et Go restent exclues du dispositif, les abonnés Plus (à partir de 23 €/mois en France), Pro, Enterprise et Edu peuvent déjà en profiter avec la promesse de quotas d’utilisation nettement plus généreux.
