articles.title: Sony's next PlayStation handheld may get exclusive access to AMD's mobile RDNA 5
articles.text:
Winners & losers: Handheld PC gaming enthusiasts have long speculated that mobile SoCs based on AMD's upcoming RDNA 5 architecture could deliver generational performance gains for the Steam Deck 2 and its rivals from other PC makers. But recent comments, some disputed, suggest that Sony's next handheld may have mobile RDNA 5 all to itself for the foreseeable future.
According to Digital Foundry, Sony might have some kind of exclusive access to the mobile variant of AMD's upcoming RDNA 5 architecture. The nature of that exclusivity remains unclear, however. Sony and AMD may have a formal deal, or Sony may simply be the only manufacturer able to justify a dedicated RDNA 5 chip.
The comment, made in DF's Direct podcast, sparked speculation that competing devices, such as a potential Xbox handheld, the Steam Deck 2, or successors to other handheld gaming PCs, might be forced to settle for RDNA 4m.
Earlier statements from trusted leaker Kepler_L2 also fueled theories that only Sony could meet AMD's shipment requirements for bleeding-edge mobile SoCs, though it remains unconfirmed whether those requirements apply to Valve or other PC makers.
In any case, Sony's previously leaked 15W chipset, codenamed Canis, is the best-documented mobile RDNA 5 design in development. Expected to outperform the Xbox Series S, it reportedly features four Zen 6c CPU cores clocked at up to 2.2GHz, 12 to 20 RDNA 5 GPU compute units, and LPDDR5X-7500 memory on a 128-bit bus.
It's still unclear whether the device will support PlayStation 5 games, PS6 games, or titles from either console that developers could update and optimize manually.
Meanwhile, other reports suggest AMD plans to debut RDNA 4m with a set of SoCs named Ryzen Z3 and Z3 Extreme, possibly in early 2027. The chips would combine RDNA 3.5's GPU architecture with RDNA 4's machine learning capabilities, enabling greater performance gains from FSR 4.1 than RDNA 2. There are reasons to both believe and doubt that a customized Z3 variant codenamed "Gainsborough" might power the Steam Deck 2.
Valve has repeatedly said it won't move forward with a successor to the RDNA 2-powered Steam Deck until an APU arrives that delivers generational performance gains without sacrificing battery life. If the company can't get its hands on RDNA 5, speculation based on Gainsborough's specifications suggests it might double the Steam Deck's performance at the same power draw.

articles.title: Steam habilitó gratuitamente un titulo de plataformas que pone a prueba los reflejos y la paciencia de los jugadores
articles.text:
Steam habilitó gratis y de forma permanente Bounce Quest, un título de plataformas en 2D que exige reflejos, precisión y paciencia para llegar a la cima de una montaña. El juego, desarrollado por Nozech, tenía un precio de 4,99 dólares, pero desde el 13 de octubre de 2026 puede añadirse a cualquier biblioteca de la plataforma sin pagar y sin una fecha límite para reclamarlo.
La novedad resulta relevante para quienes buscan videojuegos gratuitos en Steam con una propuesta centrada en el desafío. Bounce Quest no responde al modelo de las ofertas temporales que aparecen durante algunos días en la tienda de Valve: el estudio modificó su precio de manera definitiva. Los usuarios pueden incorporarlo a su cuenta y descargarlo cuando lo consideren oportuno.
Bounce Quest convierte cada movimiento en un riesgo
Publicado originalmente en 2025, Bounce Quest propone controlar a un pequeño cubo que debe ascender por una montaña llena de plataformas, desniveles y obstáculos. Su objetivo final es alcanzar la cima y descubrir el secreto que espera al final del recorrido.
El personaje dispone de tres acciones básicas: saltar, deslizarse y golpear superficies. Sin embargo, la mecánica que define la partida es el rebote. El cubo puede impulsarse sobre determinadas zonas para llegar a plataformas elevadas, superar huecos y mantener la progresión por el escenario.
Un fallo en el cálculo puede hacer que el jugador pierda una parte importante del avance conseguido. Un aterrizaje fuera de lugar, un salto con demasiada fuerza o un rebote mal dirigido pueden devolver al protagonista a sectores ya superados.
La dificultad no parte de controles difíciles de entender. El reto aparece al intentar dominar el momento exacto de cada movimiento. A medida que el cubo asciende, las plataformas se separan más y los márgenes para corregir una trayectoria se reducen.
La propuesta recuerda a los juegos donde caer es parte del desafío
El diseño de Bounce Quest guarda similitudes con producciones como Getting Over It y Jump King. En estos títulos, el progreso depende de la constancia y del control, mientras que una equivocación puede obligar a repetir una secuencia larga.
En el caso del juego de Nozech, los rebotes añaden un elemento propio. El movimiento constante del cubo reduce la sensación de control absoluto y exige anticipar la dirección que tomará el personaje después de cada contacto con una superficie.
La experiencia cuenta con seis áreas diferentes, cada una con obstáculos y condiciones que requieren una respuesta precisa. La estructura no se limita a obtener una puntuación alta ni a superar partidas breves: plantea un recorrido completo hasta la cima de la montaña.
El juego también incorpora 12 apariencias desbloqueables para el protagonista. Estas opciones cambian el aspecto del cubo, aunque no alteran la dificultad ni conceden ventajas dentro de los niveles. Funcionan como un incentivo adicional para quienes quieran completar el contenido disponible.
La frustración forma parte del planteamiento. Cada caída obliga a recuperar terreno, lo que puede convertir una sección corta en un obstáculo prolongado. Para parte del público, esa exigencia constituye precisamente el atractivo del juego, ya que cada plataforma alcanzada representa un avance que requiere atención y práctica.
Cómo añadir Bounce Quest a la biblioteca de Steam
Para obtener el juego, es necesario tener una cuenta en Steam. El proceso puede realizarse desde el cliente de escritorio o desde la versión web de la tienda:
- Iniciar sesión con la cuenta personal.
- Buscar Bounce Quest en el catálogo.
- Comprobar que el precio aparece como 0.
- Pulsar en “Obtener”, “Añadir a la biblioteca” o “Jugar”.
- Verificar que el título figure en la biblioteca del usuario.
La recomendación es añadir el juego a la cuenta antes de descargarlo. Así, el espacio libre del ordenador no impide vincularlo a la colección digital.
Los títulos adquiridos quedan asociados al perfil de Steam, lo que permite instalarlos desde distintos ordenadores que utilicen la misma cuenta. En el caso de Bounce Quest, el acceso seguirá disponible sin costo mientras la plataforma mantenga el juego dentro de su catálogo y las condiciones de la licencia asociada a cada usuario.

articles.title: I spent over two weeks with the Amazon Kindle (2026) — and it's like reading an old book with a new cover
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
With a thinner and lighter body compared to the 2024 release, Amazon's entry-level Kindle (2026) comes in some lovely colors and even a new metal body. You also get a sharper screen — which is now flush with the bezels — with improved contrast, and its general performance over its predecessor is slightly better. However, the 32GB aluminum Kindle sent for this review suffered from slight light bleed in dark mode, while the lack of any interface changes, or new features — like warm light or waterproofing — makes it a hard sell at its higher price compared to the 2026 edition of the Kindle Paperwhite.
Reasons to buy
- + Perfectly sized for small hands
- + Excellent overall performance
- + Lovely colors
- + Double storage (32GB) also available
Reasons to avoid
- - No warm or auto-adjusting light
- - Still no waterproofing
- - Lackluster battery life
- - Flush screen triggers accidental page turns
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Amazon Kindle (2026): Two-minute review
When Amazon announced its 2026 range of Kindles on October 1, I balked at the prices, particularly for the entry-level model. Then again, I should have expected it, given the current cost of components. The days of Kindles being the affordable ereader are long gone now.
Yet the 2026 entry-level Kindle does go some way in justifying its higher price compared to its predecessor thanks to all new hardware that includes new colors — now also in an aluminum chassis that gets you double the storage (32GB) — as well as a thinner and even lighter design. The power button being moved to the right edge is also a welcome change that made my colleague Lance Ulanoff especially happy.
The design changes also include the screen now lying flush with the bezels and the display offering better contrast that improves text sharpness. However, I noticed a tiny bit of light bleeding on the top edge of the screen when reading in dark mode, which Amazon has acknowledge is a flaw, and the slim bezels don't offer enough space for the thumb to rest, thus triggering accidental page turns.
The page-turn speed here hasn't visibly improved over the 2024 model, but general navigation has. Amazon says the 2026 base Kindle is 30% faster than the previous model and, while that's hard to measure, I can attest that many other functions on the latter, like opening books, accessing the Kindle Store and going through settings, and are definitely faster.
That's all that's new here, though, which is why I said the 2026 Kindle only goes 'some' way in justifying its cost. At launch, when I began my testing of this Kindle, there were no new software features to distinguish it from previous generations. However, Amazon released a new firmware just a couple of days before the publication of this review that has made a small change to how some books appear in the library tab — all titles within a series are now grouped together. This software update has also been rolled out to the previous Kindle generation, so you really aren't missing much if you don't upgrade... except for the slight increase in speed and the new screen.
There is still no warm light or auto-adjusting brightness for evening reading, and neither is there any waterproofing, not even on the aluminum version which has a screwed on back panel rather than the plastic one's pop-off option.
Yes, the rear panels can be removed now to allow users to change the battery when needed, in compliance with EU regulations, but I haven't seen any official battery packs being sold as yet. Battery life, however, is lackluster compared to the Kindle Paperwhite (both 2024 and the newer release) — it's practically half, which makes the aluminum Kindle especially harder to recommend over the 2026 Paperwhite as the prices aren't all that different.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
So while I can appreciate that a new Kindle would cost more, I'm struggling to find value in it, more so because the Kobo Clara BW comes with waterproofing and warm light temperatures at a similar price to the plastic 16GB Kindle, albeit in a now two-year-old device.
Amazon Kindle (2026) review: price & availability
- First announced October 2026
- Available in major markets, including the US, UK and Australia
- List price from $149.99 / £134.99 / AU$279
With a starting price of $149.99 / £134.99 in the US and the UK for the ad-supported 16GB plastic Kindle, it's still a cheaper option compared to the 2024 release of the Kobo Clara BW that retails for $159.99 / £149.99. However, you get a few more features with the latter that the new 2026 release of the entry-level Kindle still doesn't get you — namely, warm light and waterproofing.
If you don't want the ads, then you need to tack on another $20 / £15 to that cost, which shifts the price dynamic between the Kindle and its Kobo counterpart.
In Australia, only the ad-free version of the Kindles has always been available and the starting price is now AU$279, which is AU$10 more than the Kobo Clara BW.
The 32GB Kindle Aluminum (yes, that's what Amazon is calling it in the US and is the model sent to TechRadar for this review) is ad-free by default and will set you back $189.99 / £169.99 / AU$299. Given the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite costs just another $10 / £15 / AU$50 (with ads in the US and UK), I'm struggling to see the value in the shiny new aluminum Kindle.
• Value score: 3 / 5
Amazon Kindle (2026) review: specs
| Display type: | E Ink (possibly Carta 1300) | 
| Screen size: | 6 inches | 
| Resolution: | 300ppi | 
| Processor: | unknown | 
| Frontlight: | Yes, white light only | 
| Storage: | 16GB / 32GB | 
| Battery: | up to 6 weeks (capacity unknown) | 
| Water protection: | None | 
| Software: | Linux based | 
| Connectivity: | Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB-C | 
| File support: | 6 natively; 1 audio | 
| Dimensions: | 108 x 152.8 x 6.85 mm (4.3 x 6.0 x 0.3 inches) | 
| Weight: | 140g (4.9 oz) for plastic finish; 162g (5.7 oz) for aluminum | 
Amazon Kindle (2026) review: Design & display
- Shiny, new hardware, including fresh colors and a new aluminum model
- Thinner, lighter and more compact than before
- Gorgeous new display with better contrast and sharper text
I might have been disappointed with the 2024 edition of the base Kindle, saying it wasn't really an 'upgrade' just because it came in a lovely new color, but that's not the case with the 2026 release. This time, the entry-level Kindle truly is a worthwhile upgrade — at least in terms of hardware. Nearly everything about it is brand-spanking new and I love it.
The most obvious difference between the previous Kindle generations and the 2026 model(s) is the new chassis. Now available in two finishes — plastic and aluminum — and lovely new colors (Ube and the usual Graphite for the former, Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green for the latter), there's more choice where the base Kindle is concerned.
The other point of difference, and not just between generations but also between the two finishes, is that the aluminum version comes with 32GB of storage (like the Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft) and is ad-free by default in the US and the UK.
While I personally didn't mind the power/sleep button on the bottom edge of the Kindle, now having it just below the top right corner is a good move, putting the cheapest Kindle in the new range on a similar design footing as the current Kindle Scribes.
The flush screen on both the plastic and metal Kindles makes it look modern and more premium, although the thin side bezels triggered numerous accidental page turns during my testing. I also noticed a small amount of light bleed on the top edge of the review unit sent to me, visible in dark mode. This has been discussed on Reddit and Amazon has acknowledged there is a flaw and is ready to exchange any units with such issues.
Impressively, though, the screen and the aluminum body aren't fingerprint magnets, which is my biggest relief compared to, say, the 2024 edition of the Kindle Paperwhite that showed off every oily smudge on the front and back.
Another hardware difference — and a first for Amazon — is the replaceable battery. On the plastic model, the rear panel just pops open, but you will need tiny hex screwdriver to remove the aluminum panel if you ever need to change the battery. This is accordance to EU regulations, but I am yet to see official replacement batteries being listed on Amazon. It's early days yet, and a Kindle battery typically lasts about 10 years, so I'd expect to see official listings down the line.
In comparison, though, Kobo's 2024 ereaders — namely, the Libra Colour, Clara BW and Clara Colour — have even better repairability, with screens and motherboards also replaceable. So if longevity is important to you, Amazon still has a way to go to impress its Kindle users.
As much as I love the new colors, the star of the show here is the upgraded display. The entry-level Kindle finally gets the E Ink Carta 1300 screen tech that the 2024 model missed out on.
Admittedly it still lacks warm LEDs, which is disappointing, but despite that it's the sharpest display on the entry-level Kindle that I've seen to date. It also boasts better contrast where blacks are blacker, even the background in dark mode, and that gives text better clarity overall.
Alongside the lack of warm hues for the frontlight, the entry-level Kindle still doesn't have waterproofing, which is probably for the best at least for the plastic model where the rear pops right off to access the battery. However, it would have been nice if Amazon had deigned to provide at least one of these missing features on the aluminum version to justify the higher price tag, especially since there are hardly any new software features to speak of here.
Design & display score: 4.5 / 5
Amazon Kindle (2026) review: Software
- Books in a series are now grouped together in the Library tab
- Additional wallpapers are nice
- Not much else is new with the latest software release
If you've been using an older Kindle, you'll be intimately familiar with navigating around the 2026 release as well. At the start of my two-week testing of the new Kindle, seemingly nothing had changed with the release of the software version 5.20.1.0.1. However, just a day before this review was published, Amazon released firmware 5.20.1.02 and the only new feature here that I've come across is books in a series being grouped together in the Library tab.
There is, however, a caveat here — only items purchased or borrowed from the Kindle Store (or from Kindle+, previous Kindle Unlimited) are arranged this way. If you've sideloaded books in a series via, say, the Send To Kindle platform, they will still appear as individual titles.
This latest firmware at the time of writing has also been rolled out to the 2024 11th-generation Kindle, so this new feature will also be available on the older model.
I do appreciate that Amazon has added more wallpapers now, some which debuted on the 2025 releases of the Kindle Scribe. You can still choose to show the book covers if you don't want to cycle through the wallpapers when the device is sleeping.
The lack of significant new features on the Kindle is not a bad thing, although it would have been nice to have something different — perhaps reading stats like Kobo offers. However, the Kindle UX remains very simple to navigate around even if you're a first-time user — there is just the home screen and the library tabs, with the rest of the features and settings accessible by swiping down from the top edge of the screen.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
I still find the home screen to be too wound up in Amazon's ecosystem and looks quite cluttered compared to Kobo's homepage setup, but it at least makes it easy to find your next read if you source your content from the Kindle Store. In the same vein, if you are a Prime member or have a Kindle+ subscription, you'll be able to find something new right from the homepage based on your previous reading habits.
Audible support is no longer restricted to select countries at launch, like it was for the 2024 Kindles. Meaning if you're in, say, Australia, you can absolutely listen to Audible audiobooks by pairing the Kindle to a set of wireless headphones or earbuds (or even a Bluetooth speaker).
WhisperSync will continue narration on any Alexa-supported speaker too if you prefer to move on from using the Kindle, like when you're perhaps fixing dinner and, in a similar vein, if you ever change your Kindle to a newer device, your entire library is already available the moment you sign into your Amazon account (something I wish Kobo would offer).
• Software score: 4 / 5
Amazon Kindle (2026) review: Performance
- Excellent reading experience
- General navigation is faster compared to previous generation
- Same battery life as previous model, which is disappointing compared to the Paperwhite
New hardware aside, the overall performance from the 2026 Kindle is also better, making it a true upgrade that I was expecting to see in 2024. Amazon, however, hasn't revealed whether there's an upgraded processor under the hood but I suspect there would be, even if it's a small update.
While page-turn speed is more or less the same on the 2024 and 2026 Kindles, all other navigation and functionality happens just that much quicker on the latter, including ebook load times. Even automatic screen refreshes are so quick that I barely registered most of them — similar to what I experienced in my 3rd-generation Kindle Scribe (2025) review.
This speedy performance adds to the excellent reading experience, where the darker background in both regular and dark mode adds better contrast and makes text look sharper.
That said, I personally find 6-inch ereaders too small, and prefer the 7-inch or 8-inch ones — the sweet spot in terms of screen real estate, not too small and not too large. If you prefer larger fonts, you'll end up turning pages more often and that will then eat into the battery life of the Kindle.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
And that has not changed from the 2024 model. Battery life is still up to 6 weeks according to Amazon, based on just 30 minutes of reading per day. That is doable, if you leave Bluetooth and Wi-Fi off, switch off the frontlight completely and don't keep browsing the Kindle Store or doing anything else except read.
In my testing, where I read for 4-5 hours a day for two weeks, had Wi-Fi always on and screen brightness set to level 7 in regular mode (relatively low), I had to charge the Kindle every 2 to 3 days, which got a little annoying considering the 2024 Kindle Paperwhite I have gives me double the battery life.
Charging the battery is quick, though, with the device going from 11% to full in just about an hour when plugged into a 25W USB-C outlet and using a good-quality C-to-C cable. Three attempts at topping from 10% or 11% battery gave me the same results.
• Performance score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Amazon Kindle (2026)?
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | As lovely as the new hardware is, the 2026 Paperwhite isn't much more expensive than the 2026 Kindle (especially the aluminum version), making it a hard sell. | 3 / 5 | 
| Design & display | A full revamp of the hardware and an updated screen makes this a good upgrade from an aging Kindle. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Software | Not much has changed here, so it's still an easy-to-use interface. But the lack of new software features is still disappointing. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | Overall navigation and speed of loading books is visibly quicker compared to older generations. Battery life could have been better though. | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You're using a very old Kindle that now feels slow and clunky
For its entry-level model, Amazon has definitely done a good job with making the 2026 Kindle a worthy upgrade, if you can handle the higher price.
You want the most compact, lightest Kindle made to date
The entry-level Kindles have always been the most portable options in Amazon's ereader range, but the 2026 editions are smaller still, although the aluminum version isn't quite the lightest.
You care about device longevity
It may not be as repairable as Kobo's more popular ereaders, but at least being able to change out the battery — if official stock is made available globally — ensures your ereader will last way longer than the usual 10 years.
Don't buy it if...
Value for money is important
Admittedly the new hardware makes the 2026 Kindle a worthy upgrade over the 2024 model but, the latter — as long as it's available to buy — is cheaper and will continue getting new software features that are released for its successor, at least for a few years longer. Moreover, Kobo offers more features for around the same price, making the 2026 Kindle harder to recommend.
You prefer reading with larger fonts
Given its limited battery life and smaller screen size, you'll be better off opting for a 7-inch or 8-inch ereader with better battery capacity to support more frequent page turns.
You read a lot on holiday, by the pool or in the bath
I wouldn't recommend dropping any ereader in the ocean as salt water corrodes, but if you do read on the beach, by the pool, in the bath or just by the kitchen sink (hey, maybe you do), I'd recommend opting for an ereader that has waterproofing.
Amazon Kindle (2026) review: Alternatives
The 2026 edition of the base Amazon Kindle is good — a very worthy upgrade. However, its price might make you stop and think. So if you're keen on alternatives, I would consider the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite better value than the Kindle Aluminum, for example. I haven't tested the new Paperwhite yet, but from the existing crop of tried and tested models, the below two options are my top picks and are still some of the best ereaders you can buy.
Kobo Clara BW
As I've already mentioned earlier in this review, this 6-inch counterpart to the Kindle offers more features for around the same price as the 2026 release and is far more repairable than any Kindle. It might feel slower compared to the 2026 Kindle because it's now over two years old (at the time of publication of this review), but it's still a fabulous E Ink tablet with very good per-dollar value.
Read my full Kobo Clara BW review for more information
Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024)
For as long as this model is on the market, it's the better buy. You get a larger screen, waterproofing, warm LEDs, auto-adjusting screen light, a very good screen, excellent performance and better battery life than the 2026 Kindle.
Read my in-depth Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024) review to learn more
How I tested the Amazon Kindle (2026)
No matter the circumstances, I generally read for at least a few hours a day, so it wasn't much different when it came to testing the 2026 Kindle. I used it for two and a half weeks, reading every single day for 4 to 5 hours.
While I already have an Amazon library accessible on any Kindle as soon as I sign in, I also used the Send To Kindle app to add a few more titles for good measure. Most of the titles I read on the 2026 Kindle were borrowed from Kindle+ though. This also allowed me to try out audiobooks on the device. I paired the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones to the Kindle and also a JBL Charge 5 speaker for this purpose.
During testing, I changed screen brightness regularly to see how much affect it had on battery life, while also noting how browsing the Kindle Store affected the same. I also made a note of how much battery was lost when the device was sleeping.
Unfortunately I couldn't find the right screwdriver to access the battery under the Kindle Aluminum sent for this review, so I can't speak to how easy it would be to swap out an old pack for a new one.
Read more about how we test
[First published October 2026]
While she's happiest with a camera in her hand, Sharmishta's main priority is being TechRadar's APAC Managing Editor, looking after the day-to-day functioning of the Australian, New Zealand and Singapore editions of the site, steering everything from news and reviews to ecommerce content like deals and coupon codes. While she loves reviewing cameras and lenses when she can, she's also an avid reader and has become quite the expert on ereaders and E Ink writing tablets, having appeared on Singaporean radio to talk about these underrated devices. Other than her duties at TechRadar, she's also the Managing Editor of the Australian edition of Digital Camera World, and writes for Tom's Guide and T3.

articles.title: Nvidia is bankrolling AI accelerator supply chain buildout to reserve production capacity
articles.text:
Nvidia is bankrolling AI accelerator supply chain buildout to reserve production capacity — announces billion-dollar deals with six major suppliers across substrates, advanced packaging, semiconductor testing, and optical engines
Expanded supply to be available from 2027 through 2028
On October 21, during GTC Berlin, Nvidia announced several massive, multi-billion-dollar deals with supply chain partners across substrates, advanced packaging, semiconductor testing, and optical engines to expand production capacity. Aimed at overcoming severe bottlenecks restricting the current and future AI infrastructure buildouts, the deals feature commitments and production roadmaps stretching through 2028, securing capacity for Nvidia and ensuring resiliency and redundancy in its AI accelerator supply chain. “We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history. Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint,” said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. “Our supply chain partners are the world’s best manufacturers. I’m grateful they are expanding capacity around the globe to scale production and help us deliver the AI supercomputing systems powering this new industrial revolution.”
The deals cover two major AI accelerator supply chain categories: hardware interconnects and OSAT (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test). Under hardware interconnects, Nvidia is securing capacity for both substrates and co-packaged optics. Nvidia has signed deals with Ibiden, Unimicron, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics — three of the world's five largest substrate manufacturers — to support its production capacity expansion and reserve significant portions of that capacity for the chipmaker. The company says it plans to secure 2.5x dedicated substrate capacity over the next three years. Nvidia has also signed agreements with SPIL (Siliconware Precision Industries Co., Ltd) to expand manufacturing capacity for the optical engines used in co-packaged optics by 15x by mid-2027.
On the OSAT side, Nvidia and Amkor are targeting a 300% increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028 through expanded advanced packaging capacity in South Korea, to support higher production volumes for Nvidia's platform. The company also plans to double its semiconductor testing capacity by 2027, investing $1.1 billion to reserve capacity from KYEC (King Yuan Electronics Co., Ltd.), the world's largest semiconductor testing company, which currently handles nearly all of Nvidia's chip testing.
Nvidia currently leads the AI chip market by a considerable margin, with its extremely powerful accelerators sitting in a vast majority of AI data centers globally. These deals target major bottlenecks in the AI chip supply chain, suggesting Nvidia doesn't plan to relinquish its position soon. So, why these specific deals? What are the exact details? What's the broader play? And where do Nvidia's competitors and the rest of the AI industry stand?
Uncorking bottlenecks
The substrate base, a specialized intermediary layer in every accelerator package that connects the tiny silicon chips above it to the board below, is one of the most critical bottlenecks in the AI chip supply chain. As we detailed in our comprehensive substrates roadmap, this indispensable physical layer, manufactured by only a handful of companies, is expanding in both the X-Y and Z axes as chip makers package an increasing number of components onto one board. Nvidia's Blackwell generation places two reticle-sized GPU dies and eight HBM3E stacks on a single package. Its Rubin and Rubin Ultra architectures mount even more components. As a result, each substrate now consumes much more material and production capacity, even as demand for individual substrates soars.
Fubon Research estimates that Nvidia would supply around 12.4 million data-center AI GPUs in 2028, up from a projected 8.2 million in 2026. Each one would feature a substrate layer. Nvidia is staying ahead of the curve, with a planned 2.5x capacity expansion over the next three years, led by Ibiden. Earlier this year, the company signed a deal to provide a multibillion-dollar capacity reservation advance to support Ibiden's Ono Plant in Japan, targeting 3x the plant’s current individual capacity.
To reach its 2.5x target, Nvidia has also brought on Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Samsung's substrate-manufacturing subsidiary, as a supplier. Beyond the immediate capacity from Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ existing operations, the deal will support facility upgrades and new plants in Busan and Sejong. Nvidia is projected to account for a significant portion of the substrate manufacturer’s output by 2028. To build even more redundancy, Nvidia also signed a capacity reservation agreement with Unimicron, supporting the latter's substrate manufacturing expansion in Taiwan. The expansion will reach full capacity by mid-2028 but is expected to start providing capacity by Q2 2027.
Next on Nvidia's to-expand-capacity list announced on October 21 is co-packaged optics. As next-generation speeds surpass 224 Gbps per lane, traditional copper traces on the board consume considerable power to move data even a few inches from the processor to the edge of the board. To address this, the industry is moving the optical engine into the accelerator package itself via co-packaged optics. Nvidia had long detailed its plans for silicon photonics and co-packaged optics as the standard for future AI accelerator packages. The company has signed a deal with Taiwanese optical engine manufacturer SPIL to expand production capacity by 1,400% by mid-2027, with plans to double again by the end of 2028.
A 4x increase in packaging, double the testing, and $1.1 billion specifically for U.S. facilities
Interestingly, the world's biggest semiconductor company, Nvidia, doesn't own a single Fab. After TSMC manufactures the logic chip and binds it with memory chips on a silicon interposer, final-assembly companies such as Amkor package that integrated module with the substrate and protective casing into the final accelerator package. These final steps are increasingly incorporating co-packaged photonics chips. Nvidia’s deal with Amkor aims to expand the latter's interposer wafer capacity by more than 300% by the end of 2028, through advanced packaging capacity expansions in South Korea. Amkor confirmed the deal is worth $1.3 billion, bringing Nvidia's total investment in Amkor across its Arizona and South Korea facilities to $3 billion.
After final assembly, finished Nvidia AI accelerator packages are shipped to KYEC for extreme testing. KYEC currently handles nearly all of Nvidia's chip testing. It therefore comes as no surprise that Nvidia expects semiconductor testing capacity to double from calendar 2026 to 2027 through buildouts across KYEC’s facilities in the U.S., Taiwan, and Singapore. On October 13, Nvidia signed a deal to pay KYEC $1.1 billion to reserve testing capacity at KYEC's new $1.4 billion U.S. facility, where high-volume production is slated to begin in April 2027. The funds will build domestic testing capacity and bolster the domestic supply chain. At the same time, KYEC is aggressively expanding operations in Singapore, where it expects high-volume production to begin in February 2027.
The bigger picture
Nvidia has been aggressively securing production capacity and long-term supply commitments to meet anticipated demand for its next-generation AI accelerators. According to its August 2026 financial disclosures, the company had accumulated $279 billion in outstanding supply and manufacturing-capacity commitments by July 2026. The company has since signed several additional deals. These commitments cover future component purchases and manufacturing capacity reservations, particularly for memory and chip production. Combined with its more recent agreements, Nvidia is securing nearly every stage of its AI accelerator supply chain, from semiconductor fabrication and HBM memory to substrates, advanced packaging, optical interconnects, final assembly, and testing.
Of course, the rest of the industry isn't standing by. On May 21, 2026, AMD announced over $10 billion in investments across Taiwan's semiconductor ecosystem, specifically targeting advanced packaging and manufacturing partnerships. On October 6, CEO Lisa Su confirmed that AMD intends to increase those investments further. The company is working with TSMC, packaging partners, substrate manufacturers, and memory suppliers to increase production substantially in 2027. Google and Amazon are also aggressively expanding their custom TPU and Trainium accelerator programs.
Intel, meanwhile, is positioning its foundry and advanced packaging operations as alternatives to TSMC's increasingly constrained production capacity. The company is expanding its EMIB-T packaging technology, with reports indicating that Google has already reserved Intel capacity to package more than three million TPUs in 2028. Intel is also advancing its 18A and 14A manufacturing processes as it attempts to attract major external customers.
Samsung is expanding its semiconductor operations as well. The Korean company, which held approximately 5.9% of the global foundry market by revenue in Q2 2026, is ramping up its 2nm manufacturing technology and preparing its Taylor, Texas, facility for volume production in 2027. As detailed in our comprehensive Samsung foundry roadmap, the company is investing heavily in its manufacturing operations as it attempts to close the considerable gap with TSMC.
Perhaps the most ambitious player is new entrant Elon Musk's Terafab, a joint semiconductor manufacturing project involving Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI. The project aims to eventually manufacture the equivalent of one terawatt of AI computing capacity annually, an extraordinarily ambitious target given the industry's current scale. Intel joined the project in April, and Musk later confirmed plans to use the company's 14A fabrication technology. The project aims to deliver its first experimental chips in 2027 and begin high-volume production by the third or fourth quarter of 2028.
Nvidia and other semiconductor firms are continuously fighting against emerging bottlenecks, but compute doesn't come online overnight, and fabs aren't built in a day. So, while almost every inch of the semiconductor supply chain remains constrained, it remains likely that big-name players will continue to invest heavily to ensure that products continue to flow into neoclouds and data centers alike.
Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: Test JBL Cove P1 : JBL veut bousculer Sonos et ses arguments ne manquent pas
articles.text:
Seule enceinte sur batterie de la petite gamme connectée Cove, la JBL Cove P1 est sans doute le modèle le plus attractif du trio. Sous ses atours presque classiques, ce modèle veut briller par sa polyvalence et sa puissance sonore. Une sorte de concurrente de la récente Sonos Play en somme. De quoi placer JBL dans la course aux meilleures enceintes connectées ?
JBL ne lésine pas sur les moyens. Outre son châssis assez massif mais transportable, l’enceinte affiche une architecture ambitieuse avec woofer + radiateurs passifs, trois tweeters, et un haut-parleur vertical spécialement pensé pour la prise en charge des contenus Atmos. Le reste est tout aussi attirant, avec une batterie robuste offrant 14 h d’autonomie, une élégante base de charge dédiée, une résistance IP56, et bien sûr l’intégration dans l’écosystème multiroom JBL One.
- Son équilibré et riche, bonne ampleur
- Bonne puissance sonore, basses maitrisées
- Connectivité avancée
- Expérience utilisateur intuitive
- Qualité de fabrication et IP56
- Légère imprécision dans les haut-médiums
- Connectique spartiate
- Pas de virtualisation Atmos
Pas originale, mais réussie
Difficile, surtout pour qui ne serait pas un pur technophile, de savoir que ce totem dense de 14.6 x 23.3 x 14.7 pour 3,26 kg est une création JBL et non une énième création Sonos. Quoiqu’il en soit, cette formule ne déroute pas les utilisateurs, qui trouvent ici l’habituelle formule toute scandinave, dans laquelle rien ne déborde jamais vraiment et où les couleurs ne s’expriment, au mieux, qu’en nuances grisonnantes. Cette version blanche est toutefois plus réussie selon nous, en tous cas moins triste, que la déclinaison noire (qui révèle d’autant plus les traces de doigts).
Sérieuse malgré la présence non négligeable de plastique au toucher légèrement doux, la P1 est armée d’une grille métallique ceinturant la quasi-intégralité de sa circonférence. Bien sûr, difficile de passer à côté de la certification IP56, qui offre à ce modèle connecté et Bluetooth une polyvalence que ne peuvent revendiquer sa petite sœur M1 et sa grande sœur X1. En théorie, la Cove P1 peut s’utiliser en extérieur ou dans une salle de bain. Évitez évidemment la plage et l’eau de mer, la corrosion faisant fi d’un simple indice IP56.
De polyvalence, il en est évidemment question pour ce côté transportable, assuré par une poignée sculptée directement dans le châssis. Rien de particulier à dire, si ce n’est que cet élément totalement fixe, et surtout l’absence d’emplacement pour une lanière ou une dragonne, prouvent que la Cove P1 est un modèle transportable d’intérieur avant d’être un produit nomade.
Pour accompagner ce côté transportable, la P1 est livrée, dieu merci, avec une base de charge. Pas d’induction ici, mais un simple contact entre deux connecteurs.
La connectique est morte, vive la connectivité
Il faut s’y faire. Une enceinte de ce type, et toutes les petites enceintes connectées en général, n’ont pas pour vocation d’être des centres audio traversés de fils. La JBL Cove P1 fait plus que prendre cette logique au pied de la lettre, et… n’intègre aucune connectique exploitable. Oui il y a bien un port USB-C camouflé derrière une trappe étanche, mais celui-ci n’assure que la fonction de recharge (si la base n’est pas disponible). Sur la version américaine de l’enceinte, ce port peut lire les contenus audio sur clés, mais notre mouture européenne fait l’impasse dessus.
Au moins la connectivité n’est-elle pas oubliée, au contraire. En amuse-gueule, une puce Bluetooth 5.3 compatible LE Audio/Auracast, mais également Multipoint en Bluetooth Classic. La marque mise ainsi sur une certaine universalité, bien que le LE Audio en soit encore à ses balbutiements vis-à-vis du grand-public.
Avec sa puce Wifi 6, l’appareil entre de plain-pied dans la connectivité avancée. Sans même parler de l’application JBL One, la JBL Cove P1 est compatible avec les protocoles AirPlay, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect, Qobuz Connect, Roon Ready, et DLNA/UPnP. Ses microphones intégrés permettent également de prendre en charge l’assistant vocal Alexa+ (configuration à faire dans l’application Amazon Alexa).
Expérience utilisateur : pourquoi faire compliqué quand on peut faire simple
Les commandes intégrées, symbolisées par des touches tactiles placées sur la face supérieure incurvée de l’enceinte, assurent l’essentiel : navigation, volume, passage au Bluetooth, et déclenchement du Moment, sorte de pré-selection déclenchant une playlist ou la lecture de sons d’ambiance. L’absence de retour haptique, de véritables sensations, nous fait toujours pencher vers des solutions plus physiques à la Marshall, mais l’idée est ici de rester discret.
De son côté, JBL One est plus qu’un complément, puisque permet de configurer l’enceinte sur le réseau local, et d’effectuer la gestion de groupes et de multiroom made in JBL. En l’état, cette application a le mérite de briller par sa simplicité et son aspect très agréable. L’appairage de chaque enceinte est simplissime, d’autant que JBL ne redemande pas le code Wifi pour les nouveaux appareils.
En l’état, les réglages sonores et ergonomiques ne sont pas aussi nombreux que chez le concurrent Sonos, et la gestion des groupes et appairages spéciaux est un peu différente, mais sans doute plus clés en main. Notons qu’il est possible de créer deux types d’appairages avancés : stéréo, en associant en l’occurrence une deuxième enceinte Cove P1 (une pour le canal gauche, une pour le droit), et Surround (enceintes arrière), pour épauler l’une des barres de son de la gamme JBL Bar MK II. Nous n’avons, malheureusement, pas pu expérimenter cela dans le cadre de notre test.
Enfin, et cela n’est pas un détail sur le papier, la Cove P1, ainsi que la plus imposante Cove X1, disposent d’un haut-parleur up-firing (pointé vers le haut) utilisé pour la reproduction de pistes Atmos. Si la présence de ce haut-parleur est plutôt une bonne idée, nous pouvons regretter que la marque n’active pas une véritable virtualisation à partir de simples sources stéréo. En effet, cet élément reste inactif tant que nous ne lui servons pas une piste audio Atmos (que l’on trouve sur Tidal, Amazon, ou Apple Music), ou que nous l’association à une barre de son récente de la marque.
S’il y a peu de chances de tomber en panne de batterie chez soi, la Cove P1 est pourtant un produit assez robuste dans ce domaine. Malgré sa puissance sonore l’enceinte tient facilement 10 h en utilisation normale, les 14 h annoncés étant sans doute valables à des niveaux un peu plus modérés.
Puissante mais maitrisée
Plutôt originale, l’architecture de la JBL Cove P1 peut se définir comme 3.0.1. Les basses sont assurées par un woofer de 105 mm placé en position frontale, woofer associé à deux radiateurs passifs (d’environ 105 mm eux-aussi) intégrés sur les flancs. En façade, un tweeter de 20 mm, fonctionnant comme une sorte de voie centrale. Les deux côtés latéraux abritent chacun un plus large tweeter de 30 mm, tweeters couvrant à priori une plus large gamme de fréquences que le modèle de 20 mm. Enfin, le haut-parleur vertical est lui-aussi un modèle à dôme de 30 mm. Le tout est propulsé par une amplification annoncée à 120 W RMS (mesure à un taux de distorsion de 1%), pour une réponse en fréquences de 50 Hz – 20 kHz (-6 dB).
A l’écoute, et nous ne sommes pas surpris, force est de constater que JBL démontre une fois de plus sa maitrise du sujet du traitement sonore, acoustique comme électronique. La Cove P1 n’est pas une merveille de qualité Hifi à la manière de Kef LS50, mais elle distille un savant mélange d’équilibre et de technicité, le tout enrobé d’une puissance très confortable.
Les basses, notamment, ne présentent pas d’exagération ni de bosses, ce qui ferait paraitre la Cove P1 plus énergique qu’elle ne l’est déjà. Le montage acoustique donne un résultat plus que satisfaisant, avec une extension très prononcée, mais surtout une excellente vivacité dans ce registre. En d’autres termes, elle délivre des basses amples mais assez percutantes.
L’équilibre est également assez net dans les médiums, registre qui peut perturber en raison de cette topologie 3.0.1. Mais, selon nous, le tweeter central permet justement de mieux projeter l’écoute, de ne pas la disperser dans une représentation qui serait un peu flou. La transition médiums-aigus est toutefois le seul léger point noir, point noir sans doute imputable à cette architecture. Ici, les sons tranchants ont tendance à manquer d’un peu de technicité, notamment sur les pistes déjà chargées.
Légèrement en retrait en départ, puis légèrement scintillants, les aigus restent l’un des aspects les mieux gérés de la JBL Cove P1, qui parvient selon nous à faire mieux que Sonos sur ce domaine. On retrouve en effet une meilleure linéarité que, par exemple, sur les Era 300, ces dernières ayant un peu plus de tenue dans les haut-médiums. La Cove P1 est un produit qui n’est pas parfait, mais qui distille un son agréable en pratiquement toutes circonstances, polyvalent et riche, avec une dynamique impressionnante. En effet, pas la peine de pousser le volume dans ces retranchements pour entendre les petits détails d’un morceau, ni isoler les instruments les uns des autres.
A l’inverse, la représentation stéréo reste très relative. La largeur très réduite du produit ne permet pas de donner une véritable ampleur, une séparation très marquée entre la droite et la gauche.
Notre test de la dimension Atmos s’est malheureusement révélé assez superficielle, l’obligation de passer par des pistes vraiment dédiées restant un frein. En l’état, l’idée est assez intéressante, puisque la marque conserve là-aussi une certaine cohérence. L’effet de verticalité n’est pas immense, mais il participe à l’ampleur générale, il parvient assez bien à profiter de l’aération offerte par ce type de mixage. Pour les adeptes de l’écoute spatiale, en particulier avec un appairage stéréo, nul doute que l’achat d’une telle configuration soit justifié.
À qui s'adresse vraiment la JBL Cove P1
Cette enceinte moderne s'adresse à :
- Les amoureux de son détaillé et équilibré
- Ceux qui désirent la meilleure enceinte connectée transportable
- Les allergiques au principe d'écosystème fermé
À l'inverse, les utilisateurs déjà bien dotés en matériel Sonos ne trouveront pas ici un produit suffisamment révolutionnaire, ni un écosystème encore assez riche, pour passer chez la concurrence.
JBL Cove P1 : l’avis de Clubic
La JBL Cove P1 n’est pas une enceinte irréprochable, mais qui fait exactement ce que nous attendons d’un produit moderne de cette catégorie de prix. La marque, tout en prenant bien en main l’utilisateur, est particulièrement exigeante en matière de son.
La Cove P1 est à ce titre un produit équilibré et puissant, technique et efficace. Si les propositions sont un peu différentes, et l’écosystème matériel JBL encore à ses balbutiements, nous tenons là un véritable concurrent pour les produits Sonos. Dommage pour JBL d’imiter son concurrent sur le terrain de la connectique, inexistante, et de ne pas proposer la fonction qui lui donnerait un avantage incontestable.
- Son équilibré et riche, bonne ampleur
- Bonne puissance sonore, basses maitrisées
- Connectivité avancée
- Expérience utilisateur intuitive
- Qualité de fabrication et IP56
- Légère imprécision dans les haut-médiums
- Connectique spartiate
- Pas de virtualisation Atmos

articles.title: Ugandan startup XenFi helps hotspot operators sell, manage Wi-Fi access - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ugandan startup XenFi is helping internet service providers (ISPs) and Wi-Fi hotspot operators sell internet access, manage customers and collect payments via mobile money from a single platform.
Founded in 2025, XenFi has built a hotspot billing and management platform that also lets operators monitor transactions and manage multiple MikroTik routers from a centralised dashboard.
“Many hotspot operators need to manage customer access, sell vouchers, collect payments, monitor revenue and administer multiple routers. Handling these processes through disconnected tools or manual systems can make it difficult to track transactions, maintain operational efficiency and scale,” said Charles Wasswa, XenFi’s CEO.
“XenFi brings these functions together through a centralised platform that supports mobile money payments and simplifies the management of hotspot businesses.”
The startup is self-funded by its founders, which Wasswa said forced discipline from the start.
“Starting without relying on external investors required us to be disciplined in how we allocated resources, developed our technology and acquired customers,” he said.
That approach has paid off. XenFi is already profitable and employs more than 100 people.
“Rather than treating profitability as the end goal, we are using it to strengthen our technology, expand our operations and reach more customers,” Wasswa said.
The platform serves approximately 6,000 active users in Uganda and has customers in close to 15 African countries, including Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Gabon. XenFi has also set up a physical presence in Kenya.
“Uptake has been encouraging,” said Wasswa. “Beyond Uganda, we are seeing adoption across other African markets, with businesses welcoming our system as a solution for managing their hotspot operations and payments.”
XenFi makes money through platform charges and billing and transaction fees, which vary by service and market.
“As our customers grow and process more activity through our platform, we have opportunities to grow our revenue alongside them,” Wasswa said.
The startup competes with international hotspot billing platforms, regional providers, locally developed billing tools and operators still relying on manual systems. Wasswa said XenFi stands out through its focus on African market needs, payment integration and ease of use.
Expansion has brought its own challenges.
“Payment systems, customer expectations, connectivity infrastructure and regulatory requirements differ from country to country, making international expansion a continuous learning process,” Wasswa said.
“Customers need reliable systems that support their businesses consistently, so we place considerable importance on product reliability, customer support and continuous improvement.”
XenFi now plans to deepen its presence in existing markets, strengthen local partnerships and move into more African countries.
“We are proud of how far we have come, but we see this as the beginning of a much larger journey,” said Wasswa.

articles.title: Quantum Computing’s Energy Bill Is Coming, and It’s Unpriced - EE Times
articles.text:
UN researchers project that by 2030, data centers will use twice the power and water they used in 2025, largely because of AI. Energy has become a key constraint to consider in scaling up compute. The same goes for scaling up quantum computing, yet progress is still often only measured in raw qubit count and fidelities. Those are key, of course, but by themselves they fail to tell you what amount of useful compute power your system brings. In the end, we’re pushing our technology to get it to a useful scale, which in the most basic sense means that value per solution must outweigh cost per solution.
Quantum computers hold real promise in utility applications, be it in faster drug discovery, accelerating materials research, or enabling more efficient machine learning once they run at a useful scale. Getting there means taking the cost of running these machines as seriously as the physics behind them to make them economical. A better understanding of how much useful compute power systems generate for each unit of energy or dollar you put into it is key for that.
At utility scale, compute per watt is what counts
There are two parts of that equation. The denominator is power: Cooling and control electronics in a quantum computer draw power continuously. That power draw will be significant, as large-scale quantum computers will consume tens of megawatts. However, because quantum compute can scale exponentially with the size of the processor, the numerator of the equation is much more important. What matters most is the amount of compute power the system generates for every watt it consumes. This is driven by the QPU architecture of the system.
Classical computing encountered similar issues. For years, processors were judged by clock speed. But as data centers scaled, power became the bottleneck, and performance per watt became the metric that mattered. Since 2007, the Green500 has ranked the world’s supercomputers by computations per watt, next to the TOP500’s ranking by raw speed.
Following the emergence of AI and the hyperscale compute buildout, compute demand is still outrunning supply. The industry has spent the years since catching up, adding power and cooling retrospectively rather than designing for it from the start. Operators are now resorting to on-site gas generators to power new data centers, which is a step back. With quantum, we need to build an energy-efficient architecture before we hit that same inflection point.
From qubit count to compute per watt and per dollar
This is why the industry needs a better yardstick. Compute-per-watt should be the core metric: the amount of useful computation you get for each watt the system consumes. It pushes buyers and builders to weigh output against the energy that produced it, rather than counting the qubits and assuming the rest follows.
The metric counts the power drawn by cooling, control electronics, and classical computing on one side, and the useful quantum computation delivered on the other. If buyers and builders adopt compute-per-watt as a common measure, the whole industry will optimize for the useful processing power it can get from each unit of energy. The same logic applies to cost: Compute-per-dollar weighs that output against what the system costs to build and run.
The fix is in how the chip is built
Getting more compute per watt comes down largely to how a chip is built. On the power side, the way you design your chip and system architecture determines how much power is needed for cryogenics, control hardware, and classical compute.
On the compute side, the differences between architectures are much larger. There are two main scaling approaches for quantum computers: scaling up and scaling out. Scaling out means taking today’s QPUs and networking them together to scale your quantum computer. Scaling up means overcoming today’s scaling bottlenecks and scaling the QPU itself. Both scale qubit count, but scaling qubit count is not the same as scaling compute power.
A recent study quantifies this, showing that quantum computers built around large QPUs generate up to exponentially more compute power than a networked quantum computer. The difference is explained by the network links, which are significantly slower and more lossy than connections within a single QPU.
This networking penalty is often overlooked when the industry talks about scaling quantum computers, but it can make the difference between running a workload for one hour on 100,000 qubits and running the same workload for 10 years on 100 billion qubits. Networking will be important, but later. We first need to scale up, then scale out.
The decisions get made now
The architecture and manufacturing processes for these systems are being decided today, and those decisions set the course for the next decade. Quantum is at an earlier stage than AI, so the industry still has a choice AI didn’t: We either start measuring progress in a way that accounts for the economics and power usage today or face the consequences of neglecting these key considerations.

From Qubits to Workflows: Rethinking Quantum Computing

articles.title: Microsoft announces voluntary exit offer for employees in India, 3 other countries
articles.text:
Microsoft announces voluntary exit offer for employees in India, 3 other countries
Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India, although there is no immediate clarity on how many of them would be eligible for the voluntary exit programme.
Microsoft on Monday announced a voluntary exit programme for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK and Canada, offering financial support and career planning resources to those opting to leave the company, according to a blog post by the tech giant.
Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India, although there is no immediate clarity on how many of them would be eligible for the voluntary exit programme. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible.
It is learnt that eligible employees in India will have until December 1 to decide on the voluntary exit offer.
The package is understood to be similar to a standard severance arrangement, including one month's base salary for each completed year of service, plus health insurance and career transition services.
Microsoft's Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer Amy Coleman informed in her blog post that the voluntary exit offer (VEO), which will be available to employees at level 70 and below (internal job grades that span various levels of seniority at Microsoft) in participating teams across the four countries, is a time-limited initiative aimed at providing greater flexibility to employees considering opportunities outside the company.
The offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States, she wrote in the post.
Meanwhile, a Microsoft spokesperson said the company continues to invest in India's talent and technology ecosystem and is backing the country's AI ambitions with $20.5 billion in committed investment between 2025 and 2029 across cloud and AI infrastructure, skilling and operations.
"We are also on track to fulfil our commitment of equipping 20 million people across India with AI skills by 2030," the Microsoft spokesperson said.
Coleman - in her blog post - said the programme would provide employees with an option to make the transition with support, while allowing participating businesses to adjust their workforce according to evolving requirements.
"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organisations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," Coleman said.
The company clarified that the programme would not be implemented uniformly across its operations, with participation depending on individual business priorities, customer commitments and workforce requirements.
Eligible employees will receive emails detailing the terms of their voluntary exit offers, the blog post said.
"The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We'll learn from it," Coleman said.
She added that Microsoft would continue helping employees develop new skills and explore internal career opportunities, where appropriate.
"There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee," Coleman said, emphasising that the company would seek to balance changing business requirements with opportunities for employees to grow and contribute.

articles.title: Les nouveaux rois des smartphones photo ? Les Vivo X500 Pro et X500 Pro Max arrivent en France — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’objectif de Vivo est clair et net : s’imposer dans la catégorie des meilleurs smartphones en photo. La marque officialise ce mardi 27 octobre l’arrivée en Europe, France comprise, de ses X500 Pro et X500 Pro Max, présentés en Chine le 21 septembre. Au programme : un nouveau capteur photo principal Sony censé mieux gérer les scènes très contrastées, un zoom de 200 Mpx sur le Pro Max et des objectifs additionnels Zeiss qui permettent de zoomer bien plus loin. Sur le papier, c’est l’une des fiches photo les plus ambitieuses de 2026.
Vivo présente cette génération comme la première d’une nouvelle stratégie, qui veut mettre la vidéo au niveau de la photo.
Un capteur principal taillé pour les contre-jours
Les deux modèles partagent le même appareil photo principal, baptisé ZEISS TrueDynamic. Il utilise un nouveau capteur Sony LYTIA L910 de 1/1,28 pouce, développé avec Vivo. C’est un grand capteur pour un smartphone, même s’il reste un peu plus petit que les capteurs 1 pouce de certains concurrents.
Sa grande promesse est sa plage dynamique, c’est-à-dire sa capacité à capturer en même temps les zones très claires et très sombres d’une scène. Vivo annonce 17 EV, un niveau très élevé pour un smartphone. Le capteur produirait aussi très peu de bruit électronique, ce qui aide à garder des ombres propres.
En photographiant quelqu’un avec le soleil en arrière-plan, les nouveaux Vivo X500 Pro et X500 Pro Max sont censés pouvoir garder à la fois le ciel détaillé et le visage bien visible, en une seule prise. Aujourd’hui, les smartphones y arrivent surtout en assemblant plusieurs photos, une technique difficile à appliquer en vidéo.
Pour compenser sa taille, Vivo mise sur la technologie LOFIC du capteur, qui stocke le surplus de lumière pour éviter que les zones claires ne saturent. Ces chiffres proviennent toutefois de ses propres tests en laboratoire, et il faudra les vérifier en conditions réelles. Ça tombe bien, nous avons commencé nos tests et c’est très prometteur. Nous publierons un premier retour d’expérience plus détaillé dans les prochains jours.
Les deux modèles profitent d’une stabilisation renforcée sur l’appareil photo principal, avec un débattement de 1,5 degré sur le X500 Pro et de 3 degrés sur le Pro Max. Plus ce débattement est grand, plus le module compense des mouvements amples, ce qui limite les photos floues et les vidéos qui tremblent.
Le téléobjectif, vrai point de divergence entre les deux modèles
C’est sur le zoom que les deux smartphones se distinguent. Le X500 Pro Max embarque un téléobjectif Zeiss APO de 200 Mpx avec une focale équivalente à 85 mm. Cela correspond à un zoom optique x3,5 par rapport à l’objectif principal (24 mm), idéal pour les portraits. La mention APO (apochromatique) signifie que l’optique est corrigée pour limiter les franges de couleur sur les contours.
Son capteur de 1/1,4 pouce est très grand pour un téléobjectif de smartphone, ce qui lui permet de capter plus de lumière. Ses 200 Mpx permettent aussi de recadrer dans l’image pour zoomer davantage sans trop perdre en détails. Le X500 Pro, lui, se contente d’un capteur Sony LYTIA 610 de 64 Mpx, au format 1/2 pouce, nettement plus petit.
|  | X500 Pro Max | X500 Pro | 
|---|---|---|
| Capteur télé | 200 Mpx, 1/1,4″ (Samsung HP0) | 64 Mpx, 1/2″ (Sony LYTIA 610) | 
| Ouverture | f/2,67 | f/2,52 | 
| Focale | 85 mm | 85 mm | 
| Compatible téléconvertisseur 400 mm | Oui | Non | 
Le Pro Max ajoute un autofocus laser à 1 536 points, actif sur toutes les focales : le téléphone mesure la distance des sujets avec un faisceau laser pour faire la mise au point plus vite, y compris dans la pénombre. Il peut aussi prendre des rafales à 60 images par seconde tout en suivant le sujet. Le mode Long-Range Motion Snapshot, lui, cherche à figer un sujet en mouvement même à fort zoom. Vivo vise clairement la photo de sport, d’animaux et de concert.
Les deux modèles revendiquent une stabilisation « CIPA 7.0 » sur le téléobjectif. La CIPA est l’association japonaise qui définit la façon de mesurer la stabilisation des appareils photo. Un score de 7 signifie qu’on gagnerait l’équivalent de 7 crans de vitesse d’obturation : on pourrait garder l’obturateur ouvert bien plus longtemps sans que la photo soit floue. Le chiffre provient toutefois des mesures de Vivo, et nous le vérifierons pendant notre test.
Jusqu’à 400 mm avec les téléconvertisseurs Zeiss
Vivo reconduit sa stratégie d’objectifs additionnels qui se fixent devant le téléobjectif, à la manière d’une longue-vue. Ils multiplient la focale du téléobjectif : avec un grossissement de 4,7x, les 85 mm d’origine deviennent environ 400 mm. Deux modèles sont au programme, tous deux vendus séparément.
| Téléconvertisseur | Focale équivalente | Grossissement | Compatibilité | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Telephoto Extender Gen 2 Ultra | 400 mm | 4,7x | X500 Pro Max | 
| Telephoto Extender Gen 2 | 200 mm | 2,35x | X500 Pro et Pro Max | 
Le Gen 2 Ultra repose sur une structure optique képlérienne, le principe des lunettes astronomiques, avec 15 lentilles réparties en 2 groupes. Parmi elles, 5 lentilles à faible dispersion limitent les franges colorées, et 1 lentille asphérique améliore la netteté jusque dans les coins de l’image. L’accessoire est volumineux (116 mm de long) et, avec 248 grammes, il pèse plus lourd que le smartphone lui-même. Le Gen 2, plus compact (153 grammes pour 96 mm de long), se glisse dans une poche et fonctionne dans 10 modes de prise de vue, dont Scène, Snapshot et Vidéo Pro.
Nos tests diront si ces accessoires tiennent la comparaison avec un appareil photo bridge ou un hybride équipé d’un téléobjectif.
La vidéo au même niveau que la photo
La nouveauté vidéo phare s’appelle 4K Golden Hour Portrait Video : un mode portrait cinématique en 4K, avec arrière-plan flou, pensé pour les scènes à contre-jour au coucher du soleil. Il s’appuie sur un traitement basé sur le Log, un format qui enregistre une image volontairement terne pour conserver un maximum d’informations dans les zones claires et sombres. Il profite ainsi directement de la plage dynamique du capteur principal.
Vivo ajoute de nouveaux styles colorimétriques, dont Golden Hour (développé avec Zeiss), Sunny Day et Modern Film. Ils sont calibrés dans la chaîne de traitement maison, avec un réglage distinct pour les sujets et pour les décors.
Sur le Pro Max, le module principal et le téléobjectif atteignent tous deux la stabilisation « CIPA 7.0 », de quoi promettre des plans stables même en marchant. Les deux modèles filment aussi en 4K à 240 images par seconde, pour des ralentis, et proposent un mode Log baptisé Cinematic Pro. Ils s’appuient sur deux puces dédiées au traitement d’image conçues par Vivo, les V3+ et VS1.
La même puce MediaTek sur les deux modèles
Les deux modèles tournent sur le MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro, la nouvelle puce haut de gamme du fournisseur taïwanais gravée en 2 nm. Ils fonctionnent sous OriginOS 7, basé sur Android 17. Le X500 Pro reste un haut de gamme relativement compact avec son écran de 6,36 pouces, quand le Pro Max vise le grand format avec 6,85 pouces.
|  | X500 Pro Max | X500 Pro | 
|---|---|---|
| Écran | 6,85″, LTPO 1-144 Hz, 1 440 × 3 168 px | 6,36″, LTPO 1-144 Hz, 1 216 × 2 660 px | 
| Luminosité max | 4 400 cd/m² | 4 500 cd/m² | 
| Puce | Dimensity 9600 Pro | Dimensity 9600 Pro | 
| RAM / stockage | 12 Go, 256 Go à 1 To | 12 Go, 256 ou 512 Go | 
| Batterie | 6 750 mAh | 6 510 mAh | 
| Charge | 90 W filaire, 40 W sans fil | 90 W filaire, 40 W sans fil | 
| Dimensions | 163,32 × 76,82 × 7,95 à 8,12 mm | 151,78 × 71,92 × 7,95 à 8,12 mm | 
| Poids | 224 à 228 g | 192 à 197 g | 
| Coloris | Starry Gray, Moonlit Black | Sunny White, Moonlit Black | 
| Étanchéité | IP68 et IP69 | IP68 et IP69 | 
La batterie est le principal changement par rapport à la version chinoise. Le X500 Pro Max européen descend à 6 750 mAh, contre 8 000 mAh en Chine, avec deux cellules montées en parallèle. Le X500 Pro conserve en revanche ses 6 510 mAh. C’était déjà le cas des X300 l’an dernier, dont les versions européennes avaient elles aussi perdu en capacité.
L’écart de poids et d’épaisseur dépend du coloris : les versions noires, à dos en fibre de verre, sont un peu plus fines et plus légères que les versions en verre.
Prix et disponibilité
Les deux smartphones arrivent avec 256 Go de stockage. Les prix ? 1399 euros pour le Vivo X500 Pro et 1599 euros pour le Vivo X500 Pro Max.
En revanche, aucune date de commercialisation précise n’a encore été annoncée. Celle-ci « sera confirmée dans un deuxième temps », explique Vivo.

articles.title: CrissCross raises undisclosed investment from Circle Ventures
articles.text:
CrissCross, the South Africa-headquartered cross-border payments infrastructure company, has secured an undisclosed investment from Circle Ventures, the corporate venture arm of Circle Internet Group, the company that issues USD Coin (USDC), a digital stablecoin.
The investment, made through Stitch Group, CrissCross’s parent company, will help the company expand its local payment connections and liquidity, build more stablecoin settlement capabilities for enterprise customers, and grow the team supporting clients across the continent.
Stablecoins are increasingly being used to move money across borders, making them a growing part of Africa’s payments infrastructure. Circle’s investment marks its second notable bet on the sector in 2026. In July, it invested in Nigerian fintech Flutterwave as the company expanded USDC settlement across its payments platform, allowing businesses to collect payments locally and settle in USDC. s.
“Africa’s cross-border payments market is massive, complex, and underserved,” James Cope, general manager at CrissCross, said in a statement. “Circle Ventures’ investment validates what we’ve been building: infrastructure that can handle that complexity at scale.”
Lex Campbell and Byron Coetsee founded CrissCross to make cross-border payments more efficient for enterprise businesses operating in African markets. The company was acquired early by Stitch and now sits within Stitch Group, the South Africa-based payments group. CrissCross provides businesses with a single application programming interface (API) to collect money, make payouts, manage funds and exchange currencies across African markets.
For collections, CrissCross lets customers pay merchants using familiar local methods such as bank transfers, mobile money and cards. For payouts, businesses can send individual or bulk payments directly to local bank accounts and mobile wallets. Its treasury tools let companies manage funds across multiple currencies, while its foreign exchange infrastructure lets them convert between local currencies, US dollars, and euros.
CrissCross connects blockchain-based settlement to local fiat payment networks. A business can move value between markets using stablecoins, while the recipient can receive local currency in a bank account. The company says it chooses between stablecoin and fiat rails based on a client’s requirements. It makes money from the payments and currency conversions it processes for clients, and says its pricing varies depending on the markets, payment methods, and services each customer uses.
“Stablecoins help funds move between markets quickly and transparently, and the money is delivered in local currency to the recipient’s bank account or mobile wallet,” the company said in a statement shared with TechCabal. “We use stablecoin or fiat rails depending on what each client needs for speed, cost and compliance.”
CrissCross is trying to close the gap between global stablecoin liquidity and local payment infrastructure. In October, CrissCross partnered with Velocity, a stablecoin payments and treasury platform, to connect institutional on-chain liquidity with local collections, payouts and FX. The partnership aimed to connect global stablecoin liquidity to local bank accounts and payment rails.
Sub-Saharan Africa received more than $205 billion in on-chain crypto value between July 2024 and June 2025, up 52% from the previous year. As crypto activity grows, so does demand for infrastructure that connects digital assets to local payment systems and enables cross-border payments.
“We’re excited to support CrissCross as they bring stablecoin-powered payments infrastructure to scale across African markets — some of the most complex and underserved corridors in the world,” said Brian Schultz, vice president of corporate development and ventures at Circle.
CrissCross says it currently operates across more than 30 markets spanning West, Central, East, Southern and North Africa, including both CFA franc zones, and supports more than 20 currencies. Its customers include multinational enterprises, financial institutions and platforms that need to move money across complex African payment corridors. The company wants to become the infrastructure that lets global businesses treat Africa as one connected market rather than a collection of separate payment systems.
“We want global businesses to find it as easy to collect and pay out across African markets as anywhere else they operate,” it said. “A company operating in Nigeria, Senegal or Kenya should be able to do it through the same infrastructure, with predictable settlement and full visibility over its funds. More enterprises are building their growth plans around African markets, and we want CrissCross to be the payments infrastructure they use to do it.”
Stablecoins are becoming the layer underneath payments for African payments companies. In June, Flutterwave announced an investment from Ripple as part of its Series E and said it would integrate RLUSD, Ripple Payments, and the XRP Ledger into its payment infrastructure. It has also partnered with Polygon and Tempo to build out stablecoin settlement infrastructure.
Onafriq, which operates across more than 40 African countries, has taken a similar route. In February, it partnered with Conduit to use stablecoins such as USDC to fund accounts and rebalance treasury holdings, and announced another partnership in July with digital-asset infrastructure provider Privy to develop regulated stablecoin-powered payment services for financial institutions.
Yellow Card has shifted its focus towards businesses, providing stablecoin payment infrastructure, fiat settlement rails, custody, and local stablecoin issuance. Once associated with crypto trading, dollar-backed stablecoins are now being positioned as a way for businesses to settle transactions and move money across borders.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution.
