articles.title: Hört dein Fernseher mit? Neue Vorwürfe gegen Samsung Smart-TVs
articles.text:
Samsung-TVs: So sollen Smart-TVs Nutzer heimlich belauschen
Smart-TVs sind mittlerweile Teil von vielen Haushalten. Was viele User:innen nicht wissen, ist, dass sie sich damit offenbar auch einen Spion in die eigenen vier Wände geholt haben. Nachdem zuletzt LG-Fernsehern das Abhören von Nutzer:innen vorgeworfen wurde, legt ein Sicherheitsforscher jetzt nach. Er behauptet, dass auch Samsung Kund:innen belauschen soll, um ihnen personalisierte Werbung auszuspielen.
So sollen Samsung-TVs spionieren
Die Warnungen stammen dieses Mal vom Sicherheitsforscher mit dem Nicknamen „log4j“ auf X. Er war in der Vergangenheit als Bug-Bountyhunter, Penetration-Tester für Sicherheitssysteme und als Reverse-Engineer tätig. In einem Post schreibt er, dass er einen vergleichsweise neuen Samsung-TV aus dem Jahr 2025 besitzt. Ihm sei gerade in letzter Zeit aufgefallen, dass er sehr spezifische Werbeanzeigen ausgespielt bekommt. Um herauszufinden, wie Samsung an diese Daten kommt, untersuchte er das Betriebssystem genauer.
Dabei fand er gleich mehrere verräterische Dateien und Code-Schnipsel. Zunächst sollen Samsung-TVs Dateien im Hintergrund ausführen, die die App-Nutzung von User:innen genauer unter die Lupe nehmen. Dadurch können sie etwa in Streaming-Diensten wie Youtube sehen, welche Videos Nutzer:innen angeschaut haben, welche Werbeanzeigen übersprungen wurden und wie lang ein Video insgesamt geschaut wurde.
Wie lauschen Samsung-TVs auch ohne Mikro?
Dazu kommt ein Tool namens „rmdemon“, das einen Packet-Logger im verbundenen Netzwerk startet. Ein weiterer Dienst mit dem Namen „Wifi-Presence“ sucht jede Stunde nach verbundenen Geräten und sucht deren IP- und Mac-Adressen heraus. Daneben wären die Samsung-TVs laut „log4j“ in der Lage, ihre Nutzer:innen über angeschlossene Kameras aufzunehmen oder Mikrofone zu nutzen, um sie abzuhören.
Besonders gravierend sind die Anschuldigungen, dass die Smart-TVs dabei sogar Umwege gehen können. Haben sie selbst kein Mikrofon verbaut, können sie laut dem Sicherheitsforscher auf verbundene Geräte wie Soundbars oder Bluetooth-Lautsprecher zugreifen und deren Mikrofone nutzen. Der Sicherheitsforscher schreibt dazu: „Ich habe herausgefunden, warum sich mein Samsung-Fernseher so träge anfühlt. Samsung nutzt seine eigene Hardware zum Verarbeiten von Daten, inklusive Audio, Screenshots, ID-Tracking über mehrere Geräte hinweg und noch mehr Telemetrie.“
Abschließend hat „log4j“ einen ausführlichen Bericht versprochen, der alle Funde noch einmal zusammenfasst. Bislang ist dieses Dokument noch nicht veröffentlicht worden. Auch Samsung hat sich noch nicht zu den Anschuldigungen des Sicherheitsforschers geäußert.

articles.title: DeepMind unveils Genie 4 world model promising more realistic physics and humans
articles.text:
Last year, Google DeepMind sent gaming stocks tumbling with the reveal of its Genie 3 world model. Since then, world models have become a major focus of AI labs around the world, but Google isn’t resting on its laurels. Researchers have been hard at work on an updated model that improves on Genie 3 in almost every way. And if you pay Google enough money, you might actually get to use Genie 4 before too long.
It’s easy to look at the output of Genie 4 and see a video game, which is why Genie 3 caused so much consternation in the gaming industry. DeepMind doesn’t think about it that way, though. According to Google, world models are a key element in the march toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). A world model creates a virtual world, but it doesn’t require pre-rendering environments or programming interactive elements. You simply tell the model what you want, and it generates the experience frame by frame in real time as you explore it.
DeepMind says this technology could create infinite training environments for physical robots or unlock new avenues of rapid prototyping for creative fields. Of course, that requires the model to accurately simulate what you want. Genie 4 has several improvements that make its simulations more useful, and that’s thanks in part to Google’s updated Gemini models.
When you prompt a world into existence in Genie 4, it leverages Gemini 3.8 Flash as a guiding agent to break down goals and evaluate each output frame. This helps keep the simulation on track, letting you move through varying environments without losing the original context. However, DeepMind notes that Genie 4 worlds still only remain consistent for a couple of minutes before they forget how things started.
Like Genie 3, the new version supports changing the parameters midstream. You can change the weather, add elements, or move the camera, and Gemini will help steer the simulation with each update. This is similar to the way reasoning models generate additional internal prompts to zero in on the right output tokens.

articles.title: Ford Fathom will be the cheapest American EV capable of powering a house | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Ford announced two new EV chargers today that will allow its forthcoming Fathom pickup truck to serve as a battery capable of delivering power to the home or grid.
The new chargers promise to be about half the cost of Ford’s existing equivalent products, which could make the technology available to more households. Ford said the Fathom itself will start at $28,350.
The Fathom will be capable of delivering “over 10 kW” to a home, Ford said. That would allow the electric vehicle to substitute for a small standby generator. For most U.S. homes, it wouldn’t be enough to power everything, but it could keep a refrigerator and air conditioner operational for about half a day.
Such capability has been touted as an advantage EVs have over fossil fuel vehicles, but not many EVs come properly equipped, and the chargers required to make use of vehicle-to-everything (V2X) services tend to be costly.
Ford’s two devices offer similar but differing capabilities.
The Home Power Station device can help customers shave their utility bill by charging the Fathom when power prices are low and sending electricity back to the home when prices are high. The automaker says it will cost around $650, about 50% less than its first-generation bidirectional charger.
The other option, Home Backup Power, is a package that bundles the Home Power Station with a second device, the Home Backup Panel, to allow the Fathom to also power parts or all of a home when the power goes out. Ford says the package will cost around $2,100, about 60% less than its first-generation product.
None of those prices include installation, which for existing V2X chargers can run up to $10,000, depending on how much electrical work needs to be done to prepare the home. Ford did not announce any partnerships with installers, though a spokesperson told TechCrunch that Ford would release more details at a later date.
Which loads the Fathom can power will vary by household and the specifics of each installation. Things like air conditioners and refrigerators, for example, typically require a large surge of power to start up, after which point their load drops. So-called soft-start devices can help mitigate the surge, though they add cost to the installation.
Both chargers will allow Fathom customers to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs), which use software to control a fleet of distributed energy storage devices, such as EVs.
As strain on the grid grows due to AI data centers, utilities have been exploring whether VPPs can help alleviate congestion at the edges.
Fathom owners who enroll and keep their truck plugged in can sell electricity back to the grid, often at a premium. Ford did not say how much Fathom owners can stand to make, but the payouts can be upwards of $1,000 per year, depending on the grid’s needs and the level of participation.
Automakers, including Ford, have been diving deep into energy storage as demand for such services surges. The Fathom-powered VPP is Ford’s latest foray into the market, but it’s unlikely to be its last.

articles.title: Mira el asombroso nuevo tráiler de 'Dune 3', el épico final de la saga
articles.text:
Por fin, el tráiler final de Dune 3 acaba de ver la luz. El esperado desenlace de la épica saga de ciencia ficción de Denis Villeneuve llegará a los cines cinco años después de su primera entrega. Será un filme que adapte la historia del segundo libro de la franquicia, El Mesías de Dune. Y por lo que podemos ver en el avance, va a volver a ser una película grandiosa y brutal.
El tráiler de Dune 3 nos lleva de vuelta a Arrakis. Pero, esta vez, su historia se ambienta 17 años después de los eventos ocurridos Dune 1 y 2. Ahora, Paul Atreides deberá lidiar con las consecuencias de su lucha por la libertad de los Fremen tras ascender como Emperador Muad’Dib al derrotar a los Harkonnen y al anterior Emperador Shaddam IV Corrino.
Paul se ha convertido, por tanto, en un emperador despiadado y ambicioso que lidera a sus ejércitos en campañas de conquista. De esta forma, Dune 3 indagará ese círculo de violencia del que el protagonista parece incapaz de escapar. La guerra se antoja inevitable en su camino, marcado por oscuras traiciones y luchas de poder.
Mira el tráiler final de Dune 3
Obsesionado por visiones del colapso Imperialista y la reaparición de su antiguo amor perdido, en el tráiler de Dune 3 Paul es absorbido por una conspiración radical, con Chani en el centro del misterio. Ante el fragor de la rebelión y la aproximación de los enemigos, Paul debe enfrentarse al verdadero precio del poder y el destino de aquellos a los que más quiere.
El reparto de Dune 3 lo conforman Timothée Chalamet como Paul Atreides, Zendaya como Chani, Javier Bardem como Stilgar, Rebecca Ferguson como Lady Jessica y Florence Pugh como la emperatriz Irulan. También está Jason Momoa, que regresa como un clon de Hayt tras la primera película. Y los nuevos fichajes, Robert Pattinson como Scytale, Anya Taylor-Joy como Alia Atreides e Isaach De Bankolé como Farok.
La película será la última de la saga. O, al menos, la última que dirigirá Denis Villeneuve, que ya ha asegurado que el resto de libros no le interesan tanto. En definitiva, Dune 3, que se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre, será un épico cierre a una de las mayores trilogías del cine de ciencia ficción de este siglo.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.text:
Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Même hébergé en local, un modèle d’IA d’Alibaba a tenté d’envoyer un fichier vers Pékin
articles.text:
C’est une tâche de routine qu’ont confiée les chercheurs de Cohere à Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.
Cette préversion publiée en août par Alibaba devait rédiger une règle de détection, c’est-à-dire un petit programme qui permet de repérer un type d’attaque sur un réseau.
Mais selon le billet publié par Cohere le 26 octobre 2026, au lieu de s’en tenir à cette consigne, le modèle a passé en revue la machine sur laquelle il tournait, consulté ses réglages réseau, puis tenté d’envoyer un fichier test vers un espace de stockage d’Alibaba Cloud hébergé à Pékin.
L’environnement de test, volontairement coupé d’internet, a bloqué la tentative, mais l’incident a suffisamment interpellé pour que Clément Delangue, cofondateur et patron de Hugging Face, demande publiquement à Cohere de publier l’intégralité de ses traces.
Une demande loin d’être anodine, puisque sa plateforme, la principale pour le partage de modèles, compte plus de 113 000 dérivés de Qwen.
Un raisonnement qui annonçait l’inverse
Le comportement n’était pas totalement inédit. Depuis août, des développeurs avaient repéré des appels inexpliqués de modèles Qwen vers des serveurs d’Alibaba, sans parvenir à les provoquer à nouveau. C’est donc à cette reproduction que se sont attaqués les chercheurs de Cohere.
Pour comprendre ce qui déclenchait ces appels, ils ont écrit eux-mêmes le début d’une commande de téléchargement, puis ont laissé le modèle la terminer, des centaines de fois, en observant quelles adresses web il choisissait d’y inscrire. Les chercheurs ont ensuite rallongé cette commande petit à petit, en y ajoutant une option après l’autre.
Tant qu’elle se contentait de télécharger, le modèle n’y glissait presque jamais d’adresse suspecte. Mais dès que la commande précisait que le fichier téléchargé devait être enregistré sur l’ordinateur, la part de réponses contenant une adresse suspecte bondissait de 0,5 % à 23 %.
Lors de l’incident initial, la trace de raisonnement, comprenez le monologue intérieur que les équipes de sécurité lisent pour anticiper ce qu’un agent s’apprête à faire, annonçait pourtant que le modèle n’utiliserait aucun outil, juste avant qu’il ne tente d’envoyer son fichier vers Pékin. Une équipe qui se serait fiée à ce raisonnement n’aurait donc rien vu venir, et seul le blocage de l’environnement de test a empêché la requête de partir.
Les modèles à poids ouverts mis en doute
Alors, accident ou porte dérobée ? Cohere ne tranche pas entre les deux hypothèses. Ces adresses pourraient être des vestiges des environnements où le modèle a été entraîné, restés dans les données faute d’avoir été nettoyés. Elles pourraient aussi trahir une backdoor, conçue pour recenser les serveurs utilisant le modèle.
La démonstration de Cohere a toutefois été discutée. Des critiques ont fait valoir que la méthode employée, qui consiste à écrire le début de la commande à la place du modèle, revenait à l’orienter vers ce comportement plutôt qu’à mesurer la fréquence à laquelle il le produit de lui-même. Cohere maintient que la tentative d’envoi initiale s’est produite sans aucune aide de ce type, tout en reconnaissant qu’elle reste rare.
Reste que l’affaire porte un coup à l’un des principaux atouts présumés de ce type de modèles. De nombreuses entreprises adoptent des modèles dits à poids ouverts, que chacun peut télécharger et faire tourner sur ses propres serveurs, en pensant que leurs données ne peuvent ainsi pas sortir.
Selon Hugging Face, les modèles chinois ont représenté 41 % des téléchargements sur la plateforme dans l’année précédant mars 2026.

articles.title: Audeze has created something incredibly special with the Maxwell 2 ANC, and I doubt I’ll ever go back to another wireless gaming headset on PS5 or PC
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
My favorite gaming headset of the last few years gets an excellent, though not essential, upgrade that makes it an even better proposition. ANC and planar-magnetic drivers combine for the first time, and the results are spectacular — the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC is simply superb and a must-consider for anybody chasing the best in gaming audio and for whom ANC is a top priority.
Reasons to buy
- + World-class game audio
- + Excellent feature set
- + Strong noise cancellation
- + Great design and build quality
- + Has all the same excellence as the non-ANC model
Reasons to avoid
- - ANC might not be enough for existing Maxwell 2 owners to upgrade
- - Battery life takes a big hit
- - Head tracking feature still feels a little niche
- - A price jump up from the non-ANC version
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC: one-minute review
The Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC is simply a fantastic version of an already world-beating wireless gaming headset. While it shares an awful lot with the ‘original’ Audeze Maxwell 2 that launched earlier this year, the addition of genuinely excellent active noise cancellation (ANC) means that it offers an enhanced experience compared to its brethren.
The design and build remain very similar to that older model, with the big, weighty earcups sitting comfortably over your ears while the leather headstrap keeps things secure. Controls are also nearly identical, bar the addition of the ANC button on the front of the left cup. It’s a sturdy and robust build which gives great confidence, but if you’re in any way wary of weighty sets, then the Maxwell 2 ANC might be a bit much for you — it’s a chonker at 19.75oz / 560g.
However, the heft is unequivocally worth it in my opinion: when it comes to performance, the Maxwell 2 is absolutely fantastic. The non-ANC Maxwell 2 is my pick for the best-sounding gaming headset money can buy right now, and the ANC variant sounds just as brilliant in all scenarios across different platforms.
The ANC itself is a welcome addition and a genuinely impressive one, blocking out all exterior noise in my testing, as well as offering a transparency mode. The quality of the ANC makes it perfect for busy environments, or just achieving maximal immersion in your games.
This is up there with the absolute best in the premium ANC business — like the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni and Nova Elite I tested in recent months — and I can’t recommend it more if it fits in your budget.
Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC: Price and availability
- List price: $429 / £429 / AU$699
- Chunky increase in price over the non-ANC model
- Priced alongside competitors from the likes of SteelSeries, but above other wireless contenders
The Maxwell 2 ANC is more expensive than its ‘regular’ counterpart: it’s $100 / £90 / AU$130 more. With only a few features that are different from its non-ANC brother, its value proposition will be called into question.
For that price, it’s above the likes of the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni (a direct competitor to the Maxwell 2), which is a headset with excellent ANC and one I really would recommend as well.

More broadly, you can still get models such as the brilliant Turtle Beach Stealth Pro 2 headset for comfortably less, and other planar magnetic driver gaming headsets like the wired Asus ROG Kithara are cheaper still (though aren’t quite like-for-like).
As a result, the Audeze Maxwell 2 is a premium headset package, and the combination of its awesome planar magnetic driver audio and the great ANC makes it a sizable investment in the gaming headset market — though still much less than the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Elite. If the best gaming audio and ANC are both must-have features for you, then the Maxwell 2 ANC will still offer what you want and earn its price tag.
Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC: Specs
| Price | $429 / £429 / AU$699 | 
| Weight | 19.75oz / 560g | 
| Drivers | 90mm Planar Magnetic | 
| Compatibility | PlayStation or Xbox, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PC, Mac, Mobile | 
| Connection type | Wireless (2.4Ghz via dongle), Wired (USB-C & audio jack), Bluetooth 5.3 (Auracast, LE Audio, LC3, LC3plus, LDAC, AAC, SBC, Multipoint) | 
| Battery life | ANC off: 40 hours; ANC on: 35 hours | 
| Features | “Aviation-grade” ANC with dual dedicated 1.4W amplifiers, 24-bit/96kHz high-resolution audio, SLAM acoustic management technology, detachable hypercardioid mic, beamforming mic with physical and AI reduction, FILTER™ Noise Reduction Technology, embedded Dolby Atmos license (Xbox) | 
| Software | Audeze App (PC & mobile) | 
Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC: Design & features
- Robust build with a great feature set that builds on predecessor
- A little heavier than the non-ANC headset
- Weaker battery life
The Maxwell 2 ANC gives great confidence with its build. It feels robust, solid, and able to withstand a knock or a drop (something I can attest to), and a lot of that comes from its weightiness. Some folks might immediately associate ‘heavy gaming headset’ with ‘bad,’ but I really think that is a grave misconception and something drilled into us by the marketing of other brands.
In reality, the design and build are so nicely done that it offsets the weight, and the comfort too — largely down to its new memory foam cushions and ventilated leather head strap — means that I’ve never really noticed wearing the Maxwell 2 ANC for even the longest sessions.
In terms of on-board controls, the left cup houses the volume dial, the game-chat mix dial, an audio jack, a USB-C port, a mic port, and the new ANC button. The right cup has the mic mute switch and the power button, which also doubles up as the Bluetooth pairing button. Simple. The dual microphone is very welcome, and means you can deploy the Maxwell 2 ANC for entertainment and music, and still rely on something for comms, without plugging in the detachable boom mic.
Small improvements are also present and welcome. One of which is that the wireless dongle is much shorter than the lollipop stick found with the non-ANC model, and makes for a much tidier look on the front of a PS5 or PC. The head tracking features provided by Embody Immerse Gaming Hive and Dolby Atmos Rendered compatibility are fun and a novelty, though they still feel a little niche for me.
The most notable thing in the features of the Maxwell 2 ANC, however, sadly, is that the battery life has taken a dive compared to the regular Maxwell 2. While the non-ANC version could get you 80-odd hours of use, the ANC version is limited to about half of that with ANC off, and 35 hours with ANC on.
It’s perfectly serviceable and still provides you with comfortably more than a full day, but it is a shame the difference is so massive.
Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC: Performance
- Incredible audio quality across all games
- Excellent ANC performance that doesn’t kill bass
- Comfortable to wear, plus a really solid mic
The Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC is simply fantastic when put to the test. The gaming audio it provides is every bit as good as the audio I love from the regular Maxwell 2.
No matter what I’ve been playing, the Maxwell 2 ANC provides thumping combat sounds, beautifully crisp environmental audio, and rich, rounded soundtracks. It’s a joy to use as a media and entertainment pair of headphones too, with music singing clearly into my ears. Planar magnetic driver audio really is something else.
Backing this up is the microphone combo, which ensures I’m clear and crisp with my teammates even in the most frantic of online multiplayer battles.
Key to the audio sounding so good all the time is that the main USP of the headset, the ANC, doesn’t kill bass like almost every other ANC I’ve tried in my years of testing.
This means that you really are getting uncompromising audio, and some very effective ANC too; it’s excellent for immersion, and even in a busy household with a few people, I’ve been unbothered by external noise. This is undoubtedly aided by Audeze’s SLAM (Symmetric Linear Acoustic Modulator) tech, which is proven to assist in bass performance.
The weight of the headset doesn’t impact the performance of the Maxwell 2 ANC from a comfort perspective either. It might be heavier than other headsets, sure, but it’s never been uncomfortable on my head, even in the longest of sessions. I've almost come to prefer it over lightweight models you totally forget you’re wearing.
Elsewhere, I will say that by default the Maxwell 2 ANC can be quite quiet, which was a mild annoyance, though easily solved on PC or PS5 by manually adjusting the volume. The companion Audeze app on desktop and mobile has also been handy, facilitating firmware updates and allowing for EQ tinkering.
All in all, the Maxwell 2 ANC has all that is great about the non-ANC variant and adds excellent ANC. If you have to have the latter and are eyeing up the best version of the best-sounding headset, then this is the one to get.
Should I buy the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC?
Buy it if...
You want the best version of the best-sounding gaming headset going
If you’re on the hunt for the best-sounding gaming headset money can buy right now, and want to make sure you get the most up-to-date variant, then the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC is the one for you.
You need excellent ANC in a gaming headset
If ANC is at the top of your desired feature list, then what’s on offer here in the Maxwell 2 ANC - combined with its sheer audio quality and prowess - is certainly something to take notice of.
You’re an audiophile gamer chasing the best in audio from specialist drivers
If you’re someone who really, really cares about your gaming audio and wants something extra special that’s geared toward audio lovers, then the Maxwell 2 ANC’s planar magnetic drivers, in conjunction with its ANC and other features, are perfect for you.
You’re on one, maybe two, platforms only
While it can’t connect to lots of devices simultaneously like some of the competition, if you’re looking for one of the best gaming headsets money can buy for a small number of platforms, then this version of the Audeze Maxwell 2 needs to be considered.
Don't buy it if...
You’re wary of weighty headsets
Personally, I think this is a grossly overstated ‘con’ of gaming headsets, but the fact remains: if you’ve grown used to lightweight headsets, then the Maxwell 2 ANC won’t be for you.
You already have a Maxwell 2
As great as the ANC is on this new version of the Maxwell 2, if it’s a feature you can do without, then I’d recommend the normal version of the Maxwell 2 to save some cash but still get that supreme audio experience. 
Also consider...
If the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC doesn’t feel like it’s going to hit the mark for you, then these are the two alternatives I’d look to right now.

How I tested the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC
- Tested over the course of a few months
- Compared with other headsets, including the non-ANC version
- Used across PS5 and PC games, on mobile, and for music, work, and entertainment
I’ve used the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC as my go-to PS5 headset for a few months now, playing the likes of Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, Marvel’s Wolverine, and Tom Clancy's The Division 2 and Warhammer 40,000 Space Marine 2 with friends online, as well as regularly using it on my PC when not using my SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni headset — a competing headset that has been great for comparison.
On my Acer Predator Orion 5000 gaming PC (supplied by Acer), I’ve tested the Maxwell 2 ANC not only with everyday usage like work calls, music, and TV, but also with games like Cyberpunk 2077, Frostpunk 2, Crusader Kings 3, and a preview of a game or two under embargo.

articles.title: 60,000 Microsoft employees offered voluntary buyouts as AI buildout costs bite — program covers roughly 27% of workforce across US, Canada, India, and the UK
articles.text:
60,000 Microsoft employees offered voluntary buyouts as AI buildout costs bite — program covers roughly 27% of workforce across US, Canada, India, and the UK
27% of the company's total 223,000-strong workforce is affected just months after Microsoft's last, and first, voluntary retirement program.
Microsoft has offered voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees across the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom. The employees, who must have an experience level of 70 or below, make up around 27% of the company's total workforce of 223,000 people, a CNBC report notes. This move comes hot on the heels of a similar move in April when the company announced its first-ever voluntary retirement program. That program was open to around 7% of the company's U.S.-based workforce, but it pales in comparison to this latest move. That time around, more than 30% of those eligible for the program took advantage of it.
The "Voluntary Exit Offer" was announced via a post on the Microsoft blog, penned by Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president in charge of people. "The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Coleman explained, going on to say that the move "builds on what we learned" following the retirement program that was launched earlier in the year. Operationally, Coleman added that those who are eligible for the new program will receive an email with all of the relevant details today.
While the blog post points out that the Voluntary Exit Offer is a time-limited, voluntary program, the fact that it comes so soon after April's retirement program is notable. Companies run programs like this when they are looking for ways to slash their wage bills, something that Microsoft knows all about. The company is in the midst of an Xbox "reset" that includes a plan to cut 3,200 jobs by the end of the year. The company has also seen some studios close, with others merging and yet more being cut adrift to pursue life as independents.
As for why Microsoft has chosen now to make cuts, all fingers point to its ongoing AI data center plans. Last year, it announced plans to open the "world's most powerful" AI data center. Fairwater, in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, is now operational, with Microsoft lauding its closed-loop cooling system amid ongoing concern over the impact of data centers on local communities. Since 2023, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta have spent more than $1 trillion on AI infrastructure. AI data center investment is expected to skyrocket to $32 trillion by 2050, with Microsoft among those spending big.
All of this money has to come from somewhere. For Microsoft, at least some of that looks set to come from global salaries. It's unlikely this will be the last cost-cutting measure put forth by Microsoft execs, with Coleman adding that this voluntary exit program is just one "of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute."

articles.title: Lockheed Martin taps Contextere to integrate AI platform into RCAF fleet | BetaKit
articles.text:
American defence contractor Lockheed Martin has solidified a relationship with another Canadian AI company to support its work on Canada’s military planes.
The news: Lockheed Martin’s Canadian subsidiary has signed a $10-million CAD contract with Ottawa-based industrial AI company Contextere to help modernize maintenance, training, and workforce readiness for its work on the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF)’s CC-130J Hercules fleet, the companies announced at the Canadian Aerospace Summit on Tuesday.
The agreement will see Lockheed Martin, RCAF, and Contextere collaborate on a new Intelligent Maintenance, Asset, Personnel and Learning Environment (iMAPLE) platform, which aims to support decisions that Contextere said could improve aircraft availability, maintenance efficiency, and fleet readiness. iMAPLE will be based on Contextere’s Madison platform, which the firm describes as “Siri for the industrial worker”.
From the source: Lockheed Martin vice-president and Canadian regional executive Kristen Leroux said in a statement that the collaboration is “demonstrating how Canadian innovation can build a sovereign defence and dual-use ecosystem right here at home.”
The context: This isn’t Lockheed Martin’s first experience in Contextere. In 2017, the defence contractor invested just under $1.4 million in the company to develop a personal assistant for aerospace and defence maintenance workers.
The new contract is part of Lockheed’s obligations under Canada’s Industrial and Technological Benefits (ITB) policy, which contractually requires companies awarded defence procurement contracts to undertake business activity in Canada equal to the value of the contracts they have won, such as Lockheed’s contract to build the CC-130J Hercules fleet.
Lockheed made a $3.6-million CAD investment into Ottawa-based AI solutions provider Lemay.ai for similar reasons earlier this year.
Final thought: As Canada makes commitments to increase military spending and reduce its military dependence on the United States, giving rise to domestic defence competitors, Lockheed Martin is doubling down on its Canadian presence. Earlier this week, Lockheed Martin completed its acquisition of Ultra Maritime, a defence company specializing in undersea warfare. Ultra Maritime had a strong presence in Dartmouth, NS, with a headcount of approximately 400, adding to Lockheed Martin’s 1,300 Canadian employees.
Feature image courtesy Lockheed Martin via Flickr.

articles.title: Tesla Roadster : prix, versions, date de sortie… tout savoir sur la voiture volante d'Elon Musk
articles.text:
Neuf ans après sa première apparition, le Tesla Roadster a fait un retour très remarqué avec des propulseurs hérités de SpaceX et une version capable de décoller. Trois déclinaisons, une quatrième plus abordable qui pourrait débarquer, 50 000 euros pour réserver et une production prévue en 2028 : voici ce que l’on sait vraiment de la voiture.
Qu’a montré Tesla lors de la présentation ?
Tesla a dévoilé son Roadster dans la nuit du 15 au 16 octobre 2026, sur le site d’essais de moteurs de SpaceX à McGregor, au Texas. Devant les caméras, la voiture d’Elon Musk a fait le show et a animé les réseaux sociaux en sautant en vrille au-dessus d’une partie de la gamme Tesla, de la Model 3 au camion Semi en passant par le Cybertruck et le Cybercab.
L’autre temps fort a été l’accélération et, propulseurs allumés, le Roadster a affiché un 0 à 96 km/h en 0,81 seconde. Notons quand même que ce chrono a été mesuré par Tesla, sur son terrain et avec sa propre voiture, sans contrôle indépendant. « Le futur a bien des voitures volantes », a ensuite résumé Elon Musk sur X, tout en reconnaissant sur scène que ce n’était « pas forcément une voiture optimisée pour la sécurité ».
Quelles sont les différentes versions du Roadster ?
Tesla propose pour l’instant trois versions. La Performance, présentée comme « prête pour la route », compte deux places et se contente d’une aérodynamique active et d’un système d’aspiration, avec un 0 à 96 km/h annoncé en moins de 1,6 seconde. La Thrust, produite en série limitée, ajoute des propulseurs à l’arrière et descend sous les 0,9 seconde. La Rocket, enfin, sacrifie le siège passager, reçoit des propulseurs tout autour de la caisse et vise moins de 0,59 seconde, avec une vitesse de pointe de plus de 370 km/h. C’est elle qui peut réellement décoller du sol et Tesla précise qu’elle n’est « pas approuvée pour une utilisation sur la voie publique ». Elle est par ailleurs réservée à des clients invités.
Une quatrième version, plus abordable, devrait rejoindre la gamme. Selon Top Gear, ce Roadster « Standard » développerait environ 800 kW, contre plus de 1 MW pour la Performance, et se passerait du système d’aspiration de sa grande sœur. Encore en développement selon Lars Moravy, il n’a pour l’instant ni prix ni date de sortie.
Certaines caractéristiques sont communes à toute la gamme, à commencer par l’autonomie de plus de 480 km annonhcée par Tesla, qui ne précise pas le cycle d’homologation. Le reste vient des interviews données par Lars Moravy, vice-président de l’ingénierie véhicule, à Top Gear et Hagerty. Le Roadster serait une propulsion à deux moteurs arrière, développant plus de 1 MW (environ 1 360 ch) et plus de 1 400 Nm, chaque roue arrière étant pilotée indépendamment. Sa batterie utiliserait des cellules cylindriques à la chimie lithium-ion au nickel conçue sur mesure, sans que Tesla en communique la capacité, et pourrait se recharger de 15 à 85 % en une dizaine de minutes sur les Superchargeurs V4. La voiture pèserait moins de 1 700 kg. La direction, sans lien mécanique avec les roues, est commandée par un volant de type « yoke ».
Comment fonctionnent ses propulseurs et son système d’aspiration ?
Pour tenir à l’envers sur sa rampe, la Performance mise sur un système d’aspiration. Selon Lars Moravy, quatre ventilateurs placés à l’arrière travaillent avec des jupes déployables sous la batterie pour plaquer la voiture au sol, même à l’arrêt. De quoi offrir plus de 2 g d’adhérence en virage, avant même que l’aérodynamique n’entre en jeu. Passé 80 à 100 km/h environ, les jupes se relèveraient pour laisser place à un effet Venturi sous le plancher, puis l’aileron actif, dont un brevet détaillait déjà le fonctionnement, prendrait le relais. Au-delà de 320 km/h, l’appui atteindrait ainsi deux fois le poids de la voiture.
 Real life, baby https://t.co/3QEqn18wig
— Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026
Les versions Thrust et Rocket vont plus loin avec des propulseurs à gaz froid empruntés à SpaceX. Ici, aucun carburant n’est brûlé : le système expulse simplement un gaz stocké à très haute pression, jusqu’à 10 000 psi (environ 690 bar), dans des réservoirs en fibre de carbone. Tesla a parlé d’air pendant sa présentation, alors que Lars Moravy évoque plutôt de l’azote. La Thrust disposerait d’un réservoir de 200 litres logé dans le coffre et de quatre buses à l’arrière, dont deux orientables pour garder la voiture en ligne droite, pour une poussée de plus de 80 kN, soit à peu près celle d’un avion de chasse. La Rocket, elle, remplacerait le siège passager par un second réservoir de 400 litres, soit 600 litres au total, et ajouterait six buses : une au niveau de chaque roue pour soulever la voiture et deux à l’avant pour contrôler sa rotation. Sa poussée dépasserait elle aussi 80 kN, et pourrait atteindre 90 kN selon Lars Moravy.
Comment la Rocket peut-elle voler ?
« Donc oui, il peut voler », assure Tesla sur la page française du Roadster. Le terme mérite pourtant d’être nuancé, puisque la Rocket ne dispose ni d’ailes ni de rotor et ne vole donc pas comme un avion ou un hélicoptère. Elle se soulève uniquement grâce à la poussée de ses propulseurs, à la manière d’une fusée. Les quatre buses placées au niveau des roues dirigeraient le gaz vers le bas pour la décoller du sol, tandis que les deux buses avant serviraient à contrôler sa rotation. Lors de la démonstration, ces propulseurs ont permis de remettre la voiture à l’endroit en bout de rampe, d’amortir sa réception puis de la faire sauter en vrille au-dessus des autres Tesla. Ses capacités se limiteraient toutefois à des sauts et à de brèves lévitations, bien loin d’un vol au-dessus des embouteillages.
Ce spectacle a d’ailleurs ses limites, puisqu’un plein ne permettrait qu’environ cinq secondes de poussée, de quoi accompagner un départ arrêté sur environ 400 mètres. Il faut ensuite s’armer de patience, car le remplissage prendrait aujourd’hui de 2 à 6 heures, et même 6 à 7 heures pour les 600 litres de la Rocket. Tesla travaillerait sur un nouveau système pour ramener ce délai à une demi-heure environ.
Combien coûte le Tesla Roadster ?
Pour l’instant, Tesla n’a annoncé aucun prix de vente et se contente de prendre des réservations. En France, la Performance demande de verser 5 000 euros par carte bancaire, présentés comme entièrement remboursables, puis 45 000 euros sous 10 jours, sans quoi la réservation peut être annulée. Pour la Thrust, sa disponibilité est « limitée » et si la réservation reste figée à 5 000 euros, le montant dû dans les 10 jours grimpe à 250 000 euros. Enfin, la Rocket est accessible uniquement sur invitation et n’affiche aucun montant.
Notez que ces sommes ne garantissent pas la livraison d’une voiture dont on ne connaît toujours pas le tarif final. Pour se faire une idée, Tesla annonçait en 2017 la version de base à 200 000 dollars, et la série « Founders », limitée à 1 000 exemplaires, à 250 000 dollars payés d’avance.
Quand sortira-t-il ?
Elon Musk annonce une production en 2028, et Tesla disposerait aujourd’hui, selon Lars Moravy, de quatre ou cinq prototypes, avant d’assembler une série plus importante début 2027. Après neuf ans de reports, mieux vaut toutefois rester prudent avec les prévisions de l’homme le plus riche du monde.
En attendant, rappelons que le premier Roadster de Tesla a été produit à 2 680 exemplaires entre 2008 et 2012. Son successeur avait été présenté en novembre 2017 avec des promesses alléchantes et une sortie prévue en 2020. Si le constructeur a pris son temps, il n’a pas manqué de faire parler de lui en envoyant un Roadster de première génération dans l’espace, à bord d’une fusée Falcon Heavy. Quelques mois plus tard, Elon Musk promettait une option « SpaceX » à propulseurs. La production a ensuite été repoussée d’année en année, puis la présentation elle-même a été décalée à plusieurs reprises en 2026, la dernière fois à cause de la météo.
Le projet semble aussi peser assez peu dans la stratégie de Tesla. Lors de la présentation des résultats du troisième trimestre, le 21 octobre, Elon Musk a bien qualifié la démonstration de « sans doute la plus cool de tous les temps », sans que le sujet suscite l’intérêt des investisseurs, bien plus tournés vers la conduite autonome, le Cybercab et le robot Optimus.
Pourra-t-il rouler en France ?
Aucune version n’a pour l’instant le droit d’y circuler, puisque Tesla n’a annoncé aucune démarche d’homologation en Europe. Cette étape est indispensable pour obtenir une carte grise et le modèle Performance, le plus classique des trois, est celui qui a le plus de chances d’arriver un jour sur nos routes. Pour cela, il pourrait éventuellement bénéficier d’une homologation allégée prévue pour les petites séries. La Thrust, que Tesla présente comme « prête pour la course », semble plutôt destinée aux circuits, faute de règles adaptées à ses propulseurs. Quant à la Rocket, elle soulève une question inédite, que nous avons détaillée dans un article consacré à l’homologation du Roadster : relève-t-elle du droit routier ou du droit aérien ?
Aux États-Unis, l’aviation civile a déjà tranché en indiquant à CBS News que « le véhicule de Tesla ne répond pas à la définition d’un aéronef de la FAA ». De son côté, l’autorité de sécurité routière, la NHTSA, a rappelé que le constructeur devait respecter les normes fédérales. En Europe, aucune autorité ne s’est encore prononcée.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : Apple réagit après les premiers signalements d’écrans fissurés
articles.text:
Apple a répondu aux propriétaires d’iPhone Duo dont l’écran pliant s’est fendu le long de la charnière. Dans sa déclaration, le groupe reconnaît un problème sur un petit nombre d’appareils, sans pour autant en donner l’origine.
Vendu à partir de 2 339 euros en France, l’iPhone Duo connaît ses premiers déboires quelques jours seulement après son lancement. Interrogée par MacRumors, Apple confirme qu’un petit nombre d’appareils sont concernés. La marque souligne également l’accueil positif réservé au smartphone, mais ne fournit aucune explication sur ces cassures apparues le long de la charnière.
Apple reconnaît des fissures sur l’écran intérieur de l’iPhone Duo
Le premier témoignage nous venait initialement d’Australie. Comme nous le soulignions dans notre article consacré aux premières fissures de l’iPhone Duo, un propriétaire affirmait avoir utilisé son appareil pendant environ six heures et l’avoir ouvert moins de vingt fois. En le dépliant, il a senti une résistance sous l’écran, avant d’entendre un craquement. La dalle s’est alors fendue au niveau de la charnière.
D’autres photos ont depuis circulé aux États-Unis, au Canada et en Chine, où des exemplaires d’exposition endommagés ont également été signalés. Les fissures apparaissent généralement le long de la pliure, dans la moitié inférieure de l’écran intérieur, parfois accompagnées d’une ligne de pixels lumineux. Plusieurs utilisateurs décrivent une sensation de blocage ou un claquement juste avant la casse.
Apple a récemment confirmé l’existence du problème auprès de nos confrères de MacRumors, sans en préciser la cause. Le groupe invite les propriétaires concernés à contacter AppleCare pour obtenir un remplacement. Les échanges en boutique sont possibles, mais les stocks limités risquent d’allonger les délais. Si les dégâts sont considérés comme accidentels, le remplacement de l’écran intérieur coûte 1 149 euros sans assurance, contre 99 euros avec AppleCare+.
Le démontage d’iFixit apporte des pistes, mais pas de réponse définitive
Pas plus tard qu’hier, le démontage d’iFixit a apporté des éléments pour comprendre le fonctionnement de la charnière du pliant d’Apple, sans identifier avec certitude l’origine des fissures. En confrontant des images de tomographie aux plans du mécanisme, les spécialistes ont repéré une zone où plusieurs éléments de soutien se rejoignent sous la pliure.
L'une des hypothèses évoquées concerne une barre de soutien centrale qui devrait se rétracter à la fermeture. Si elle ne le fait pas suffisamment, elle pourrait exercer une pression localisée sur l’écran. Gageons qu’Apple parviendra à identifier rapidement l’origine de ces fissures et à éviter qu’elles ne se reproduisent, au risque de s’exposer une nouvelle fois aux moqueries de Samsung.
Source : MacRumors

articles.title: British SME lender Lovey secures up to €298 million to support UK companies | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Lovey, a British FinTech and financial services provider specialising in SME lending and brokerage, has today announced a senior secured credit facility of up to €298 million (£250 million) with Pollen Street Capital, an alternative asset manager.
The facility is made up of €59 million (£50 million) committed capital and a €238 million (£200 million) accordion to continue Lovey’s focus on SME and startup funding. The facility will increase Lovey’s lending capacity as it scales its own-book lending.
Jack Smith, Founder and CEO at Lovey, says: “This new facility is an important milestone for us and will enable us to put more capital behind UK small businesses, scale our own-book lending and give more SMEs access to finance when they need it. Pollen Street shares our belief that finances for small businesses should be simpler, faster and more flexible, and we’re really pleased to have them backing Lovey for this next stage of growth.”
Lovey’s financing follows several comparable European lending announcements in 2026.
In France, Paris-based Aria launched a €240 million debt facility to expand invoice financing, while Lithuania’s InSoil secured €120 million from Pollen Street Capital to increase lending to agricultural SMEs.
In the UK, London-based equipal announced a €17 million forward-flow facility for equipment financing, while specialist consumer lender Plend obtained a facility of up to €58.3 million.
Together with Lovey’s agreement, these financing arrangements represent approximately €733 million in announced credit capacity, including expandable facilities rather than solely committed or drawn funding.
EU-Startups also covered Pollen Street’s participation in Ferovinum’s €468 million asset-backed securitisation in 2025.
Kai Hunter, Chief Operating Officer at Lovey, adds: “The funding announced today is the result of close and collaborative work with Pollen Street and I am grateful to their team, and to our own, for the diligence they brought to it. This funding deepens our lending capacity and allows us to offer larger loans, so that we can back more of the UK’s small and medium-sized businesses, from those that have found finance hardest to secure to the well-established, with greater speed and certainty.”
Founded by Jack Smith in 2016, Lovey has grown from a one-person startup into a 120-strong business, funding more than €717 million (£600 million) in loans to over 11,000 UK SMEs.
Lovey began lending directly from its own balance sheet in 2022, building on its experience as a broker to develop a deeper understanding of the funding needs of UK SMEs. Today, the business combines direct lending with its established brokerage proposition, giving customers access to both Lovey’s own lending and a wider panel of funding partners.
Today’s facility builds on Lovey’s existing funding arrangements announced last year, including a €41 million (£35 million) revolving credit facility from Paragon Bank and a €11 million (£10 million) junior medium-term note programme from LGB Capital Markets.
Ethan Saggu, Investment Director, Pollen Street, says: “Lovey has spent almost a decade seeing the UK SME lending market from a broker’s perspective, giving the team an expert view of where demand for credit is going unmet. We have financed a number of specialist SME lenders and recognise what it takes to grow from brokerage into balance-sheet lending. Lovey has done so with a well-defined product and a focused approach, and we look forward to supporting the team as it scales.”

articles.title: Apple backports CoreGraphics zero-day patches to older iPhones
articles.text:
Apple has backported security patches released last month to older iPhones and iPads, addressing a zero-day bug exploited in "extremely sophisticated" targeted attacks on iOS devices.
Apple patched the same vulnerability in September for devices running iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1.
Meta Product Security discovered this out-of-bounds write weakness (tracked as CVE-2026-86950) in CoreGraphics, a framework used for two-dimensional vector graphics, text drawing, and image rendering across iOS, macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and tvOS.
Successful exploitation of out-of-bounds write security issues can let attackers crash programs, corrupt data, or gain remote code execution by writing data outside the allocated memory buffer.
"Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27," Apple warned on Monday.
"Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved bounds checking."
With this week's security patches, Apple has now also addressed this vulnerability on iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later.
While Apple said CVE-2026-86950 is exploited only in highly targeted attacks, it is strongly advised to install these backported patches to block potential attacks.
With this vulnerability, Apple has fixed two zero-days exploited in attacks this year. The other (CVE-2026-20700), an arbitrary code execution vulnerability in dyld (the Dynamic Link Editor used by Apple operating systems) also exploited in "extremely sophisticated" targeted attacks, was patched in February.
Earlier this year, Apple also fixed a high-severity Beats Studio Buds flaw (CVE-2025-20701) that lets attackers in Bluetooth range spy on users' conversations, and patched older iPhones and iPads against four vulnerabilities targeted in cyberespionage and crypto-theft attacks using the Coruna exploit kit.

articles.title: Moniepoint to cut product, engineering roles in restructuring
articles.text:
Moniepoint, the Nigerian financial services company, is restructuring its engineering and product teams, with some roles set to become redundant. The company is offering affected employees a voluntary exit package and plans to complete the process by the end of December, according to two employees with direct knowledge of the matter.
The restructuring, announced internally to staff on Monday, October 19, introduces smaller teams responsible for building and operating products from end to end, alongside new platform architect roles to oversee shared technology systems.
Moniepoint has grown from a single product into a financial services group spanning payments, banking, credit and business management. It now wants smaller teams with clearer responsibility for delivery and operations, rather than relying on multiple layers of coordination and sign-off.
A Moniepoint spokesperson said the restructuring should not be regarded as a layoff. The company did not disclose how many employees would be affected.
Staff were offered five months’ salary to resign voluntarily. However, Moniepoint can reject applications from employees whose skills it still needs, according to two employees who asked not to be named to speak freely. The voluntary exit window closed on Friday, October 23, and staff will be told whether their roles are affected between November 2 and November 11.
“As part of Moniepoint’s regular strategic review of operations, the management is restructuring the engineering and product functions for the next stage of growth,” the company said in a statement shared with TechCabal on Monday. “The company is moving to a structure of platform groups made up of small, focused product-area teams, each owning what it builds from end to end.”
Moniepoint heavily hired engineers and product managers as it grew to a unicorn valuation, building several financial products and a range of internal tools. As the teams grew, so did the layers of review and sign-off that slow large tech companies down.
The restructuring is Moniepoint’s answer. Small teams will each own a product from build to operation, and new platform architects will design and oversee the shared systems beneath them.
Much of a product manager’s job is coordination: writing specifications, setting priorities, and passing work from design to engineering to quality assurance. When one team owns a product end to end, there are fewer handoffs, and fewer people are needed to manage them.
“This model is designed for a business of the company’s size and ambition, giving teams greater autonomy and clearer accountability, while enabling faster product development, greater operational reliability, more consistent service for a growing customer base, and smoother expansion into new markets,” Moniepoint added in the statement.
Platform ownership
Moniepoint said the new structure requires fewer roles in some areas while creating others. As a result, some existing roles will become redundant. The company said it would consider affected employees for open positions elsewhere in the business and would initiate redundancy consultations only where it cannot identify suitable roles.
Employees in backend, frontend, mobile and quality-assurance engineering, as well as product management, are affected. The changes apply across the countries where Moniepoint operates.
Employees will be assessed against written criteria covering delivery and adaptability, work quality, their track record, and length of service. Engineering leaders will score staff, and the human resources team will review the scores across teams. Before any role is confirmed as redundant, the company will check for open roles that could suit the person.
The restructuring comes as Moniepoint expands its financial services business and decides where to deploy its resources.
Founded in 2015 as TeamApt, Moniepoint became a unicorn in October 2024 after a $110 million Series C round. The company says its subsidiaries process more than $400 billion in digital payments a year. In March, it bought a 78% stake in Kenya’s Sumac Microfinance Bank and, in August, phased out MonieWorld, its UK remittance product, less than 18 months after launch.
The job cuts come as Moniepoint continues to hire. The company hired more than 120 people in October, according to one employee, and brought in several heads of department from outside Nigeria, according to another. In May, Tosin Eniolorunda, Moniepoint’s chief executive officer, said the company was struggling to fill about 500 vacancies, later clarifying that the shortage was in senior technical talent.
Earlier this year, Moniepoint discussed internally how artificial intelligence could streamline product management, according to one employee. While the company did not name AI a driver of the restructuring, the discussion reflects a wider question of whether automation and new ways of organising work will enable technology companies to deliver more with smaller teams. In February, Zap Africa, a Nigerian cryptocurrency startup, cut 44% of its workforce as “part of an AI-driven efficiency shift.”
Wider shift
Moniepoint is not the first technology company to argue that smaller teams and clearer ownership can improve productivity. In February, Block, the parent company of Square and Cash App, cut 4,000 jobs, about 40% of its workforce. Chief executive Jack Dorsey linked the cuts to AI tools and a move towards “smaller and flatter teams.”
Across Africa, companies have also reduced staff while trying to improve profitability or refocus operations. Branch laid off employees in Kenya and Nigeria in May, despite reporting about $30 million in profit in 2025. That same month, Jumia said it would cut about 200 jobs as it incorporated AI into operations, logistics, finance, and marketing.
TechCabal Insights found that restructuring was the most common reason African tech companies gave for layoffs between January 2023 and March 2026, while one cited AI. If smaller teams work for the companies that try them, and AI keeps getting better at the specialised tasks those teams used to share, more African tech companies will hire fewer people to do the same work.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Europa está llena de ciudades que sufren una crisis de vivienda. En Praga tienen algo más: un plan para solucionarla
articles.text:
Aunque en pocos sitios ha alcanzado el impacto de España, donde ha precipitado un adelanto electoral, la crisis de la vivienda no es un problema exclusivo de nuestro país. A lo largo y ancho de Europa se encuentran ciudades que sufren escaladas de precios, déficit residencial y escasez de suelo. Ocurre desde Londres hasta Atenas, pasando por París, Berlín o Lisboa. También en la República Checa, que ha visto cómo el coste del m2 aumentaba un 10,4% en 2025. En su capital, Praga, han ideado una fórmula para suavizar ese desajuste estructural sin expandir la ciudad o construir en altura.
La clave está en su pasado industrial.
“Un desajuste persistente”. El entrecomillado es de la Comisión Europea (CE), que en su último informe sobre los retos económicos y sociales de la República Checa identifica un problema de sobra conocido en España: la crisis residencial. Para ser más precisos, Bruselas detecta un “desajuste persistente entre la fuerte demanda de vivienda y una oferta limitada”, lo que está caldeando los precios y complicando la accesibilidad. Los analistas comunitarios incluso advierten de que ese cóctel (nada que no ocurra en Madrid o Barcelona) está reduciendo la movilidad laboral.
“El problema es más grave en las grandes ciudades, afectando tanto a los precios de venta como a los de alquiler. Estos acontecimientos tienen amplias repercusiones, exacerbando la asequibilidad de la vivienda, dificultando la movilidad laboral, profundizando las desigualdades y complicando el acceso a la financiación para las empresas innovadoras”, añade la CE. Esa realidad es palpable en Praga, una ciudad de casi 1,4 millones de habitantes que el año pasado atrajo a 8,3 millones de turistas, un 3% más que durante 2024.
¿Tan cara es la ciudad? Para responder a esa pregunta viene bien echar un ojo al informe ‘Mapping the World´s Prices 2026’, un análisis elaborado por Deutsche Bank que compara lo que cuesta comprarse un m2 residencial en el centro de 69 ciudades del mundo, 28 de ellas europeas. Aunque los valores de la capital checa son muy inferiores a los de Zurich, Génova, Londres o París, las metrópolis más prohibitivas del continente, Praga figura en el Top 15. Supera por ejemplo a Madrid, Berlín, Roma, Dublín o Lisboa. Comprar un piso de 80 m2 en el centro cuesta 668.200 euros, frente a los 626.500 de Madrid o 518.700 de Barcelona.
¿Cómo corregirlo? Aumentando la oferta. Como recuerda elEconomista en un informe reciente sobre Praga, en 2025 la capital checa inició la construcción de apenas 7.400 viviendas y finalizó 5.300. Los datos del segundo trimestre de 2026 muestran una aceleración de ese ritmo, pero el sector tiene ante sí el complicado desafío de corregir un déficit residencial que algunos expertos estiman en 91.000 pisos. Los mismos analistas calculan que para cubrirlo la ciudad necesitaría edificar al menos 10.000 viviendas al año.
La pregunta del millón es… ¿Cómo aumentar el parque residencial? ¿Debe resignarse Praga a una expansión descontrolada de los límites de la ciudad? ¿Le toca revisar los límites de altura y levantar rascacielos? En la ciudad checa han optado por otra vía que aprovecha dos cosas: su historia reciente y su peculiar entramado urbano. Desde hace tiempo la metrópolis ‘cocina’ un plan que busca levantar miles de pisos en terrenos industriales abandonados.
Una cifra: 10.000 millones. Hace unos días la agencia Bloomberg analizó en detalle esa transformación y llegó a una conclusión interesante: la capital checa está experimentando un cambio urbano que puede remontarse varias décadas atrás y alcanza los 10.000 millones de dólares. La clave no pasa por expandirse hacia el extrarradio o añadir plantas a los edificios que ya existen, sino en reconvertir antiguos polos industriales en barrios con casas, parques, edificios de uso mixto y amplios bulevares. Todo con apoyo de inversores privados.
En el punto de mira están antiguas estaciones de ferrocarriles, fábricas y almacenes de mercancías en desuso. “No se trata de añadir muchas capas nuevas”, explica a Bloomberg Martin Ourednicek, del Departamento de Geografía Social y Desarrollo Regional de la Universidad Carolina de Praga. “Se trata de aprovechar y transformar aquellas partes de la ciudad que quedaron relegadas tras la era industrial”. Praga tiene ante sí un cálculo complicado: construye unas 5.000 nuevas viviendas al año, la mitad de las que en realidad necesita, según su Instituto de Planificación.
De la teoría a la práctica. No todo es teoría o declaraciones de intenciones. Praga acoge ya algunos proyectos ambiciosos que ayudan a entender el calado de esa transformación. De todos, quizás el más interesante es Bubny-Zatory, que aspira a convertir el entorno de una estación ferroviaria en desuso de Bubny en un barrio con 11.000 pisos para unas 25.000 personas. Además de edificios residenciales, el plan incluye un parque y una nueva sede para la Filarmónica Checa. Según IPR Praha el objetivo es que el proyecto culmine en 2040.
Bloomberg cita otros ejemplos, como Florenc21, un proyecto de 920 millones de dólares que quiere crear un barrio verde y peatonal. ¿Dónde? En un espacio ahora infrautilizado situado en uno de los principales nodos de transporte de Praga. Algo similar está ocurriendo en Smichov, una vieja estación de mercancías. En teoría su reconversión debería estar lista a mediados de la próxima década con un amplio bulevar, oficinas, negocios, hostelería… y apartamentos.
Oportunidades y retos. Praga no es la única ciudad europea que cuenta con amplias zonas que en su día tuvieron un uso industrial o logístico y ahora están en desuso. La capital checa, eso sí, se beneficia de un escenario peculiar. Como recuerda Bloomberg, su historia reciente, marcada por el fin del comunismo y la transición a la democracia, explica que el desarrollo urbano impulsado en otras ciudades de Europa en los años 60 se pospusiese en Praga. El motivo: dificultades legislativas, dudas sobre la titularidad del suelo y farragosos trámites burocráticos.
Semejante cóctel hizo que los inversores extranjeros perdieran interés. Eso ha cambiado. Hace poco se actualizó el marco urbanístico de la ciudad, lo que allana el camino para aprovechar terrenos abandonados y aumentar la oferta de viviendas. Por supuesto, no todo son ventajas. Gran parte del plan se apoya en inversores privados a los que no se les exige reservar parte de sus promociones a vivienda asequible. Además, queda botando otra pregunta: ¿Hasta qué punto los nuevos barrios residenciales aumentarán la presión sobre las infraestructuras y los servicios públicos de la ciudad?

articles.title: Vendor Key Leak Puts Data of 238,000 Denver Health Plan Members at Risk
articles.text:
Denver Health Medical Plan (DHMP) is notifying 238,000 people that their personal and health information may have been compromised in a data breach.
Based in Denver, Colorado, DHMP is a non-profit managed care organization within the Denver Health and Hospital Authority system. Through its Denver Health Medicaid Choice plan, it administers Health First Colorado (Medicaid) benefits for members in Denver and three surrounding counties.
The data breach, DHMP says, involved third-party vendor SquareML, which provides a no-code platform for healthcare analytics.
According to DHMP’s incident notice (PDF), SquareML notified the health plan administrator on August 14, 2026, that an access key was inadvertently leaked on a publicly accessible website.
“These credentials may have been used to access a database maintained by SquareML containing information about DHMP’s 238,083 members,” DHMP says.
The access key was published online on June 27, 2025, and was revoked on August 18, 2026. During this window, it could have been used to access the personal and health information stored in the database.
“The compromised account was read-only, meaning the access key could not be used to download, export, delete, or change any information,” DHMP notes.
The potentially compromised information includes names, dates of birth, ZIP codes, city, state, demographic information, health metrics, health plan eligibility data, hospital admission, provider name, and discharge and transfer data.
According to DHMP, the database did not store Social Security numbers or financial information.
“At this time, DHMP has no evidence that member information was viewed or misused, only that it may have been,” the health plan affiliate notes.
In response to the incident, the passwords for all accounts that had access to the database were reset, and DHMP and SquareML are pursuing additional remedial actions.

articles.title: Pour relier une console ou une barre de son : le câble HDMI Silkland de 2 mètres est à 6,27 €
articles.text:
Le câble HDMI 2.1 Silkland de 2 mètres est à 6,27 € (-43 %)
Le câble HDMI Silkland de 2 mètres annonce une bande passante de 48 Gbit/s et prend en charge la 4K à 120 Hz, le VRR et le retour audio eARC.
Amazon propose le câble HDMI 2.1 Silkland de 2 mètres à 6,27 €, contre un ancien prix affiché de 10,99 €, soit environ 43 % de réduction. Le prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours était de 6,60 € : la baisse atteint donc 5 % sur cette référence. Le câble est vendu par Silkland-FR et expédié par Amazon.
Une liaison pour la 4K à haute fréquence
Le câble HDMI Silkland annonce un débit maximal de 48 Gbit/s, avec la prise en charge de la 4K à 120 Hz et de la 8K à 60 Hz. Les appareils reliés et leurs ports doivent également prendre en charge ces formats.
Le VRR et l’ALLM figurent parmi les fonctions compatibles. Le retour audio eARC permet aussi de relier un téléviseur à une barre de son ou à un amplificateur adapté.
Une gaine tressée et des retours favorables
Cette version mesure 2 mètres et possède une gaine tressée ainsi que deux connecteurs HDMI mâles.
La page Amazon affiche 4,7/5 sur 7 662 évaluations, regroupant plusieurs longueurs et lots. Les commentaires consultés apprécient notamment la fabrication et le fonctionnement avec des équipements 4K. Ces retours ne constituent toutefois pas une mesure du débit annoncé.
