articles.title: Paso a paso para activar el modo Halloween en Alexa, el asistente de Amazon
articles.text:
Alexa puede activar un modo temático para Halloween que combina música, relatos, juegos y respuestas especiales mediante comandos de voz. La función permite adaptar la ambientación de una casa antes de una reunión familiar, una fiesta o un día de películas de terror.
El asistente de Amazon puede interactuar con luces inteligentes compatibles y modificar su color para acompañar la temática. Con una orden breve, los usuarios tienen acceso a recursos pensados para sumar sonidos, historias y dinámicas de juego durante la celebración.
Cómo activar el modo Halloween en Alexa
El primer paso consiste en decir: “Alexa, activa el modo Halloween”. El comando habilita una experiencia temática que cambia algunas de las respuestas del asistente y ofrece contenidos vinculados con la fecha.
La activación no requiere ajustes manuales complejos desde la aplicación. Después de reconocer la orden, Alexa puede reproducir canciones asociadas con Halloween, dar historias de terror y ofrecer alternativas para continuar la interacción desde el dispositivo.
Qué sucede si hay luces inteligentes conectadas en el hogar
Las viviendas que cuentan con luces inteligentes compatibles pueden incorporar un componente visual a la experiencia. Alexa puede sincronizar los dispositivos de domótica con colores relacionados con Halloween, entre ellos rojo, naranja y violeta.
Para que esa opción funcione, las lámparas deben estar previamente configuradas en la cuenta del usuario y vinculadas con el asistente. La iluminación temática puede acompañar la música, las historias y los juegos de audio, lo que permite organizar un ambiente acorde sin recurrir a controles individuales para cada dispositivo.
Cómo pedir historias de terror a Alexa para toda la familia
Una de las opciones disponibles es el comando: “Alexa, cuéntame una historia de terror”. A partir de esa petición, el asistente puede narrar leyendas y relatos asociados con el imaginario de la festividad, como La Llorona o El Jinete sin Cabeza.
La elección del contenido conviene adecuarla a la edad de quienes escuchan. En una reunión con niños, la supervisión de un adulto permite decidir si el relato es apropiado y si conviene interrumpirlo o elegir otra actividad. Las historias pueden servir como una alternativa de entretenimiento sin necesidad de pantallas.
Asimismo, quienes busquen una dinámica de interpretación pueden decir: “Alexa, activa el modo bruja”. Con esa frase, el asistente adopta una voz y respuestas asociadas con un personaje de hechicera, que puede proponer un hechizo dentro de la conversación.
Esta función está pensada para juegos en grupo, disfraces o actividades de Halloween en casa. Puede utilizarse como un recurso para iniciar una ronda de desafíos, inventar personajes o acompañar una búsqueda de dulces.
Qué pasa al decir “mi casa me da miedo” a Alexa
El comando “Alexa, mi casa me da miedo” activa una respuesta diseñada para sorprender a quienes se encuentran cerca del parlante. El asistente puede responder con sonidos o frases inesperadas que se incorporan al clima de una reunión temática.
La función es útil para introducir un momento de juego entre familiares o invitados. Como ocurre con los relatos de terror, se sugiere considerar la presencia de niños pequeños o personas sensibles a ruidos repentinos. El objetivo es sumar una reacción breve al encuentro, sin necesidad de preparar efectos de sonidos.
Cuáles juegos tiene Alexa para Halloween
Alexa cuenta con un juego de audio interactivo al que se accede con el comando: “Alexa, abre casa embrujada”. La propuesta plantea un recorrido virtual por una mansión fantasmal, donde cada participante debe elegir entre distintas opciones para avanzar en la historia.
Las decisiones modifican el desarrollo del juego y convierten al grupo en parte de la narración. Esta modalidad puede funcionar durante una reunión familiar porque invita a responder en voz alta y acordar qué camino tomar. El juego combina relato, elecciones y efectos sonoros dentro de una misma actividad.

articles.title: Planeta coberto de lava desafia cientistas ao manter atmosfera contra todas as expectativas
articles.text:
Um planeta coberto por rocha derretida está desafiando as expectativas dos astrônomos. Localizado a cerca de 280 anos-luz da Terra, o exoplaneta TOI-561 b parece manter uma atmosfera significativa, apesar de receber tanta radiação de sua estrela que, segundo os modelos tradicionais, deveria ter perdido seus gases há bilhões de anos.
Observações do telescópio espacial James Webb indicam que o planeta reflete aproximadamente 75% da luz estelar que recebe. Uma possível explicação é a presença de nuvens brilhantes formadas por minerais vaporizados, que funcionariam como uma espécie de protetor solar natural.
Os resultados foram publicados na revista científica The Astronomical Journal e ajudam a aprofundar uma descoberta anterior: a de que esse mundo rochoso extremamente quente aparentemente possui uma atmosfera substancial.
Um planeta que deveria ter perdido sua atmosfera
- O TOI-561 b pertence à categoria das chamadas super-Terras, planetas rochosos maiores que a Terra. Ele tem aproximadamente 1,4 vez o raio do nosso planeta e completa uma volta ao redor de sua estrela em apenas 10,6 horas;
- O exoplaneta está cerca de 40 vezes mais próximo de sua estrela do que Mercúrio está do Sol. A proximidade faz com que uma de suas faces permaneça constantemente voltada para a estrela, enquanto a outra fica permanentemente na escuridão;
- Se fosse apenas uma rocha escura e sem atmosfera, a temperatura do lado iluminado poderia chegar a aproximadamente 2.700 °C. As observações do James Webb, porém, indicam temperatura próxima de 1.800 °C, centenas de graus abaixo do esperado para um corpo sem uma camada gasosa capaz de redistribuir calor ou refletir a radiação recebida;
- A diferença levou os pesquisadores a investigar o que poderia estar impedindo o planeta de absorver tanta energia.
Nuvens minerais funcionariam como um protetor solar
Para entender o comportamento do exoplaneta, a equipe utilizou o James Webb para observá-lo durante 37 horas, acompanhando quase quatro órbitas completas ao redor de sua estrela.
Os cientistas analisaram as mudanças no brilho e na emissão de calor do planeta ao longo desse período. Os dados revelaram que o lado permanentemente escuro não é quente o suficiente para explicar sozinho a diferença de temperatura observada na face iluminada.
A conclusão é que o TOI-561 b reflete aproximadamente três quartos da luz que recebe. Para explicar esse resultado, os pesquisadores compararam as observações com simulações computacionais do clima do planeta.
Os modelos indicam que nuvens compostas por minerais de silicato, como dióxido de silício e silicato de magnésio, poderiam se formar na atmosfera. Essas partículas refletiriam parte da radiação estelar antes que ela atingisse a superfície, reduzindo o aquecimento.
O efeito seria semelhante ao de um protetor solar em escala planetária. Além disso, a atmosfera aparentemente transporta parte do calor do lado iluminado para o lado escuro, contribuindo para diminuir a temperatura da face voltada para a estrela.
A composição exata dessas nuvens, contudo, ainda não foi confirmada diretamente. Elas são uma explicação sugerida pelos modelos para os dados observados.
Leia mais:
- Uma explosão cósmica durou 27 dias; o que a manteve ativa?
- Simulação impressionante recria os primeiros bilhões de anos do Universo
- James Webb encontra galáxia em forma de anel que pode ter nascido de colisão rara
Como o planeta consegue manter gases por bilhões de anos?
A existência de uma atmosfera significativa é especialmente intrigante porque o TOI-561 b está submetido a uma intensa radiação estelar. Em condições assim, os gases de um planeta rochoso relativamente pequeno deveriam escapar para o espaço ao longo do tempo.
Uma possibilidade é que o exoplaneta tenha começado sua história com uma reserva excepcionalmente grande de gases. Outra hipótese é que seu interior continue reabastecendo a atmosfera.
Os pesquisadores consideram que a superfície do TOI-561 b pode ser coberta por oceano global de rocha derretida. Esse material funcionaria como uma gigantesca fonte vulcânica, liberando gases continuamente e compensando parte das perdas para o espaço.
O interior e a atmosfera também poderiam trocar material: enquanto gases escapam da região derretida e alimentam a camada externa, parte deles pode retornar ao interior do planeta.
Essa dinâmica ajudaria a explicar como a atmosfera consegue persistir durante bilhões de anos, mesmo em ambiente tão extremo. Ainda assim, o mecanismo exato permanece em investigação.
Atmosfera pode lembrar Vênus ou uma lua vulcânica
Os cientistas ainda não sabem quais gases predominam na atmosfera do TOI-561 b. Uma das possibilidades é uma camada densa de dióxido de carbono, semelhante à de Vênus, mas em condições muito mais quentes. Outra hipótese envolve o dióxido de enxofre, gás associado à atividade vulcânica de Io, uma das luas de Júpiter.
A equipe pretende realizar novas observações do planeta com o James Webb em comprimentos de onda maiores. Os dados poderão ajudar a determinar a composição química da atmosfera e esclarecer como o exoplaneta mantém seus gases apesar da exposição prolongada à radiação estelar.
Embora as condições do TOI-561 b sejam incompatíveis com a vida como a conhecemos, compreender seu funcionamento pode ajudar os astrônomos a descobrir como atmosferas se formam, evoluem e sobrevivem em mundos rochosos muito diferentes da Terra.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: US government says hackers are now exploiting critical PHP web bugs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA has confirmed that hackers are now actively exploiting a pair of critical security vulnerabilities in the widely used PHP web software and has ordered civilian federal agencies within the U.S. government to fix their systems within the next three days.
The urgent new warning to patch comes less than a week after the makers of the decades-old PHP web programming language rolled out patches for the two bugs, which allow hackers to remotely break into a vulnerable system over the internet without the need for passwords. The PHP software is reportedly used by some 70% of web-facing servers, putting major websites and applications at risk. The severity of the bugs prompted some governments and big companies to take their sites offline to fix them.
While the bugs are rated critical, meaning they can be highly damaging if exploited, security researchers said that developing a working exploit to hack into vulnerable systems was initially challenging — but not impossible. Confirmed in-the-wild exploitation now puts extra pressure on organizations to patch their systems to prevent malicious compromises, disruption, and data breaches.
CISA did not provide details about who was exploiting the bugs in its Monday statement, but its statement comes soon after security researchers said they found evidence that the PHP bugs were being exploited.
The bugs, known as PHP2Shell, exploit vulnerabilities in the software that went undiscovered for years. The bugs were initially uncovered two years ago but the nonprofit foundation that maintains the software said there was no practical way for hackers to exploit them, leaving the bugs unpatched. That was until earlier this year, when researchers at security research firm Calif uncovered a way to exploit the two dormant vulnerabilities with the assistance of an AI model.
The two bugs in PHP are among countless vulnerabilities that have not yet been discovered or have been deprioritized for years but now pose a risk due to advances in AI models’ ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities, including by chaining multiple flaws together.
PHP is one of many aging web technologies that help keep the internet and modern technologies running, but that have been under-resourced and under-funded for years, making it difficult for open source projects like PHP to pay for security reviews that might have uncovered flaws sooner.

articles.title: From cheap tool to premium subscription: When a beloved app's price skyrockets
articles.text:
How much are you willing to pay to keep using your favorite app?
Maybe you’ve used it for years. Perhaps it performs a function so essential and specific that you couldn’t imagine what you’d do without it. But when the developer announces an extraordinary price hike, you’re forced to consider how much you really value that app.
Earlier this year, Evernote, a note-taking app, changed its subscription tiers, forcing some users to go from paying $130 per year to $250. The highest tier now costs more than 3.3 times as much as the most advanced tier did in 2023 and 10 times more than what Evernote charged for annual subscriptions from its 2008 launch until 2016.
That’s just one example of many longstanding consumer pieces of software that have seen dramatic price hikes in recent years. A lifetime pass to Plex, for example, was $75 in 2012. Today, it’s $250. Individual plans for Quicken, Robokiller, and Inkdrop have each doubled in price.
It’s easy to assume that the developers are miscalculating the value of their app or the loyalty of their users. But an unconventionally honest assessment regarding price hikes from Evernote owner Bending Spoons illustrates how owners of legacy software can apply pressure to loyal customers to extract additional revenue.
Evernote puts a fresh squeeze on old customers
When Bending Spoons bought Evernote in 2023, the app had a sizable customer base. In a June SEC filing, Bending Spoons explained that it was attracted to Evernote’s 200 million accounts and high user engagement.
“We… valued its robust subscriber retention, driven by a rich feature set and a highly engaged and tenured customer base,” the filing says. “Many customers had thousands of notes stored in Evernote and had developed personalized workflows on and around the product. At the time of acquisition, the average customer tenure was 7.2 years.”

Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
articles.text:
Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink’s terms of service before the recent slowdown, as reported earlier by Ars Technica. According to Musk, “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” however Ukrainian officials have denied that happened, or that it is actually possible for them to do.
Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
Musk accuses Ukraine’s military of using Starlink to carry out drone strikes, which officials have denied.
The statement comes nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of putting limits on the military’s satellite internet service that disrupted its drone missions and operations. As reported by Axios, Ukraine uses Starlink for communications, logistics, and to defend against incoming drones. For offensive missions, officials say that Ukraine uses Starshield, the US military-controlled variant of Starlink.
Musk points to a post from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which said Ukraine uses “Starlink from mid-range strikes against enemy military targets,” in violation of Starlink’s policies. However, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, pushed back on this in a post on Telegram, saying Starlink’s systems can only connect to devices traveling between 70 and 90 kilometers per hour (around 43 and 55 miles per hour) and don’t work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” Beskrestnov wrote.
Ars Technica also points out a tweet from another former Ukrainian advisor, Serhii Sternenko, that went into more detail, saying that while stationary terminals could be registered (with Starlink) by military personnel or civilians, “for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system… In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield services had been fully restored. With the restriction lifted, Ukraine’s military can now connect to devices traveling at speeds of more than 400km/h (248mph), the Kyiv Independent reports.
Though Musk initially offloaded the blame for the slowdown in Ukraine onto the US government, President Donald Trump responded by saying he “wasn’t involved” and didn’t know who throttled SpaceX’s services. A report from The Wall Street Journal later said Trump asked Musk to lift restrictions on Ukraine.

articles.title: AWS named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
AWS named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service
I’m proud to share that Amazon Web Services (AWS) has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS) for Amazon Connect for the fourth consecutive year. We believe this recognition reflects years of work pushing on what’s possible in customer experience.
When we launched Amazon Connect Customer, we set out to evolve how businesses serve their customers: to make personalized, intelligent experiences possible without giving up efficiency, flexibility, or control. That belief still drives how we build today.
Customer expectations have shifted. People expect you to recognize them, understand what they need, and stay consistent across every channel. They don’t want to repeat themselves. They don’t want to navigate disconnected systems to solve a simple problem. They want interactions that feel natural, relevant, and genuinely helpful. Meeting that takes more than traditional contact center technology, it takes a comprehensive solution that brings together customer context, AI, and the flexibility to adapt. That’s what we’re building with Amazon Connect Customer.
Customer experience without compromise
What matters most to your customers hasn’t changed: they want to be known, they want their problems fully resolved, and they want to trust you in the moments that matter. Read the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant to know why we are recognized.
Experiences that start with knowing the customer. Connect Customer builds a living picture of every customer: who they are, what they’ve been through, what they need next. Every touchpoint draws on that intelligence. Your customer feels known before a single word is exchanged. That’s what personal actually looks like.
Resolution that carries all the way through.
Most of the industry is still optimizing for deflection: getting customers away from humans as fast as possible. We took a different path. Connect Customer is built for the hard things: the disputed claim, the renegotiated mortgage, the disrupted itinerary that needs real action and can’t go wrong. We carry those interactions all the way through to resolution, and we make them feel natural and personal.
Generative and agentic AI push this further: understanding what a customer needs and acting on it. Every action is auditable. Humans step in when the moment calls for it. You get enterprise scale and the confidence that nothing slips through the cracks.
Building for what’s next
The companies that win the next decade of customer experience won’t be the ones with the most channels or the fastest bot. They’ll be the ones whose customers feel known, whose problems actually get resolved, and whose trust is earned in the moments that matter most. Connect Customer exists to make that real for businesses of every size.
I’m proud of the Connect Customer team for receiving this recognition for the fourth year in a row. Our engineers, product teams, partners, and customers shaped what we’ve built. This is a moment to celebrate how far we’ve come, and a signal of what’s ahead.
Every customer is unique. Every interaction should reflect that.

articles.title: No bank account required: how blockchain works at the last mile - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme – supported by Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation – UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Kenya-based Kotani Pay’s co-founder Samuel Kariuki, spoke with us about what the early work with UNICEF taught the team and how the company grew from a feature phone ready SMS wallet into a business serving multiple markets.
What did you see in those early days that told you there was a problem Kotani Pay could solve?
We started as a bunch of educators teaching people in Nairobi about blockchain, around 2018. We soon hit a problem: Africans pay through mobile money, and mobile money couldn’t connect to the blockchain. In one basic-income pilot in Nairobi’s informal settlements, people received digital money they couldn’t spend. A local agent swapped it for cash, and he quickly became a target.
We thought someone should be able to move from the blockchain to Kenya shillings, and from Kenya shillings back to the blockchain, using the readily available payment channel, which is mobile money. We experimented, and it was a eureka moment for us. We felt we had a product we could build a team around.
What did your first product allow someone receiving money to do?
Through our work with UNICEF Office of Innovation, we did projects in Ghana and Kenya, mainly with people living in refugee camps. If you look at Africa as a whole, the people who struggle financially – whether refugees or others – have feature phones and have trouble connecting to the internet. By designing infrastructure where someone can use any device to connect to the blockchain, what we provided was an SMS wallet: a user could simply dial a code to see what funds they had received and convert it into, local currency through mobile money making it possible to spend digital funds.
What did working with those early users teach you about building the product?
It was a phenomenal experience, to customize a product that resonates. Building a product that meant blockchain payments worked on basic phones and seeing the excitement of someone actually spending that money in the local economy, was very good for us, because it made a case that this is a product that can be replicated at scale.
UNICEF supported Kotani Pay to develop its model. What did the experience give you beyond funding?
The early projects also made a case for us to raise money, because we could tell investors: look, this is what we have been able to achieve, this is what we have been able to learn, these are some of the gaps we are identifying, and we think we can do more.
Beyond that, we had amazing support in terms of product design, market penetration and understanding the fundamentals of the business, and all of this was given for free.
Kotani Pay began with an SMS wallet and now provides payment infrastructure to businesses. What led to that change?
We decided to focus specifically on Application Programming Interfaces (API), tools that allow different software systems to connect and exchange information. With the projects in Kenya and Ghana, we had built a platform that could be used to transfer funds into two different markets, and that’s a very big value proposition. People in the Web3 ecosystem were asking whether they could have a pathway to move crypto into local currency in different countries.
How does Kotani Pay’s payment infrastructure work?
Money moves through something we call the ‘stablecoin sandwich’. The first leg of a transaction is fiat [traditional currency], the second leg is stablecoin, and the last leg is fiat again. Our API is multi-chain infrastructure: on one end it connects to local payment channels – whether that’s banking or mobile money – and on the other end it connects to the blockchain protocols.
Why is blockchain finding such practical uses in Kenya?
Most emerging markets tend to be victims of how financial services are structured. For me to make a trade with someone in Uganda, I have to exit from Kenya shillings into the dollar, then exit from the dollar into Ugandan shillings!
Say I sell phones on a street in Nairobi. I go to a local bank and tell them I want to make a payment to China to import goods. The process of settlement is so long, and most of this business is first-come-first-served, so if it takes one week for my funds to reflect on the other side, the product may have been sold to someone else. These frustrations are forcing people to look for alternatives, and one of the strongest alternatives has always been crypto, specifically stablecoins.
Kotani Pay now focuses on businesses. Is the social purpose of your early work still part of the company?
Social good is still something so close to our hearts. We still believe in it. We open-sourced our solution, and being in the UNICEF portfolio, we are known as people who have infrastructure that people can experiment with.

articles.title: Pytorch erklärt: Was das KI-Framework leistet – und warum nicht mehr nur Nvidia profitiert
articles.text:
Pytorch erklärt: Was das KI-Framework leistet – und warum nicht mehr nur Nvidia profitiert
Bis vor wenigen Jahren war das Trainieren und Ausführen von KI-Modellen wenig effizient. Statt wie heute auf Grafikbeschleuniger zurückzugreifen, auf denen mehrere Berechnungen gleichzeitig ausgeführt werden können, musste man dafür reguläre Prozessoren nutzen. Zwischen 2015 und 2017 wurden gleich zwei Frameworks von konkurrierenden Softwarefirmen veröffentlicht, die die dazugehörigen Prozesse deutlich beschleunigten und auch heute noch zum Goldstandard im maschinellen Lernen zählen: Tensorflow von Google und Pytorch von Facebook. Während ersteres auf die Google-Infrastruktur, die Nutzung im Mobile- und Edge-Kontext und die hauseigenen TPU-Chips optimiert ist, ist zweiteres besonders in der Forschung beliebt.

articles.title: Nazara Technologies swings to profit in Q2; revenue jumps 53% to Rs 803 Cr
articles.text:
Nazara Technologies swings to profit in Q2; revenue jumps 53% to Rs 803 Cr
Nazara Technologies swung to a profit of Rs 35.3 crore in Q2 FY27, as revenue surged 53% year-on-year to a record Rs 803 crore. Gaming revenue more than doubled, driven by growth in mobile gaming and the consolidation of Bluetile and BestPlay.
Nazara Technologies on Monday reported a profit after tax of about Rs 35.3 crore for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, against a loss of about Rs 34 crore in the year-ago period, as the gaming company clinched a "record quarter" in revenue.
For the second quarter of FY2026-27, the revenue rose 53% year-on-year to a record Rs 803 crore.
The EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a measure of a company's operating profitability - grew 93% to Rs 120 crore, with the margin expanding 311 basis points to 14.9%.
Profit after tax from continuing operations was Rs 35 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 34 crore in Q2FY26.
Q2 FY27 is the first quarter to include Bluetile and BestPlay, consolidated from August 1. In their first two months, the two businesses generated revenue of Rs 329 crore, up 49%, and EBITDA of Rs 64 crore, up 64%, at a margin of 19.4% against 17.5%.
Gaming revenue grew 122% to Rs 656 crore at a 21.5% EBITDA margin, accounting for 82% of consolidated revenue.
Mobile gaming revenue jumped 167% to Rs 550 crore.
Among existing studios, WildWorks grew revenue 41%, Kiddopia 21% and Curve Games 27%, with Curve's EBITDA rising 61%.
"This quarter demonstrates the company we are building: a portfolio of high-quality games on a single, shared platform," Raymond A. Stauffer, CEO, Nazara Technologies, said.
He added: "Every game we launch and every studio we acquire benefits from proven capabilities from the outset, enabling us to scale faster and more profitably."
Stauffer, founder of Bluetile and BestPlay, became CEO on September 16. Mithun Sacheti, founder of CaratLane, joined as Executive Director on October 12, subject to shareholder approval, and Arun Agarwal joined as Chief Financial Officer on October 16.
Together, the team brings global gaming, operating and financial depth to scale Nazara's platform, the release said.

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.text:
Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- RIKEN
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
- Share:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.
Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors
Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.
Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.
This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.
To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.
"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%
The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.
When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.
The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors
The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.
This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.
"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."
The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.
"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

articles.title: How Venn helped Dominion Dynamics scale its finance operations | BetaKit
articles.text:
Long before Dominion Dynamics closed its $139-million Series A round this summer, it faced a more basic financial problem.
The Ottawa-based startup was growing fast and quickly becoming a major player in Canadian defence technology. But its legacy bank was holding it back. Supplier transactions couldn’t be processed, and payments were delayed. For a company in hypergrowth, a single missed payment could stall manufacturing.
“Sovereignty is a huge part of our focus, and the fact that Venn is Canadian made it a very easy choice.”
Mitch Carkner, Dominion
“[It was] very siloed, difficult from an onboarding perspective. Payments and cards were a very difficult thing, and in 2026 they shouldn’t be,” said Mitch Carkner, Dominion’s Chief Operating Officer.
The final straw came when the bank de-platformed Dominion altogether, leaving the company in urgent need of a new financial provider.
That’s when a friend pointed Carkner to Venn, the Toronto-based FinTech that lets businesses move money, manage team spending, and sync transactions with their accounting software—all from one platform.
Carkner signed up and within an hour received a call from Venn co-founder and co-CEO Saud Aziz. He walked through the challenges Dominion had faced, and the company was onboarded that same day.
“We use Venn for payments and individual cards. On Mondays, our finance team gets together, we look at all our payments, check invoices, and then execute on the platform,” said Carkner.
Built for companies scaling fast
Dominion’s experience illustrates the problem Venn set out to solve. Its founders, Aziz and Ahmed Shafik, saw Canadian startups and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as being underserved by traditional banks.
For companies trying to scale quickly, new employees need to hit the ground running on day one, suppliers need to be paid on time, and finance teams need to be able to see where all the money is going. Handling those tasks across separate systems only adds to the workload as the business expands.
A simpler way to manage spending
For Carkner, Venn’s appeal is in its simplicity and the ease of its systems and automations. Dominion now pays suppliers on time and manages employee purchases through individual cards, earning one percent cashback on its spending. Both run through the same platform, replacing the separate systems that made its earlier setup difficult.
As Dominion adds suppliers, Venn offers ACH/EFT payments, wire transfers, and Interac e-transfers, alongside global transfers to more than 180 countries. Businesses can schedule recurring bills automatically, reducing the work of handling regular payments as their vendor lists expand.
And, as new people join the team, Dominion can issue them a virtual card through Venn right away, so they can buy what they need to get to work without waiting for a physical card. Managers set spending limits and decide which purchases need approval, while finance can see who’s spending what in real time.
Venn Intelligence, the platform’s built-in AI tools, reads uploaded receipts and matches them to transactions. It uses the company’s accounting history to suggest expense categories and proposes rules to automate recurring patterns. Finance teams can then review those suggestions and send categorized transactions and matched receipts to QuickBooks, reducing the manual data entry necessary. Venn says businesses using the tools save around 10 hours a month on accounting work.
Dominion has used Venn since pre-seed, through its $21-million seed round and recent $139-million Series A. Carkner expects the platform to continue supporting the company as its workforce and supplier network expands.
Sovereignty first
At Dominion, Carkner points to the simplicity of the platform and its automations as benefits for the team. The company manages supplier payments and individual employee cards together and earns one percent cashback on its spending.
They’ve used Venn since pre-seed, through a $21-million seed round and their $139-million Series A round in June. Carkner expects that relationship to continue as Dominion grows. Alongside those practical benefits, he said Venn’s Canadian roots sealed the deal when Dominion was looking for a new financial partner.
“Dominion is building a Canadian company for our military,” he said. “Sovereignty is a huge part of our focus, and the fact that Venn is Canadian made it a very easy choice for our capital and our payment solution.”

articles.title: Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane
articles.text:
In its latest gift to oil and gas companies, the Trump administration is expected to announce plans today to weaken rules that guard against methane leaks.
Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane
The Environmental Protection Agency is lowering standards meant to keep methane from leaking from oil and gas infrastructure.
Methane is a smog-forming pollutant and a powerful greenhouse gas that’s up to 80 times as potent as carbon dioxide on a 20-year horizon. It’s the primary component of what the fossil fuel industry calls “natural gas” that routinely leaks from oil and gas wells and pipelines.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is reversing course on its previous efforts to plug those leaks. As part of President Donald Trump’s deregulatory agenda, the EPA plans to undo Biden-era rules that were expected to cut methane emissions by 80 percent over 14 years.
Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming
The EPA teased the rule change earlier this month, saying in a press release that it was “days away” from making the proposal. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin says the rollbacks will save oil and gas companies $45 billion, while the previous rules would have incurred $18 billion in regulatory costs.
“This proposal takes on many of the problems American [oil and gas] producers and operators have raised with us,” Zeldin said in the October 7th press release. “The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential.”
The agency is expected to step back standards for so-called “marginal wells” — old wells that produce little fuel but create an outsize amount of methane pollution from leaks. These wells are responsible for half of the industry’s methane emissions despite only producing 6 percent of US oil and gas, ProPublica reports. The EPA is also expected to end the Super Emitter Program that notified oil and gas infrastructure operators of large releases of methane reaching 100 kilograms per hour or more.
Trump plans to make the announcement from a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, today, Bloomberg reports. Not only is Texas the top oil- and gas-producing state in the US, it’s also the world’s biggest data center market. With more data center capacity under construction than any other state, Texas has become emblematic of the challenges energy-intensive AI models pose. In just five years, data centers could undo decades of air quality improvements in Texas, according to a recent report by the Houston Advanced Research Center.
Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming so far. But unlike carbon dioxide, which can linger in the atmosphere for hundreds or thousands of years, methane dissipates in a little over a decade. That makes eliminating methane emissions, particularly from unintentional leaks, one of the fastest and most straightforward ways to stop global temperatures from rising.
The EPA’s rollbacks quickly triggered furor from health and environmental advocates. “Any proposed rollback to the federal methane rule is a slap in the face to families who are exposed to oil and gas pollution where they live, work, and play,” Celerah Hewes, a senior manager for state field campaigns at Moms Clean Air Force, said in an email ahead of the expected announcement. “For over a decade, [our group] has been fighting for methane protections for our families—and we were making progress. Today’s announcement from EPA is a massive blow to the efforts to safeguard our children’s health and our climate.”
The Biden-era methane rules were estimated to bring in up to $98 billion in benefits by reducing climate risks and health costs from air pollution, even after factoring in the costs of compliance. Plugging leaks was supposed to lead to up to $13 billion worth of recovered natural gas.

articles.title: Singapur llevará a los tribunales a seis conductores de bus y camión por saltarse los límites de velocidad tres veces en dos días
articles.text:
Que te pillen por exceso de velocidad en la carretera es algo que le puede pasar a cualquiera, a pesar de que debamos siempre no sobrepasar los límites en todo momento. Pero si te pillan mientras llevas un autobús o un camión, ahí la cosa se pone más seria. Esto es precisamente lo que ha pasado en Singapur, donde seis conductores de autobuses, un camión y una cabeza tractora van a comparecer este martes ante un tribunal por delitos de exceso de velocidad. Fueron pillados en varias ocasiones entre julio y agosto de 2026 en autovías, según un comunicado de las autoridades del país. Tal y como informan, los conductores tienen entre 38 y 64 años, y cuatro de los seis casos involucran a conductores de autobuses.
Ir por encima del límite de velocidad en una vía con un vehículo pesado es bastante más serio, no solo por cuestión de dimensiones, sino porque al ser más pesados, van con mucha más inercia que los coches y pueden causar auténticos estragos en el caso de que acaben chocando.
En el comunicado, compartido por el medio AsiaOne, se advierte que los conductores que superan los límites “se ponen en riesgo” y aumentan significativamente las posibilidades de sufrir lesiones graves o la muerte para otros usuarios de la vía.
En detalle. En la Autovía Bukit Timah (BKE), en dirección al puesto de control de Woodlands, cuatro conductores, de 47, 56, 59 y 64 años, fueron pillados en este tramo. Según el comunicado, tres conducían autobuses con un límite de 60 km/h, registrados a velocidades de entre 73 km/h y 76 km/h. El cuarto, un camionero de 59 años, fue registrado a 74 km/h en un vehículo limitado también a 60 km/h.
Tal y como comparte el medio Mothership, en otro tramo, en la Autovía Ayer Rajah (AYE), en dirección a la autovía costera de Marina, un conductor de autobús de 52 años fue pillado a 81 km/h el 1 de agosto. Y al día siguiente, un conductor de cabeza tractora de 38 años fue registrado a 63 km/h en un vehículo limitado a 50 km/h.
Según el medio, uno de los conductores de autobús fue pillado tres veces en dos días: dos veces el 26 de julio (76 km/h y 73 km/h) y de nuevo el 27 de julio (73 km/h), todo ello en la BKE. Otro de los conductores de autobús también fue pillado un par de veces, el 18 de julio a 73 km/h y de nuevo el 26 de julio a 75 km/h.
A qué se enfrentan. Según las leyes del país, una primera condena por exceso de velocidad conlleva una multa o una pena de prisión de hasta tres meses, o ambas cosas. Tal y como comparte el medio, una segunda condena o posterior eleva el máximo a 2.000 dólares singapurenses, hasta seis meses de cárcel, o ambas cosas. Los infractores también pueden ser inhabilitados para conducir toda clase de vehículo. La policía de tráfico afirmaba, según Mothership, que “no tolerará” el exceso de velocidad, especialmente por parte de vehículos pesados.
Entre líneas. Los vehículos pesados están sujetos a límites de velocidad inferiores a los de los coches, y muchos están equipados con limitadores de velocidad. Así que si todos ellos rebasaron la velocidad, tiene sentido que la policía también quiera revisar el equipo instalado en los vehículos. Por eso cualquier vehículo pesado pillado superando su límite debe ser inspeccionado para comprobar que su limitador funciona correctamente.
Limitadores. Según cuentan desde AsiaOne, las normas sobre los limitadores en Singapur se están endureciendo por fases, con un segundo plazo legal que entró en vigor el 1 de julio para los camiones matriculados antes del 1 de enero de 2018, y con un peso máximo autorizado de carga de entre 3.501 kg y 5.000 kg. Tal y como comparte el medio, los propietarios de camiones matriculados a partir del 1 de enero de 2018, con un peso máximo autorizado de carga de entre 5.001 kg y 12.000 kg, tienen hasta el 1 de enero de 2027 para instalarlos.

articles.title: Cómo activar el doblaje automático de YouTube para traducir tus videos a otros idiomas
articles.text:
El doblaje automático de YouTube permite crear pistas de audio traducidas para que un mismo video pueda reproducirse en distintos idiomas. La función busca ampliar el alcance de los creadores sin que tengan que grabar de nuevo cada contenido ni contratar una voz para cada mercado.
Un video publicado originalmente en español puede ofrecer una versión de audio en otro idioma, mientras el espectador conserva la opción de volver a la pista original. YouTube identifica estas publicaciones con la etiqueta “con doblaje automático” en la descripción.
YouTube genera el audio traducido tras publicar el video
El sistema de doblaje automático está disponible de forma predeterminada para los canales que cumplen los requisitos establecidos por YouTube. Cuando un creador sube un video nuevo, la plataforma puede generar las pistas de audio en idiomas compatibles y publicarlas según la configuración elegida en YouTube Studio.
La opción no requiere una activación manual para quienes ya tienen acceso. Sin embargo, algunos canales pueden solicitar el acceso anticipado desde el apartado de configuración avanzada. La disponibilidad de idiomas se amplía de forma gradual, por lo que las opciones pueden variar entre cuentas y videos.
El proceso utiliza herramientas de reconocimiento de voz y traducción para producir un nuevo audio. Los espectadores pueden definir sus preferencias para el idioma del sonido, los títulos y las descripciones. También pueden alternar entre la pista original y cualquiera de las versiones dobladas disponibles.
Los doblajes se generan de forma automática y pueden publicarse al mismo tiempo que el video o quedar pendientes de revisión.
Cómo habilitar el doblaje automático en un canal
Quienes hayan desactivado la función o dispongan de acceso anticipado deben entrar en YouTube Studio desde un ordenador. La ruta para habilitarla es sencilla:
- Acceder a Configuración
- Seleccionar Canal
- Entrar en Configuración avanzada
- Marcar la casilla Permitir el doblaje automático
- Pulsar en Guardar
En esa misma pantalla aparece una alternativa para controlar el proceso antes de que las pistas lleguen al público. Basta con marcar la opción Revisar manualmente los doblajes antes de publicarlos.
Esta configuración permite escuchar el resultado, comprobar la transcripción y decidir si cada idioma debe publicarse, mantenerse sin publicar o eliminarse. La administración detallada de las versiones dobladas solo está disponible en la versión de escritorio de YouTube Studio.
La revisión manual ayuda a evitar errores de traducción
Aunque la herramienta acelera la adaptación de contenidos, YouTube advierte que el doblaje automático puede cometer errores. La calidad depende de elementos como la pronunciación, los acentos, la velocidad de la voz, el ruido de fondo y la complejidad de las expresiones utilizadas en el video.
Los nombres propios, la jerga y los modismos pueden presentar traducciones imprecisas. También pueden surgir diferencias entre la voz original y la voz sintetizada que interpreta el contenido en otro idioma.
Por ese motivo, resulta importante configurar correctamente el idioma original del video antes de publicarlo. Si ese dato es incorrecto, el sistema puede identificar mal el audio de partida y generar una traducción equivocada. El creador no puede editar directamente la pista doblada, pero sí puede corregir el idioma original para que la plataforma vuelva a generarla.
La revisión previa permite detectar fallos antes de que el audio doblado quede disponible para la audiencia.
Qué videos no pueden usar esta herramienta
No todos los contenidos son aptos para el doblaje automático. La plataforma excluye, entre otros casos, los videos que superan los 120 minutos, aquellos sin diálogos o con predominio de música, y las publicaciones cuyo idioma original no puede detectarse.
También pueden quedar fuera los materiales con una velocidad de habla demasiado alta, ya que la versión traducida podría resultar acelerada y difícil de entender. Los reclamos por derechos de autor constituyen otro motivo de exclusión.
Para revisar un doblaje específico, el creador debe abrir el video en YouTube Studio, seleccionar la pestaña Idiomas y elegir la versión correspondiente. Desde allí puede reproducir una vista previa, consultar la transcripción y administrar su publicación.
El lip sync busca ajustar los labios al nuevo audio
Algunos canales cuentan además con acceso anticipado a lip sync, una función experimental que adapta el movimiento de los labios de la persona que aparece en pantalla al audio doblado. La herramienta solo funciona con determinados idiomas y videos que cumplen las condiciones técnicas.
Para activarla, hay que mantener habilitado el doblaje automático en la configuración avanzada del canal y marcar la opción de sincronización labial experimental. Si el ajuste no aparece, significa que la cuenta todavía no tiene acceso.
La expansión de estas funciones dependerá de los idiomas disponibles y de las pruebas de YouTube. Mientras tanto, el doblaje automático ofrece una vía para acercar los videos a públicos de otros países, aunque exige supervisión antes de confiar por completo en la traducción generada por la plataforma.

articles.title: Apple iPhone Duo review: Two screens, two experiences, two thousand dollars
articles.text:
I understand the appeal of foldable phones—they let manufacturers keep expanding screen sizes while still producing devices that can reasonably fit in a pocket. In practice, though, every foldable Android phone I’ve seen in public has had a ridiculously visible seam between the two halves of the screen, often with what looks like delamination from the underlying surface, giving the display an ugly, bubbly appearance.
Back when Android phones began shipping with bigger and bigger screens and the iPhone was stuck at a miserly four inches, I was jealous. But I’ve never looked at anyone using a chunky, fragile-looking foldable phone in public and pined for Apple’s take on the idea.
Nevertheless, that take has arrived, in the form of the iPhone Duo. This $1,999-and-up foldable is the biggest change to the iPhone in years, with both hardware and software updates that dramatically change how you interact with the device.
Like most Apple products, it looks and feels solid, and Apple has managed to engineer its way around at least some of the problems that have bedeviled other foldables (in particular, it has wrangled the between-screen crease so close to invisibility that I rarely thought about it while using the phone unfolded).
But like most first-generation Apple products, it has some odd rough edges and costs more than most people will want to spend. Some aspects of its design feel like steps backward from the standard iPhone design, as exemplified by the current iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro.
The result is something that is technically impressive but not always enjoyable to use. As a little iPad, it’s surprisingly good. As an iPhone, though, I struggle to think of a single way I prefer it to a regular old iPhone.
The iPhone Duo in phone mode
The iPhone Duo (left) feels squat and cramped compared to a typical iPhone (see the 17 Pro, right).
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo (left) feels squat and cramped compared to a typical iPhone (see the 17 Pro, right).
Andrew Cunningham
The camera side of the Duo is the phone’s only quadrant that isn’t made out of screen.
Andrew Cunningham
The camera side of the Duo is the phone’s only quadrant that isn’t made out of screen.
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo (left) feels squat and cramped compared to a typical iPhone (see the 17 Pro, right).
Andrew Cunningham
The camera side of the Duo is the phone’s only quadrant that isn’t made out of screen.
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone I’ve used in a long time that comes with a learning curve. It’s the first time since 2018’s iPhone X that a hardware update has fundamentally changed how you interact with the software.
For the first day or two, I found this pretty off-putting. I kept losing track of the iPad-style button-mounted Touch ID sensor and flipping the phone around with the camera upside down. When fully opened, the phone acts like an iPad: It’s orientation-agnostic, and it will work in portrait or landscape, regardless of which end is up. But in its folded one-handed mode, the Duo still has a right-side-up and an upside-down just like any iPhone, and it took a couple of days of retraining my muscle memory before I was consistently pulling it out of my pocket and looking at it the right way without thinking about it.
When folded up, the iPhone Duo has a more compact footprint than Apple’s other phones and a screen that’s both shorter and wider. The titanium frame looks and feels a lot like last year’s iPhone Air, which plenty of people (us included) pegged as a half-step toward a foldable design. The outer screen looks and feels like a typical glassy iPhone screen, and the “back” of the phone where the camera is (the only quadrant of the phone that isn’t a screen) uses familiar-looking and -feeling Ceramic Shield glass.
Despite having a familiar-looking camera cutout and Dynamic Island on the front screen, the Duo totally lacks a Face ID scanner, which is a pretty big behavioral change following years of face-scanning phones. The Touch ID button has been migrated to the power button, iPad-style, which is in the upper-right corner of the phone when it’s folded (when unfolded, the positioning depends on which direction is “up” because the phone flips its screen orientation no matter which way you’re holding it).
The outer screen of the iPhone Duo has a camera pinhole and Dynamic Island but no Face ID.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The outer screen of the iPhone Duo has a camera pinhole and Dynamic Island but no Face ID.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
In general, the Duo’s button positioning is strange. The power button’s position is… fine. It’s the only placement that makes Touch ID authentication even remotely possible with one hand, even though I felt like I was about to drop the phone every time I tried. But the volume buttons are on the top of the phone in this mode. The left button is volume down and the right button is volume up in this orientation, like on a landscape iPad, even though the volume indicator itself is a tiny bar that lives in the Dynamic Island and travels up and down vertically.
The Duo’s other physical button is the Camera Control button. I would vastly prefer it be a customizable Action Button, which I use constantly on my iPhone 17 Pro. For a phone with this many acres of edge, it feels like the Action Button should have room to exist somewhere, but it doesn’t.
That shorter, wider screen leads to the biggest and most noticeable of the iPhone Duo’s software design changes, at least in folded-phone mode: Your dock moves to the right edge of the screen, and that’s where most app controls move, too. Controls for apps that normally appear on the top or the bottom of the screen are now generally relocated to the right side of the screen, which is still something I’m still getting used to, even after nearly a week of daily use.
These side-mounted controls feel like they’re swimming upstream against almost two decades of smartphone app design—and they don’t even really solve the “lack of vertical space” problem because as soon as the iOS keyboard pops up, the viewable area still shrinks to just a few lines of text.
This right-hand navigation area also feels weirdly underutilized, given the percentage of the front screen it takes up. Your dock is there, but Apple still limits it to four icons, leaving a ton of unused space above and below it. The nav area feels too wide, with too much negative space.
In the end, I only really liked the Duo in folded-down phone mode when it was sitting on a desk, couch, or table next to my laptop, serving as a separate compact notification screen—in other words, when I was not actively holding or touching it. And this isn’t something no other phone can do; it’s just a regular phone thing that the Duo doesn’t make worse.
Lefty troubles
The Duo has a TouchID sensor in its power button, which will usually be on the right or top edge of the phone, depending on how you’re using it. There’s also a Camera Control button, but no user-customizable Action Button.
Andrew Cunningham
The Duo has a TouchID sensor in its power button, which will usually be on the right or top edge of the phone, depending on how you’re using it. There’s also a Camera Control button, but no user-customizable Action Button.
Andrew Cunningham
The volume buttons are usually either on the top or left edge of the phone, and they function differently depending on whether you’re in portrait or landscape mode.
Andrew Cunningham
The volume buttons are usually either on the top or left edge of the phone, and they function differently depending on whether you’re in portrait or landscape mode.
Andrew Cunningham
The Duo has a TouchID sensor in its power button, which will usually be on the right or top edge of the phone, depending on how you’re using it. There’s also a Camera Control button, but no user-customizable Action Button.
Andrew Cunningham
The volume buttons are usually either on the top or left edge of the phone, and they function differently depending on whether you’re in portrait or landscape mode.
Andrew Cunningham
While folded, the Duo is fundamentally designed for right-handed use. Controls throughout iOS and Duo-optimized apps have been scooted to the screen’s right edge to make up for the loss of vertical screen area. The screen is wide enough that any attempt by lefties to reach across with their thumbs to tab that part of the screen will be difficult to impossible, and I say this as someone with fairly large hands.
The Touch ID sensor—integrated, iPad-style, into the phone’s long, flat power button—is also mounted on the right side. Even if iOS did flip around the other way when you hold the Duo with the rounded edge on the left (and it doesn’t, to be clear), the camera would then be on the bottom of the phone, blocked by your fingers.
But even as a right-hander, I don’t find the Duo to be especially comfortable to use one-handed. Sure, I can reach everything, but the phone is so heavy and thick that the standard “rest the phone on my pinkie and use it with my thumb” move is fatiguing. A left-handed friend who held and tested the Duo found it extremely uncomfortable, particularly the stretch you need to do to hit any app icon in the side-mounted dock.
The iPhone Duo as a tablet
I much preferred using the Duo as a small iPad.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
I much preferred using the Duo as a small iPad.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
As frustrating as the Duo is when it’s folded, I genuinely enjoy it when it’s unfolded. Think of an iPad Nano, and you’ll be pretty close to what the experience is.
To answer the biggest question first: Yes, you can see and feel the seam between the screens if you’re looking for it. But most of the time, if you’re just holding it and watching video or reading a webpage and using a thumb to scroll in the corner of the screen, you just don’t notice it. Apple has gotten very close to making it invisible.
Frankly, I’m much more bothered by the under-screen camera, which is visible pretty much constantly. The seam is visible from some angles if you go looking for them. The under-screen camera pinhole is only invisible from some angles if you go looking for it. It’s out of the way enough not to be experience-ruining, but I did find it distracting, and I don’t know that I find it to be a net improvement over the actual-pinhole-with-Dynamic-Island solution that Apple has used for the last few iPhone generations.
When unfolded, the Duo’s screen expands from a squat 5.4 inches to a more comfortable 7.6 inches, which isn’t so far off from the new iPad mini’s 8.5-inch screen. The dock is still limited to four app icons, like a regular iPhone, but it moves back to a familiar place at the bottom of the screen, and apps have more room to breathe.
In landscape, apps usually retain the same side-mounted controls you see on the phone’s front screen, but when you pivot to portrait mode, they revert to more familiar positioning at the top and bottom of the screen—portrait mode looks pretty much like an iPad, while landscape mode looks more like a pair of iPhone home screens next to each other (more on that in a minute).
The inner screen has a matte nano-texture finish, which shares a name with the technology used in some Macs and iPads. But Apple says that both the materials used and the actual nano-texture pattern are both different, changes that were necessitated by the fact that this is a foldable phone and not an inert glass slab. A slightly raised rim around the edge of the screen keeps it from resting directly on a table or desk and leaves room for tiny bits of dust or crud to get trapped without grinding into the screen. If the inner screen does get damaged, this cover layer can apparently be removed and replaced without too much trouble.
You feel the seam between screens more than you see it, but it’s at its most visible against flat fields of black, white, or color.
Andrew Cunningham
You feel the seam between screens more than you see it, but it’s at its most visible against flat fields of black, white, or color.
Andrew Cunningham
The circle on the left of the screen here is the under-screen camera pinhole, which is visible almost any way you hold or look at the phone.
Andrew Cunningham
The circle on the left of the screen here is the under-screen camera pinhole, which is visible almost any way you hold or look at the phone.
Andrew Cunningham
You feel the seam between screens more than you see it, but it’s at its most visible against flat fields of black, white, or color.
Andrew Cunningham
The circle on the left of the screen here is the under-screen camera pinhole, which is visible almost any way you hold or look at the phone.
Andrew Cunningham
I find the screen mostly pleasant to look at and interact with, and I really appreciate the lack of glare. My only gripes are that it picks up smudges that are slightly harder to wipe off than they are on regular glass and that contrast (particularly for dark/black elements) is visibly worse than on the front glassy screen. The inner screen does use OLED display panels, the same as the front screen, but this specific benefit of OLED is missing from the inner screen.
While an unfolded Duo is decidedly iPad-like, it’s still running iOS, not iPadOS, and Apple has gone back to the drawing board for yet another take on split-screen iDevice multitasking. What the company landed on is most similar to the iPad’s old Split View interface, but with some limitations and benefits that help it feel somewhat more at home on the Duo.
Moving an app to one or the other half of the screen.
Andrew Cunningham
Moving an app to one or the other half of the screen.
Andrew Cunningham
Once one app has been pinned, the other side of the screen essentially starts acting like an independent iPhone.

Andrew Cunningham
Two apps at once.
Andrew Cunningham

Apps can be launched and dismissed from either side independently.
Andrew Cunningham

Andrew Cunningham

Andrew Cunningham
Apps can be launched and dismissed from either side independently.
Andrew Cunningham
To enter split-screen multitasking, open an app and swipe up from the bottom of the screen, then drag the window to the areas that appear on the left and right of the screen. Once you’ve anchored an app in this way, the unused half of the screen simply becomes a standard iPhone home screen, with all your icons, widgets, and the side-mounted dock (which can appear on the left side of the screen when the phone is unfolded).
Launch another app from that home screen, and it will take up the other half of the screen. Both apps can be used and dismissed independently, as though you were using two separate iPhones next to each other; you can even launch the same app twice if you really want to.
The center of the screen, where the fold is, is mostly treated as a dead zone by default, but drag it one way or the other to resize one of the apps to full screen, and tap the divider to lock two apps together so they always appear and are dismissed in tandem. If you close the phone’s screen, what you were doing on the right half of the inner screen is preserved on the outer screen, giving the transition a seamless feel.
The hardware’s design makes sense when you look at multitasking mode. Half of an unfolded iPhone Duo is exactly the same as using the iPhone Duo in its folded-down phone mode. The side-nav is pinned to the left side of the screen instead of the right side, but it otherwise feels very similar to having a pair of iPhones you can use in tandem (I would say “two iPhones for the price of one,” but that doesn’t work when the base Duo model is even more expensive than buying two regular iPhones).
Third-party apps need to be updated in one way or another to support the Duo, with baseline support granted at least partly for “free” to apps that target the Xcode 27.1 SDK. Apps that haven’t been updated look mostly OK on the outer screen, since its strip of usable space is roughly the same width as a regular iPhone. Apps that haven’t been updated look like iPhone apps running on an iPad when the screen is unfolded, though: little phone-sized windows with black borders all around, with an option to expand them so they take up the entire screen.
I’ve been surprised how many apps have added Duo support in the few days since the device came out, given that Apple didn’t even make these tools available to developers until just a few weeks ago. But early adopters will run into tons of apps that don’t know what to make of the Duo’s larger inner screen, and I suspect it will be a while before you can assume that any given app will work properly on it.
The iPhone Duo in between
The StandBy screen when the iPhone is in tent mode.
Andrew Cunningham
The StandBy screen when the iPhone is in tent mode.
Andrew Cunningham
“Laptop” mode doesn’t always give you a new view, but some app developers are treating it that way.
Andrew Cunningham
“Laptop” mode doesn’t always give you a new view, but some app developers are treating it that way.
Andrew Cunningham
The StandBy screen when the iPhone is in tent mode.
Andrew Cunningham
“Laptop” mode doesn’t always give you a new view, but some app developers are treating it that way.
Andrew Cunningham
The Duo can be a phone. The Duo can be a tablet. But it also supports several liminal states that exist somewhere in between the two (nomenclature mine):
A “tent mode,” where the phone functions as its own stand and the outer screen shifts to one of several dedicated StandBy views.
A sort of “bent tablet” mode, where content scoots away from the middle of the screen and treats the hinge area as a dead zone.
A “laptop/clamshell” mode, with one half of the inner screen lying flat on a table and the other half sticking up. The device’s hinge will hold its position at almost any angle rather than opening to a few specific hinge points, so how you use it and the angle you choose is pretty much up to you.
Not all apps that support the Duo do different things in every one of its modes, but apps can treat them all as their own unique views if they want to. (I asked a developer from the New York Times Cooking team at an Apple-hosted developer showcase how many distinct views they needed to support to cover every possible position that an app can appear in on the Duo. “Seven. It’s seven,” he replied without hesitation.)
Home screen with the phone unfolded.
Andrew Cunningham
Home screen with the phone unfolded.
Andrew Cunningham
With a bent screen, the two home screens nudge away from each other to leave space in the middle for the fold.
Andrew Cunningham
With a bent screen, the two home screens nudge away from each other to leave space in the middle for the fold.
Andrew Cunningham
Home screen with the phone unfolded.
Andrew Cunningham
With a bent screen, the two home screens nudge away from each other to leave space in the middle for the fold.
Andrew Cunningham
When the screen is unfolded, normally things look pretty iPad-y…
Andrew Cunningham
When the screen is unfolded, normally things look pretty iPad-y…
Andrew Cunningham
When the screen bends, the keyboard scoots away from the crease.
Andrew Cunningham
When the screen bends, the keyboard scoots away from the crease.
Andrew Cunningham
When the screen is unfolded, normally things look pretty iPad-y…
Andrew Cunningham
When the screen bends, the keyboard scoots away from the crease.
Andrew Cunningham
But we’ve already seen a few examples of developers doing things that wouldn’t be at home on a regular iPhone or an iPad. The Headroom app uses a remote desktop connection to connect to a remote Mac and simulate a tiny MacBook; the Delta emulator app has been updated with a Nintendo DS mode; and the Tiny Computers app will change it into arguably copyright-safe facsimiles of distinctive classic computers. I can’t vouch for the quality of any of these apps, and Headroom and Tiny Computers in particular have a distinct air of “quickly vibe-coded to catch the wave of early adopter interest” to them. But the ideas are interesting, and they wouldn’t work as well on different hardware.
About those cases
The iPhone Duo Folio case and its kickstand.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo Folio case and its kickstand.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
Along with the review unit, Apple included a $79 iPhone Duo Case and a $129 iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand. The case provides a basic level of protection without really changing anything about how the Duo works (though the fact that it sticks to the phone using adhesive raises concerns about its longevity).
The Folio is more interesting. It attaches with magnets, and it has a retractable strip between its two halves that stretches to cover the hinge when the phone is folded and retreats into the case when it’s opened. The kickstand that props the phone up in tablet mode is genuinely useful; in phone mode, it solves one problem while creating another.
Here’s the problem it solves: By default, if you’re using the Duo in tablet mode and you fold it closed, the phone transitions your current app to the outer screen rather than putting the phone to sleep. Flipping the Folio cover open and closed does put the phone to sleep and wake it up. It makes the question of “is my phone awake or isn’t it” easier to answer.
The problem it creates is that this cover is opaque, and when you fold it around to the back of the phone, it covers both the camera and the flashlight. These are two things I regularly need fast access to when I pull my phone out of my pocket, and the Folio case asks you to leave the cover flopping around, remove the case temporarily, or snap the phone open into tablet mode instead of using it in phone mode.
Internals and performance
The chip and the camera in the iPhone Duo are way less interesting than the brand-new hardware and software changes, so apologies if this section feels like an afterthought. But it kind of is.
The Apple A20 Pro is Apple’s first 2 nm phone chip, and its second 2 nm chip overall after the M6 that debuted in the new Mac mini. It still uses two large CPU cores and four efficiency cores, the same as the last few generations of A-series chips, but it’s the first phone chip to include “super” cores instead of performance cores. Unlike the M6, which ships all three kinds of cores, the A20 Pro just uses super and efficiency cores.
The A20 Pro does ship with 7 GPU cores, up from the 5-6 cores in the A19 Pro, plus Apple’s upgraded 32-core Neural Engine (Apple usually refers to this as a “dual Neural Engine” with 16 cores each). The A20 Pro still includes 12GB of RAM, the same as the A19 Pro (both upgraded from the 8GB of RAM in the A18 Pro—either chip would be a solid upgrade option for a future MacBook Neo).
In the benchmarks I ran, Apple’s performance promises for the A20 Pro end up in the ballpark of the figures Apple has published: around 20 to 30 percent better single- and multi-core CPU performance compared to A19 Pro, and between 40 and 50 percent faster GPU performance (the 73 percent performance improvement for the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme test is an outlier). If you own any iPhone made within the last three or four years, the chip isn’t the reason to buy the phone, but it’s a respectable upgrade.
Cameras
The iPhone Duo’s camera system is roughly equivalent to the one in the basic iPhone, not the Pro.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo’s camera system is roughly equivalent to the one in the basic iPhone, not the Pro.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The Duo’s camera system is fine. Like the iPhone Air, this hardware is priced well into iPhone Pro territory while lacking the camera system that makes the Pro my default iPhone choice.
The Duo uses the same basic camera configuration as the basic iPhone. It has one 48 MP main sensor and one 48 MP ultrawide sensor, both of which enable a 2x optical zoom feature by cropping a 12 MP patch out of the middle. (Apple’s tech specs page also claims that the ultrawide lens can zoom out by 2x, giving it a “4x optical-quality zoom range,” which feels hand-wavy even if you accept “optical-quality zoom” as an accurate description of what Apple’s cameras are doing).
What keeps me away from the standard iPhone these days is that I find the ultrawide lens to be by far the least useful one Apple ships and the telephoto lens to be the most useful. The Duo’s camera asks you to make the same kind of downgrade from a Pro iPhone, though it at least improves on the one-camera setups Apple ships in the iPhone 17e and iPhone Air.
Once you get past the lack of a telephoto lens, the Duo’s camera system is perfectly competent. Apple’s year-to-year camera quality improvements generally happen around the margins—a little less noise here, a little better low-light performance there—and that’s what I observed while comparing it to my iPhone 17 Pro. To my eye, the differences between the 17 Pro and Duo in good lighting were minimal, but the Duo did capture marginally better detail in low light (see the cat pictures). Of course, when you try comparing the Duo’s digitally zoomed 4x and 8x photos to the 17 Pro’s telephoto lens, there’s zero contest.
