The front cameras, like Face ID, are another casualty of the Duo’s design changes. There are technically two front-facing cameras: a typical-ish pinhole cutout on the front of the outer screen and the one hidden underneath the inner screen (as we discussed before, “hidden” is generous; the camera is almost always visible underneath whatever you’re looking at).
The outer camera is lower-resolution than most other iPhones (12 MP, down from 18 MP), but it’s in the ballpark when you’re on a FaceTime call or taking a selfie. The under-screen inner camera is noticeably worse, capturing noisier video and photos that look excessively digitally sharpened to try to cover for its reduced quality and lack of detail. Apple doesn’t list a resolution for the inner camera, but its 2432 x 1824 resolution works out to around 4.4 megapixels, just one-third the resolution of the outer camera.
That the inner camera is so much worse than the outer camera is made even more obvious by the fact that the inner screen is twice as large; when you fire up a FaceTime call, you’re looking at a lower-resolution image on a larger screen. This isn’t a dealbreaker; the bi-directional FaceTime call that shows the person on the other end of the line on both the outer and inner screens remains genuinely cool, even with the potato-esque quality of the inner camera. But it’s yet another place where the core/traditional iPhone experience is degraded to make room for the Duo’s hero features.
Wrapping folding things up
The iPhone Duo.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
In some ways, foldable phones remind me of the PC industry’s push toward convertible tablet PCs in the early 2010s. In the wake of Apple’s original iPad, Microsoft and its partners clearly thought that they had to figure out tablets or get left behind, but even the designs with staying power (mainly Microsoft’s Surface and Lenovo’s Yoga) aren’t as good at being laptops as a purpose-built laptop or as good at being tablets as a purpose-built tablet.
For me, the iPhone Duo straddles a similar line between the iPhone and the iPad. As a regular one-handed iPhone, it feels deeply compromised—too thick and heavy to comfortably hold in one hand for long, no Face ID, no action button, and power/volume/camera button positioning that feels like it was dictated by “where the buttons can physically fit on the phone” rather than ergonomics. It costs nearly twice as much as the iPhone Pro but has an inferior camera system.
I do really like the Duo as a Kindle-sized iPad. But if that’s what I want, I can buy something like it for less money without saddling myself with a regular phone I don’t particularly like using.
I see the promise of the Duo. It feels well-built—some users have had problems with screen breakage, but it’s not something we ran into. Its hardware and software are cleverly designed. It mostly solves the visible-seam problem that most Android foldables come with. An updated version of the Duo with Face ID support would be just about the best possible version of this form factor, given the limits of battery technology and physics. But for me personally—and for many happy iPhone users—it requires too many compromises to enable features I don’t want badly enough.
The good
A premium look and feel with a satisfying hinge. We didn’t encounter any issues with screen breakage.
Seam between screens is functionally invisible most of the time, a big step up from most other foldables.
Thoughtfully designed multitasking.
Comfortable to hold and use when unfolded.
Apps are being updated to support it reasonably quickly.
Characteristically competent camera system.
Characteristically excellent performance, thanks to the Apple A20 Pro chip.
The bad
$2,000 entry price. That’s more than a pair of iPhone 17s and the same price as the cheapest MacBook Pro.
Outer screen feels cramped.
Camera system isn’t as good as the iPhone Pro’s.
Visible pinhole camera on the inner screen is sometimes distracting.
Matte finish on inner screen shows smudges and makes black levels look less black.
Tacked-on Apple Pencil support.
Fundamentally right-aligned in a way that may be frustrating for lefties.
The ugly
The lack of Face ID and the awkward positioning of the Touch ID button is a small speed bump, but it’s one you’ll hit nearly every time you interact with the phone.
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

articles.title: The Download: Anthropic’s IPO, smarter power grids, and exercise pills
articles.text:
The Download: Anthropic’s IPO, smarter power grids, and exercise pills
Plus: Anthropic's listing could determine the future of the AI investment boom.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Will the real Anthropic please stand up?
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world.
But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology.
These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic.
—Will Douglas Heaven
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.
As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses.
The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.
Find out how solid-state transformers could help meet rising electricity demand.
—Casey Crownhart
Are we there yet? Exercise in a pill
We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks, without the workout.
The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.
Discover how close researchers are to developing an exercise pill.
—Cassandra Willyard
This story is part of “Are we there yet?” from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review. The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Anthropic has filed for its blockbuster IPO
The listing could determine the future of the AI investment boom. (CNBC)
+ The filing warns of catastrophic AI risks and huge compute costs. (BBC)
+ And exposes safety failures and a month-long training pause. (Reuters $)
+ The prospectus reveals soaring revenues but also staggering losses. (NYT $)
+ Anthropic’s founders will retain voting control after the IPO. (Verge) 
2 Solar is quietly overtaking nuclear as a global power source
Cheap panels and batteries are accelerating the shift. (BBC)
+ The balcony solar boom is coming to the US. (MIT Technology Review)
3 OpenAI has announced three new science discoveries
They span mathematics, computer science, and physics. (Verge)
+ It’s enlisted expert "shepherds" to publish its breakthroughs. (Gizmodo)
4 Microsoft is offering buyouts to a quarter of staff amid rising AI costs
Around 60,000 employees are eligible for the buyout program. (Bloomberg $)
+ Microsoft plans $190 billion in AI spending this year. (NYT $)
5 The plastics industry knew microplastics could enter the body decades ago
Company documents reveal concerns dating back to 1974. (LA Times $)
+ No part of the globe is free of human fingerprints. (MIT Technology Review) 
6 A demonstration of lighting Earth from space has sparked alarm
Startup Reflect Orbital used space mirrors for the California test. (Guardian)
+ The tech could jeopardize the night sky. (MIT Technology Review)
7 The US has designated helium a critical material
The move is due to its importance to semiconductor production. (AP)
8 Hundreds of Boston Dynamics staff have protested its ICE deal
They’ve called for a halt to sales of the robot dogs. (Ars Technica)
9 Treatments for age-related infertility are being developed at last
Two startups aim to reduce chromosome errors in eggs. (Economist $)
+ Here’s how tech transformed babymaking. (MIT Technology Review)
10 Grok says its AI-generated Odyssey is “not historically accurate”
The bot itself admitted Elon Musk’s filmmaking plan has failed. (Wired $)
Quote of the day
“It’s as if they’re making a promise and crossing their fingers behind their backs.”
—Kate Brennan, who leads policy at the AI Now Institute, tells the New York Times that the voluntary safety pledges AI executives recently made are toothless and unenforceable.
One more thing
The problem with thinking you’re part Neanderthal
There’s a theory that many of us have an “inner Neanderthal.” The idea is that Homo sapiens and its cousin species once bred, leaving some people today with a trace of Neanderthal DNA.
This DNA is arguably the 21st century’s most celebrated discovery in human evolution. But in 2024, a pair of French geneticists called into question the theory's very foundations.
They proposed that what scientists interpret as interbreeding could instead be explained by population structure—the way genes concentrate in smaller, isolated groups.
Find out what it all means for human evolution.
—Ben Crair
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ See how fast the planets spin with this dizzying animation that puts faces on each one.
+ A flask of mercury, a little neon, and some shaking produce this mesmerizing homemade light.
+ What can the USA’s earliest restaurants teach us about the country? This digital collection explores the answers.
+ Rick and Morty asked the crucial question: could a lightsaber really drill its way to Earth’s core? Science now has an answer.

articles.title: HPE Patches Dozens of Critical Flaws in Networking Products
articles.text:
HPE last week released patches for 72 vulnerabilities in the AOS-8 and AOS-10 wireless operating systems of its Aruba networking products, including 33 critical-severity flaws.
The security updates address eight max-severity bugs: CVE-2026-79844, CVE-2026-79845, CVE-2026-79846, CVE-2026-79847, CVE-2026-79848, CVE-2026-79849, CVE-2026-79850, and CVE-2026-79851.
Successful exploitation of these security defects could allow unauthenticated attackers to achieve remote code execution (RCE), bypass authentication to gain administrative privileges, run arbitrary commands, and completely compromise the affected systems.
HPE Networking’s AOS versions 8.10.0.24, 8.13.3.1, 10.4.1.14, 10.7.2.7, and 10.8.1.2 contain fixes for all eight bugs and have been rolled out across mobility conductor, controller, gateway, and access point products.
The remaining critical-severity issues resolved with the updates could lead to unauthenticated RCE, command execution, information disclosure, authentication bypass, file tampering, administrative access, and complete system compromise, HPE notes in its advisory.
HPE also resolved 31 high-severity vulnerabilities across its networking products, including over a dozen that could be exploited without authentication, eight medium-severity flaws, and one low-severity weakness.
The company notes that all “hardware, mobility solutions (such as conductors, controllers, and gateways), access points, or virtual machines (VMs)” that are compatible with the vulnerable wireless operating systems are also affected by these security issues.
“To minimize the likelihood of an attacker exploiting these vulnerabilities, HPE Networking recommends that the CLI and web-based management interfaces be restricted to a dedicated layer 2 segment/VLAN and/or controlled by firewall policies at layer 3 and above along with accounting controls for tracking and logging user activities and resource usage,” HPE notes.
The company says it is not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, but urges customers to apply the patches as soon as possible.

articles.title: Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs
Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits. Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress. For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job. Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs, which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job.
With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy-loads your container image. It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes. You adopt it by pointing to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image. Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels. The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure.
SOCI-indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance. As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks.
This post shows how to adopt SOCI indexing: what it is, the results we measured, and how to turn it on for your own jobs.
The challenge
SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance. It decompresses and writes every layer to disk.
For small images this takes seconds. But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more. That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time. The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime.
How SOCI indexing works
Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images. Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately. It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it.
A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image. You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI-compliant artifact linked to your original image. Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid.
SageMaker AI checks for an index automatically
When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly:
| Scenario | What happens | 
| The image includes a SOCI index | SageMaker AI lazy-loads the image and starts your container before the full download completes | 
| The image has no SOCI index | Standard download, no change in behavior | 
| The index can’t be read, or lazy loading doesn’t succeed | The job falls back to a standard download and continues running | 
Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running. You only gain faster startup. You never risk breaking an existing workflow.
What we measured
We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI-indexed lazy loading. We then ran full training jobs from both to measure the effect on training speed.
Setup
- Eight images, 1.8–35.4 GB compressed.
- GPU and CPU instances ml.g4dn, ml.g5, ml.g6, ml.g6e, ml.g7, ml.g7e, ml.p4d, ml.p5, and ml.m7i, from xlarge to 48xlarge, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) and the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1).
- Download time measured from the start of the image pull until the container is ready to run. All figures are medians of repeated runs.
Result 1: Download time drops from minutes to seconds at every image size
| Image size (compressed) | Standard download | Lazy loading | Improvement | 
| 1.8 GB | 48 s | 3-11 s | ~8x | 
| 13.2 GB | 3 min 42 s | ~6 s | ~34x | 
| 35.4 GB | 7 min 17 s | 3-11 s | ~38x | 
The following chart compares container image download time for a standard Docker pull against SOCI lazy loading across eight image sizes, from 1.8 GB to 35.4 GB.
Each image size shows two bars. The Docker download time bar (blue) grows steadily with image size, from 48 seconds at 1.8 GB to 7 minutes 17 seconds at 35.4 GB.
A speedup label above each pair shows the ratio of Docker time to SOCI time. Speedups range from approximately 10x for the smallest image to over 35x for the largest.
Standard download time grows with image size because every file is decompressed and written. Lazy loading stayed at 3–11 seconds regardless of size, an 8x–46x improvement. The bigger the image, the more minutes you save.
Result 2: The saving holds on every instance type and size
Running the 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type/size combinations, standard download ranged from 3 min 16 s to 4 min 20 s, while lazy loading held at 6-8 s. That is about 34x faster on every configuration. You don’t need to change instance type or size to benefit.
Result 3: Training performance is unaffected beyond a first-epoch penalty
We ran two kinds of full training jobs from the Docker-pulled and from the SOCI-indexed image and compared every epoch:
- Image classification on ResNet-50 on Imagenette (9,469 images) 
         
  - Container images: PyTorch (13.2 GB DLC) and TensorFlow (9.9 GB DLC)
  - Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g7e.48xlarge, ml.g7.48xlarge, ml.g6e.12xlarge, ml.g6e.24xlarge, and ml.g6e.48xlarge.
- Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning: full-parameter supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Qwen2.5-0.5B on alpaca-cleaned (51,760 examples) with the Hugging Face Trainer. 
         
  - Container image: 9.4 GB Hugging Face PyTorch DLC.
  - Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g6.48xlarge.
The following chart breaks job startup into image download time and first training epoch time, comparing a standard Docker pull with a SOCI-indexed image across GPU and CPU configurations for both workloads.
- From the second epoch on, time per epoch is the same (within run-to-run variation) on every instance, for both workloads.
- The first epoch takes 3–16 s longer from the lazy-loaded image, while files the framework touches for the first time are fetched. This first-epoch cost is the same on every instance size.
- Net: each job finished 1-6 min sooner. That is the download saving minus the one-time first-epoch cost, a fixed saving per job.
Test this on your own workload
These numbers are from the two workloads described earlier. The first-epoch cost depends on your image and what your code touches at startup:
- Lazy loading wins when the first training step needs only a fraction of the image, the rest streams in while you train.
- If your entry point reads most of the image before training starts (for example, scanning, checksumming, or preloading its contents), the first epoch waits for roughly the same bytes a full pull would have fetched. The net improvement would be small.
- Front-loaded starts still came out ahead in our tests: 
         
  - torch.compile and a just-in-time (JIT) built CUDA extension added 7-15 s to the first epoch (net saving still 3 min 25 s–3 min 56 s)
  - A 6 GB model baked into the image streamed its weights at load time, adding 2-3.5 min, but the overall job still finished 2-2.5 mins sooner on the indexed image.
Getting started
You can adopt SOCI indexing two ways: use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container or create an index for your own custom image.
Option 1: Use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container
AWS publishes SOCI-indexed variants of several popular Deep Learning Containers, identified by the -soci suffix on the image tag:
Pre-indexed variants are available for PyTorch Training, TensorFlow Training, vLLM, and SGLang, including arm64 variants for some frameworks. To adopt lazy loading, update the image tag in your job definition to the -soci variant. Browse the full list in the AWS Deep Learning Containers Gallery.
Note: If you build your own image FROM a DLC base image, you must create a SOCI index for your final image. The index from the base image does not carry forward to derived images.
Option 2: Create a SOCI index for your own image
To index a custom image, you need a Linux host (such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance running Amazon Linux 2023) with containerd, the SOCI snapshotter, and either Finch or nerdctl installed.
- Set your environment variables.
- Install the required tools.
- Authenticate to Amazon ECR.
- Pull your original image.
- Create the SOCI-indexed image.
- Push the indexed image.
This creates two artifacts in your repository: the SOCI index and an OCI-compliant image index manifest linking your image to the index. Your original image and its digest remain unchanged.
Automate index creation in CI/CD
To generate indexes automatically on every push, deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder. It uses an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect Amazon ECR image push events and build the index. No changes to your build pipeline are required.
Use the indexed image in your SageMaker AI job
Reference your SOCI-indexed image exactly as you would any other image. No API changes are needed. Only the tag differs.
Training example (SageMaker Python SDK)
Verify that your image includes a SOCI index
Before launching, confirm your tag resolves to an indexed image:
Look for a child manifest whose artifactType begins with application/vnd.amazon.soci.index. alongside your platform manifest. If it isn’t there, the tag does not point to an indexed image.
Things to keep in mind
- Amazon ECR private repositories only. Images in other registries, or pulled through a private Docker registry (TrainingRepositoryAccessMode set to Vpc), are not eligible for lazy loading.
- Improvement scales with image size. Images smaller than roughly 4 GB see relatively small improvements.
- Check for Docker-specific assumptions. SOCI-indexed images run on a containerd-based runtime. Review entry points and setup scripts for code that calls the Docker CLI, reads /var/run/docker.sock, or derives identifiers from cgroup paths. SageMaker AI mounts a /.dockerenv marker for backward compatibility, but avoid adding new dependencies on it.
- SOCI indexing for SageMaker AI jobs is available across all AWS Regions.
Conclusion
With SOCI indexing, you can minimize container image download time from your SageMaker AI training and processing jobs. Add a SOCI index to your images, or switch to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container. Either way, you cut startup time from minutes to seconds, reduce total job cost, and accelerate your machine learning (ML) iteration cycle. And your existing job definitions, API calls, and data pipelines stay exactly the same.
To learn more about Amazon SageMaker AI and start using SOCI indexing, explore the following resources:
- Pick a SOCI-indexed Deep Learning Container. Browse the Deep Learning Containers Gallery and append -soci to your image tag. For framework-specific guidance, see SOCI index for AWS Deep Learning Containers.
- Index your own custom image. Follow the step-by-step walkthrough in the SageMaker AI Developer Guide, or refer to the SOCI snapshotter getting-started guide for advanced options.
- Automate indexing in your CI/CD pipeline. Deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder to generate indexes automatically on every image push. No pipeline changes are required.
- Test locally with Finch. Use the Finch lazy-loading walkthrough to validate your image on a containerd-based runtime before you submit a job.
- Dive deeper into the technology. Read Reducing container cold start times using SOCI index on DLAMI and DLC on the AWS Machine Learning Blog for benchmarks, or explore Under the hood: Lazy loading container images with Seekable OCI and AWS Fargate on the AWS Containers Blog to understand the lazy-loading mechanism in detail.
Faster container startup is only one image tag away. Try it on your next SageMaker AI job and see the difference.

articles.title: Cette borne d’arcade Street Fighter II avec 20 jeux Capcom est disponible en précommande : voici où la réserver
articles.text:
Sorti en 1991, Street Fighter II a marqué durablement l’histoire du jeu vidéo et contribué à populariser les jeux de combat en un contre un. Avec ses personnages emblématiques, ses coups spéciaux et ses affrontements exigeant autant de réflexes que de maîtrise, le titre de Capcom est devenu un incontournable des salles d’arcade, avant d’envahir les foyers du monde entier.
La licence a ensuite donné naissance à plusieurs versions enrichies, avant de s’étendre à de nombreux épisodes et séries dérivées. La borne Iconic Arcade XT veut faire revivre cette époque et réunit plusieurs classiques de Capcom dans une seule machine.
Où précommander la borne d’arcade Street Fighter II de Capcom ?
Affichée à 999,99 €, la borne Iconic Arcade XT Capcom Street Fighter II est annoncée pour le 19 novembre 2026.
Voici les marchands chez qui vous pouvez précommander la borne :
Une borne à l’échelle 9/10 pour retrouver l’ambiance des années 90
La borne Iconic Arcade XT reprend les proportions d’une véritable machine d’arcade, à l’échelle 9/10. Sa fiche technique indique 158 cm de hauteur, pour 56 cm de largeur, 50 cm de profondeur et 26,5 kg. Son design reprend les codes visuels de Street Fighter II, avec une bande lumineuse au-dessus de l’écran et une fausse fente à pièces également éclairée. La machine est livrée en kit à assembler, avec une notice et une vidéo de montage.
Pour faire tourner ses jeux, la borne s’appuie sur un Raspberry Pi 5 et des ROM d’arcade sous licence officielle Capcom. Elle dispose d’un écran LCD de 19,5 pouces de diagonale, ainsi que de commandes de type arcade pensées pour retrouver les sensations des bornes d’époque. Une sortie Micro HDMI permet aussi d’afficher le jeu sur un autre écran ou de diffuser ses parties en streaming. Le fabricant promet enfin le multijoueur en ligne via une future mise à jour, sans donner de date.
La borne ne se limite pas au jeu qui lui donne son nom. Elle embarque 20 classiques de l’arcade Capcom. Côté combat, on trouve plusieurs versions de Street Fighter II, dont Street Fighter II Turbo et Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition, Street Fighter Alpha 2 et Street Fighter Alpha 3, ainsi que Power Stone et Power Stone 2, deux jeux de combat en arène. Les beat’em up Final Fight, Captain Commando, Knights of the Round et Warriors of Fate représentent l’action.
Côté shoot’em up, on trouve GigaWing, GigaWing 2, ProGear, 1944: The Loop Master et Carrier Air Wing. Le beat’em up Dynasty Wars complète la liste. Avec ses 20 jeux préinstallés, cette borne vise ainsi autant les nostalgiques de Street Fighter que les collectionneurs désireux de retrouver plusieurs classiques de l’éditeur sur une machine dédiée.

articles.title: La NASA prépare une solution à un vieux problème d'Orion pour retourner sur la Lune
articles.text:
Orion peut emmener des astronautes jusqu'à la Lune, mais ses réserves de propulsion ne suffisent pas pour rejoindre une orbite lunaire basse et assurer ensuite le retour sur Terre. La NASA prépare un étage de fusée plus puissant pour rapprocher la capsule de la surface.
Les quatre astronautes d'Artemis II ont survolé la Lune en avril 2026 sans entrer en orbite basse autour de notre satellite. Pour les prochaines missions, deux membres d'équipage devront quitter Orion et rejoindre le sol à bord d'un alunisseur. La NASA avait prévu leur rendez-vous sur une orbite très éloignée, afin de préserver les réserves de propulsion du module de service européen de la capsule.
À la conférence du 23 octobre, l'administrateur Jared Isaacman a annoncé un changement de méthode. United Launch Alliance (ULA), qui avait fourni les étages supérieurs des deux premiers vols Artemis, développera une version allongée de Centaur V pour la fusée SLS. La NASA veut ainsi conduire Orion sur une orbite plus basse, afin de réduire le carburant nécessaire aux alunisseurs de SpaceX et Blue Origin.
Un nouvel étage Centaur V pour atteindre une orbite lunaire basse
Avec les plans précédents, Orion devait rejoindre une orbite très allongée autour de la Lune, accessible avec les moyens de propulsion de son module de service européen. La station Gateway devait également circuler sur cette trajectoire. Orion pouvait ainsi économiser son carburant, mais les alunisseurs devaient parcourir une plus grande distance pour déposer deux astronautes sur le sol lunaire et les récupérer ensuite.
Après l'abandon de Gateway en 2026, les ingénieurs ont dû repenser les rendez-vous entre les véhicules. Jared Isaacman a reconnu que rapprocher Orion de la surface imposait de résoudre des problèmes « de propulsion et d'intégration du vaisseau laissés sans réponse depuis bien trop longtemps », d'après le compte rendu de la conférence publié par Ars Technica.
L'agence compte donc sur un nouvel étage supérieur de SLS. Dans son communiqué consacré à Centaur, ULA a précisé que le Centaur 180K emporterait environ 50 % d'ergols supplémentaires par rapport à la version actuelle, grâce à des réservoirs plus longs. Le constructeur modifiera aussi leur matériau et devra adapter l'électronique de bord, avant de qualifier l'ensemble pour un vol habité. Il prépare un exemplaire d'essai et un étage de vol pour une mission Artemis envisagée en 2028.
La NASA n'utilisera pas ce nouvel étage pour Artemis III. Pour cette mission prévue en orbite terrestre en 2027, les équipes de la NASA ont commencé à assembler une version adaptée de SLS. Les quatre astronautes testeront les amarrages avec les prototypes des deux alunisseurs. ULA devra, de son côté, avoir qualifié son nouvel étage pour une mission lunaire envisagée en 2028.
SpaceX et Blue Origin devront rejoindre Orion par des trajets différents
Chez SpaceX, le trajet commencera par une série de lancements de Starship-citernes. D'après le plan de vol présenté par la NASA, SpaceX remplira un dépôt orbital avec ses vaisseaux ravitailleurs, puis transférera le carburant vers le Starship lunaire. Celui-ci rejoindra Orion sur une orbite terrestre haute, puis propulsera l'ensemble vers la Lune. La NASA devra adapter Orion pour lui permettre de supporter cette poussée. Une fois en orbite lunaire basse, deux des quatre astronautes descendront à bord de Starship, tandis que leurs collègues les attendront dans Orion.
Quand le comité consultatif de sécurité de la NASA a évoqué environ 22 vols de ravitaillement, Elon Musk a contesté son estimation et avancé une fourchette de six à huit lancements, rapporte Ars Technica. Jared Isaacman a jugé possible l'estimation du patron de SpaceX, mais seulement lorsque Starship aura atteint son plein potentiel. D'ici là, les transferts de carburants cryogéniques devront être démontrés à grande échelle.
Blue Origin a choisi d'éviter ces transferts pour ses premières missions habitées. Quatre décollages de New Glenn sont prévus, dont trois pour placer en orbite des étages de transfert et un dernier pour lancer l'alunisseur Blue Moon Mark 2. Les étages supplémentaires l'accompagneront ensuite vers la Lune, avant qu'Orion ne rejoigne Blue Moon sur une orbite lunaire elliptique d'environ 8 500 kilomètres d'altitude.
La NASA étudie aussi un rendez-vous à quelques centaines de kilomètres de la Lune. Avec Orion sur une orbite plus basse, Blue Moon consommerait moins de carburant pour descendre puis remonter. En cas d'urgence, les astronautes auraient aussi davantage d'occasions de retrouver rapidement leur capsule. Cet été, Victor Glover, pilote d'Artemis II, avait alerté sur les délais de retour imposés par certaines orbites lunaires.
Avant de transporter un équipage, SpaceX et Blue Origin devront réussir chacune une démonstration d'alunissage sans astronautes. La NASA choisira ensuite l'entreprise chargée de la première descente habitée d'Artemis IV, toujours annoncée pour 2028.

articles.title: Apple iPad Mini 2026: Das kann das neue KI-Tablet wirklich
articles.text:
iPad Mini: Warum Apples kleinstes Tablet jetzt zum KI-Kraftpaket wird
Eigentlich war die Rede davon, dass Apple das neue iPad Mini im Rahmen des „Pro and tell“-Events am 28. Oktober 2026 vorstellen soll. Nun ist das Unternehmen dem zuvorgekommen und hat das neue Tablet schlicht per Pressemeldung angekündigt – vielleicht auch, um von etwaiger Kritik rund um brechende Bildschirme beim iPhone Duo abzulenken. Das ansonsten in den vergangenen Jahren eher stiefmütterlich behandelte Gerät kommt 2026 gleich mit mehreren Neuheiten, die es vom Vorgänger deutlich unterscheiden.
Dünnes Gehäuse, neues OLED-Display
Da wäre zum einen das Gehäuse. Das iPad Mini ist jetzt nur 5,4 Millimeter dick. Bei der letzten Version waren es noch 6,3 Millimeter. Auch in der Höhe (195,3 Millimeter) und in der Breite (132,6 Millimeter) ist es kompakter als der Vorgänger. Trotzdem wächst der Bildschirm. Der misst jetzt nicht mehr 8,3, sondern 8,5 Zoll. Statt eines LC- kommt jetzt ein OLED-Display zum Einsatz. Die Technik liefert sattere Kontraste und stärkere Farben. Wie beim Vorgänger ist das Display laminiert. Es gibt also keinen Hohlraum zwischen Glas und Bildschirm. Gegen Aufpreis ist das iPad Mini auch mit dem sogenannten Nanotexturglas, also einer matten Beschichtung, erhältlich.
Im Inneren taktet jetzt der A20-Pro-Prozessor, der auch in den neuen iPhone-Modellen 18 Pro (Max) und Duo zum Einsatz kommt. Apple spricht von einer bis zu 4,5-mal höheren KI-Performance als beim vorherigen iPad Mini. Die Grafiklistung sei laut 2,7-mal schneller. Zudem dürfte die Leistung im Alltag steigen. Der Hersteller von 1,6-fach schnellerer Performance. Apple-Chips liefern hier allerdings seit jeher mehr als genug Power.
Eine Besonderheit stellt die Variante mit 512 Gigabyte Speicher dar. Deren Prozessor soll mit einer Neural Engine mit 16 Kernen ausgestattet sein und sich für lokale KI-Modelle eignen. So oder so: Das iPad ist mit dem Prozessor fit für Apple Intelligence.
Neben dem Prozessor ist das iPad Mini zudem mit Apples eigenem N1-Chip ausgestattet, der für WLAN- und Bluetooth-Verbindungen zuständig ist. Er unterstützt Wi-Fi 7 und Bluetooth 6 und seine Stärken besonders bei 5-Gigahertz-Verbindungen in drahtlosen Netzwerken aus. Die gegen Aufpreis erhältliche Mobilfunk-Variante ist wie das iPhone 18 Pro mit dem C2-Modem ausgestattet.
iPad Mini: Entertainment und Arbeit
Ein Tastaturfolio für das iPad Mini bietet Apple nach wie vor nicht an, bewirbt das Tablet aber doch als Arbeitsgerät – in Verbindung mit dem Apple Pencil. Das iPad Mini funktioniert sowohl mit dem günstigen Apple Pencil mit USB-C (89 Euro) als auch mit dem Apple Pencil Pro (149 Euro). Darüber hinaus unterstützt das Mini mit dem Update auf iPadOS 27.2 auch den Modus „erweitertes Display“. So sollt ihr auf einem großen Monitor bequemer mit Apps und Fenstern arbeiten können.
Eine weitere Neuerung betrifft ebenfalls den Bildschirm. Apple spricht vom „Accoustic Display“. Hinter dem Bildschirm befinden sich demnach Hoch- und Tieftöner, die den Sound verbessern sollen. Wie gut das klingt, lässt sich natürlich nur anhand eines Tests aussagen.
Das iPad Mini lässt sich ab dem 28. Oktober um 18:10 Uhr vorbestellen und ist regulär ab dem 6. November erhältlich. Es ist in Weiß und Schwarz mit 128, 256 oder 512 Gigabyte Speicher und gegen jeweils Aufpreis mit Mobilfunk und Nanotexturglas erhältlich. Das Basismodell mit WLAN startet bei 749 Euro.

articles.title: Finnish DefenceTech Arctic RAVN secures €2.5 million in loan commitments before its first product launch | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Arctic RAVN, an Espoo-based DefenceTech startup, has secured €2.5 million in convertible loan commitments, surpassing its original €2 million target in under a week.
The round, launched in October 2026, saw investor commitments arrive within just five days, a pace that is a reflection of mounting demand for European-made drone components as Western militaries push to reduce reliance on Chinese-origin supply chains.
“Investors committed to the round within days, even though we have not yet officially launched a single product,” said Matti Vansén, CEO, Arctic RAVN.
Arctic RAVN was founded in 2025 as a studio company within Finnish Defence House, a DefenceTech venture studio that identifies, funds and builds companies. The company manufactures drone electronics designed specifically for battlefield conditions, and its product range includes electronic speed controllers (ESCs), flight controllers (FCs), motors, and a modular frame system.
All products are engineered and assembled in Finland, with components sourced entirely from Europe and NATO-allied countries. The company explicitly positions itself as an answer to Western defence’s long-standing dependency on Chinese-origin drone components.
Arctic RAVN says it has already invested more than €1 million in scaling up manufacturing of its electronic speed controller and aims to produce tens of thousands of ESC units before the end of 2026, with a significant share already reserved by customers. The company says its customers already include several well-known European defence industry players, though it has not publicly named them.
With the next production phase, it plans to shift its focus to flight controllers. Arctic RAVN’s raise comes as European governments and NATO allies accelerate their effort to move away from Chinese-origin drone components and build indigenous drone supply chains.
Arctic RAVN structured the raise as a convertible loan, a financing instrument commonly used by early-stage companies that allows investors to convert their debt into equity at a later date, typically at a discount. With the loan commitments closing 25% above target without a single product launched, it shows demand for the company’s products and trust in its ability to execute.
“Follow-up orders and discussions with several leading defence manufacturers indicate a need for high-performance European drone electronics. We are now scaling our manufacturing capabilities for industrial-level output and strengthening Europe’s ability to produce critical drone electronics,” added Vansén.
The fresh capital will support two immediate priorities: production scale-up and product development. The startup says it has already received follow-up orders and is in active discussions with several leading European defence manufacturers.
It has set itself an ambitious target of annual production capacity of up to two million circuit boards per year, the scale that would immediately position it as one of Europe’s major producers of drone electronics.

articles.title: Talent diplomacy may become the next driver of global economic growth
articles.text:
Talent diplomacy may become the next driver of global economic growth
As ageing populations and skill shortages weigh on economies worldwide, countries are looking beyond immigration to build structured talent partnerships. India has an opportunity to emerge as a trusted global hub for workforce readiness, backed by skills training, tech and verifiable credentials.
The drivers of economic power have always traditionally been accessing to capital, energy, technology, and markets; but more nations are now running up against that much more difficult resource to generate fast talent.
Unlike capital, talent is not something that can be conjured out of thin air overnight, it takes years to educate, train, and ready the workforce. But at the same time that world economies are in need of more workers, the number of people available is declining.
Healthcare offers one of the most transparent indicators of this situation. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates a shortfall of 11. 1 million health and care professionals worldwide by 2030. Other sectors including manufacturing logistics hospitality, construction, and trades are experiencing similar pressures. Workforce numbers in many advanced countries are declining even as the need for core functions increases. There are declining numbers of people undertaking physically demanding jobs, leaving serious structural deficits difficult to address solely through large-scale migration.
What's left unsaid is huge: skills shortages are no longer an employment issue. They are a drag on economic growth. Countries are free to scale up investments in infrastructure, industrial capacity and technological advances, if they lack the people to run them, where is the growth?
Talent partnerships reshape economic diplomacy
Demographic decline is prompting governments to reconsider avenues for future growth. One-third of the EU population will be over 65 by the year 2050 and countries, including Japan and Germany, are already experiencing dire skill shortages within care and the healthcare sector.
Their answer has gone further than simply immigration reform. Germany's Skilled Immigration Act, Japan's increases of avenues for foreign workers and the EU's Talent Partnerships are part of a bigger change: policy makers are now starting to see "talent as a strategic asset".
These agreements are increasingly targeted on preparing the work force, recognising qualifications and moving workers, not only on visas. As countries used to compete for market access, energy, and supply chains, they are now forming partnerships to enjoy access to skilled people.
That may be one of the biggest changes to economic diplomacy in the coming decade.
India can become a global hub for workforce readiness
India’s opportunity should not be framed as the export of labour. It lies in becoming a trusted global centre for workforce readiness.
India’s domestic healthcare requirements must remain central to this approach. Responsible mobility should generate additional training capacity rather than draw indiscriminately from areas that already.
Encouragingly, this shift is already visible in policy. India plans to establish 30 Skill India International Centres focused on preparing individuals for overseas employment, while NSDC has certified over 22,455 candidates for international mobility over the past three years. The 2026 International Mobility Framework released by NITI Aayog further signals a shift in thinking, calling for greater state participation in global workforce mobility. Collectively, this suggests a larger shift where mobility of the workforce is a national asset helping create stronger economic partnerships, talent corridors, and help make India a trusted partner for the global workforce.
Technology must build trusted talent corridors
As opposed to taking over the role of educators, AI technology can assist in individualised learning, language training, workplace simulations, and competency evaluation.
Technology may minimise the information discrepancies, which have traditionally plagued international recruiting efforts. Employers require assurance that the credentials and experience are legitimate, while applicants require assurance about the legitimacy of the offer itself, along with its costs and conditions of employment.
This is increasingly becoming a competitive differentiator. ASEAN chases digital recognition of qualifications and credentials to enable smoother cross-border mobility.
For India, the opportunity is to make workforce readiness portable, verifiable and trusted. Technology can become the infrastructure that allows Indian professionals to prove their preparedness across markets, reducing friction for both employers and destination countries.
Though India's demographic weight is not the only one in an increasingly crowded field of developing countries, that invested years in creating structured talent corridors with host countries. Globally, over 8,000 nurses from Germany's Triple Win programme through government to government-built recruitment and training setups, while Japan's long standing health mobility corridors with Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam span language training, credentialing, and governance.
The real competition, therefore, is not for vacancies. It is for trust. Workforce shortages as a strategic challenge for ageing economies creates diplomacy where workforce readiness determines which nations become indispensable partners in supporting global growth.
(Mayank Kumar is the Co-founder & CEO of BorderPlus)

articles.title: Energy giant ENGIE discloses data breach affecting customers
articles.text:
French energy giant ENGIE, one of the world's largest power and natural gas providers, confirmed that attackers stole customer data after breaching a marketing platform used by business partners.
ENGIE operates in renewable energy, infrastructure, and customer energy supply in 30 countries, employs over 90,000 people, and reported €71.9 billion in revenue last year.
An ENGIE spokesperson told BleepingComputer that it cut off the attackers' access to the compromised platform and that they didn't breach the company's internal systems.
"ENGIE's internal IT systems were not compromised. ENGIE recently identified unusual data access activity within a tool used by partners as part of their customer prospecting activities and the marketing of energy offers," the spokesperson said.
The ENGIE spokesperson didn't say how many customers were affected, but told BleepingComputer the incident is limited to customers in France.
Since the attack, ENGIE has notified relevant authorities and contacted affected customers to inform them of the breach.
"The investigations conducted to date indicate that the data concerned is limited to customers' contact details and certain information relating to their energy contracts. No banking data is affected," ENGIE told BleepingComputer.
"In the interest of transparency, ENGIE individually informed each customer concerned and reminded them of the precautionary measures they should take to protect themselves against potential fraud or phishing attempts."
Although the company didn't share what customer information was stolen in the attack, it said in breach notification letters sent to affected customers that the threat actors gained access to their first and last names, mailing address, email address, phone number, Delivery Point (PDL) or Metering and Estimation Point (PCE), customer ID, and contract number.
ENGIE didn't attribute the attack to a specific threat group, and no ransomware operation or extortion gang has claimed the ENGIE breach before publication.
One year ago, the Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters extortion group also leaked records they claimed to have stolen after allegedly breaching a Salesforce instance of Engie Records, the retail energy supply subsidiary of ENGIE North America.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Hiding Capabilities in AI Models - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Hiding Capabilities in AI Models
Interesting research: “AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities”
Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.
K.S • October 27, 2026 12:35 PM
Does difficulty of elicitation also corresponds to difficulty of detecting presence? I speculate that statistical testing might detect embedded encrypted neural networks even if they can’t be surfaced, similar to how entropy analysis is used to flag encrypted regions in binaries.

articles.title: Installez-vite iOS 27.2 sur votre iPhone, Apple corrige plus de 160 failles de sécurité
articles.text:
Ce lundi 26 octobre, Apple a déployé iOS 27.2 sur tous les iPhone compatibles. C’est la première grande mise à jour d’iOS 27, et elle n’est pas avare en nouveautés. La mise à jour propose plusieurs améliorations de Siri AI, qui s’ouvre enfin à cinq nouvelles langues, dont le français. L’assistant IA reste néanmoins indisponible dans l’Union européenne jusqu’à nouvel ordre.
À lire aussi : Apple corrige une faille zero-day sur iPhone, iPad et Mac, installez vite la mise à jour
Des failles d’Apple Intelligence et de Safari
Surtout, iOS 27.2 corrige plus de 160 vulnérabilités de sécurité dans le système d’exploitation d’Apple. Le géant de Cupertino a notamment colmaté une faille d’Apple Intelligence, sa suite d’outils d’IA générative. En exploitant la brèche, un pirate pouvait accéder à des données sensibles tout en restant à distance.
Citons aussi un bug de « Masquer mon adresse e-mail », la fonction qui génère des adresses e-mail aléatoires pour masquer la vraie, pour des raisons de confidentialité. Au lieu de cacher l’information, la fonction exposait au contraire dans certains cas la véritable adresse de l’utilisateur. Apple a aussi colmaté plus de 30 failles dans WebKit, le moteur qui fait tourner Safari, et une quinzaine dans le noyau du système.
Une grande partie des correctifs visent à empêcher des applications malveillantes d’accéder à vos données ou au hardware de l’iPhone sans permission. La caméra, le Bluetooth, votre photothèque, vos contacts ou même la liste des applications installées font partie des éléments qui sont scrupuleusement préservés par Apple.
Quelques failles débusquées par l’IA
Bonne nouvelle, Apple précise qu’aucune des failles n’a été activement exploitée par des pirates. Une fois que les détails des failles ont été rendus publics, les appareils qui n’ont pas encore été mis à jour deviennent néanmoins des cibles. Il faut s’attendre à ce que des cybercriminels ne tardent pas à se servir des vulnérabilités dans des cyberattaques. Notez que l’intelligence artificielle a joué un rôle dans la découverte de plusieurs vulnérabilités. En effet, Anthropic et OpenAI sont respectivement crédités dans 3 et 4 correctifs.
Pour installer la mise à jour, rendez-vous dans Réglages > Général > Mise à jour logicielle, puis appuyez sur « Télécharger et installer ». Par sécurité, Apple recommande de sauvegarder votre iPhone, de le brancher au Wi-Fi et de vérifier qu’il dispose d’au moins 50% de batterie avant de lancer l’opération. Sans surprise, Apple n’oublie pas les iPhone trop anciens pour passer à iOS 27. Le groupe américain a en effet déployé en parallèle iOS 26.7.2, une mise à jour qui embarque une grande partie des correctifs de sécurité d’iOS 27.2.

articles.title: El parque eólico de Muel sustituye 27 aerogeneradores por solo tres y aumenta su producción más de un 50%
articles.text:
Algo está cambiando en Aragón. Por lo menos, en el paisaje. El parque eólico de Muel (Zaragoza) ha sustituido 27 aerogeneradores antiguos por tres de última generación que tendrán una potencia instalada de 19,97 MW.
Es uno de los primeros proyectos eólicos terrestres de la región que se somete a un plan de modernización tan ambicioso, El proceso de repotenciación comenzó en 2025 y culminó con la puesta en marcha del nuevo parque a finales de ese año. El 8 de octubre de 2026 se celebró oficialmente su nueva etapa.
Al final de su vida útil. Tras años proporcionando electricidad, las 27 turbinas originales que se instalaron en 1997 con una capacidad combinada de 16,2 MW llegaron en 2025 al final de su vida útil. El saldo de casi tres décadas produciendo ha sido de un total de 800 gigavatios hora, según cuentan desde RWE Renewables Iberia, la empresa titular de la explotación.
Este proyecto de repotenciación ha recibido financiación del Mecanismo de Recuperación y Resiliencia a través del PRTR/NextGenerationEU, así como la consideración de iniciativa ejemplar por su impacto positivo en la economía local, como indica el Heraldo.
Menos unidades, más energía. Ahora, estas unidades antiguas han sido sustituidas por tan solo tres turbinas nuevas de 6,6 MW cada una, con una capacidad total instalada de 19,97 MW. Cada nueva turbina tiene alrededor de 11 veces la potencia de cada una de las antiguas.
RWE asegura que la producción permitirá pasar de abastecer unos 9.400 hogares a unos 21.000. Como cuenta El Español, el incremento en la producción ha sido de más de un 50% y, al mismo tiempo, se ha mejorado la integración ambiental del parque y se ha reducido su impacto paisajístico.
El entorno, uno de los factores clave. Precisamente el impacto ambiental es uno de los aspectos más debatidos en la transición energética. Aunque son innegables los beneficios que genera como fuente de energía limpia, un parque eólico altera inevitablemente la percepción del paisaje y la configuración natural del entorno, con una intrusión visual a gran escala. Los aerogeneradores pueden superar fácilmente los 100 metros de altura y su constante movimiento puede crear efectos indeseados en los pueblos cercanos, como por ejemplo, el shadow flicker: un efecto de parpadeo de sombras que puede resultar bastante molesto.
De ahí que la reducción de unidades como esta de Muel pueda contribuir a mitigar ese lado menos amable de la transición energética.
No todo acabará en chatarra. Otra buena noticia de este ‘renove’ es que, según RWE, el desmantelamiento se hará de acuerdo con soluciones de economía circular y cero residuos que reciclarán gran parte de los componentes. La empresa que lo llevará a cabo será RenerCycle y se encargará de reacondicionar 1.350 componentes antiguos que se utilizarán en otros parques eólicos de RWE. También recuperarán 1.825 toneladas métricas de material férrico y conseguirán reciclar el 95% de los materiales.
En cuanto a las palas, estas se reciclarán en la planta de reciclaje de palas eólicas Waste2Fiber®, a través de una tecnología de tratamiento térmico que permitirá reutilizar las fibras en diferentes aplicaciones industriales.

articles.title: Un look de Classe G pour une fraction du prix : les SUV chinois iCaur arrivent en France dès 2027 — Frandroid
articles.text:
Arrivé fin 2025 en France avec sa marque Omoda Jaecoo, le groupe chinois Chery semble être là pour rester et étend patiemment sa toile.
Après avoir lancé sa gamme éponyme le 1er septembre 2026, le groupe de Wuhu (province d’Anhui) compte lancer en 2027 des marques supplémentaires.
    Pour aller plus loin
Le nouveau Volkswagen ? Comment le géant chinois Chery a dépassé BYD en Europe avec 7 marques de voitures électriques et hybrides
            
Outre Lepas, à mi-chemin entre le généraliste et le premium, nous avons appris que Chery compte également lancer sa marque iCaur, dédiée aux SUV électriques et à prolongateurs d’autonomie, avec trois modèles au look qui feront à coup sûr parler d’eux.
Trois SUV et un nom modifié
En Chine, la marque s’appelle iCar – pour l’export, Chery a dû la rebaptiser en un assez maladroit iCaur pour d’évidentes raisons de propriété intellectuelle ; à vrai dire, on ne sait même pas comment Apple a autorisé ce nom en Chine. Passons.
iCaur s’est spécialisée dans les SUV au look pour le moins différenciant, mêlant des inspirations à vrai dire peu subtiles de Jeep Wrangler, de Mercedes-Benz Classe G ou de Land Rover Defender, mais efficaces et adroitement remis au goût du jour.
Trois modèles seront vendus en France. La gamme débutera par le V23, un petit SUV électrique de 4,22 m de long proposé en Chine avec deux batteries : une de 60 kWh, offrant 401 km d’autonomie selon le cycle chinois CLTC (environ 340 km WLTP selon notre estimation, le modèle n’étant pas encore homologué en Europe), et une de 80 kWh, boostant l’autonomie à 550 km CLTC (environ 460 km WLTP). Une alternative sacrément originale aux Renault 4 E-Tech ou un Volkswagen ID. Cross.
Pour la taille au-dessus, il faudra passer à l’iCaur V25 de 4,64 m de long, qui s’offre ici les services d’une motorisation électrique à prolongateur d’autonomie (un moteur essence sert de générateur pour recharger la batterie de 33,67 kWh). La version la plus évoluée propose jusqu’à 1 240 km d’autonomie cumulée CLTC (environ 1 050 km WLTP), dont 210 km CLTC sur les batteries (environ 175 km WLTP).
Enfin, l’iCaur V27 chapeautera la gamme du haut de ses 5,07 m de long. Ici aussi, le choix du prolongateur d’autonomie a été retenu, mais la batterie peut atteindre 51,2 kWh, de quoi parcourir 300 km CLTC sur les batteries (environ 250 km WLTP) et 1 300 km CLTC en ajoutant le plein d’essence (environ 1 100 km WLTP).
Encore quelques questions en suspens
Selon nos informations, iCaur arrivera début 2027 en France avec le V25 et le V27 ; le V23 suivra dans un second temps, des évolutions structurelles étant nécessaires avant son homologation – nous n’en savons pas plus.
De même, nous n’avons pas eu de certitude sur les motorisations retenues. En France, les voitures électriques à prolongateurs d’autonomie cumulent les tares : comptabilisées par l’Union européenne comme des voitures électriques, elles subissent les surtaxes douanières ; comptabilisées en France comme des voitures hybrides, elles subissent le malus masse. De quoi possiblement grever leur attractivité tarifaire.
Côté tarifs, seuls les prix chinois sont connus : le V23 débute à 109 800 yuans (environ 14 700 euros), le V25 est en prévente depuis le 19 octobre à partir de 139 800 yuans (environ 18 700 €), le V27 démarre à 169 800 yuans (environ 22 700 €). Ces montants ne préjugent pas des prix français : droits de douane, transport, équipement et malus viendront s’y ajouter, et iCaur n’a encore donné aucun tarif européen.
Le réseau de distribution sera lui aussi à construire en parallèle de celui de Chery et d’Omoda Jaecoo ; bref, encore quelques étapes à franchir, mais cette marque pourrait bien apporter un sacré boost d’image pour ce groupe chinois, plutôt connu pour ses SUV hybrides aux tarifs bien positionnés.

It’s Moonshot week! ☀️ ️️️
We’re officially renaming Q4 the “IPO quarter.” Any company that went public before October may have to do the whole thing again, properly this time.
But on a serious note, Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, filed to list on Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” on Monday, joining an already busy quarter for public market debuts.
Closer to home, Quickmart, Kenya’s second-largest supermarket chain, has expanded the cornerstone allocation in its KES 15 billion ($116 million) IPO to 48% after three more institutional investors joined the offer.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Startups
Klump shuts down after five years of trying to make BNPL work
Klump wanted to make taking a loan feel as quick as buying a pair of shoes online. Five years later, the Nigerian buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) startup is shutting down after discovering that fast credit still needs one expensive ingredient: money to lend.
What happened? Klump, founded in 2021 by Celestine Omin and Olufunbi Falayi, has closed after raising about $1.2 million across two rounds. The startup let shoppers split purchases into instalments at checkout and eventually powered financing for hundreds of merchants, including Jumia, Konga, SLOT, and iStore. Seedcamp, the UK-based investor, led its $780,000 pre-seed round in 2022.
Explain like I’m new here: Klump initially funded loans from its own books. Owning the loan book meant it could decide who qualified and return a credit decision in minutes, exactly what an online checkout needed.
But lending at scale requires far more capital than building software, Omin wrote on October 25. Klump tried to raise debt to fund more loans but could not secure enough.
So it changed the model. Instead of lending, Klump became the pipe connecting shoppers and merchants to banks and other lenders. By July, shoppers on e-commerce platform Jumia could choose financing from multiple lenders directly at checkout.
Between the lines: The pivot solved one problem and created another. Klump no longer needed to finance every purchase, but its growth now depended on banks. Integrations took six to 18 months, sometimes years. Lenders decided which sectors they would finance, how much they would lend, and how much risk they would tolerate.
Klump’s problem captures BNPL’s difficult economics. Finance the loans yourself, and you need a deep pool of debt. Let banks fund them and your product moves at bank speed.
Zoom out: Klump explored acquisition options before shutting down, including talks with Kenya’s Lipa Later, which itself entered administration in 2025. Its founders now say BNPL may work better as a feature inside a larger financial services company than as a standalone business.
Klump proved people wanted instalments at checkout. It could not build enough control over the capital behind them.

Banking
FNB, South Africa’s second-largest bank, fined $60,000 for exposing private customer data
Because of their business, banks usually hold valuable and sensitive customer information—names, ID numbers, addresses, salaries, account details, and loan applications. Keeping that data safe is a great responsibility. When banks fail to do so, it sends ripples throughout the ecosystem.
First National Bank (FNB), South Africa’s second-largest lender, unfortunately became susceptible to that risk. On October 23, the Information Regulator fined the bank R1 million ($60,000) for that failure.
What happened? South Africa’s privacy regulator said FNB violated the country’s data protection law, the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA). An error in FNB’s banking system wrongly classified some account holders as employees, giving 696 unauthorised people access to personal information belonging to 88 home-loan applicants.
Explain like I’m new here: South Africa’s POPIA governs how organisations handle personal data. The regulator found that FNB breached several provisions, including unlawfully processing an account number. It also said FNB was alerted twice, in March and May 2022, but only acknowledged the second complaint in September.
There’s more: The regulator also flagged how FNB collected and kept personal data. It said the bank wrongly used newspaper reports to build databases on people linked to money laundering and politically exposed persons, because newspaper articles do not count as public records under POPIA.
FNB’s retention policy was also criticised for keeping some records—including cancelled tax certificates, asset ownership records, and securities registers—indefinitely without a stated legal basis.
What now? FNB has 30 days to pay the R1 million ($60,000) fine, agree to pay in instalments, or take the matter to court. If it does none of these, the regulator can recover the fine as a civil judgment.
More value with Mycoverai
You already have a great product. With MyCover.ai, create tailored insurance for your customers across fintech, e-commerce, logistics and more, built around your product, and their needs. Get started here.
Ecommerce
Pick n Pay closes 19 more stores as losses narrow
Pick n Pay is shrinking in size to get healthy again. The South African supermarket chain has closed another 19 stores over the past year, while its half-year headline loss narrowed nearly 32% to R299 million ($18 million).
What happened? Pick n Pay’s turnover was almost flat at R36.4 billion ($2.2 billion) in the six months to August, but gross profit rose 3.9%, and its trading loss narrowed 16.9% to R516 million ($31 million). Online sales were a bright spot, growing 35.4%.
The company now has 520 supermarkets and is targeting a return to profit in its 2029 financial year.
Explain like I’m new here: Pick n Pay is one of South Africa’s oldest and best-known supermarket brands. Raymond Ackerman bought four stores in Cape Town in 1967 and built them into a national retailer. But more than a decade of losing market share to rivals such as Shoprite—the country’s largest supermarket chain by revenue and store count—eventually left its core supermarket business in trouble.
The rescue began in 2024. Pick n Pay raised R4 billion ($240 million) through a rights issue, then sold 34.4% of its faster-growing Boxer discount chain for R8.5 billion ($510.5 million). The money reduced debt and bought the company time to repair the Pick n Pay business.
Between the lines: The turnaround is entering a different phase. Closing bad stores, cutting costs, and staff management can improve the numbers. Now Pick n Pay needs shoppers back.
It is also turning to sports to drive that strategy after backing Springboks, South Africa’s world-champion national rugby team. Its six-year Springboks sponsorship is part of that push. Rugby collectables are bringing customers into stores, while Pick n Pay has exclusive rights to sell cheaper Springbok merchandise. Sean Summers, the company’s chief executive officer, said merchandise sales have been “absolutely phenomenal.”
The first phase of the turnaround was about survival. The next is about relevance.
What to watch: Same-store sales. Pick n Pay’s company-owned South African supermarkets recorded 2.4% same-store sales growth in the first half of 2026. Closing another weak store improves the cost base; getting more people through the remaining stores is what eventually gets Pick n Pay back to profit.
Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world!
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
Pay-TV
DStv is cutting Kenya prices to win back viewers
DStv, the pay-TV platform owned by MultiChoice, has been reshuffling its prices and packages. First in South Africa, now in Kenya. What caught our attention is that MultiChoice has unbundled sports into a standalone package in both markets. Meanwhile, Nigeria is still waiting for the same treatment.
What happened? Canal+-owned MultiChoice is replacing six DStv packages with four in Kenya. From November 5, prices will range from KES 750 ($6) for Starter to KES 7,300 ($56) for Ultimate, down from KES 11,700 ($90) for Premium. That is a 38% cut at the top end.
The Sports package will cost KES 3,000 ($23) and include Premier League and UEFA Champions League matches, plus UFC and WWE.
Explain like I’m new here: DStv is trying to stop a subscriber decline that has been building for years. MultiChoice ended 2025 with 14.4 million subscribers, down from 14.9 million in the previous year. Canal+ has responded with a €100 million ($112 million) growth plan built around simpler packages, lower entry costs and stronger distribution, while shutting down loss-making Showmax to cut costs. MultiChoice expects a €140 million ($157 million) loss in 2026, hit by weaker revenue and rising costs
Will cheaper DStv bring people back? DStv has already tried cheaper packages and promotions in markets such as South Africa, but price alone cannot fix the subscriber problem. Its competition is no longer limited to pay-TV rivals such as StarTimes and Zuku.
Viewers can instead spend their time and money on Netflix, YouTube, TikTok, and other streaming services. Interestingly, Netflix, one of Africa’s widely-streamed platforms, is facing its own problems, as watch hours decline globally.
Is it an attention span problem, electricity outages, cost, or are users just deprioritising entertainment services in the pecking order?
MultiChoice is approaching the problem from all angles that it can control. GOtv gives price-sensitive customers another option within the same group. Canal+ is betting that cheaper entry points and easier access to sports will give DStv a reason to stay in the monthly budget.

articles.title: Unexplained DreamHost Incident Prompts Email, FTP Password Resets
articles.text:
Over the weekend, web hosting provider DreamHost suspended its File Manager service and reset some user passwords.
The company says it took protective actions in response to “an issue” with its systems, which affected File Manager at files.dreamhost.com and DreamHost webmail.
“As a precaution, we are resetting passwords for some email and FTP/SFTP users,” the company warned on Friday.
It also notified DreamHost account owners via private communication (shared on Reddit), noting that users would need to set new passwords when logging in, and underlining that DreamHost would not request password resets via email.
“We are contacting you because you are the DreamHost account owner, and only you will be able to set new passwords for these users. DreamHost is unable to contact individual mailbox or FTP users directly, so they may not know about this until you tell them,” the company said.
“If they used the old password anywhere else, they should change it there too,” DreamHost told account owners.
Users complained about DreamHost’s lack of transparency, and some speculated that the passwords may have been compromised and questioned whether they were properly hashed.
In the meantime, DreamHost says it has created and deployed a fix to the File Manager and restored access to http://files.dreamhost.com.
“We are monitoring the situation to ensure that the File Manager is back in a fully operational state,” the company said on Monday.
SecurityWeek has emailed DreamHost for information on the number of affected users and the root cause of the incident and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: "Se acabó, la IA ganó": Google Gemini 4 Argon destruye una conjetura de fusión nuclear de 59 años en solo unas pocas horas
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Argon de Google ha ayudado a descubrir nuevas soluciones matemáticas relacionadas con la fusión nuclear. Los primeros candidatos se encontraron en cuestión de horas, según los investigadores. Esto supone una mejora con respecto al trabajo anterior, que refutó una conjetura formulada en 1967. Las aplicaciones prácticas se refieren a las pruebas del software que simula campos magnéticos para la investigación en fusión.
La conjetura lleva el nombre del físico Harold Grad. Aborda las ecuaciones que rigen el equilibrio del plasma y el campo magnético que lo rodea. El objetivo es identificar equilibrios estacionarios tridimensionales compatibles con un conjunto dado de condiciones de presión y simetría.
Cómo se encontraron las nuevas soluciones
La investigación que se publicó en arXiv es el resultado del esfuerzo conjunto de Opal Issan, Jonathan Citrin, Matt Landreman y Brendan Tracey. Los autores generalizaron las dos familias de soluciones anteriores mediante un parámetro en cada una, que rompe la simetría de stellarator. Los stellarators son dispositivos de fusión que utilizan campos magnéticos tridimensionales para contener el plasma.
Con el fin de encontrar generalizaciones de las familias de soluciones conocidas, los autores entregaron la investigación de Landreman y sus preguntas abiertas a un pequeño equipo de agentes de Gemini 4 en Google Antigravity. Los avances mencionados por los investigadores se lograron en cuestión de horas.
El Argon de Google también contribuyó a la escritura de partes del manuscrito, así como a la codificación de comprobaciones simbólicas y numéricas. Los autores humanos supervisaron el proceso de investigación y realizaron varias rondas de revisión adversarial, así como la reescritura del manuscrito.
Los investigadores volvieron a derivar y comprobar simbólicamente cada desarrollo y asumieron la responsabilidad del resultado final. El tiempo mencionado se refiere al periodo en el que unos agentes de IA encontraron los primeros candidatos prometedores.
A la vista del ejemplo mencionado anteriormente, cabe afirmar que se repartió el mérito. Gómez-Serrano, Liehr y Taylor habían expuesto otros contraejemplos a Grad el 21 de septiembre de 2026. Sus soluciones no presentan las simetrías de reflexión planar, axial o helicoidal que postula la conjetura. El resumen de su investigación incluye un sello de aprobado en Lean 4, un asistente de prueba matemática.
A continuación, Landreman presentó sus soluciones analíticas el 22 de septiembre de 2026. Según contó, las soluciones analíticas que él pudo encontrar con la ayuda del GPT-6 Astra Pro fueron comprobadas manualmente por él. La versión revisada se publicó el 28 de septiembre. Cuando se les presentó el problema a los agentes de Gemini, ya disponían tanto de las soluciones de Landreman como de preguntas concretas que requerían respuestas.
El sello de aprobado en Lean 4 figura en la investigación de Gómez-Serrano y sus colaboradores. El artículo de Gemini también menciona otra comprobación. Los investigadores también realizaron cálculos que se verificaron simbólicamente. El manuscrito mencionado anteriormente no declara un sello de aprobado en Lean para los hallazgos. La mención del código de comprobación simbólica y numérica tampoco permite dar por sentado dicho sello.
El acceso a Argon y la publicación científica
En la hemeroteca de septiembre de 2024 hay más ejemplos de formas en que la inteligencia artificial ha facilitado la investigación en fusión nuclear. Los científicos han utilizado la nueva tecnología en la investigación de patrones de turbulencia y en la detección de defectos en soldaduras.
Google mencionó la investigación cuando anunció el 13 de octubre de 2026 el lanzamiento del Argon para su uso comercial. Argon está ahora disponible a través de la API y para suscriptores de Google AI Pro y Ultra en la aplicación Gemini y en el Modo IA del buscador, y de Google AI Ultra en Antigravity.
Se han abierto también las solicitudes para que 10.000 científicos reciban gratuitamente seis meses de acceso al nivel de mayor uso de Antigravity, sujetos a los requisitos de acceso, la capacidad y la selección del programa.

articles.title: Windows 11 : terminé le raccourci Bing, Microsoft intègre un vrai de test de débit
articles.text:
Windows 11 : terminé le raccourci Bing, Microsoft intègre un vrai de test de débit
Microsoft va enfin corriger le tir avec son pratique, mais très imparfait outil de test de vitesse de connexion Internet sur Windows 11. Il s'agit cette fois d'une véritable intégration au système d’exploitation.
Microsoft Windows 11 Professionnel
En septembre 2025, Microsoft annonçait l'arrivée dans Windows 11 d'un outil fort pratique : un speedtest, ou test de débit de la connexion à Internet. Logé dans les paramètres rapides de l'OS via un nouveau bouton dédié, celui-ci a finalement eu l'effet d'une douche froide. Plutôt que de réaliser le test directement depuis l'interface de Windows 11, l'outil actuel lance une recherche Bing pour effectuer la mesure dans votre navigateur par défaut (au moins, ce n'est pas forcément Microsoft Edge). En ce mois d'octobre 2026, Microsoft a décidé de faire mieux.
Test de débit Internet : un speedtest enfin intégré à Windows 11
Dans la nouvelle build en test depuis le 23 octobre 2026, cet outil fonctionne enfin comme il aurait dû le faire depuis le début, à savoir directement dans l'interface de Windows 11. En une poignée de clics, la vitesse de téléchargement et téléversement, ainsi que le ping, s'affichent dans une fenêtre dédiée, sans jamais ouvrir le navigateur.
Trois méthodes permettent d'accéder à ce nouvel outil : un clic-droit sur l'icône de réseau, dans le volet wifi ou réseau mobile, ou depuis une tuile dans les paramètres rapides. Microsoft note que ce test de débit s'appuie sur le moteur actuellement disponible via le navigateur.
Comme toujours, la date de déploiement de cette nouveauté auprès du grand public, via une mise à jour stable, n'est pas encore connue. Il s'agit en tout cas d'une preuve supplémentaire que Microsoft écoute les retours des utilisateurs, tâchant d'améliorer un Windows 11 initialement mal-aimé.
Smartphone Android : des commandes étendues depuis les paramètres rapides
Cette amélioration du speedtest est accompagnée d'une autre nouveauté dans la dernière build à destination des testeurs, à savoir un contrôle de son smartphone depuis les paramètres rapides. Dans un encart dédié, des boutons pour régler certaines fonctionnalités d'un terminal Android compatible (ne pas déranger, vibration/son...) sont ainsi proposés.
