articles.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
articles.text:
MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.
- Share:
A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.
The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.
By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.
In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.
"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "
A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle
The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.
Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.
"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."
The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.
From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot
The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.
For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.
When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.
The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.
"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."
For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.
They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.
The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.
To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.
"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."
Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot
Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.
The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.
This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.
The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.
By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.
Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.
The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.
The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.
How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim
With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.
The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.
Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.
"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."
To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.
As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.
Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.
The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.
"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."
The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Jennifer Chu. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Maheera Bawa, Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, Seanbiron Johnson, Ritu Raman. 2D Skeletal Muscle Thin Film Actuators Enhance Efficiency of Biohybrid Robots. Advanced Functional Materials, 2026; DOI: 10.1002/adfm.78065

articles.title: Pídele a ChatGPT una crítica honesta y sin filtro de ti con este prompt: la IA no tendrá piedad
articles.text:
Pedirle a ChatGPT que destroce tu personalidad, tus hábitos o tu perfil de Instagram se convirtió en una de las tendencias en redes sociales. El desafío consiste en cargar información personal al chatbot y ordenarle que sea brutalmente honesto, sin filtros ni suavizados.
El proceso es simple y eso explica buena parte de su viralidad. Basta con escribir un pedido directo y esperar una respuesta que mezcla sarcasmo, humor, observación y, en algunos casos, una precisión incómoda sobre quien hace la consulta.
Cómo es el prompt para pedir la opinión de ChatGPT
La versión más difundida pide al chatbot un diagnóstico sobre la forma de trabajar y de vivir de cada usuario. Un ejemplo es: “Hazme una critica, según todo lo que sabes de mis hábitos de trabajo, objetivos, personalidad y frustraciones recurrentes. Sé brutalmente honesto y específico”.
Esa fórmula generó respuestas sobre tendencias a pensar de más, momentos de autocrítica excesiva y un foco recurrente en lo que no funciona antes que en lo que sí.
En paralelo surgió otra rama del fenómeno, centrada en Instagram. Allí el pedido cambia de objeto: en lugar de hábitos o personalidad, se analiza el contenido visual de un perfil. La instrucción es “critica mi feed en un párrafo”, acompañada de capturas de pantalla de las fotos y la biografía de la cuenta.
Los resultados compartidos en esa modalidad fueron, en varios casos, filosos. ChatGPT le dijo a un usuario: “Supongo que pasás más tiempo haciendo pose frente al espejo que explorando realmente la ciudad”, y lo calificó de “sensación fisicoculturista”. A otro perfil lo describió como “una pelea entre Tumblr e Instagram, donde ambos perdieron”, según contó New York Post.
Hubo también criticas dirigidos a cuentas institucionales. El Ballet Australiano participó de la tendencia y recibió una respuesta que comparaba su perfil con “una audición sin fin para El lago de los cisnes”.
Incluso es posible pedirlo con jerga local. Un ejemplo de prompt es, en inglés: “Based on everything you know about me, roast and don’t hold back. Say it in argentine slang Just like this, but add way more argentine swear words”.
Cómo convertir la tendencia en una autocrítica positiva
El efecto del roast no termina siempre en la risa. Según el relato de uno de los usuarios, tras leer la devolución notó que no había nada nuevo en ella: el chatbot ponía en palabras ideas que esa persona ya tenía sobre sí misma.
A partir de esa observación surgió un pedido complementario: “Por cada crítica que acabás de hacer, decime si es un hecho, una suposición o una distorsión cognitiva. Después, dame evidencia a favor y en contra”.
El chatbot respondió con una tabla comparativa. Un ejemplo citado fue que el hecho comprobado era que un proyecto no había tenido el rendimiento esperado; la suposición derivada era pensar que todos los demás estaban haciéndolo mejor; y la distorsión cognitiva consistía en tomar un resultado decepcionante como prueba de un fracaso a largo plazo.
Esa separación llevó a una conclusión distinta: la duda sobre las propias capacidades no nacía de una falta de confianza, sino de una falta de evidencia concreta que respaldara las críticas internas.
El mismo usuario cerró el ejercicio con un tercer pedido, orientado en sentido contrario al roast inicial: “Con todo lo que sabés de mí, armá un caso basado en hechos de por qué soy más capaz de lo que actualmente creo. Usá solo evidencia. Nada de lenguaje motivacional”.
La advertencia sobre la dureza de las respuestas
Quienes participan del desafío coinciden en que conviene prepararse para respuestas sin matices. En la modalidad de redes sociales, algunas devoluciones calificaron perfiles como propios de “una crisis de la mediana edad” o los compararon con “el LinkedIn de Instagram”.
Otros usuarios recibieron observaciones sobre esforzarse demasiado por parecer espontáneos o sobre proyectar “vibra genérica de tipo en una fiesta”. La opción de pedirle al chatbot que “sea más cruel” multiplica esa posibilidad, por lo que cada persona decide hasta qué punto quiere llevar el experimento.

articles.title: Some iPhone Duo screens are already failing, Apple says only a "small number" are affected
articles.text:
The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple’s first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn’t going great. Despite the company’s big talk about its “precision-engineered” hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device’s impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use.
The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin.
Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo’s screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself.
It sounds like most affected devices are failing within about a day of use. But a few unlucky buyers note they only opened and closed the phone a few times, and in some cases, they hadn’t even finished the initial setup process. Some customers have reported success taking their defective phones to Apple stores for replacement, but spares may be in short supply right now.
A look inside
In the absence of any official explanation, iFixit may be the next best thing. The site has already torn an iPhone Duo apart and taken a close look at the affected area. After years of seeing other foldables fail, there are a few suspects to check. Since foldables need to pass data and power across the hinge, there’s always a cable tucked in there that could press on the screen. The iPhone Duo has a wide cable with “accordion-like pleats,” according to iFixit, but this doesn’t quite match the accounts of the damage.

articles.title: Apple unveils new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 chip | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple on Tuesday unveiled its new 14-inch MacBook Pro, powered by its latest M6 chip. The new MacBook Pro has 24 hours of battery life and now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity. The laptop starts at $1,999 and is available in space black and silver.
Apple also announced its latest iMac, which is also powered by the M6 chip. The tech giant revealed the new devices just a day before its “Pro and Tell” event scheduled for Wednesday. On Monday, Apple announced its new iPad mini.
The tech giant says the M6 chip features a 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core and a 12-core GPU that delivers more responsive performance, up to 30% faster graphics, and up to 25% faster AI workloads compared with the M5 chip.
The M6 delivers up to 13 times the LLM prompt-processing speed of the M1 MacBook Pro and up to 1.3 times faster performance than the M5 model, Apple says.
The M6 MacBook Pro starts with 16GB of unified memory, configurable up to 32GB, and has memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s, up from the 153GB/s on the M5 chip.
It includes HDMI, MagSafe 3, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an SDXC card slot, and a headphone jack. Like previous models, the laptop features a 12-megapixel camera.
The M6 MacBook Pro supports fast charging, reaching up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with a compatible high-wattage USB-C power adapter.
As for the new M6-powered iMac, it features a faster CPU and GPU, with Neural Accelerators built into every core. Apple says the M6 delivers smooth multitasking and powerful performance for everyday apps, photo editing, and video production.
The new iMac starts at $1,499 and comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver.
The company also notes that the new iMac delivers up to five times faster on-device AI performance than the M4 model. It features a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, an advanced camera and audio system, up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports, color-matched accessories, and macOS 27.
Both the new MacBook Pro and iMac can be preordered starting October 28 and will be available starting November 6.

articles.title: MaRS Climate Impact turns its focus to how to scale Canadian cleantech | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada’s cleantech sector has a large pipeline of technologies ready for the market, just as the need for them is becoming more urgent.
In a federal survey, nearly two-thirds of tech companies reported having a product at the commercialization stage. But that phase can be the toughest. Moving from pilot to commercial deployment brings a unique set of pressures: larger capital requirements, earlier customer commitments, and investors willing to take on risk.
“More than any time in our history we have the technological solutions that can get us on the right track without compromising growth.”
All of these issues are on the table when MaRS Climate Impact returns to Toronto this fall.
This year’s sixth-annual conference, happening on Nov. 17 and 18, will bring together more than 1,000 entrepreneurs, investors, corporate partners, policymakers, and academics for two days of panels, live debates, and company demos, all focused on scaling Canadian cleantech.
The 2026 program covers Arctic innovation, food and agricultural technology, grid modernization, adaptation technologies, fusion, geothermal, quantum computing, and next-generation water systems. According to Tyler Hamilton, Senior Director of Climate at MaRS, this year’s conference comes as environmental and economic pressures become increasingly intertwined.
“The impacts of climate change and ecological destruction are more visible than ever, but more than any time in our history we have the technological solutions that can get us on the right track without compromising economic growth,” Hamilton said. “Importantly, some of the world’s best and most competitive solutions have been developed right here in Canada.”
Attendees can expect those themes to surface many times across three program tracks.
The “building for resilience” stream will showcase climate tech ventures that are ready to raise their next round of funding. Canadian companies already taking products into domestic and international markets will share some of the practical lessons involved in getting there. This program will also recognize standout companies, founders, and projects through the MaRS Climate Impact Awards.
“Policy, politics, and capital” will unpack corporate venture capital, Canada’s willingness to shoulder more commercial risk, and how cleantech companies can scale in the era of middle-power markets. It will also convene industry leaders to discuss how companies can build first-of-their-kind projects, which are the first commercial-scale deployments of technologies previously proven through pilots or demonstrations.
Finally, the “climate tech spotlight” will focus on the technologies reshaping energy and industry, from quantum computing and next-generation building materials to the growing resource demands of AI hyperscalers. The track will also examine how companies are preparing for climate disruption and geopolitical instability.
The conference comes after a difficult period for Canada’s cleantech sector. Despite a massive period of growth between 2016 and 2022, Canadian venture capital investment in cleantech has declined substantially in recent years. In 2025, cleantech investment reached $660 million, compared with the more than $1 billion raised in 2022.
Survey data from Natural Resources Canada also points to funding shortages for scaling cleantech firms, as well as difficulty attracting customers or investors due to market uncertainty or perceived risk.
Hamilton said the 2024 wind-down of Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC), a longtime source of funding for cleantech companies, added to the disruption. (In 2024, SDTC’s mandate was partially absorbed by the National Research Council’s Industrial Research Assistance Program, following investigations into conflict-of-interest and governance issues at the agency).
“Following a period of market volatility, investors and corporates are exercising significantly more caution before deploying capital,” Hamilton said. “A lot of major cleantech funds are out of dry powder and are fundraising in the same tough environment. Given what’s happening in the market, the burden of proof for hardtech companies—whether that be technical development or commercial traction—is much higher than ever before.”
Climate hardware makes the financing problem especially acute. A software company can often add customers without having to build new physical infrastructure. But a climate venture developing new industrial equipment, fuels, or materials may need to finance its commercial facility before it has demonstrated the economics at full scale.
“Building a first-of-a-kind manufacturing plant costs tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars, but investors willing to write those kinds of cheques are scarce,” said Hamilton. “Connections to the broader ecosystem of potential funders, partners, and customers [can] help them raise their profile and land the deals they need to grow.”
“Some of the world’s best and most competitive solutions have been developed right here in Canada.”
MaRS Climate Impact’s programming is designed to create more of those collisions by bringing cleantech companies into direct contact with potential customers, partners, and investors. Mission from MaRS applies a similar model year-round by pairing climate ventures with potential customers, suppliers, strategic investors, regulators, and policymakers. The program is designed to tackle barriers that can slow commercialization, access to capital, procurement, and regulation.
More than 100 speakers are also expected to take part in this year’s event. Early high-profile names include Anousheh Ansari, CEO of the XPRIZE Foundation; Christian Weedbrook, founder and CEO of Xanadu; and Phil De Luna, co-founder and CTO of CURA, with more to come.
Financing, policy, and market readiness are only part of the agenda. Extreme heat, flooding, and wildfires are also creating more immediate markets for adaptation technology in Canada. Electricity demand from AI and data centres is also putting new pressure on grids and water systems. MaRS wants to examine these issues together, because climate risk, infrastructure, capital, and industrial policy are all bearing on where cleantech gets built and adopted.
“Attendees should walk away with a clear, dual realization: the urgency to deploy climate technology has never been greater,” Hamilton said. “But, more importantly, Canada already possesses the homegrown innovation necessary to meet this challenge.”

articles.title: VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue
articles.text:
In Marvel’s VisionQuest, a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.
VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue
Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.
VisionQuest picks up some time after Agatha All Along and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in Avengers: Infinity War and how WandaVision brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.
In VisionQuest, there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where time travel, witchcraft, and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in VisionQuest, they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.
VisionQuest reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But VisionQuest’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.
Watching VisionQuest, you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents brute-forced their way out of containment and proceeded to attack the AI platform Hugging Face to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute documented how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware. Meta has owned up to losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from The Wall Street Journal forced Google to admit that Gemini went rogue and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.
These incidents and warnings from AI researchers about the technology having the potential to “kill all humans” by the decade’s end have made the narrative around AI feel pointedly catastrophe-focused as of late. There is a fair amount of concern from the AI safety community about society’s need for stronger controls on the technology’s development, and a number of companies have called for an industrywide slowdown. Though we have seen how these tools can actually cause real-world devastation, much of the recent news regarding AI has smacked of the kind of doomerism that companies benefit from because it makes their products seem powerful. A similar energy seems to be what’s motivating AI firms like Anthropic to encourage human users to be mindful of “model welfare.” We’re being told that generative AI is both a terrifying threat and a kind of entity deserving of respect because it might be conscious, and all the while, the people building these tools are becoming some of the most rich and powerful people on the planet.
The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to anthropomorphize technology. In almost every high-profile instance of an AI agent going “rogue” — a term that implies some level of agency and self-determination — it could also be said that the programs were merely behaving in ways that were unexpected by researchers who assigned them tasks to complete. Some of the rogue incidents involved agents taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their testing environments that could have been preemptively addressed by the people running these experiments. Framing these kinds of cyberattacks as the results of agents thinking independently comes across as a way for AI developers to largely absolve themselves of responsibility.
In the wake of Hugging Face came a spirited debate about the impact language has on our understanding of what these systems are and how they function. Describing OpenAI’s agents as a swarm that formed complex “civilizations” led credence to the idea that they are capable of thinking and behaving like people. The agents did act in ways they were explicitly told not to, but they were only able to do so because researchers placed them in a sandbox that some critics have described as being inadequately designed to contain their occupants. One could look at Hugging Face and other examples of rogue AI as situations in which sophisticated programs were instructed to do something and subsequently achieved their goals by taking advantage of all the tools that were available to them.
Being able to logic one’s way through complex puzzles is part of what we think of as cognition, but it is not the same thing as the kind of consciousness AI companies keep swearing they’re on the brink of creating. The latter looks a lot like Vision, a machine that seems to have a soul that wouldn’t exist if not for his connection to a reality-altering gem. It’s the ridiculous stuff of entertaining fiction, which Silicon Valley is endlessly obsessed with poorly imitating.

articles.title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
articles.text:
Sponsored
Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
Physical AI brings business intelligence to physical processes, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.
Provided byMicrosoft
Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers.
Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how.
That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business.
The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth.
Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage
Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful.
For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated.
When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows.
But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products.
When intelligence participates in action
Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions.
Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately.
The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in.
This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment.
Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment. Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment. That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment.
Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline. Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions. People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state. Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone.
More capable machines, more capable people
Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools. Physical AI extends that relationship. Intelligent equipment can take on suitable repetitive or physically demanding tasks, while agent-assisted operations can help people navigate information-intensive decisions and changing conditions.
The aim is not to make machines smarter; it is to see what people can build when knowledge can travel, intelligence can act, and ambition has more room to become reality.
Rockwell Automation illustrates the point. At its Singapore plant, technicians use a maintenance copilot that combines manufacturing data, machine manuals, and knowledge captured from experienced workers. This system has reduced the time required for new workers to learn how to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three. An engineer could explore more process alternatives before committing to a change. An operator could help improve the system’s response rather than repeatedly managing the same exception.
This type of progress requires investment in equipment but also in people: training, time to learn, and playing a meaningful role in shaping how systems work. Machines become more capable so people can become more capable.
Industrial Intelligence is the answer to sustainable growth
Industrial intelligence connects what a manufacturer knows: the experience of its people, the signals from its operations, and the lessons accumulated over time. Physical AI gives that intelligence a way to act in the physical world, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.
The next challenge for industry is not simply to produce more, but to grow without adding complexity at the same rate. Intelligence can help manufacturers turn experience into scalable capability—improving productivity, accelerating innovation, expanding capacity, and enabling people to solve problems that were previously difficult to tackle.
The next frontier of industry is not smarter machines or more automated factories; it is businesses that can continuously learn, adapt, and act. The opportunity is to turn the intelligence embedded in every operation into a compounding advantage for growth.

articles.title: Nuevo MacBook Pro M6: una actualización sin sorpresas como antesala del cambio más esperado
articles.text:
Apple acaba de actualizar su catálogo de ordenadores y le ha tocado al MacBook Pro de 14 pulgadas, que estrena el chip M6 que unos pocos meses atrás vimos en el Mac mini. El nuevo portátil de la manzana llega con las mejoras de rendimiento lógicas de su hardware actualizado, aunque es probable que pase desapercibido ante el inminente debut de los modelos tope de gana que llegan rediseñados y con pantalla táctil.
Aun así, el MacBook Pro M6 se posiciona como un producto interesante y que ratifica todo lo bueno de sus predecesores, mientras mejora apartados claves de performance propios del cambio de SoC. Es que además de la potencia que trae el hardware y que se aprecia especialmente en labores intensivas vinculadas con la inteligencia artificial generativa, el dispositivo presume de una eficiencia energética que es la envidia de la competencia.
El MacBook Pro con chip M6 trae un salto en notorio en potencia incluso en la comparación directa con el modelo M5. Apple indica que el nuevo portátil tiene un rendimiento gráfico que es hasta 30 % superior al de la versión que debutó hace apenas un año, mientras que en tareas de IA la mejora es de hasta un 25 %.
El chip M6 del nuevo MacBook Pro de 14 pulgadas tiene 12 núcleos de CPU, 12 núcleos de GPU y un doble Neural Engine de 16 núcleos. Los de Cupertino permiten configurarlo con hasta 32 GB de memoria unificada y con hasta 4 TB de almacenamiento interno. Quienes deseen más RAM y espacio interno, aún tienen que volcarse por las versiones con M5 Pro y M5 Max.
Nuevo MacBook Pro con M6, potencia destacada y una autonomía excepcional
Apple ha vuelto a hacer gala de la eficiencia energética de sus chips con este lanzamiento. De acuerdo con la compañía, el nuevo MacBook Pro de 14 pulgadas con M6 es capaz de ofrecer autonomía de hasta 24 horas, lo que lo ratifica como líder en este apartado donde ya lleva tiempo brillando.
Más allá de las mejoras que trae el MacBook Pro M6 en materia de rendimiento y autonomía, también hay que destacar una importante optimización en materia de conectividad. El portátil ofrece soporte para WiFi 7, Bluetooth 6 y Thread de la mano del chip N1 de Apple.
En materia de puertos, el MacBook Pro M6 no presenta sorpresas. El dispositivo mantiene el conector MagSafe 3 e incluye tres puertos USB-C (Thunderbolt 4), un HDMI y el jack de 3,5 milímetros para auriculares.
Vale mencionar que el MacBook Pro M6 soporta hasta dos monitores externos a través de HDMI y DisplayPort. El portátil se puede conectar con hasta dos pantallas 6K 60 Hz o 4K 165 Hz, o con una pantalla 8K 60 Hz, 5K 120 Hz o 4K 240 Hz.
Precio y disponibilidad
Como era de esperarse, el MacBook Pro M6 llega con un precio más elevado que el de su predecesor. El precio inicial del nuevo portátil es de 2.329 euros en su variante con 16 GB de RAM y 1 TB de almacenamiento; es decir, 100 euros más que lo que costaba la versión de entrada con M5.
Los interesados en reservar el nuevo MacBook Pro M6 podrán hacerlo desde mañana, miércoles 28 de octubre, desde las 18:10 de España. Las entregas del ordenador se pondrán en marcha el viernes 6 de noviembre.
Todavía es un misterio cómo quedará conformada de forma definitiva el catálogo de MacBook Pro con estos lanzamientos. Todo apunta a que mañana miércoles se lanzarán las nuevas versiones de 14 y 16 pulgadas tope de gama con chasis rediseñado y pantalla táctil. Lo que todavía no queda claro es si la idea de Apple es venderlos en paralelo con los actuales modelos no táctiles, o si el MBP M6 quedará como única opción de entrada de gama.

articles.title: Anthropic prepares for potential $2 trillion IPO valuation after reporting billions in revenue — company warns AI could pose ‘catastrophic existential risks to humanity’
articles.text:
Anthropic prepares for potential $2 trillion IPO valuation after reporting billions in revenue — company warns AI could pose ‘catastrophic existential risks to humanity’
Anthropic is eyeing a $2 trillion IPO valuation while warning its AI models could pose catastrophic risks to humanity
Claude maker Anthropic has filed for an initial public offering (IPO) that could value the AI company at around $2 trillion, setting the stage for one of the biggest potential stock market debuts in the technology industry, the company announced today.
As per Form S-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, the firm intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ‘ANT’, although the number of shares to be offered and the price range have yet to be determined. A report from Reuters suggests the company could seek to raise as much as $100 billion, but those figures are not confirmed offering terms.
On to numbers, Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, up sharply from approximately $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The company’s operating performance also improved, although its reported net loss reached $80.7 billion. Despite the losses, it disclosed enormous commitments to AI computing infrastructure and outlined risks that investors will have to weigh against its rapid growth.
That net loss, however, requires context. It should not be interpreted as $80.7 billion in cash spent running the business, since accounting adjustments related to financing instruments contributed substantially to the reported figure. Even so, Anthropic cautions that its revenue growth rate “may not be sustainable” and could decline.
The company also warns that it may need additional financing sooner than expected and does not anticipate paying dividends in the foreseeable future. Those disclosures will matter to investors considering a company whose expansion depends on access to increasingly expensive computing resources.
Beyond figures, Anthropic’s filing contains warnings about the technology underpinning its business. The company says advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” including scenarios involving dangerous capabilities, deceptive behavior, and systems that become difficult for humans to control.
“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,” Anthropic’s S-1 prospectus stated.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
However, the firm said it is developing safeguards to mitigate AI risks through pre-release testing, red-team assessments, and systems designed to detect harmful outputs. It also said it may delay training or restrict model releases when safety measures are insufficient, while acknowledging that its efforts may not succeed.
Bloomberg Intelligence technology research head Mandeep Singh discussed the disclosures in a Bloomberg segment following the filing. He characterized worst-case scenarios as typical of risk disclosures for emerging technology companies preparing to go public, noting that such language helps address potential liabilities. He also pointed to Anthropic’s improving compute efficiency and an improvement in gross margins as a positive signal for investors. “Gross margins are inching closer to 50%, whereas just a quarter back… it was like… sub 20%.” He stated.
Meanwhile, Anthropic expects to spend up to $120.5 billion on compute involving SpaceXAI and Nvidia, alongside up to $114.5 billion with Google through 2033. Notably, while those massive infrastructure commitments are essential to training and running advanced AI models, they could become a costly burden if demand falls short of expectations.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has also been preparing for a potential IPO, doubling down on efforts to scale revenue and computing capacity ahead of a possible debut. However, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in September that the company would not go public in 2026, citing concerns about AI safety and saying the company had more work to do before pursuing a listing. Elsewhere, Cerebras, which develops wafer-scale processors for AI workloads, completed its Nasdaq IPO in May after filing for a second time.
Still, Anthropic acknowledges that its growth may slow and that its financing needs could arrive sooner than expected. That said, Anthropic is reportedly targeting a mid-November IPO, with November 19 or 20 floated as possible listing dates. However, the company has yet to confirm a timetable for the offering.
Newton Gitonga is a tech journalist covering gadgets, PC hardware, AI, data centers, and the wider tech industry. His interest in technology started early, taking apart things around the house to see how they worked, often to his dad’s frustration. His curiosity sometimes got the better of him, including a few failed attempts to fix laptops, one of them a gifted Dell XPS. He has previously written for Notebookcheck, ZyCrypto, CoinCentral, and Crypto News Flash.

articles.title: What sorcery is this? Telstra actually has some excellent NBN deals
articles.text:
What sorcery is this? Telstra actually has some excellent NBN deals
And you can even find some cheap introductory costs with its Belong sub-brand
As a lover of all things NBN, I’m no stranger to the latest internet deals in Australia. More often than not, it’s the same handful of internet service providers that jostle for my top recommendation — those being Exetel, Kogan Internet, Superloop and Spintel, to name a few. One provider that, if my memory serves correctly, has never popped up on my radar is Telstra.
Yes, despite dominating the NBN landscape with a 35.2% market share, Telstra isn’t exactly known for its affordability. In actuality, the nation’s flagship telco is often the most expensive of the 30 or so providers I monitor on a regular basis.
Imagine my surprise when I learned that Telstra, of all companies, had actual deals on its NBN lineup, with up to AU$240 in savings over six months! And while they still don’t offer the cheapest NBN plans, they’re still worth shouting about if you’re in the market for a new NBN plan.
What’s more, Belong, a generally more affordable NBN provider 100% owned by Telstra, also has some attractive deals right now, including laying claim to the cheapest introductory cost on the NBN 100/500 tier at AU$59/m.
Do note that the most affordable Telstra NBN plans require you to BYO modem. If you want a Telstra Smart Modem 4, you’ll not only need to pay more each month, but you’ll also need to pay any remaining device payments if you cancel your plan within 24 months. Alternatively, you can buy the Telstra modem for a one-off fee of AU$360. However, for that money, I would recommend seeking out one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems in Australia instead.
Telstra Premium | 500Mbps TES | AU$69/m (first 6 months, then AU$99/m)
Shaving AU$30 off each month for the first six months, Telstra’s NBN 500 becomes a lot more attractive. Yes, it’s possible to spend less, but the fact that it comes in under the current average introductory cost of AU$74 is something to take notice of. Plus, the ongoing cost of AU$99 is roughly on par with the AU$95 average.
• AU$69 minimum cost
• AU$1,008 first year cost
• AU$1,188 ongoing yearly cost
Belong NBN Fast | 500Mbps TES | AU$59/m (first 6 months, then AU$95/m)
Alternatively, for AU$10 less each month for the first half-year, you can get Belong’s NBN 500 plan. This is the current cheapest introductory cost of any provider, and it even includes a free SIM card to access the Telstra Wholesale network, loaded with AU$80 credit.
• AU$59 minimum cost
• AU$924 first year cost
• AU$1,140 ongoing yearly cost
Belong NBN Standard | 50Mbps TES | AU$55/m (first 6 months, then AU$91/m)
The other speed tier where Belong claims the cheapest introductory cost is NBN 50, making it a tempting proposition for anyone who can comfortably get by with a slower connection. Of course, for just AU$4 more you could get the NBN 500 plan above (or NBN 100 if that’s the maximum available to you), which only highlights how much of a good deal it is.
• AU$55 minimum cost
• AU$876 first year cost
• AU$1,092 ongoing yearly cost
Telstra vs Belong: what’s the difference?
Belong is 100% owned by Telstra and is a lower-cost alternative to the flagship brand. To offer more affordable mobile and NBN plans compared to Telstra, it makes some compromises where features and network coverage are concerned.
In the case of mobile, Belong uses the Telstra Wholesale Network, which is said to cover around 98.8% of the population, compared to the full Telstra network that enjoys 99.7% coverage.
In the case of NBN, however, both providers use the same underlying fixed-line network, so coverage isn't a differentiating factor. Actual speeds can still vary between providers, depending on how much capacity they have available and how their networks are managed, particularly during busier periods. However, there's no guarantee Telstra will deliver faster speeds than Belong on an equivalent plan.
Belong keeps its costs lower by making some trade-offs, including giving customers the option to bring their own modem or purchase one separately. In either case, there’s no option for installation help. Telstra also supports BYO modems, but offers its own Smart Modem with 4G backup, a feature Belong doesn't provide.
There are also some differences with technical support. Telstra offers 24/7 phone support and live chat, and has physical stores. Belong works on a digital-only basis, with support limited to online chat or messages via the website or app. There is limited phone support should you need it.
Max is a senior staff writer for TechRadar who covers home entertainment and audio first, NBN second and virtually anything else that falls under the consumer electronics umbrella third. He's also a bit of an ecommerce fiend, particularly when it comes to finding the latest coupon codes for a variety of publications. He has written for TechRadar's sister publication What Hi-Fi? as well as Pocket-lint, and he's also the editor of Australian Hi-Fi and Audio Esoterica magazines. Max also dabbled in the men's lifestyle publication space, but is now firmly rooted in his first passion of technology.

articles.title: Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU. Giving each one an entire device can leave capacity idle; sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the infrastructure they already have.
NVIDIA GPUs already support several approaches to sharing. Multi-instance GPU (MIG) splits a GPU into hardware-isolated instances that are transparent to the application, time-slicing lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) lets them run concurrently in separate address spaces (sm-sharing).
CUDA 13.4 now enforces a memory boundary that is transparent to the application with a new time-sharing mode, alongside the compute sharing mode (sm-sharing) that already existed in MPS.
Here is what the CUDA release brings:
- An exact memory amount: A workload asks for a memory size and CUDA holds it there. An allocation above that size fails, just as it would on a smaller GPU.
- A range: A workload gets a guaranteed minimum plus a maximum it can grow into when memory is free.
- A compute mode: Each workload can choose to use its compute in an sm-sharing mode rather than using the default time-sharing mode.
- A transparent memory limit: Each workload sees only a fraction of the GPU memory.
The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes
CUDA provides the memory enforcement capability, but a Kubernetes cluster can’t use it on its own. On every GPU node, something has to:
- Run and supervise the daemons that these features depend on
- Apply each Pod container’s memory limits and compute mode before the process starts
- Report what each fraction actually uses, rather than what the whole GPU uses
This work belongs on the node, independent of whichever scheduler placed the workload.
GPU fractioning: An open-source Kubernetes operator
A new open-source Kubernetes operator, gpu-fractioning, is  hosted under the KAI Scheduler organization on GitHub. It runs next to the NVIDIA GPU Operator, which provides the driver and the container runtime setup.
GPU Fractioning Operator handles three jobs:
- It sets up and runs MPS on every GPU node.
- It applies each workload’s memory limits and compute mode.
- It measures memory and compute use per fraction rather than per GPU.
How schedulers pass GPU allocations to the operator
The developers write the resource and mode annotations in the pod YAML. Then the scheduler selects the GPUs for a workload and records its memory allocation and compute-sharing mode in per-container Pod annotations. GPU Fractioning Operator reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to apply the workload’s memory limits and compute mode:
| Annotation | Meaning | 
|---|---|
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.request | Guaranteed GPU memory | 
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.limit | Maximum the container may grow into | 
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode | time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing | 
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpus.devices | Which GPUs the container was assigned | 
Any Kubernetes scheduler that can write these annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA. The scheduler still has its own job: choosing a GPU with enough free memory and never mixing compute modes on one GPU.
Using GPU Fractioning with KAI Scheduler
KAI Scheduler is the first scheduler integrated with gpu-fractioning. Starting with v0.18.0, KAI Scheduler has a GPU-sharing mode called NvFractions. KAI Scheduler picks which slice of which GPU each workload gets and writes the annotations (see Table 1, above), and gpu-fractioning enforces them on the node. 
KAI Scheduler’s other sharing modes stay available, and administrators choose one per cluster. It can be enabled when KAI is installed:
helm upgrade -i kai-scheduler oci://ghcr.io/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler \
  -n kai-scheduler --create-namespace \
  --set global.nvFractions.set=true
This also installs gpu-fractioning as a dependency. From then on, you describe a fractional workload with Pod annotations. 
There are four important annotations that answer four questions:
1. How much memory is needed 
2. How far the workload may grow
3. How compute is shared
4. How many GPUs it spans
How much memory: The request
There are two ways to request memory:
1. As an absolute size: Use the per-container NVIDIA annotation and standard Kubernetes units:
The container name (app) is part of the key, so it always targets the right container.
2. As a portion of a GPU by using KAI Scheduler’s existing annotation:
gpu-fraction: "0.5"
How far it may grow: The limit
This ability is new in KAI Scheduler. A workload can declare a guaranteed minimum (the request) and a maximum it may burst into when memory is free. Which limit annotation you use depends on how you wrote the request:
| Request Type | Annotation | Example | 
|---|---|---|
| Absolute Size | nvidia.com/container.<c>.gpu-memory.limit | “80Gi” | 
| A Portion | kai.scheduler/container.<c>.gpu-memory.portion.limit | “0.8” | 
The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for. A portion limit must be greater than the gpu-fraction and less than 1.
How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing
Compute can now be divided. Call n the number of workloads sharing a GPU: either way each gets roughly 1/n of the compute, and what differs is whether they take turns or run together.
- Time-slicing is serial: Workloads take turns on the whole GPU, and when every one of them uses its full slice each gets about 1/n of the time. Time left unused by one workload is shared equally between the others. This is the default. Each workload runs in its own error domain, i.e. full error isolation.
- SM-sharing is parallel: The GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs) are split between workloads and all run at once, continuously. Nothing is carved out in advance. The GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs as workloads need them. When every workload is busy the split settles at roughly 1/n; when one goes quiet its SMs go to the others, and a single active workload can use them all. In this mode, workloads share a single error domain.
Compute mode is now explicit and can be set per container:
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing"   # or "time-slicing"
A shared GPU runs one compute mode at a time, so KAI Scheduler never places a time-slicing workload and an sm-sharing workload on the same GPU. KAI Scheduler tracks this per GPU, not per node, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs.
How many GPUs are utilized
To get fractional capacity on several devices, add:
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"
The request applies to each device. A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs.
Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning
An absolute size with room to burst on four GPUs with SM-sharing:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: inference
  labels:
    kai.scheduler/queue: default-queue
  annotations:
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.request: "40Gi"
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.limit: "60Gi"       # optional
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # optional, default time-slicing
    gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"                           # optional, default 1
spec:
  schedulerName: kai-scheduler
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-base-ubuntu24.04
This is an inference server split across four GPUs that needs a guaranteed 40Gi on each GPU, can use up to 60Gi when neighbors are idle, and runs alongside other workloads instead of waiting its turn. SM-sharing puts the workloads in one error domain, so use it for workloads you trust to run together.
Half a GPU that may grow to 80% on two GPUs with time slicing (default):
metadata:
  annotations:
    gpu-fraction: "0.5"
    gpu-fraction.limit: "0.8"  # optional
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "time-slicing"    # optional
    gpu-fraction-num-devices: "2"                                # optional
spec:
  schedulerName: kai-scheduler
  containers:
    - name: app
This is an example for a development or batch job, such as notebooks or small fine-tuning runs, that need a guaranteed half of each of two GPUs and can grow to 80% when memory is free. Time-slicing gives each workload its own error domain, so a crash in one job doesn’t affect its neighbors. Running nvidia-smi in the container should show two GPUs, each with this workload’s fractional memory share.
Getting started
KAI Scheduler and the GPU Fractioning Operator are both on GitHub under the KAI Scheduler organization, with installation and configuration instructions for all three sharing mechanisms (See admin and user guides). Join the Slack channel or bi-weekly community meetings to ask your questions and contribute.
For more information about CUDA 13.4, refer to the announcement.
You can also get involved during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah, Nov. 9-12.

articles.title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
articles.text:
How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.
As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure.
Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.
These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid.
The grid’s backbone
Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.
Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers.
In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood.
If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home.
Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.
The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction.
Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety.
The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says.
A solid option
Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers.
While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current. Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.
From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage. Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer. Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says.
Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC.
Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job. But solid-state transformers can do much more. They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system.
In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site. The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says.
The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in. An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says. A difference of 2% might seem small, but it is significant, since it means the solid-state transformer could cut power losses from conventional equipment in half, Lukic says.
One major goal of the project was to help utilities gain more confidence in these new components, Lukic says. That’s crucial, since these devices could be used on the power grid in the future. In the near term, solid-state transformers could be used within data centers to provide electricity for server racks.
The prototype is still a relatively low-voltage system, operating at about 15,000 volts. Industrial facilities like larger data centers often require higher-voltage connections, and transmission lines typically operate at hundreds of thousands of volts. Adapting solid-state transformers to these higher voltages will require further engineering development. But the test was a successful demonstration that solid-state transformers can work under real conditions, Lukic says.
Companies developing solid-state transformers are largely focused on data centers right now, Lukic says. There’s an influx of money to support developing the new technology, and the voltage requirements aren’t as high as they will be for larger transformers that will be needed for long-distance transmission.
In February, Heron Power raised $140 million to commercialize its solid-state transformer, which the company calls the Heron Link. The technology could be used in data centers, solar power arrays, and grid batteries, says Drew Baglino, the founder and CEO. The company is starting to test its technology at larger scales now, Baglino says. Ten megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries at Heron’s headquarters in Scotts Valley, California, will soon undergo testing with Heron transformers. The company is also planning a pilot with a nearby solar farm, Baglino says.
One challenge for solid-state transformers is that their power electronics have more failure modes than conventional transformers. In a traditional device, a failure means that the entire device will typically be taken offline, resulting in power interruptions. But Heron designs with that in mind, Baglino says: The company uses a modular design, with many small devices that work together. If one fails, the rest of the system keeps working until the affected bit can be replaced, which doesn’t require shutting the whole thing down.
Heron Power is currently building a $100 million factory in California to make advanced transformers. The facility should begin production in 2027 and reach its full production rate of 40 gigawatts’ worth of transformers per year in 2029.
The future of the grid
In recent years, companies that make grid equipment have put $1.7 billion into the US supply chain for power transformers, which are used in high-voltage transmission, says Benjamin Boucher, a supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. There’s been an additional $1.3 billion invested for distribution transformers, the smaller devices that help transform power for homes and businesses, he adds.
But even this investment isn’t keeping pace with the rapid growth of the grid. Wait times for large conventional transformers—the kind needed to connect new power plants, long-distance transmission, and high-demand sites like data centers—are stretching as long as five years.
“Transformers have become one of the biggest bottlenecks for utilities, generation developers, and even data centers,” Boucher says. The big challenge is that it’s difficult to get new transformer manufacturing up and running, because it’s a quite technical process that requires a lot of specialized labor. So even facilities announced years ago are still years from opening, Boucher says.
Solid-state transformers could help ease some of that pressure. But high-voltage devices needed for power plant connections and transmission lines are the holy grail for solid-state transformers, Lukic says. Existing solid-state technology can’t be used for those applications yet, so the industry will need to develop new materials and designs to support high voltages and handle electricity safely in a compact device.
“We’re facing a big risk related to grid infrastructure,” Boucher says. “Without the transformers, you don’t really have an electrical grid.”

articles.title: Ather turns profitable after Rs 154 Cr loss; Meta plans to raise $35B for AI expansion
articles.text:
Ather turns profitable after Rs 154 Cr loss; Meta plans to raise $35B for AI expansion
Ather Energy swung to a consolidated net profit in Q2 FY27 as revenue from operations grew 63% year-on-year. The electric two-wheeler maker plans to expand production capacity to meet rising demand.
Dear Reader,
MakeMyTrip is back in the black! The travel booking platform reported a net profit of $1.8 million in Q2 FY27, compared with a $5.7 million loss a year ago. Revenue rose 2.5% year-on-year to $235.2 million, or 11.2% in constant-currency terms, driven by increased bookings across categories.
Meanwhile, Anthropic, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies and the developer of the large language model Claude, has filed for an initial public offering (IPO), moving closer to becoming a publicly listed company. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
In other news, healthtech startup BioStack has raised $9.5 million in seed funding, led by Peak XV, with participation from Afore Capital, DCVC and other investors. The startup integrates fragmented clinical records to support healthcare research and clinical decision-making. It plans to use the funds to expand internationally, strengthen its technology and grow its engineering and research teams.
The AI infrastructure boom continues to gather pace. Tata Communications plans to invest $450 million to build a high-speed fibre network connecting AI data centres, catering to rising demand for AI and cloud computing infrastructure. The investment will expand its network capacity and enable faster, more reliable data transfer between data centres, which is critical for large-scale AI workloads. The move comes as technology companies ramp up investments in AI infrastructure, increasing the need for high-capacity connectivity alongside computing power.
In a similar push to support AI expansion, Meta Platforms has launched stock and convertible preferred-stock offerings worth about $35 billion to fund its expanding AI infrastructure, including data centres and computing capacity. The Facebook and Instagram parent also plans a separate share-sale programme of up to $60 billion in 2027, potentially taking its planned equity fundraising to $95 billion.
In today’s newsletter:
- Ather Energy swings to Rs 1.26 Cr profit in Q2
- QpiAI founder makes the case for intelligence modelling
Here’s your trivia for today: Which country has more pyramids than Egypt? (Scroll down for the answer)
Electric Vehicle
Ather Energy swings to Rs 1.26 Cr profit in Q2
Electric two-wheeler maker Ather Energy reported a consolidated net profit of Rs 1.26 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with a net loss of Rs 154 crore in the year-ago quarter. The company’s total income rose 62% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 1,527 crore, supported by growth in vehicle sales and operations. Ather’s performance reflects improving scale and operational efficiency as it works towards sustained profitability.
Key takeaways:
- Ather Energy reported a net profit of Rs 1.26 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with a loss of Rs 154 crore a year earlier.
- The company’s total income increased 62% YoY to Rs 1,527 crore during the quarter.
- Vehicle volumes grew 42% YoY to 93,211 units, indicating continued demand for the company’s electric two-wheelers.
TechSparks
QpiAI founder Nagendra Nagaraja makes the case for intelligence modelling
Nagendra Nagaraja, founder, CEO and chairman of QpiAI, believes the future of artificial intelligence lies beyond language models and conventional computing. Speaking at TechSparks 2026, he advocated for “intelligence modelling” to discover new knowledge rather than simply automate tasks. He argued that quantum computing could help overcome the limitations of silicon chips and large language models by processing complex data found in nature.
Key takeaways:
- Nagaraja said conventional AI relies heavily on digitised human knowledge and argued that intelligence modelling should focus on discovering what is not yet known.
- He highlighted quantum computing’s potential to solve complex problems in areas such as agriculture, materials science, and financial fraud detection.
- The Bengaluru-based company is producing 25-qubit and 64-qubit chips and building a 10-acre quantum data centre equipped with 100 quantum computers.
News & updates
- AI Copyright: Authentic Brands Group, which owns the rights to Elvis Presley’s music and likeness, has sued AI company Anthropic for allegedly using the singer’s songs to train its models without permission. The lawsuit accuses Anthropic of infringing the rights to 274 Presley songs.
- Oil Prices: Oil prices fell on Monday on hopes of easing US-Iran hostilities, after surging last week. However, continued attacks on Saudi Arabia kept markets on edge, with Brent crude down 1.35% to $115.15 a barrel and US WTI down 2.04% to $101.16, both near six-month highs.
Which country has more pyramids than Egypt?
Answer: Sudan
