articles.title: Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Japanese internet company GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders.
The IT and internet services giant said on its blog that it believes the attacker has published information allegedly linked to customers and its business. However, the contents are still being verified and the full extent of the incident remains unclear.
GMO Internet has since advised customers to reset their passwords, amid receiving reports of “unauthorized operations” performed on customer trading accounts. The company said 27,000 servers may be affected by the breach.
A spokesperson for GMO Internet did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.
The incident comes about a week after the Japanese firm’s cybersecurity unit separately reported finding evidence that a Chinese AI-enabled penetration testing tool called Artex had been used in hacks targeting companies across Japan. However, the company said it has not publicly established a connection between Artex and the breach of Onamae.
The Artex tool was also used to hack financial institutions in South Korea in September, according to a report by CrowdStrike earlier this month. The attacks largely relied on exploiting weak security controls, such as a lack of multi-factor authentication. Artex’s Chinese developer has since stopped public updates and made the AI security tool closed-source after it was linked to cyberattacks targeting banks, per Reuters.
A spokesperson at Japan’s Financial Service Agency (FSA) told TechCrunch that it issued guidance in May urging financial institutions to prepare for a rise in cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The regulator called for stronger basic defenses, including “vulnerability management, defense-in-depth and incident preparedness,” while encouraging firms to use AI and other security tools, the spokesperson added.
Here’s the timeline of the Onamae breach.
October 21: GMO Internet shut down its Onamae Desktop Cloud service after discovering unauthorized access had occurred to its systems without permission. The IT firm also received an email from hackers demanding about 8 billion yen (~$50 million).
October 22: The Japanese company reported the incident to Japanese police and shared another public update.
October 24: GMO Internet said it would offer customers compensation and alternative service while seeking help from government agencies.
October 25-26: The company began collecting devices from customers to detect malware and better understand the damage.
October 27: The Japanese IT firm said a suspected attacker had posted information that appeared to be linked to the company and its customers. GMO said it was still checking whether the information was genuine.

articles.title: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization
Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems that deliver reliable power for energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers. Its flagship product, the Exowatt P3, captures solar energy through optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long-duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand through a heat engine. Unlike grid-tied photovoltaic solar systems, P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, helping data centers come online without waiting in multi-year grid interconnection queues. Exowatt builds a fleet of AI agents that monitor and triage live alarms and support operational decisions for solar systems, often at the edge, with limited or no connectivity. As its fleet scales from test benches toward manufacturing and thousands of deployed field units, the intelligence layer that operates these systems must scale with it.
In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline. The pipeline produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost.
The two models described here are the first outputs of that pipeline rather than the end goal. The more durable result of the engagement was the pipeline itself: a repeatable path from raw operational data to a certified training set, a fine-tuned model, and an evaluated deployment artifact. Exowatt can now run this path in days rather than months. Alarm triage and energy-market analysis are two of many narrow, high-value tasks where the same approach applies.
The challenge: AI on physical energy infrastructure
Exowatt’s energy management system (EMS) runs across a growing fleet of operational sites. Each site continuously produces alarms: a hardware component operating out of spec, a dropped connection, an out-of-range voltage reading, and similar events. As the fleet scales toward thousands of field units, a human operator can’t monitor every site in real time. Exowatt needed an AI agent that could read the alarm state on each site and take or recommend the correct next action autonomously and reliably.
A frontier model couldn’t solve this problem for three reasons:
- The task is narrow and proprietary. Alarm triage on Exowatt’s EMS depends on their specific hardware, data, and operating logic. A general-purpose frontier model isn’t specialized for it.
- It must run at the edge, with no GPU and often no internet. Many sites have limited or intermittent connectivity, so an agent that depends on a cloud call to a frontier model leaves the operator without coverage when the connection drops.
- Cost doesn’t scale at fleet level. Routing every operational decision to a frontier model across thousands of sites is not economical for a decision that repeats continuously.
This is where Exowatt turned to model customization. Exowatt’s initial fine-tuning workflow relied on selecting an open-weight model, building a container, and creating a custom training recipe before any experiment could run. This was a major blocker for model experimentation. Additionally, they had to decide GPU hardware requirements of model fine-tuning. As the team increased the pace of experimentation, each run first required choosing a specific GPU instance type and then waiting for that self-selected capacity to become available. When a chosen instance type was unavailable, this could delay the start of a run or block it entirely.
They needed a model small enough to run on a no-GPU edge controller, yet accurate enough compared to the frontier model on the specific task to act autonomously. Fine-tuning closed that gap: a compact, task-specialized model that is both deployable in the cloud and at the edge.
Solution overview
Exowatt addressed these challenges by adopting a cloud-native, serverless model customization approach on Amazon SageMaker AI. The same training pipeline produces fine-tuned models for two deployment targets: the edge and the cloud.
Exowatt implemented this approach on the Qwen3-1.7B model for the first use case, edge alarm triage, then applied the same approach to the Qwen3-14B model for the second use case, cloud energy-market analysis. The company plans to reuse this solution to build smaller, task-specific models across the fleet.
The following seven AWS services power the AI pipeline, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints to manage:
| AWS Service | Purpose | 
| Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) | Data, manifests, model artifacts, and test sets | 
| Amazon SageMaker AI serverless fine-tuning | Every fine-tune run, launched from Public Hub recipes | 
| Amazon SageMaker AI serverless evaluation | 2,000 answers per candidate scored as a managed job | 
| SageMaker Model Registry | Every completed fine-tune with its evidence and metrics | 
| Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import | Hosts the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B for Cloud EMS, invoked privately from the Cloud EMS service. No idle cost | 
| Amazon Bedrock (Claude, Qwen3) | Paraphrase (three rewrites per answer in the training data) and frontier model benchmarking Alarm-triage paraphrases use Qwen3-VL-235B on Amazon Bedrock. Energy-market paraphrases use Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. | 
| AWS Lambda + Amazon EventBridge | Serverless-evaluation scorer and a scheduled keep-warm invocation of the custom model | 
The workflow is organized into three stages:
Model customization (cloud): Exowatt fine-tunes open-weight base models using serverless model customization, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on SageMaker AI. Because serverless training allocates capacity on demand, the team runs multiple experiments per day rather than waiting for self-selected GPU. After evaluation, the best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry.
Edge deployment: For latency-sensitive, connectivity-constrained work such as alarm triage, the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B model is frozen, quantized to the GGUF format, and run with llama.cpp inside Kubernetes pods at the edge using on-site controllers. This path requires no GPU and operates without internet connectivity.
Cloud deployment (elastic): For internet-connected, fleet-level analysis, the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B energy-market model is served through Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, which runs with no idle cost and bills only while the model is active.
Why Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization
Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization service provides a wide selection of open-weight models with ready-made fine-tuning recipes from the SageMaker Public Hub, so the team avoided building and optimizing a custom training container, work that can otherwise take weeks. For Exowatt, this turned fine-tuning from a scarce, scheduled event into a routine, on-demand one. This makes a rapid experimentation-and-test loop practical while keeping experimentation cost low.
Fine-tuning on provisioned GPUs requires choosing a specific instance type, requesting that capacity, waiting for it to become available, running the job, and paying for the instance for as long as it is held. The held time typically includes the idle time between experiments when a dedicated instance is kept running. For a small team running many experiments, this slows down innovation and increases cost. Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization automatically manages and orchestrates the infrastructure required to run the fine-tuning job, removing the pain of capacity management, and charges only for the time the fine-tuning job runs.
Use case 1: Edge alarm triage with Qwen3-1.7B
Exowatt sites raise alarms around the clock. A compact on-site model reads each alarm together with the site’s own status and telemetry and returns one of a small fixed set of classifications with cited evidence (such as an offline system, derated component, or sensor mismatch) or an explicit abstention when the evidence is insufficient.
Model selection and training data
The team first tried Qwen3-8B with prompting and guardrails, which plateaued below the target (0.735 macro-F1). A fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B changed that: it outperformed the Qwen3-8B plus prompting setup on this narrow, single-turn task at roughly one-fifth the parameters, while staying small enough for GPU-free edge inference. Thirteen fine-tuned Qwen3-8B candidates across 12 dataset versions never beat the prompted 8B baseline. The smaller model with more varied data did.
The training set was small and curated: 2,522 examples built from 684 verified decisions on generated site scenarios plus 1,838 certified paraphrases that kept each decision fixed while rewriting the prose. The paraphrases were generated by Qwen3-235B on Amazon Bedrock for about $3.72. Each paraphrase was kept only if deterministic checks confirmed that the decision, labels, evidence citations, and every number were unchanged (1,838 of 2,218 candidates passed). One fault family was held out of training entirely, and 320 cases were reserved for testing.
Training and deployment
Training completed in about 32 minutes on SageMaker serverless fine-tuning for roughly $20–$25. Quantized to 8 bits (about 1.71 GiB), the model runs offline in a 6 GiB llama.cpp pod on the site’s existing CPU server. It also runs on a t3.2xlarge instance type.
Use case 2: Cloud energy-market analysis with Qwen3-14B
Dispatchable storage turns timing into an operational decision: each site must continually decide how much stored energy to hold for its load and when to release it, and for grid-connected sites market conditions feed into that choice. The fine-tuned model reads a six-hour packet of live market data (about 90 rows of real-time prices, day-ahead forecasts, and grid notices) and returns one of five market events (such as a price spike or scarcity adder) in about four seconds. Every claim is tied to a specific data row to inform the dispatch strategy.
Why Qwen3-14B
Qwen3-14B was chosen because it is supported by Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, it ships as a SageMaker Public Hub model with a ready LoRA recipe (no custom container or instance type to manage), and at about 28 GiB it is small enough to serve cost-effectively.
Training data and process
Exowatt fine-tuned the model on public Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market data drawn from five years of history (about 163 million rows across 12 tables). The team rule-labeled this data into 25,000 examples (22,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,000 held out for testing). They then expanded the training set to 86,281 rows by having Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock rewrite the prose of each example while its labels and numeric fields stayed fixed.
Training was a single LoRA epoch (rank 16, alpha 32), completed in about 8.5 hours of managed serverless fine-tuning with up to four jobs running at once. The team ran 23 jobs and about 155 hours of managed training in the six days from initial plan to a champion model serving in Cloud EMS.
The decisive improvement came from paraphrase diversity: adding three rewrites per answer lifted macro-F1 from 0.950 to 0.975. The base model scored only 0.415 macro-F1. It produced valid JSON but did not yet know the market. Fine-tuning fixed that.
Deployment
The merged checkpoint was imported to Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import in about 14 minutes. The model runs with no idle cost and bills at $6.86 per hour only while active.
Benchmark results
On the edge alarm-triage task the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B went from a model that couldn’t produce a valid answer to 0.911 macro-F1 with 320 test cases, ahead of every frontier baseline. Applying the identical fine-tune-and-evaluate loop to the energy-market task with 2,000 test cases, the Qwen3-14B reached 0.975 macro-F1, again ahead of the frontier baseline and at a fraction of the cost. In both cases a small, fine-tuned model beat far larger general-purpose models on the specific task.
Both models return strict JSON in which every claim cites a specific input data row. Any unsupported claim is dropped before it reaches an operator, which is what lets the team trust small models in autonomous, physical settings.
| Model | Macro-F1 | $ / 1,000 decisions | Offline? | 
| Claude Haiku 4.5 | 0.519 | ~$4.70 | No | 
| Claude Opus 4.7 | 0.680 | ~$22 | No | 
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 0.698 | ~$15 | No | 
| Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B | 0.911 | $0* | Yes | 
| Base Qwen3-1.7B | No score (failed the validity gate) |  |  | 
Table 1: Edge alarm triage results, fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B compared to frontier models
$0 per 1,000 decisions means no metered API or GPU inference cost. The quantized model runs on the site’s existing CPU.
| Model | Macro-F1 | Event Acc. | Valid JSON | $ / 1,000 answers | 
| Base Qwen3-14B | 0.415 | 0.54 | 0.834 | $0.64 | 
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 0.538 | 0.584 | 0.991 | $17.79 | 
| Claude Opus 4.7 | 0.625 | 0.718 | 0.9995 | $29.26 | 
| Fine-tuned Qwen3-14B | 0.975 | 0.983 | 1.000 | $0.60 | 
Table 2: Cloud energy-market analysis results, fine-tuned Qwen3-14B compared to frontier models
Costs are Amazon Bedrock list prices times measured tokens per answer. Fine-tuning lifted an open model from last place to first: +0.35 macro-F1 over Claude Opus 4.7 (95 percent confidence interval 0.324 to 0.371) at about 49× lower cost per 1,000 answers ($0.60 compared to $29.26). The model held 0.968 macro-F1 on a second, later test set.
Business benefits
Faster iteration and faster time to market: Exowatt moved its customized model from experimentation to production in only nine days. This process could have taken months if the team had to build and optimize custom containers and training recipes, provision GPUs, and manage infrastructure. With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, the team trained Qwen3-1.7B in about 32 minutes and Qwen3-14B in about 8.5 hours, with no capacity requests and up to four training jobs running concurrently. For the energy-market use case, Exowatt ran 23 jobs totaling about 155 hours of managed training and moved from the base model to a fine-tuned model serving in Cloud EMS in six days. The merged checkpoint was imported into Amazon Bedrock in about 14 minutes. The end-to-end pipeline used seven AWS serverless services, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints for Exowatt to manage.
Higher accuracy compared to frontier models: Both fine-tuned models beat the larger frontier models on their own task: Qwen3-1.7B at 0.911 macro-F1 (compared to 0.698 for Claude Sonnet 4.6) and Qwen3-14B at 0.975 (compared to 0.625 for Claude Opus 4.7).
Lower cost across both deployments: In the cloud, the Qwen3-14B serves at $0.60 per 1,000 answers versus $29.26 for Claude Opus 4.7 (about 49× lower), with no idle cost and $6.86 per hour only while active on Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import. At the edge, the quantized Qwen3-1.7B runs on the site’s existing CPU with no per-inference cost and no dependency on connectivity.
Grounded, low-risk outputs: Across both models, the evidence fence removed every uncited claim (any evidence citation whose source, field, or value does not literally match the input), and the edge model abstains rather than guesses when unsure. This is what let the team run it autonomously in shadow mode on a cloud-hosted replica of a site.
Lessons learned
For specific tasks, smaller fine-tuned large language models can outperform large frontier models: Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-14B models each outperformed frontier models on the target task, delivering higher accuracy at a fraction of the cost with significantly smaller models.
Data quality and variety outweigh raw volume and extra epochs: For tightly scoped tasks, data quality mattered more than model size or data volume. On the alarm-triage model, more verified training variety moved macro-F1 from 0.584 (trained on the 684 verified decisions alone) to 0.911 (with the paraphrase-expanded 2,522-row set). Simply running more epochs over the same rows did worse: a control run that trained on the 684 original rows for 11 epochs (the same number of steps) reached only 0.879. Curated data mattered more than dataset size throughout.
Removing the provisioning step changes how a team works: When a training run no longer requires waiting for GPU capacity, fine-tuning shifts from a rare event to a routine, iterative one.
One training pipeline serves two deployment targets: Separating model training from deployment lets Exowatt use the same pipeline for both offline edge deployment and connected fleet-level analysis, simplifying operations and accelerating model deployment in the cloud.
Conclusion
Exowatt now has one reusable AI pipeline that took a task from model specific data preparation to model deployment. Rather than tuning one model for different tasks, Exowatt plans to apply the same fine-tuning principles to different tasks, each with its own data, specific models, and evaluations, across the fleet as new device types and market tasks come online.
The pattern generalizes beyond energy industry segments. AI engineers, data scientists, and customers across industry segments can adopt the same principles. Use Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization as a low-overhead AI pipeline to fine-tune small, task-specific models, then deploy them where the work happens: at the edge when connectivity or latency requires it, and through a managed cloud endpoint such as Amazon SageMaker AI for elastic workloads.
To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization and Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: Meta’s $25 billion legal loss just put blood in the water
articles.text:
When attorneys general from across the US announced a $17 billion settlement with Meta this summer, the sum was unprecedented. But a ruling last week by a New Mexico judge blew that number out of the water. The judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to resolve claims that Meta misled users around the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and related incidents. Similar claims were resolved by the settlement with most other states. The outcome raised an obvious question: Should these states have asked for more?
Meta’s $25 billion legal loss just put blood in the water
Should states have sought more in their kids online safety settlement?
The answer depends on a mix of factors, including whether the $25 billion order stands up to Meta’s legal challenges. Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement that the company is “confident we will prevail on appeal” and called New Mexico’s lawsuit an attempt to impose “a tax on speech.” If the fine sticks, however, it could create a new appetite for Big Tech’s opponents to stick it out in court — or ask for bigger payouts to settle.
“For the settling AGs, they’re going to look at this and maybe experience some regret for all the claims that they waived, and start looking around and trying to figure out what’s left that they didn’t waive, if they can try to get some money like this too,” says Daphne Keller, director of platform regulation at the Stanford Program in Law, Science & Technology. For the many individuals, school districts, and tribes with outstanding claims, “this is very encouraging and will make them hopeful that continuing to litigate aggressively will lead to a big payout,” Keller says.
The $25 billion court order covered millions of violations of New Mexico’s unfair practices law, after a jury found Meta had misled users about how it protected their data and policed misinformation and hate speech – claims stemming from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal. In most states, such claims were covered by a section of the kids online safety settlement, resolved with a $459 million payment.
While that number looks comparatively puny, there were upsides to taking it. A settlement provided more certainty and an expedited payout for states even though Meta will be making the payments over 10 years. It also secured product commitments from Meta, like restrictions on teen usage, that might have been more difficult to get from a court ruling. And it allowed those to be implemented soon after the settlement was approved, which advocates say is important to prevent further harm to kids. Other state attorneys general also may have been working with different laws or evidence that could result in outcomes different from those obtained in New Mexico.
“Assuming that even a fraction of this award gets upheld, then they clearly took pennies on the dollar compared to New Mexico”
But New Mexico’s win, combined with other recent legal victories for AGs and private plaintiffs — including a separate judgment of nearly $1 billion against Meta in New Mexico — may embolden anyone still litigating privacy and kids online safety cases. “Assuming that even a fraction of this award gets upheld, then they clearly took pennies on the dollar compared to New Mexico,” Keller says of the settling states. Imagining she’s an AG with similar claims — like public false statements about privacy or content moderation — “I become less willing to settle in those cases,” Keller adds. “Or if I do settle, I ask for more.”
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose state avoided joining the Meta settlement, seemed to take the latest New Mexico ruling as a validation. “As I said at the time, the multi-state settlement with Meta was a slap on the wrist,” Utheimer wrote on X. “Florida isn’t going to sell out to Meta. We’re going to hold them accountable.” The District of Columbia could be the next place to test whether New Mexico’s win can be replicated since it did not settle its Cambridge Analytica claims and has continued pursuing its lawsuit in court.
“Any one, or 10, or 50 of them could hit the jackpot”
While the AGs who joined the settlement can’t pursue covered claims against Meta anymore, they could still push for more in cases against other social media defendants, including TikTok, YouTube, and Snap. And those who weren’t part of the Meta settlement, including school districts and individuals, may be encouraged to continue pushing ahead. “Realistically, there’s so many cases, it’s not feasible that every single case can have an outcome like this,” says Keller. “Meta actually would go broke because the multipliers are so large. But any one, or 10, or 50 of them could hit the jackpot.”
States have stepped in to pursue tech policy and competition cases where the federal government has declined to, but the wide range of potential outcomes for each state presents its own challenges. As Congress has stalled on major tech policy bills and the Trump administration has often favored lighter regulation on tech, Colorado Law associate professor Blake Reid sees recent cases as a “move toward state-level tech policy.”
“The trick of that is, now you have 50 states that all have different sets of resources, and different sets of politics, and different sets of incentives, and frankly just different skill levels in terms of the sophistication that it takes to do litigation at this scale,” Reid says. “And it’s the same Meta, but now it’s up to 50 small opponents that are going to break in different ways.”
As for whether the $25 billion ruling makes other states rethink their strategy, Reid says there could be a range of approaches, depending partly on whether the figure is upheld on appeal and whether Meta loses yet more cases. “Is that a game that every state attorney general wants to play?” he asks. “And I think the settlement in the other case suggests maybe not.” Still, the new figure may change what AGs think they can achieve in court. And the more losses Meta and other tech companies rack up, the more ambitious they might get.

articles.title: Cómo convertir una pelea entre Las Guerreras K-pop vs Los caballeros del Zodiaco en una lámina para colorear
articles.text:
Una escena de Las Guerreras K-pop de Netflix frente a Los caballeros del Zodiaco puede convertirse en una lámina para colorear si la imagen se diseña desde el inicio para impresión.
Gemini, la herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) de Google, permite crear una composición original con referencias generales a ambos universos y adaptarla luego a un dibujo de contornos negros.
El resultado depende del texto que se entregue a la plataforma. La indicación debe evitar la reproducción exacta de rostros, armaduras, trajes, logotipos y escenarios reconocibles.
En su lugar, conviene describir guerreras ficticias de pop coreano y caballeros inspirados en constelaciones, con una escena de acción simple y espacios amplios para que los niños puedan pintar.
Cuál es el primer paso para crear imágenes con IA
El primer paso es abrir Gemini desde un navegador o desde la aplicación para celulares e iniciar sesión con una cuenta de Google. La plataforma recibe instrucciones escritas en el cuadro de conversación, genera una propuesta visual y ofrece opciones para revisarla o descargarla.
Aunque el teléfono permite completar todo el proceso, una computadora o una tableta facilitan la revisión de los contornos. Antes de escribir el prompt, hay que decidir el tamaño de papel, la orientación y el tipo de enfrentamiento que mostrará la lámina digital.
Qué escena funciona mejor para una hoja destinada a niños pequeños
Una composición clara puede mostrar a tres guerreras ficticias de pop coreano en un extremo y a tres caballeros con armaduras inspiradas en el cielo nocturno en el otro. Cada grupo puede sostener elementos separados, como micrófonos, espadas estilizadas, escudos, amuletos o símbolos de constelaciones.
Para niños pequeños, es preferible reducir el número de personajes y objetos. Una escena con seis figuras principales y un fondo limitado permite reconocer mejor cada sector. Estrellas, notas musicales, planetas sencillos o rayos de energía pueden completar el espacio sin cubrir la hoja con detalles difíciles de colorear.
Cómo redactar un prompt que no infrinja derechos de autor
El prompt debe describir características amplias, sin solicitar copias de personajes existentes. En lugar de mencionar nombres concretos o atuendos idénticos, se puede pedir un grupo de heroínas con vestuario futurista de escenario y un equipo de guerreros con cascos, capas y armaduras vinculadas con signos astrales.
Un ejemplo de prompt puede ser: “Crea una página para colorear en blanco y negro de tres guerreras ficticias de pop coreano enfrentadas a tres caballeros fantásticos con armaduras inspiradas en constelaciones. Las heroínas usan accesorios musicales y espadas estilizadas. Los caballeros llevan escudos y capas”.
Qué instrucciones convierten la imagen en una lámina para colorear
La frase “lámina para colorear” debe aparecer de forma expresa. Ayudan indicaciones como “dibujo en blanco y negro”, “líneas gruesas y limpias”, “sin color”, “sin sombras”, “sin degradados”, “espacios amplios para pintar” y “contornos nítidos”.
Si la escena está orientada a chicos de menor edad, se pueden añadir pedidos como “rostros simples”, “figuras redondeadas”, “pocos detalles en las armaduras” y “objetos separados entre sí”. Las líneas anchas y los sectores despejados facilitan el uso de lápices, crayones o marcadores.
Asimismo, la orientación del papel forma parte del prompt. Una pelea con dos equipos ubicados frente a frente suele funcionar en formato horizontal. Una figura central acompañada por criaturas, símbolos musicales o elementos celestes puede adaptarse mejor a una hoja vertical tamaño carta.
Cómo descargar y preparar la imagen para imprimir
Cuando se elige una versión, hay que utilizar la opción de descarga junto a la imagen generada. Desde la versión web, el archivo puede guardarse en el dispositivo; en la aplicación, queda disponible en la galería o en el gestor de archivos.
Antes de imprimir, hay que comprobar que los contornos estén definidos, no haya logotipos ni textos y las figuras entren completas en la página. La impresión puede hacerse en papel común, en tamaño A4 o carta según el formato solicitado.

articles.title: Vistara Growth goes evergreen with launch of sixth private credit fund | BetaKit
articles.text:
Vancouver-based private credit investor Vistara Growth has officially launched its sixth fund, for which it ultimately hopes to raise $500 million USD ($700 million CAD).
Vistara hopes to secure an initial close of between $200 million and $250 million USD for the Vistara Growth Structured Opportunities Fund by the end of November. The firm is already well on its way to that target thanks to an anchor commitment of up to $125 million from longtime limited partner (LP) Ryan Beedie through his family office.
“Raising a new fund every two years is not simple.”
Randy Garg, Vistara Growth
The Vancouver billionaire revealed that commitment this summer, alongside news his Beedie Capital had purchased a 50-percent ownership stake in Vistara’s general partnership (GP), splitting Vistara’s 20-percent share of gains from the new fund and annual management fee.
While the strategy behind Vistara’s sixth fund will remain the same as its predecessors, providing a combination of debt and equity to mid- and later-stage technology companies across North America, the fund structure will be significantly different.
Since 2015, Vistara has raised and deployed five closed-end funds that have grown progressively larger. Though it had seen success with this approach, the firm saw what it thought was a better path forward through its latest investment vehicle, Vistara founder and managing partner Randy Garg told BetaKit in an exclusive interview.
“Raising a new fund every two years is not simple,” Garg said. “It’s very distracting. It takes a lot of effort.” It had also become a burden for its LPs navigating capital calls and distributions across so many different vehicles, he added.
RELATED: Vistara Growth closes $321-million USD fund after “friend-raising to the max”
Garg said many of Vistara’s LPs are “set-it-and-forget-it-type investors,” noting that when they approached Vistara with the idea of instead creating a permanent fund that they could take the income out of and let their principal compound over a longer period, the firm listened.
According to Garg, the Vistara Growth Structured Opportunities Fund’s permanent, evergreen structure allows the firm to offer greater flexibility on its repayment terms. It also permits Vistara to hold its warrants and convertible positions for longer because it isn’t on the same clock.
“It doesn’t have a number on it because this is going to be the flagship forever fund,” Garg said.
Vistara closed its $321-million USD fifth fund a year ago after “friend-raising to the max” in a nearly two-year process that ultimately fell short of its initial, $386-million USD goal. At the time, Garg indicated that the firm hoped to raise a larger sixth fund and emerge from the so-called “tweener” category by rallying institutional LPs and securing more support outside of British Columbia. To date, over 90 percent of that capital has come from BC.
The 15-person firm focuses on mid- and later-stage private tech companies with between $10 million and $100 million CAD in annual recurring revenue in areas like AI, FinTech, and healthtech. While it typically invests in venture-backed businesses at the Series B stage and beyond, it also finances bootstrapped firms seeking capital to finance organic growth, mergers and acquisitions, or shareholder liquidity initiatives without diluting ownership.
Vistara creates tailored investment structures composed of debt, equity, or some combination of the two, providing credit to those businesses while also obtaining equity sweeteners like warrants to buy their stock at a future date, or convertible debt. Those equity sweeteners can help Vistara boost its returns if clients later close equity funding or sell at a higher valuation.
“Vistara has built an exceptional team, established a disciplined investment approach, and consistently delivered strong results.”
Ryan Beedie, Beedie Capital
To date, Vistara has raised close to $700 million USD and returned $600 million USD, Garg said. The firm has invested in 46 companies and exited 26, posting a net annualized internal rate of return of approximately 13 to 14 percent. Thus far, the firm has fully returned its first two funds to LPs, has posted a 120-percent-plus return on its third, and is approaching the 100 percent mark on Fund IV. Some of its funds have been ranked top performers in their asset class by market research company Preqin.
Beedie and Garg have been friends for decades and colleagues for more than 15 years: Garg spun Vistara out of a Beedie Capital fund he was running at the time. Beedie Capital has been its biggest LP since then, anchoring all of its funds to date. Garg described Beedie’s latest commitments as “huge,” noting that the family office’s GP stake creates greater alignment and reflects both the trust they have built and the room they see for Vistara to grow from here.
“Over the past decade, Vistara has built an exceptional team, established a disciplined investment approach, and consistently delivered strong results,” Beedie told BetaKit over email. “Our acquisition of a 50-percent stake in the management company and anchoring its new evergreen fund, reflects our confidence in the broader organization and the significant growth opportunity ahead.”
As Vistara gears up to raise and deploy its new fund, the firm has also promoted two longtime investment team members, John O’Donoghue and Neil Kenley, to partner, and hired Jyotin Handa as CFO. Handa previously spent a decade helping fellow Canadian private credit provider Espresso Capital structure and manage its own evergreen funds.
While Vistara could potentially create other new funds in the future, Garg said the firm has no intention of doing that at this time, and may just look to raise additional capital for the Vistara Growth Structured Opportunities Fund.
With the right team, an aligned anchor partner, and a new fund structure in place, Garg said, “The table is now set for growth.”
Feature image courtesy Vistara Growth.

articles.title: ¡Adiós al Oscar! La nueva película de Taika Waititi y Jenna Ortega es tan mala que cancela su estreno en España
articles.text:
Hace varios meses, el estreno de Klara y el Sol, la nueva película de Taika Waititi con Jenna Ortega, levantaba una enorme curiosidad. Sony Pictures había programado su estreno para finales de octubre. Unas fechas que suelen estar destinadas a proyectos ambiciosos y con posible recorrido en la temporada de premios. De hecho, su presencia estaba confirmada para eventos tan importantes como el Festival de Cine de Londres.
Por todo ello, muchos ya auguraban que Jenna Ortega podría incluso entrar en la contienda para acabar nominada a los Premios Oscar como mejor actriz. La intérprete es uno de los rostros favoritos de Hollywood y, con un buen trabajo, este filme se antojaba como la oportunidad ideal para reconocerla al fin con esa primera nominación. Pero todo ha salido justo al revés.
Klara y el Sol se proyectó en el Festival de Cine de Londres hace unos días y las críticas fueron absolutamente desastrosas. Los profesionales especializados atacaron con muchísima dureza a la película, situándola como una de las peores del año. En Rotten Tomatoes cuenta con un catastrófico 25% de valoración. Tan mal fue que Sony Pictures tomó una decisión drástica.
En Estados Unidos, Klara y el Sol tenía programado su estreno para el 23 de octubre en casi 2.000 salas. Pero, finalmente, el estudio recortó enormemente su distribución y ha llegado a menos de 900. Y eso no es lo peor. En otros territorios, entre los que se encuentra España, la compañía directamente ha cancelado su estreno.
Taika Waititi, a la cárcel de los directores
Klara y el Sol tenía marcada su fecha de estreno en España para el 30 de octubre. Pero esto no sucederá. La película no pasará por la gran pantalla. Lo más probable es que en los próximos meses o años llegue, eventualmente, a alguna plataforma de streaming que quiera adquirir sus derechos. En resumen, la cintan se ha convertido en un nuevo fracaso total para Taika Waititi después de Thor: Love & Thunder y El peor equipo del mundo.
Hay quienes incluso consideran que el cineasta podría entrar en la "cárcel de los directores", expresión que se usa cuando los estudios de Hollywood se niegan a trabajar con algún director por considerarlo sinónimo de fracaso. Una situación terrible para quien también dirigiera filmes de la talla de Jojo Rabbit, Thor: Ragnarok o Lo que hacemos en las sombras.
De qué va Klara y el Sol
Cuando Klara (Jenna Ortega), una “Amiga Artificial” cuyo único deseo es encontrar el hogar perfecto conoce a Josie (Mia Tharia), ambas perciben de inmediato que son almas gemelas. Josie tiene una relación tensa con su madre (Amy Adams) y ambas han sufrido una gran pérdida, pero la inocente curiosidad y la inquebrantable lealtad de Klara comienzan a sanar a la familia y a iluminar el complicado mundo de Josie.
Escrita y dirigida por el ganador de un Óscar Taika Waititi, Klara y el Sol está basada en la novela superventas del ganador del Premio Nobel Kazuo Ishiguro. El filme lo protagonizan Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams y Mia Tharia, con Steve Buscemi y Natasha Lyonne, entre otros.

articles.title: The imec Report: Scaling Optical Interconnects For The AI Era
articles.text:
Unprecedented demand for bandwidth calls for bringing optics closer to silicon through a fundamental rethinking of the optical interconnect roadmap.
The explosive growth of cloud computing and AI – from generative, and reasoning, to (ultimately) agentic systems – is creating unprecedented demand for bandwidth, as the amount of data that must be moved both within and between data centers continues to surge. In turn, this exposes growing limitations in the underlying interconnects that not only span the data center fabric and rack level but also extend deep inside servers – down to where they link XPUs, memory, and other system components at the package and die level.
Copper-based (electrical) interconnects have long been the industry’s workhorse thanks to their low cost, simplicity, and reliability. Yet today, they are increasingly hitting fundamental limits: while highly energy-efficient electrical links can be realized, they are typically confined to very short reaches (on the order of millimeters). At longer distances and higher lane rates, power consumption rises sharply, thermal constraints intensify, and signal integrity degrades. In other words, electrical I/O is rapidly becoming a key barrier to scaling next-generation AI and machine learning systems.
Optical interconnects have emerged as a critical path forward. By transmitting data using light rather than electrical signals, they are far less sensitive to distance, enabling much better energy efficiency while mitigating many of the crosstalk and thermal challenges inherent to copper links. However, even optical technologies are now being pushed to new extremes – as the need emerges for (multi) terabit-per-second interfaces, ultra-high energy efficiency, and extremely low (sub-microsecond) latency.
Meeting these requirements will take more than incremental innovation. It calls for a fundamental rethinking of the optical interconnect roadmap; one that progressively brings optics closer to the silicon – from the front panel, into the package, and ultimately firmly integrated into the wafer stack.
For more than two decades, pluggable optical transceivers have been the backbone of high-speed telecom and datacom networks – powering everything from enterprise workloads and video streaming to today’s hyperscale cloud infrastructure. Inserted into standardized ports on switches, routers, and servers, pluggables convert electrical signals from the host into optical signals for transmission over fiber – and back again on the receive side.
They deliver:
Across successive generations, pluggable optical transceivers have scaled from 100/200G to 400G and 800G by pushing baud rates (the number of symbols transmitted per second on a single optical lane), adopting higher-order modulation (such as PAM-4), and increasing the number of parallel lanes.
And despite their maturity, pluggable optics continue to evolve. First-generation 1.6T pluggable transceivers, for instance – relying on 200Gbps per-lane data rates, combined in an eight-lane parallel architecture – are approaching sampling and early deployment, targeting direct-reach (DR) intra-data center links as well as forward-reach (FR) connections over single-mode fiber.
The key enabler is silicon photonics (SiPho), which underpins this scaling through a combination of (silicon-based) optical and electronic building blocks, including Mach–Zehnder modulators that play a central role in enabling cost-effective 200Gbps per-lane operation while keeping power consumption in check.
Looking further ahead, toward the end of the decade, the industry is eyeing the 3.2T pluggable optics milestone. Yet, achieving these performance levels will require continued advances in high-speed electronics, packaging, and thermal management – as well as a substantial expansion of the silicon photonics (SiPho) toolbox. On the transmit side, for instance, optical modulators will need to support bandwidths beyond 100GHz while maintaining low insertion loss and high modulation efficiency – requirements that are becoming increasingly difficult to meet with conventional silicon devices alone.
Fig. 1: Pluggable optics have delivered an order-of-magnitude leap in performance in the past few years – both in bandwidth density and power efficiency. Source: imec.
Addressing these limitations is driving interest in the heterogeneous integration of higher-performance electro-optic materials such as lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) and lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃). Techniques such as micro-transfer printing offer a promising path to integrate these materials onto silicon photonics platforms. Early results are encouraging, but further research is ongoing to scale these approaches to high-volume manufacturing – so that future 3.2T modules can be built with the same practicality, reliability, and cost discipline that made pluggable optics the industry’s workhorse in the first place.
In parallel, alternative scaling approaches are also being explored. Concepts such as extreme pluggable optics (XPO) target capacities up to 12.8T by further increasing bandwidth density, albeit at the expense of significantly higher system complexity and the need for liquid cooling, which – at least for now – impacts both cost and practical deployment.
As optical interconnects (need to) push beyond today’s 200Gbps-per-lane standard, GeSi-based devices increasingly struggle to deliver the required combination of bandwidth and energy efficiency. While GeSi modulators have demonstrated scaling to 400Gbps per lane in the C-band, such performance has not yet been achieved in the O-band. To unlock the next performance leap in pluggable optical interconnects, researchers are therefore investigating the heterogeneous integration of advanced electro-optic materials – such as lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) and lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃) – onto silicon photonics, paving the way for a new class of high-speed modulators and photodetectors.
A promising enabler is micro-transfer printing, which enables the precise placement of thin-film materials onto SiPho wafers without the material waste, post-bonding complexity, and cost typically associated with conventional wafer bonding. Two world-first results highlight its potential:
First, researchers from imec and Ghent University showcased an O-band 320Gbps unamplified optical link over 2km of single-mode fiber. This was achieved using a high-bandwidth 100GHz germanium photodiode in combination with transfer-printed thin-film lithium niobate Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZMs), integrated onto a SiPho platform and co-packaged with custom-designed traveling-wave drivers and TIAs. This work marked the first seamless integration of LiNbO₃ modulators onto a silicon photonics platform using micro-transfer printing.
Fig. 2: The first seamless integration of LiNbO₃ modulators onto a silicon photonics platform using micro-transfer printing. Source: imec.
The team also achieved the first-ever heterogeneous integration of a LiTaO₃ modulator on a silicon photonic integrated circuit. Using the same micro-transfer printing technique previously applied to lithium niobate, the researchers achieved full compatibility with the entire wafer stack, enabling co-integration with other photonic building blocks such as heaters, filters, and germanium photodetectors without compromising their performance.
While these modulators are still relatively large, they offer a viable path for further scaling pluggable transceivers, where footprint constraints are less stringent. At the same time, alternative device concepts are being explored to meet the tighter size and integration requirements of future co-packaged optics. These include compact, ultra-high-speed GeSi-based modulators operating in the C-band, as well as emerging approaches based on the integration of III-V materials into silicon photonics platforms.
Further work is required to scale these heterogeneous integration approaches to high-volume manufacturing. Nevertheless, the results highlight a promising route toward integrating >100GHz electro-optic devices on SiPho – a capability widely seen as essential for future 3.2T pluggable modules and next-generation optical interconnects supporting AI-driven infrastructure.
Pluggable optics, however, are not the answer to every challenge. The rapid rise of (generative) AI workloads is pushing optical (inter)connectivity ever deeper into compute servers and accelerator clusters – all the way down to the chip-to-chip level.
At this scale, a new set of constraints emerges. Pluggable optical transceivers rely on very high baud rates, in combination with sophisticated digital signal processing (DSP) to compensate for signal degradation. While this works well at the rack or data center level, the power consumption and latency associated with heavy DSP become increasingly problematic for short-reach, chip-to-chip optical interconnects in AI and machine learning systems. Instead, they require intrinsically clean optical channels with extremely low bit-error rates, allowing each lane to operate without excessive equalization or DSP overhead.
This shift is precisely what drives the adoption of fast-and-narrow co-packaged optics (CPO). In a CPO system, the optical components are placed in close physical proximity to the (switching) silicon or compute die, shrinking the electrical path from several centimeters (as in pluggables) to just a few millimeters – or even less. By moving the electro-optic conversion point directly adjacent to the ASIC (within the same package), CPO greatly improves signal integrity, minimizes electrical losses, and reduces latency – without relying on power-hungry DSP. This makes CPO a compelling architecture for scaling next-generation AI and high-performance compute systems.
Fig. 3: Co-packaged optics shorten the electrical path between the optical engine and the host IC, enabling higher bandwidth density and eliminating the need for digital signal processing, thereby improving power efficiency. Source: imec.
But as early CPO deployments begin to emerge, integration complexity remains one of the defining challenges of the technology. Unlike pluggable optics – where the optical module is (largely) self-contained – CPO requires tight co-design and co-optimization, including photonic integrated circuits (PICs), electronic ICs (EICs), switch ASICs, fiber‑coupling strategies, thermal management, and advanced packaging. Addressing this multidisciplinary challenge is a central objective of imec’s Optical Interconnect Program.
In the CPO domain (also referred to as OIO2.5D), imec’s key research targets include:
Reaching these targets depends heavily on advanced semiconductor packaging technologies that support dense integration of photonic and electronic components – think of 2.5D interposer architectures, through-silicon vias (TSVs), fan-out wafer-level packaging (FO-WLP), and (increasingly) 3D integration enabled by hybrid bonding – as well as the use of advanced (III-V) materials.
And then there’s the light source. While the long-term goal is to integrate lasers directly on the photonic chip, early CPO systems will still rely on externally mounted laser sources. This approach simplifies thermal management and mitigates long-standing reliability concerns of operating lasers near hot ASICs. The trade-offs: higher output power to compensate for optical losses, greater packaging complexity, and the need for additional fibers and connectors to route light into the package.
In October 2025, imec announced a major advance for next‑generation optical interconnects: a beyond-110GHz C-band GeSi electro-absorption modulator (EAM) delivering a net data rate of 400Gbps per lane.
Leveraging the Franz-Keldysh effect, the device combines compact size, high speed, and low power consumption. And thanks to its GeSi foundation, it integrates seamlessly on 300mm CMOS-compatible SiPho platforms, offering a clear route to high-volume manufacturability.
This breakthrough reflects more than a decade of coordinated progress at both the device and system levels. On the device side, imec optimized footprint, doping schemes, and epitaxial growth processes. At the system level, a robust PAM-4 IM/DD transmission setup validated sustained net-400Gbps per-lane operation, demonstrating the practical readiness of GeSi EAM technology for future high-lane-rate optical engines.
As AI and machine learning systems scale to thousands of tightly interconnected accelerators, each linked to high-bandwidth memory stacks and peer processors over distances of only a few millimeters, the demands placed on optical interconnects become even more extreme. Over the next decade, they are expected to support bandwidth densities approaching (and surpassing) 10Tbps/mm, energy efficiencies well below 1pJ/bit, and ultra-low latencies (<100ns). These targets extend beyond what even advanced CPO architectures can achieve.
To meet these requirements, optics must move beyond the package and into the wafer stack itself. This is the foundation of 3D integrated optics. By collapsing the electrical path to micrometer-scale distances, OIO3D enables ultra-short, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient optical links that make dense chip-to-chip optical fabrics feasible.
Fig. 4: By collapsing the electrical path to micrometer-scale distances, OIO3D enables ultra-short, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient optical links that make dense chip-to-chip optical fabrics feasible. Source: imec.
Realizing 3D integrated optics requires overcoming several major technology challenges. These include scalable laser integration, the development of high-efficiency, high-bandwidth electro-optic components (e.g., based on GeSi, lithium niobate, lithium tantalate, indium phosphide, or barium titanate), and robust thermal management in densely stacked environments. Equally crucial are ultra-precise bonding and alignment techniques at wafer scale.
An evolutionary step beyond CPO, OIO2.5D combines high‑density photonic integration with manageable packaging complexity by placing photonic and electronic dies side‑by‑side on a shared silicon interposer. Photonic layers are integrated using die‑to‑wafer Cu‑based hybrid bonding, a technique that enables ultrashort, low‑parasitic electrical paths.
This architecture initially targets optical engines in the 8-32Tbps range. It leverages 32-64 Gbps per‑lane rates, optimized for low‑power, DSP‑free operation to minimize latency and heat. Wavelength‑division multiplexing (8-32 wavelengths per fiber) further boosts aggregate bandwidth without increasing fiber count. The technology roadmap aims for bandwidth densities of 2Tbps per millimeter and energy efficiencies near 2 pJ/bit.
OIO3D represents the most advanced and ambitious vision for optical interconnects. Here, photonic layers are stacked directly above or below the compute silicon, creating a true chip‑scale optical fabric that collapses electrical paths to micrometer‑scale distances.
This approach relies on both die‑to‑wafer and wafer‑to‑wafer hybrid bonding, enabling extremely fine‑pitch vertical interconnects. With this level of vertical integration, OIO3D aims to extend bandwidth capabilities to tens of terabits per second (and beyond), while targeting energy efficiencies around 2 pJ/bit – with a longer‑term trajectory toward sub‑pJ/bit operation.
A key research vector is on‑wafer laser integration, using heterogeneous III‑V approaches such as quantum‑dot GaAs‑on‑Si. This is actively being explored within the EU Chips Act pilot lines for future large‑scale photonic systems.
In January 2026, Veeco Instruments Inc. and imec announced a 300mm high-volume-manufacturing-compatible process for integrating barium titanate (BaTiO3, BTO) on silicon photonics.
With exceptional electro-optic properties, BTO enables high-speed, low-power modulators for applications ranging from optical transceivers to quantum photonics, LiDAR, and AR/VR. Historically, however, bringing BTO to silicon at scale has been difficult due to cost, uniformity, and manufacturability constraints.
Leveraging a collaboration with imec, Veeco recently delivered its first molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) cluster system tailored for 300mm wafers. The platform supports the growth of single-crystalline BTO thin films on silicon – using solid and hybrid MBE – improving repeatability, material quality, and cost of ownership compared with conventional MBE solutions.
Looking across the evolution of optical interconnects, it is clear the different approaches are progressing along different timelines.
Pluggable optics, already deployed at global scale, are entering a phase dominated by incremental technical optimizations rather than fundamental breakthroughs. Their roadmap continues – toward 1.6T and 3.2T modules – and pluggables will remain competitive for many use cases while new architectures ramp up.
Co-packaged optics are also approaching a stage of (relative) maturity. Key building blocks are transitioning into pilot-line support, supply-chain preparation, and wafer-level services – even as the industry continues to pursue higher bandwidth, faster lane rates, and better energy efficiency. The start of broad, large-scale CPO deployments is expected from 2027/2028 onward.
3D integrated optics remain in an earlier R&D stage. Current efforts focus on pathfinding and building the device/integration toolbox. First proof-of-concept demonstrators are anticipated within three to five years, with wider commercialization expected on a five- to ten-year horizon.
Through its optical interconnects research program, imec develops the key building blocks for future optical transceivers, anticipating market needs years before commercial deployment.
Imec’s strength lies in being a true one-stop R&D environment, bringing together expertise in silicon photonics, advanced CMOS, 3D integration, materials research, and system-level modeling. This breadth allows researchers to explore novel concepts far more rapidly than is possible in high-volume manufacturing settings, enabling short development cycles, and the freedom to pursue unconventional (integration) approaches. The program is further strengthened by imec’s cross-technology optimization (XTCO) strategy, which drives scaling across technology domains.
A critical accelerator is the close collaboration between imec’s optical interconnect research teams and IC-Link, imec’s semiconductor manufacturing pillar. While imec’s early‑stage research focuses on pathfinding and prototyping, IC‑Link helps bring technologies toward higher technology‑readiness levels by refining process flows, improving manufacturability, establishing test strategies, and engaging the broader supply chain. Through IC-Link, industrial partners can also access and evaluate these technologies via imec’s 200mm and 300mm iSiPP silicon photonics platforms, providing a pathway from early-stage innovation to industrial deployment.
Beyond IC-Link, imec maintains close engagement with industrial partners through a variety of collaboration models. These span guided projects (in which imec and its partners jointly explore emerging technologies), to targeted bilateral programs (driven by partner-specific requirements), all the way to long-term core partner engagements. In parallel, imec collaborates closely with equipment suppliers, enabling early validation of advanced tools and process capabilities – well before they enter commercial use.
Together, these interactions ensure that imec’s optical interconnect research stays firmly grounded in real‑world system requirements, while accelerating the translation of advanced technologies into market-ready solutions.
Peter Ossieur received the M.Sc. degree in electrical engineering from Ghent University, Belgium in 2000, and the PhD degree in electrical engineering from the same university in 2005. From 2005 till 2009 he was a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University, after which he joined Tyndall National Institute, where he became senior staff researcher. His research interests included electronic integrated circuit design and optical transmission systems. In 2017, he joined imec-IDlab, an imec embedded group at Ghent University. Today, he is director for XTCO Fabric and Optical Interconnect at imec, and holds a parttime appointment as professor at Ghent University. Peter Ossieur is a member of the ISSCC wireline subcommittee.

articles.title: Sur World of Warcraft Forever, vous pouvez réserver votre pseudo, mais il faut payer
articles.text:
Envie de vous faire un nom sur World of Warcraft ? Avec WoW Forever, c’est possible sans réaliser le moindre exploit en jeu : cette troisième version du célèbre MMORPG de Blizzard introduit un second nom, que Blizzard compare lui-même à un nom de famille. Une première pour WoW. Pour celles et ceux qui craignent de ne pas obtenir l’identité de leur rêve, Blizzard ouvre une réservation anticipée des noms, à condition de passer à la caisse.
À partir de ce mardi 27 octobre, à 18 heures (heure de Paris), la réservation anticipée des noms de personnages pour World of Warcraft Forever ouvre, et cela jusqu’au 3 novembre. Les joueurs et joueuses qui tiennent à leur pseudo peuvent donc le réclamer plus d’une semaine avant la sortie du jeu, fixée au jeudi 5 novembre à minuit (heure de Paris).
Premier arrivé, premier servi, et il faut payer
Il y a cependant trois limites à connaître. D’abord, Blizzard gère les demandes sur la base du premier arrivé, premier servi. Rien ne garantit donc d’obtenir la combinaison prénom + nom de son choix. Dans WoW Forever, il n’y a plus vraiment de serveur : chaque nom complet doit être unique dans toute la région (l’Europe, pour les joueurs français), et plus seulement sur un royaume.
Ensuite, cette réservation est… payante. Elle est réservée aux joueurs qui ont préacheté l’un des trois packs payants : le pack héroïque des Éolides, le pack épique des Éolides ou la Warcraft Forever Collection. Ils coûtent respectivement 29,99, 59,99 et 79,99 euros, et chaque pack reprend le contenu du précédent en y ajoutant ses propres bonus.
Ce système comporte une troisième limite : vous ne pouvez réserver que trois noms au maximum, quel que soit le coffret pré-acheté. On devine que cette règle vise à limiter de potentiels abus, avec quelqu’un qui préempterait plein de pseudonymes d’un coup.
La limite vaut pour tous les ensembles de règles confondus : si vous créez deux personnages en JcJ, il ne vous en reste qu’un pour le mode Normal ou Jeu de rôle. De quoi sécuriser votre personnage principal et deux personnages secondaires.
Avant la réservation des pseudonymes, vous aurez également à choisir sous quel ensemble de règles vous voulez jouer tel ou tel personnage. Ces ensembles de règles remplacent les serveurs habituels. Il vous faudra choisir entre Normal, JcJ (joueur contre joueur), Jeu de rôle et Extrême, le mode hardcore où la mort a des conséquences durables. Ce dernier n’arrivera que quelque temps après la sortie, et Blizzard n’a pas encore donné de date.
