articles.title: Trump quer proibir o termo "inteligência artificial" nos EUA
articles.text:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou, nesta terça-feira (27), que pretende proibir oficialmente o uso da expressão “inteligência artificial” em documentos e outros contextos. Em publicação na rede social Truth Social, ele voltou a defender que a tecnologia passe a ser chamada de “superinteligência”, por considerar o nome atual impreciso.
A declaração foi feita em crítica ao jornal americano The Wall Street Journal, que, segundo Trump, ainda não adotou a terminologia de sua preferência.
“Em pouco tempo, vamos PROIBIR oficialmente o termo ‘IA/inteligência artificial’ em todos os documentos relevantes e em tudo mais, devido à sua imprecisão”, escreveu o presidente.
A manifestação amplia iniciativa que Trump já havia colocado em prática no governo. Em 29 de setembro, ele assinou uma ordem executiva determinando que departamentos e agências do Executivo federal adotassem os termos “Super Intelligence” e “SI” em correspondências oficiais, comunicações públicas e documentos de políticas públicas, deixando de usar as expressões “Artificial Intelligence” e “AI”.
A nova declaração, no entanto, não esclarece como uma eventual proibição mais ampla funcionaria, quais outros contextos seriam afetados nem quando as novas medidas entrariam em vigor.
Leia mais:
- Anthropic expõe os custos e os riscos da inteligência artificial antes de IPO
- IPO da Anthropic pode mudar o mercado global de inteligência artificial
- Bolha de IA estoura na China e faz mercado perder US$ 480 bilhões
Por que Trump quer mudar o nome da inteligência artificial?
- Trump considera que a palavra “artificial” transmite uma ideia equivocada sobre a tecnologia. Em discurso na Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas (ONU), em setembro, o presidente argumentou que o termo faz a inteligência parecer falsa, quando, na visão dele, as capacidades desses sistemas seriam extraordinárias;
- A preferência por “superinteligência” também foi incorporada ao discurso oficial do governo estadunidense, que apresenta a mudança como uma forma de reconhecer os avanços tecnológicos;
- O conceito, porém, tem significado específico no campo da tecnologia. A superinteligência costuma ser associada a sistemas capazes de superar as habilidades cognitivas humanas em praticamente todas as áreas intelectuais. Trata-se de categoria distinta da inteligência artificial (IA) em sentido amplo, que abrange desde sistemas de reconhecimento de imagens até ferramentas generativas, como o ChatGPT;
- Em análise publicada pela revista científica Nature em outubro, pesquisadores destacaram justamente essa diferença: a superinteligência é uma categoria aspiracional de sistemas tecnológicos, e não uma descrição consolidada de todas as ferramentas de IA existentes atualmente.
O que muda na prática?
Por enquanto, a mudança estabelecida pela ordem executiva de setembro se concentra no Poder Executivo federal. A declaração mais recente de Trump sugere a intenção de ampliar a substituição da terminologia, mas não apresenta detalhes suficientes para determinar o alcance de eventual proibição.
Também não há, na publicação citada, uma definição federal definitiva que estabeleça quais tecnologias se enquadrariam na categoria de “superinteligência”. A própria Casa Branca informou, ao anunciar a ordem executiva, que o governo deveria elaborar uma definição oficial para os termos “Super Intelligence” e “SI”.
Assim, a iniciativa representa uma mudança na linguagem adotada pelo governo estadunidense, mas não significa que todas as tecnologias atualmente conhecidas como inteligência artificial tenham passado a ser tecnicamente classificadas como superinteligência.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Anduril, Qualcomm launch BlueChip, a new kind of US-made laptop | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anduril founder Palmer Luckey is vowing to bring computer manufacturing back to the U.S. And by that, he doesn’t just mean assembly, but the production of every individual component, some of which are exclusively made in China today.
Anduril is partnering with Qualcomm to achieve that mission with a new computer called BlueChip, the companies announced Tuesday. BlueChip will be available for preorder in 2027.
While technical details are scant — Anduril hasn’t even finished contracting with all its component suppliers yet, according to Luckey — this first product will be a hardened laptop. It will be designed to withstand the most grueling physical environments and meet the security-conscious needs of the military, government, first responders, and law enforcement.
For the first generation, about 90% of its components will be made in the U.S. or in allied countries, Anduril says, most notably its CPU. BlueChip will run on a Snapdragon X Series built at TSMC’s massive new facility in Arizona. The CPU uses the same architecture that powers other laptops, including the Microsoft Surface, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said during the press conference.
“As of right now, the laptop’s bill of materials is about 90% U.S. and allied [ally countries], and we have a technical roadmap to get to 100% domestic over time,” Luckey said. “The intent in the long run is to have an option that is made entirely in the United States, 100% domestic. And I mean everything. I mean the displays. I mean the metallics. I mean the the magnetics. All of it.”
Right now, for instance, Luckey says he’s found an American supplier for the glass that covers the display, but the display itself is one of several components he says are only manufactured in China.
While Luckey says consumers are welcome to order a BlueChip — the company may even create a waiting list for interested consumers — this first PC won’t be designed for them. For one thing, as a hardened computer, it will be heavy and have battery-life constraints because of the engineering required to withstand rain, dust, and other rugged conditions.
The bigger point is to offer U.S. government agencies a product that complies with regulations requiring them to buy U.S.-made computers. In this case, the selling point is a transparent supply chain that customers can track and audit.
“These computers are the anti-surveillance computer. You fully control it,” Luckey described in a recent interview. “You know everything that is in it, every single component, and you know every software component that is running on it.”
Anduril is also working to ensure that the Arm-based machine works well with Windows apps, apps built for certain Linux distributions used by the government, and even archaic software that various agencies still run.
While Anduril hasn’t yet announced pricing, Luckey estimates it will cost about 20% more than typical high-end PCs.
“As much as I love BlueChip, if I was just a normal consumer making a rational decision without a kind of patriotic basis, I’d be better off buying a Dell laptop than an Anduril laptop because it’s going to be cheaper. I’m just talking about your average-person consumer, right, who doesn’t have any real need for this,” Luckey said.
But Luckey clearly hopes Anduril will eventually make U.S.-made laptops more in line with consumer desires. He said the product is the first in what he envisions as a full line of BlueChip computers, noting that he began his career making virtual reality headsets for consumers.
“I’m buying American cars, and then I buy a computer that’s made on the other side of the world, not just China, but you know, Japan, Korea,” he said. “It’s kind of humiliating that as an American and my birthright is computers, in my opinion, because America invented them, that I’m not able to buy an American computer.”
As for the potentially expensive folly of trying to take on China’s electronics components manufacturing industry single-handedly, Luckey joked about his internal reputation for “being a nut” with such big ideas. (He admits that he pushed his board to spend $900 million to build a factory for a jet before the company had even won a contract.)
“This is not one of those things. My investors do not think I’m a crazy person in this particular area,” he said. In fact, rugged computers are already about a $5 billion market.

articles.title: Google’s next Genie AI model generates more realistic experiences
articles.text:
Google announced today its Genie 4 world model for generating interactive experiences using AI. The company says the model has four main updates: It allows for more realistic worlds, lets users update an experience in real time with a natural language prompt, can generate audio, and uses Gemini 3.8 Flash under the hood to help with its simulations. It also can create experiences that are about two minutes long, up from one minute for the previous Genie 3 model.
Google’s next Genie AI model generates more realistic experiences
The Genie 4 world model offers more realism and can create audio to accompany its interactive worlds.
Google is pitching Genie 4 as a tool that could be helpful for things like pre-visualization for filmmakers, prototyping game ideas, and making training scenarios for robots. But the company warns that, as simulations run longer, details and object permanence can shift over time.
I haven’t been able to try Genie 4 for myself — it’s launching first as a “research preview” to “trusted testers” — so I can’t tell you how it compares to the Genie 3-powered Project Genie, which I used to generate bad Nintendo knockoffs. articles.title: “Hay que tener más miedo a perder el empleo por no usar IA que por usarla”: Jon Hernández, divulgador de inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
Jon Hernández era fotógrafo. En 2023 le llegó un artículo de Eliezer Yudkowsky en la revista Time, se puso a leer sobre inteligencia artificial y hoy es una de las voces más seguidas sobre IA en español, con un canal de YouTube que supera los 800 mil suscriptores. Hace unos dos años vendió todas sus cámaras.
“No fue un cambio voluntario”, dice. Su sensación, cuenta, era la contraria a la del que huye: él iba a ser el fotógrafo que usara la IA para quitarles el trabajo a otros fotógrafos. Ese es el eje de toda la charla: la IA no es una amenaza que esquivar, es una ventaja que tomar antes que el resto.
Su primer libro, La hostIA que viene, salió este año por Planeta y pregunta qué pasará el día que una IA se niegue a obedecer. Pero la conversación arrancó por algo más urgente: qué hace hoy un chico de 20 años y qué hace alguien de 45.
Al de 20 le pide que no guarde rencor y al de 45 que no mire para otro lado
“Al de 20, que se prepare para cambios y que la mochila de lo que ha invertido no sea un freno”, dice. Sabe que muchos estudiaron programación porque los adultos les dijeron que ahí estaba el futuro. “Tienen razón, les hemos jodido. No va a servir de nada estar enfadado.”
Al de 45 le pide que no esconda la cabeza. “Esto incluso al que tiene 60 le va a afectar. Nadie está a salvo.” Su fórmula tiene dos preguntas, cómo me afecta y cómo le saco partido. Entender por qué funciona la tecnología es perder el tiempo, porque mañana funcionará de otra manera.
Y una advertencia para el empleado que cree que ocultarle la IA al jefe lo protege. “Es más probable que pierdas tu trabajo porque tu jefe es negacionista de la IA que porque sea favorable”. Los despidos, dice, van a caer en las empresas que no supieron aplicarla, no de forma pareja en todas.
Para explicar por qué no hay escapatoria, usa la imprenta: las ciudades que la adoptaron primero crecieron un 60% más rápido que las demás, un dato que el economista Jeremiah Dittmar midió entre 1500 y 1600. Pero al final todas la adoptaron. “Lo puedes hacer primero con una ventaja competitiva o lo puedes hacer después arrastrado por la marea.”
Lo que más lo sorprendió: la IA dejó de responder y empezó a hacer
Le pregunté qué lo sorprendió en estos tres años. No dudó: diciembre del año pasado, cuando los modelos empezaron a usar herramientas y nacieron de verdad los agentes, programas que ejecutan tareas por su cuenta. Entre enero y febrero armó los suyos con OpenClaw y dejó de usar ChatGPT y Claude. Ahora que las plataformas integraron eso, volvió.
El otro salto fue a mitad de año: Claude Cowork y ChatGPT Work, las aplicaciones que manejan la computadora del usuario. Lo que la IA ganó en capacidad de hacer cosas, dice, es más “que en todos los años anteriores combinados”.
Su lectura del mercado va contra la intuición. OpenAI no tiene el mejor modelo, pero tiene el mejor agente. Lo compara con un auto de motor muy potente y sin volante: “No sirve para nada”. Lo que decide hoy, dice, es cómo se integra la IA en las herramientas de cada uno, no los modelos.
Sus hijos usan IA con supervisión y uno ya lo dejó sin respuesta
Hernández sostiene que cuanto más se trata a la IA como a una persona, mejor funciona. ¿Hasta dónde? “No estoy seguro de que en el futuro seamos capaces de diferenciar cuando hablamos con un humano y cuando con una máquina.” Cree que sus hijos, de 10 y 12 años, tendrán amigos humanos y amigos IA sin notar la diferencia.
Uno de sus hijos quería un aparato que él había traído de la oficina. Le pidió una nota escrita a mano y se la devolvió con faltas de ortografía. El chico le sacó una foto, se la mandó a ChatGPT y volvió con la nota corregida. “¿Qué le vas a decir? ¿Qué es trampa?”
Tenía un problema, dice, pensó cómo resolverlo y lo ejecutó a la perfección. Le dio el juguete.
Admite que esa delegación cognitiva, dejar que la máquina piense por uno, puede ser un problema en chicos cuyo cerebro todavía se forma. No tiene la respuesta. “Si veo que mi niño se está volviendo idiota por utilizar inteligencia artificial”, dice, siempre puede volver a la calculadora.
Qué revisa y qué no: la vara no es la dificultad, es la consecuencia
Dice que casi todo se puede delegar ya, porque los modelos revisan su propia respuesta y citan fuentes antes de entregarla. Pero la vara no es si la tarea es fácil o difícil, sino qué pasa si sale mal. Si le pregunta a qué hora sale su vuelo y se equivoca, toma el siguiente.
Si le pregunta la dosis de un remedio para sus hijos, va al prospecto. “Como haya alucinado, igual me cargo a mi hijo.”
Le mencioné la nota que publiqué el día anterior en Infobae sobre Jamie Dimon, el CEO de JPMorgan Chase: los bancos evalúan cortar el acceso de los chatbots a las cuentas o hacer responsable al cliente que lo habilita. Su respuesta fue al revés: “Lo que JPMorgan tiene que hacer es crear un acceso para mi agente, con los permisos que yo le dé. Si no lo va a hacer, lo va a hacer Revolut”.
Sobre los videos falsos con su voz: “No se puede hacer nada”
Circulan videos con su voz que nunca grabó. ¿Cómo se protege la gente? “No se puede hacer nada. Con diez segundos de audio tuyo te puedo clonar la voz. Todo el mundo tiene diez segundos de audio en internet.” El momento para evitarlo, dice, fue 2022, cuando los deepfakes, los videos y audios falsificados con IA, se veían lejanos y nadie reguló.
Lo que le preocupa es la repetición: la misma gente que avisaba en 2022 hoy advierte sobre ciberseguridad y biología, “y de nuevo no les estamos haciendo ni caso”.
Ve a Latinoamérica con más ganas de IA que a una Europa acomodada
Como la nota se lee en Argentina y en la región, le pregunté si veía diferencias con Europa. Aclara que cuando viaja ve la burbuja de la IA y no el país entero, pero ve más gente en los eventos, preguntas más profundas y más medios cubriendo el tema que en España.
La ven, dice, como el trampolín que les hace falta para nivelar. Europa lleva 20 años de bienestar y se acomodó: “Eso nos va a pasar factura”.
El próximo salto no es la cuántica, es la robótica
La computación cuántica, dice, está lejos: “La IA está haciendo más por la cuántica que la cuántica por la IA”. Lo que sigue no pasa en la pantalla, sino en la calle. “Ahora mismo estamos viendo todo lo que la IA puede hacer en una pantalla. En cuestión de meses, lo veremos en la calle.”
Reservó, con un depósito de USD 200, el Neo, el robot doméstico de la empresa noruego estadounidense 1X, que empieza a entregarse en Estados Unidos este año. Calcula que el “momento ChatGPT” de la robótica llega en 2027 y que en 2028 un robot para las tareas de la casa costará entre USD 25 mil y 30 mil.
“El mundo que nos merecemos y no el que nos podemos permitir”
Usa la IA para todo, desde que se levanta hasta que se acuesta. “No es una herramienta, es infraestructura.” Su grupo de empresas, con unas pocas decenas de empleados, produce como cientos. Trabaja más que nunca y no volvería atrás: “Me daría muchísima pereza volver al mundo anterior”.
Su definición sirve para el optimista y para el pesimista: “Hemos creado máquinas capaces de hacer cosas de humanos, para lo bueno y para lo malo”. Del lado bueno pone la salud sin listas de espera de seis meses, un tutor para cada chico y, si se hacen bien las cosas, la pobreza como problema resoluble. “El mundo va a ser el que nos merecemos y no el que nos podemos permitir.”
Del lado malo, la facilidad humana para volverse mediocre, delegar todo y terminar como en Wall-E. “Dejas de tener el control, dejas de tener el criterio y a partir de ahí te puedes convertir en una ameba inútil.”
Me quedo con la nota con faltas de ortografía. Su hijo no hizo trampa: entendió antes que nadie cómo funciona el mundo que le toca. La pregunta es cuántos adultos pueden decir lo mismo.
Cuando Hernández dice que la IA no es una herramienta sino infraestructura, está diciendo algo simple: nadie elige si usa la electricidad. Lo único que todavía se elige es cuándo. Y esa ventana se está cerrando.

articles.title: How a Fake Signal Could Fool Every Robot Safeguard
articles.text:
This article is brought to you by VicOne.
A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal.
But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path.
In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation.
At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe.
How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior
A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.
Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models, a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task.
In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement.
VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did.
In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack.VicOne
Safety-related decisions have inputs too
An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated?
At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved.
A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall.
Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information.
Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm.VicOne
Deliberate attacks challenge safety assumptions
A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed.
Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research, a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once.
Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated.
Security testing strengthens robot safety evidence
Safety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated.
That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots. IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems. The EU Machinery Regulation, which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions.
Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne
Before deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team.
VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community, VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. VicOne’s Radeis helps teams validate potential effects before deployment, while Rthena provides visibility into risks and behavior during operation.
Five questions safety and security teams should answer together
The central test is whether a robot’s safeguards still protect people when the information they rely on is manipulated. Safety and security teams can begin by tracing the inputs behind each protective decision, challenging them, and revisiting the evidence as the robot changes. They can start with these five questions:
1. What does each protective function read? Map the readings, estimates, messages, and confirmations. Identify which safeguards operate independently of the robot’s AI decisions.
2. How does that information arrive? Check how inputs are produced, transmitted, authenticated where appropriate, and handled when they are missing or implausible.
3. What happens if an input is manipulated? Test false distances, drifting position estimates, and other relevant scenarios against the robot’s safety limits.
4. Can one action mislead several inputs? Check whether sensor fusion or seemingly independent safeguards share a point of failure.
5. When should the evidence be revisited? Reassess after changes to software, models, sensors, or operating conditions. Agree on bounded responses to suspicious behavior with the safety team in advance.
The goal is not only to show that a protective function works. Teams also need evidence that it remains protective when the information behind its decision is wrong or deliberately manipulated — and that another safeguard can catch the resulting hazard when needed. As robots change, that evidence needs to change with them.
For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”
VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.

articles.title: Meta recaudará hasta USD 97.500 millones con acciones, una de las mayores emisiones de la historia
articles.text:
Meta Platforms elevó a USD 97.500 millones el monto que busca recaudar con la venta de acciones para financiar su expansión en inteligencia artificial. Según Bloomberg, es una de las mayores emisiones de capital de la historia. La empresa informó los precios de colocación en un comunicado la noche del lunes 26 de octubre.
La parte ya colocada suma USD 37.500 millones. La compañía vendió acciones comunes por USD 25.000 millones a USD 625 cada una, por encima de los USD 22.500 millones previstos al inicio. Además, colocó 250 millones de certificados de acciones preferentes a USD 50 cada uno, que suman USD 12.500 millones.
Las acciones preferentes son un título que se convierten en acciones comunes en una fecha fijada. En este caso, la conversión está prevista alrededor del 15 de agosto de 2029, según el comunicado de la empresa. Morgan Stanley y Goldman Sachs lideran las ofertas, informó Bloomberg.
El resto, hasta USD 60.000 millones, llegaría mediante un programa de venta gradual: la compañía coloca acciones en el mercado, a precios del momento, en tandas sucesivas. Meta aclaró que todavía no firmó ningún acuerdo y que el calendario y las condiciones no están definidos.
Qué empresas están entre las compradoras
Nvidia, AMD y Broadcom aceptaron comprar en conjunto hasta USD 5.000 millones de las acciones comunes, según Meta. Nvidia precisó en otro comunicado que aportará USD 3.000 millones. Las tres fabrican chips que Meta compra para sus centros de datos.
Reuters señaló que esa participación alimenta la preocupación por un flujo de dinero circular en la industria de la IA: los proveedores de chips ayudan a financiar a uno de sus mayores clientes.
Meta usará los fondos para infraestructura de IA y lo que llama “superinteligencia personal”. Las acciones de la empresa cayeron 1,9% en la mañana del lunes tras el anuncio inicial, informó CNBC.
El gasto superó al dinero que genera el negocio
En el tercer trimestre, Meta tuvo un flujo de caja libre negativo de USD 2.120 millones, el primero en más de una década. Un año antes había sido positivo en USD 10.630 millones. Los ingresos del trimestre subieron 26%, hasta USD 64.600 millones, según CNBC e InvestmentNews.
La compañía prevé inversiones de capital por entre USD 135.000 millones y USD 145.000 millones en 2026. Reuters calculó que sus compromisos de gasto futuro suman unos USD 825.000 millones, sobre todo en centros de datos, infraestructura de IA y capacidad de cómputo en la nube.
Meta sostiene que financiará ese gasto con una combinación de flujo operativo, deuda con grado de inversión, alianzas y capital propio. La empresa informó que generó USD 97.000 millones de flujo operativo en los primeros tres trimestres y que tenía unos USD 82.000 millones en efectivo e inversiones al cierre del tercero.
Las acciones sin voto protegen el control de Zuckerberg
El programa gradual se hará con acciones Clase C, una nueva categoría sin derecho a voto que Meta anunció el 21 de octubre. Reuters explicó que permite captar capital sin diluir el poder de Mark Zuckerberg, fundador y director ejecutivo, que concentra alrededor del 60,6% de los votos.
Las acciones Clase C empezarían a cotizar en el primer trimestre de 2027. Bloomberg indicó que el inicio de la negociación está previsto para enero, y el programa de USD 60.000 millones comenzaría después de ese debut.

articles.title: What Took the Internet Offline in Q3 2026
articles.text:
What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026
The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event.
In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters.
Disruptions at a glance
Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq, while renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region showed how quickly connectivity can become part of a broader political and humanitarian crisis. Outages within the United States, Japan, and Portugal — countries with a relatively strong history of Internet resilience — remind us that no country is immune to disruption.
In total, Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 disruptions during the quarter. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 incidents, including 18 exam shutdowns in Iraq. Power outages followed with 14 incidents, while natural disasters accounted for five.
Power failure was a leading cause of disruptions
The Internet is designed to be distributed and resilient, but that resilience still depends on electricity. When power fails, routers, mobile base stations, data centers, interconnection facilities, and the networks that connect them can fail with it. Over the past three months, that dependency was one of the clearest patterns in Radar’s disruption data. Power outages were the second-most common cause of disruptions by incident count this quarter, behind government-directed exam shutdowns.
In Cuba, Internet disruptions followed the erratic patterns of an unstable power grid. Radar observed four power-related outages across the quarter, meaning connectivity was affected by grid failures at least once a month. The outages took place July 6, July 14, August 3, and a three-day blackout from September 18 to 20. The traffic volume decreases ranged from 18% on July 14 to 59% on August 3.
Honduras illustrated how a localized infrastructure failure can produce national-level effects. A power failure on September 10 at an interconnection facility affected at least 11 major providers, showing how concentrated traffic exchange points can become single points of failure. The outage lasted approximately three hours, during which HTTP traffic across the country fell by 63%.
Two notable exceptions were the cross-border provider Telecomunicaciones de Guatemala (AS14754) and mobile carrier Celtel (AS52262), which were unaffected. This suggests that their Honduran connectivity may rely more heavily on infrastructure outside the country.
On July 5, a power outage in Sevastopol, Ukraine, caused an eight-hour blackout, with HTTP traffic dropping by 98%. A little over a month later, on August 12, drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure caused another power outage, resulting in a ten-hour Internet disruption and up to a 95% decline in traffic volume. As discussed in more detail below, geopolitical conflict remains a major driver of Internet disruptions. These incidents also show how conflict, energy infrastructure, and Internet connectivity are fundamentally intertwined.
Also of note: on August 13, a cooling system failure at a data center in the U.S. city of Phoenix caused a near-total drop in Internet traffic from Namecheap (AS22612). Outages such as these will be important to watch as the role of cooling systems becomes increasingly critical.
Beyond the larger outages in Cuba, Honduras, and Ukraine, power-related disruptions also appeared across a wide range of countries, including Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Some of these events were caused by sudden failures, while others, such as planned load-shedding in Eswatini, reflected deliberate efforts to manage constrained power supply. Their scale and duration varied, but together they point to the same underlying dependency: when power systems become unstable, Internet connectivity often becomes unstable with them. In total, Radar observed 14 power-related disruptions across 10 countries during the quarter.
The physical world takes the virtual world offline
Last quarter, Radar reported on the impact of Super Typhoon Sinlaku, as it moved through the Mariana Islands, knocking out power and, in turn, Internet connectivity in Guam, where HTTP traffic took four days to return to typical levels.
Super Typhoon Bavi followed Sinlaku by less than three months, giving Guam two major storm-related connectivity disruptions in a single year. Officials appeared to take earlier preparedness steps ahead of Bavi, including declaring a state of emergency before peak storm conditions. Even so, the storm caused widespread power outages. The Guam Power Authority reported that strong winds brought down key transmission lines, leaving only about 25% of distribution feeders online at one point. From a connectivity perspective, the outcome was familiar: widespread power outages, downed transmission lines, and a multi-day recovery period for Internet traffic.
In Japan, an earthquake of similar magnitude, 7.1, prompted evacuation orders affecting roughly 150,000 people in Kumamoto. The impact on Internet connectivity primarily appeared in desktop traffic, while mobile traffic remained largely unaffected.
In Colombia, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake in August caused building collapses, injuries, mass evacuations, and a four-and-a-half-day Internet disruption. Damage to fiber-optic infrastructure, compounded by the wider earthquake aftermath, drove a significant drop in traffic from Colombia Telecomunicaciones (AS3816).
Finally, in Nepal, sudden flash floods swept through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems on August 26, affecting communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. The flooding damaged homes, infrastructure, and essential services, including power, which in turn disrupted regional Internet connectivity. The outage recorded on Radar lasted two hours, during which HTTP traffic dropped by up to 18%.
Exam shutdowns continue in Iraq
Government-directed shutdowns were the largest cause of disruptions in Q3, the majority of which occurred in Iraq with separate scheduled shutdowns occurring throughout the quarter. The shutdowns took place on a strict schedule 03:30–04:00 UTC, lasting about 15-90 min each. The majority occurred between August 26 and September 28, with three occurring between July 1 and 8.
Per Internet Society Pulse, “In a video message, Minister Mustafa Sanad, Iraq's Minister of Communication, confirmed the shutdown and vowed to develop a digital system that would eliminate the need for centralized exam distribution and, by extension, the need to shut down Internet access on exam days.” Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor the country’s networks as the development of the new system progresses.
Notably, Syria and Sudan, two countries that have also frequently used exam-related Internet shutdowns in recent years, did not record similar disruptions this quarter. However, this likely reflects differences in exam calendars rather than a clear shift in policy. Radar will continue to monitor whether future national exam periods bring renewed shutdowns in either country.
Disruptions coincide with political events
In Ethiopia, renewed conflict in the Tigray region was accompanied by a government-directed Internet shutdown that lasted 10 days. Traffic dropped by 100%, signaling a full-scale shutdown.
The disruption revived memories of the extensive blockade imposed during Ethiopia’s civil war from 2020 to 2022, when Tigray was largely cut off from telecommunications, electricity, banking services, fuel, and humanitarian aid (France24), which the World Health Organization described as a “de facto blockade.” Although this latest outage appears to have remained localized to Tigray, its impact was still visible in country-level traffic, with HTTP traffic falling by up to 30%.
On September 19, during nationwide elections, fiber-optic cable damage in Russia’s Far East caused regional connectivity disruptions affecting Chukotka, Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka Krai, and Sakhalin Oblast. Rostelecom described the incidents as deliberate damage to backbone fiber lines and said connectivity was restored using backup channels. Radar data alone cannot determine whether the cable damage was related to the elections, but the timing is notable.
A quarter shaped by shutdowns and power outages, but also resilience
Across Q3 2026, government-directed shutdowns were the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by Iraq’s exam-related shutdowns. Power outages were close behind, affecting networks across Cuba, Honduras, Ukraine, Eswatini, Botswana, Tajikistan, Kenya, Saint Lucia, Georgia, and Gabon. Natural disasters and conflict added another layer of disruption, reminding us that Internet resilience depends on far more than routers and cables. It depends on electricity, physical infrastructure, policy decisions, and the ability of networks to route around failure.
Radar also observed outages inside individual networks, including One Communications (AS19863) in Guyana following a cable cut, MEO (AS3243) in Portugal following a reported “mass attack”, Digicel Haiti (AS27653), TurkNet (AS12735) in Turkey, and Fanap Telecom (AS206065) in Iran.
Each of these events demonstrates the Internet’s fragility, but also its resilience. Many disruptions were brief: 14 saw traffic return to typical levels in under an hour, and 16 recovered in less than three hours. But short outages can still have real consequences for the people affected, especially during storms, earthquakes, conflict, or political unrest. Access to the Internet is often access to information, coordination, safety, and help.
Cloudflare Radar will continue to monitor Internet disruptions around the world and share what we see from Cloudflare’s global network. Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

articles.title: Jamais Microsoft n’avait fait ça : pour financer l’IA, plus de 25 % de ses salariés sont incités à partir d’ici la fin de l’année
articles.text:
Jamais Microsoft n’avait fait ça : pour financer l’IA, plus de 25 % de ses salariés sont incités à partir d’ici la fin de l’année
Volontaire jusqu’à nouvel ordre : Microsoft garde les licenciements en réserve
Soixante mille employés de Microsoft ont reçu lundi une proposition sans précédent dans l'histoire du groupe : quitter l'entreprise avant la fin de l'année, avec une indemnité. Personne n'est poussé vers la sortie, du moins officiellement. Mais Redmond prévient déjà que les licenciements restent sur la table. Combien vont partir, et qui aura le dernier mot ?
Le 26 octobre 2026, Amy Coleman, vice-présidente exécutive chargée des ressources humaines de Microsoft, a publié sur le blog officiel du groupe un programme d'offre de départ volontaire. Environ 60 000 personnes y ont droit, soit près de 27 % des 223 000 salariés que comptait le géant fin juin, selon CNBC. Les volontaires devront se décider en décembre et quitteront l'entreprise le 31 décembre.
Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees. This latest exit offer is available to far more employees than the previous retirement one, and comes just months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees. Full details here 👇https://t.co/WHKz3Hdc4P
— Tom Warren (@tomwarren) October 26, 2026
Qui peut quitter Microsoft, et à quelles conditions
Le dispositif couvre quatre pays : les États-Unis, le Canada, le Royaume-Uni et l'Inde. Il concerne les salariés de niveau 70 et en dessous dans la grille interne, soit presque tous les effectifs, certains vice-présidents compris. Chaque division choisit d'y participer ou non. D'après une source citée par Reuters, Copilot, la finance, les ressources humaines, Xbox et Windows + Devices en font partie. Le marketing, l'activité commerciale et la sécurité restent à l'écart.
L'indemnité correspond au barème de licenciement standard du groupe, a précisé Microsoft à GeekWire. Elle s'accompagne d'un accompagnement pour la suite de carrière.
	
L'offre de départ volontaire est nouvelle pour nous. Nous en tirerons des leçons.
Un premier essai a déjà eu lieu au printemps. En avril, Microsoft avait proposé une retraite anticipée à environ 8 750 salariés américains dont l'âge et l'ancienneté cumulés atteignaient 70 ans. Un peu plus de 30 % ont accepté. Cette fois, le groupe dit s'attendre à une proportion nettement plus faible. Il prévient aussi que les licenciements restent possibles selon la conjoncture.
L'IA en arrière-plan, la France hors du dispositif
Microsoft prévoit 175 milliards de dollars d'investissements en 2026, en grande partie pour ses centres de données et ses puces dédiées à l'IA. Selon Reuters, cette offre de départ doit justement contenir les coûts et aider à financer ces dépenses colossales.
Les effectifs, eux, fondent depuis plus d'un an : 6 000 postes supprimés en mai 2025, environ 9 000 en juillet 2025, puis 4 800 en juillet 2026, dont une large part chez Xbox. Le groupe assure pourtant que cette offre ne signale pas un besoin de réduire ses équipes. Les marchés se feront leur propre idée mercredi 28 octobre, avec la publication des résultats trimestriels.
Les quelque 2 000 salariés de Microsoft France ne sont pas concernés. Ils ont déjà connu leur propre plan. En septembre 2025, la filiale a lancé une rupture conventionnelle collective, signée avec tous les syndicats représentatifs, qui portait sur environ 200 postes. C'est le mécanisme prévu par le droit du travail français pour ce type de départs volontaires.

articles.title: Le Danemark abandonne en silence son test d’un Office open source, sans même en tirer le bilan
articles.text:
Le ministère danois de la Numérisation a mis fin à son expérimentation d’une alternative open source à Microsoft Office, révèle Computerworld le 20 octobre. Le projet, lancé à l’été 2025 avec 38 agents, ne sera pas repris et n’a fait l’objet d’aucun bilan. Entre-temps, ce ministère a disparu : il a été fusionné en juin avec celui de l’Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche.
À l’époque, la ministre de la Numérisation, Caroline Stage, présentait ce test comme un pas vers l’indépendance technologique vis-à-vis des États-Unis, et saluait un « pas bienvenu dans la bonne direction ». Le ministère espérait se passer d’Office 365 avant la fin de l’automne 2025.
Les agents testaient Collabora, une suite bureautique britannique basée sur LibreOffice, fournie par le Danois cBrain et reliée à F2, son système de gestion de dossiers. Le test visait notamment à vérifier l’échange de documents entre les formats de Microsoft et les formats ouverts.
Un test arrêté avant d’être évalué
L’expérience aurait pris fin au moment où la Première ministre a convoqué des élections anticipées, fin février 2026. Un porte-parole du ministère aurait confirmé qu’aucune reprise n’est envisagée.
Des agents auraient buté sur la mise en forme des documents, des pages blanches inexpliquées et le suivi des modifications. Rien ne dit si ces difficultés ont été résolues, ni si elles ont pesé dans la décision d’arrêter.
C’est justement ce que regrette Mikkel Flyverbom, professeur à la Copenhagen Business School. « Tester des alternatives dans un projet pilote est une bonne idée », a-t-il indiqué par courriel à Tom’s Hardware, mais il aurait souhaité que le ministère en tire des enseignements et les partage avec le reste du secteur public. Sans évaluation, impossible de savoir si le ministère aurait pu fonctionner sans Office.
La souveraineté numérique à l’épreuve de l’usage
L’épisode danois survient trois semaines après celui de la Commission européenne, où Element Pro, déployé cet été comme solution de secours à Teams, a été vivement critiqué par des fonctionnaires sur une messagerie interne. Les deux cas n’ont ni la même ampleur ni les mêmes causes : d’un côté un outil de secours jugé décevant, de l’autre un test arrêté sans bilan. Mais ils posent la même question : que vaut une alternative souveraine face à des outils aussi installés que Teams ou Office ?
Le PDG d’Element reconnaissait lui-même des « soucis de jeunesse » inévitables quand on quitte un outil aussi répandu que Teams. Au Danemark, les difficultés qu’auraient rencontrées les agents (mise en forme, suivi des modifications) concernent des gestes du quotidien, qui comptent beaucoup dans l’adoption d’un outil. L’envie, elle, existe : un sondage Eurobaromètre montrait en juin que 83 % des Français jugent souhaitable de réduire la dépendance numérique aux acteurs américains, mais nommer une alternative crédible aux outils du quotidien reste plus difficile.
D’autres alternatives européennes continuent d’avancer. Euro Office, qui s’appuie sur OnlyOffice et non sur LibreOffice, vient de proposer son client de bureau sur Windows, macOS et Linux. Elle prend en charge les formats .docx, .xlsx et .pptx, comme nous l’annoncions en septembre.

articles.title: FritzOS 8.50: Diese Fritzboxen können das Update jetzt laden
articles.text:
FritzOS 8.50: Diese Fritzboxen können das Update jetzt laden
Schon seit geraumer Zeit warten Fritzbox-User:innen auf das große Update FritzOS 8.50. Hersteller Fritz hatte erste Neuerungen zunächst mit der Labor-Version 8.40 testen lassen. Jetzt ist die Beta-Phase für erste Fritz-Router vorbei und die finale Version von FritzOS 8.50 wird Schritt für Schritt für die einzelnen Geräte freigegeben.
Welche Fritzboxen bekommen FritzOS 8.50 jetzt?
Die Liste der Fritzboxen, die jetzt mit der Release-Version FritzOS 8.50 ausgestattet werden, wächst dadurch langsam an. In den kommenden Wochen und Monaten dürfte Fritz noch mehr Modelle für die Aktualisierung freigeben. Wer nicht so lange warten möchte, kann wie erwähnt bei manchen Modellen das Labor-Update zu FritzOS 8.40 installieren, das erste Funktionen von FritzOS 8.50 mit sich bringt. Beachte allerdings, dass es sich um Testversionen des Updates handelt, die noch Probleme bereiten können. Diese Modelle dürfen schon die finale Version von FritzOS 8.50 laden:
- Fritzbox 7530 AX
- Fritzbox 7690
- Fritzbox 5630
- Fritzbox 5690
Was steckt in FritzOS 8.50?
Die größte Neuerung von FritzOS 8.50 ist ein DNS-Filter. Dadurch kannst du Werbeeinblendungen auf einer Vielzahl von Geräten im Netzwerk einfach ausblenden. Das gilt etwa für Smartphones, Tablets und verbundene Smart-TVs. Daneben bietet die Myfritz-App in Verbindung mit FritzOS 8.50 einen Smart Check. Darüber wird dir in der App der Status deiner Fritzbox und deines gesamten Netzwerks angezeigt. Die App gibt dir zusätzlich Empfehlungen, mit denen du dein Heimnetz verbessern kannst.
Ferner integriert Fritz mit FritzOS 8.50 eine automatische Priorisierung, die Echtzeitverbindungen wie Videoanrufe vor alle anderen Verbindungen stellt. Dadurch wird die nötige Bandbreite für Meetings und Co. freigegeben, falls andere Verbindungen die Leitung belasten. Für alle Smarthome-User:innen integriert FritzOS 8.50 vordefinierte Routinen wie beim Verlassen des Hauses. Bei selbsterstellten Routinen lassen sich künftig auch mehrere Auslöser festlegen und das Geofencing wurde verbessert.

articles.title: Cybersecurity Issue Forces a Major New Mexico Hospital to Divert Patients and Close Clinics
articles.text:
A major hospital network in New Mexico raced to fix a cybersecurity issue on Monday that forced it to send ambulances to other hospitals and left the state without an emergency department capable of treating the most serious injuries.
The University of New Mexico Health System told people not to show up at its main hospital in Albuquerque and canceled appointments at its more than 30 clinics. It said it was working to resolve the issue, the extent and nature of which was not immediately clear.
The hospital network conducts about 900,000 outpatient visits and receives 100,000 emergency room visits each year, according to its website. It operates the state’s only Level 1 trauma center.
Presbyterian Healthcare Services and Lovelace Health System, two other major healthcare providers in New Mexico, said they were coordinating with the UNM Health System, including taking additional patients.
The UNM Health System said in a statement that its hospitals and clinics began resuming operations in phases later in the day.
Multiple UNM Health System employees said they heard messages across their computers while working late Monday morning that claimed to have stolen student and employee data and patient information.
A spokesperson for the health system wouldn’t comment, saying that the incident remains an active law enforcement investigation. FBI spokesperson Margot Cravens in Albuquerque said the agency was “assisting our partner” but declined further comment.
The Associated Press left emails and phone messages seeking comment from the Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office and the Albuquerque Police Department.
The incident comes amid growing concern about the security of digital systems that underpin essential services, from banking to medical care.
Incidents affecting hospitals, including demands for ransom. have been going on for a decade, said Josephine Wolff, a professor of cybersecurity policy at Tufts University.
Breaching a system to play a message on computers is pretty unusual, Wolff said. Monday’s incident, she said, shows “how much work we still have to do to get better at defending ourselves.”
On Monday afternoon, at the main entrance to its Albuquerque hospital, employees in turquoise staff shirts sat on chairs that blocked the waiting room and told patients their appointments might be canceled.
At a medical center in the Albuquerque suburb of Rio Rancho, two security guards at the entrance told patients arriving for appointments to reschedule.
UNM’s Health Sciences Center, the state’s largest academic medical center, canceled classes Monday.
Related: Cyberattacks on Hospitals Are Likely to Increase, Putting Lives at Risk, Experts Warn

articles.title: Smart Window adds new form filling and page watching features | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
Skip the busywork with Smart Window
The days might be getting shorter, but your to-do list is only getting longer. Whether you’re getting a head start on holiday shopping or planning your next career move, Smart Window’s newest features will help you keep up.
Firefox’s opt-in AI browsing experience can now use information from tabs you choose to help fill out forms. It can also watch web pages and notify you about specific changes you’ve asked it to track.
Let your open tabs fill in the blanks
Job applications ask for your work history; event registrations ask for a professional bio. If those details are already in your open tabs, Smart Window can now use pages you choose to suggest what to enter, saving you extra clicks and some Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V.
For example, Smart Window could use information from your online portfolio or professional profile to fill in your work history, or draw on those details to draft an answer to a question like “Tell me about a time when…” Firefox’s regular autofill still handles saved information such as your name and address, which can be entered directly into forms without relying on AI models.
To get started, click into a form field. If the form has at least four text fields that Smart Window can help fill, you’ll see “Fill from sources” appear in the dropdown, along with a recommended source page. Select “Fill from sources” to continue, or click the pencil icon to open “Edit sources” if you want to change or add tabs. Once you’ve chosen your sources, review the suggestions before filling out the form. You can edit the results before submitting; Smart Window won’t submit the form for you.
When you choose to use this feature, information from your selected source pages is shared with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model used for detecting the fields and extracting relevant information from your selected tabs. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same, and saved autofill values stay on your device. Learn more about how form filling works.
This feature currently supports text fields on web forms and does not save any generated form fill data. We’re exploring support for more field types, including dropdown menus, as well as PDF forms and ways to save and manage generated information for future forms.
Give your refresh button a break
A watched pot never boils, and refreshing a web page won’t make an update appear any sooner.
Smart Window can now watch a page for a specific update, whether that’s an item going on sale or a new job listing that includes a job title or company name that you’re following. Each task can follow up to five pages, so you can keep an eye on several stores or job boards at the same time.
Type “/watch” in the Smart Window chat to set up a task. Describe what you’re looking for, add the pages to watch, and choose whether Firefox should check for updates on a daily or weekly basis. Those checks run only while the browser is open.
When there’s a match, you’ll see an update through the Tasks button in the toolbar. With desktop notifications enabled, Firefox can also notify you directly; click the notification to open the watched pages. You can have up to 15 active tasks at a time, and you can edit, pause or delete tasks. Smart Window will automatically pause tasks after 60 days without a matching change. If 90 days pass without a change, it will stop checking altogether.
Page monitoring uses the Qwen AI model to identify changes that match what you’re looking for. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same. Learn more about creating and managing tasks.
Try the latest additions
These two new features are available in the Smart Window beta on desktop, in English in the U.S. and Canada, and will roll out to additional markets in the coming months.
Try Smart Window and share your experience on Mozilla Connect. We’d love to hear how you’re using Smart Window to get things done and what you’d like it to help with next.

articles.title: General Compute raises $100 million Series A, countering the neocloud disaster narrative | TechCrunch
articles.text:
CoreWeave, a publicly traded neocloud that rents out computing power for AI, has seen its stock price fall to a 12-month low, and Elon Musk is flexing $40 billion in debt for buying computing capacity and predicting that “200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.” It’s not exactly the ideal week to announce a Series A for a neocloud.
General Compute co-founder and CEO Finn Puklowski is unfazed. He’s bullish on CoreWeave’s chances, and thinks Musk is just talking his book to drive down the prices of the GPUs he wants to buy. Fears of a chip-led collapse are “massively overstated. I have people calling me up every single week asking me to do TPUs, GPUs, any chip, to get them more compute.”
Just as important, he says, Anthropic’s bullish S-1 is “settling fears for today.”
General Compute has found a niche building its cloud out of specialized inference chips built by Nvidia rivals. The company struck a $400 million deal to purchase new chips from SambaNova — the first debt financing of inference chips — and now has added Positron and Cerebras to its portfolio of chip suppliers.
A deal with a large customer worth $100 million in annual recurring revenue has paved the way for the company to raise $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird Ventures and Abstract Ventures. Valued at $60 million after a May seed round, General Compute is now worth $800 million post-money to its investors.
The startup’s strategy is to zig where others zag. It focused on chips built for inference while everyone else chased GPUs. And instead of taking on a complex effort to build huge data centers, it uses smaller power sources, rents space in other companies’ data centers, and converts former bitcoin-mining sites into places that run AI models.
That approach means General Compute isn’t going to catapult into the top ranks of neoclouds or compete with hyperscalers any time soon. But it’s also not subject to the constraints that come with building data centers from scratch. When General Compute has chips, it will have someplace to plug them in. Puklowski expects the company to deploy 75 megawatts of computing capacity in 2027, and he suspects he will have access to 200 megawatts of power — “more than we can probably fund and get hardware for.”
Still, the plan has a limit. Puklowski’s financing work isn’t done — “capital is going to be a full-time job for me, both on debt and equity,” he told TechCrunch.
The startup has found key customers in cloud companies that specialize in offering developers high-speed inference; General Compute provides the bare metal, or raw servers with no software layered on top, for them to bring their offerings to market. James Palmer, a principal at Blackbird who co-led the round, said his firm’s confidence in General Compute comes in part from an investment in Baseten, an inference cloud company.
“We’ve been proximate to their journey over the last 10 months and observing the wild growth story that [Baseten] has gone on, and the demand for open weight inference, and for companies owning their own intelligence,” Palmer told TechCrunch. When it comes to General Compute, he said, “Cerebras, Positron, SambaNova, all need distribution partners who can take them to scale, who can navigate the complexity of the physical world.”
Executives at all three chipmakers sang General Compute’s praises to TechCrunch, each noting the importance of the company’s focus on making the economics of AI cloud compute work. “Everyone in this market is selling speed,” Rodrigo Liang, SambaNova’s CEO and co-founder, said. “The real question is whether you can make money doing it.”

articles.title: How AI Is Changing the Pace of Discovery for Millions Living With Dementia
articles.text:
There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease.
The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), working with NVIDIA, is using AI to change that.
Alzheimer’s disease is one of today’s leading global health challenges, with over 10 million new dementia cases diagnosed each year. Despite a 7x increase in National Institutes of Health funding in the last 15 years — reaching $3.9 billion annually — no treatment has been found to stop, prevent or reverse the disease yet.
The bottlenecks are not enough high impact scientific findings, too much data living in institutional silos and too slow a pace of synthesis to keep up with the research that is published.
C-BRAIN, led by Dr. Randall Bateman and a consortium of 18 member institutions across academic, philanthropic, pharma and research organizations, launched in November 2025 to help scientists make better, faster discoveries by accelerating the research that makes new treatments possible.
“We have a window of opportunity with artificial intelligence to do research fundamentally different than we’ve ever done before, in a way that accelerates discoveries to help patients,” said Bateman, founder and director of C-BRAIN and the Charles F. and Joanne Knight Distinguished Professor of Neurology at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He described their work as “AI tools built by scientists, for scientists.”
The consortium is building a system that harnesses previously untapped Alzheimer’s research data to support scientists’ work.
Speeding Research From Weeks to Hours
Essential assets in Alzheimer’s research are datasets that have never been publicly accessible to AI tools or human researchers. This includes unpublished findings, negative results and governed proprietary data from member institutions.
“A lot of life sciences data doesn’t make its way into the frontier models,” said Dr. Ade Ojewole, chief technology officer of C-BRAIN. “The consequence of that is we’re leaving a lot of intelligence on the table.”
C-BRAIN refers to this as “dark data,” which slows down Alzheimer’s research.
Some dark data is directly deposited into secure computer systems for AI tools to access. To use this data without compromising patient privacy or institutional governance, C-BRAIN uses a hybrid centralized and federated approach — where AI models learn from data at each institution without that data ever having to leave its walls. This kind of infrastructure is technically demanding to build and scale, which is part of what NVIDIA brings to the collaboration.
C-BRAIN currently runs 64 NVIDIA data center GPUs on premises alongside cloud-based nodes on Microsoft Azure, with additional NVIDIA GPU capacity, including NVIDIA Blackwell systems, on the horizon as the consortium’s ambitions scale.
To explore how AI and accelerated computing can advance Alzheimer’s research while navigating its technical demands, C-BRAIN is working with NVIDIA to incorporate technologies including the NVIDIA BioNeMo open developer platform and the MONAI framework for C-BRAIN’s research pipelines.
“The C-BRAIN collaboration with NVIDIA aims to unlock those models in a way that they can deliver something quite impactful and important,” said Bateman.
“A great deal of optimization is going to be needed as we push the boundaries of what today’s spatial omics machine learning architectures can model,” Ojewole said. “NVIDIA software is definitely going to come into play there.”
Researchers at C-BRAIN have already built two tools: OpenScientist — built with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in an effort led by research scientist Justin Reese — and InsightEngine, built with 387 Labs.
OpenScientist is an open source agentic AI co-scientist that takes a scientist’s research question and dataset, then semi-autonomously generates hypotheses, runs analyses and produces verifiable, auditable insights. InsightEngine is an open source research platform that uses agentic AI to test hypotheses against the scientific literature, analyzing user-supplied datasets, exploring a biomedical knowledge graph and checking every claim against evidence to catch hallucinations before researchers commit to costly experiments.
In published case studies, OpenScientist completed analyses in minutes that domain scientists estimated would take weeks to months, at a cost of under $10 per run. At C-BRAIN’s current reach of over 200 research groups, this capability could release substantial research capacity, potentially exceeding one million hours annually at scale.
From Correlation to Cause
Looking ahead, C-BRAIN aims to build a multimodal biological foundation model trained on the full breadth of its data — neuroimaging, multi-omics, fluid biomarkers and longitudinal clinical measures.
By year three, it aims to discover new causal mechanisms of brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease, moving to testable scientific principles using the full scope of available research and data.
Bateman said, “AI that can think and reason has the potential to accelerate discoveries that will lead to powerful and implementable preventions and treatments for the entire population.”

articles.title: Nvidia invertirá USD 3.000 millones en las acciones de Meta, su propio cliente de chips
articles.text:
Nvidia invertirá USD 3.000 millones en la emisión de acciones de Meta, según anunciaron las dos empresas el 27 de octubre. El fabricante de chips se convierte así en accionista de uno de sus mayores clientes, en el marco de una alianza ampliada para el asistente de inteligencia artificial Muse de Meta.
La compañía informó que ambas firmas colaborarán para mejorar el rendimiento de entrenamiento y de uso de los modelos Muse, la familia de modelos de IA que sostiene al asistente de Meta. Según el comunicado, el acuerdo responde a la demanda de usuarios por asistentes capaces de ejecutar tareas.
Meta, por su parte, ampliará el uso de infraestructura de Nvidia en sus centros de datos. Incluye los procesadores Vera Rubin y Vera, que alimentarán a sus asistentes de inteligencia artificial, además de la tecnología de redes Spectrum-X y BlueField-4.
Las empresas también evaluarán otras colaboraciones, como OpenShell, una arquitectura de Nvidia para desplegar asistentes de forma segura, y Sentry, un sistema para vigilar su comportamiento.
El director ejecutivo de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, dijo en un comunicado que ambas compañías amplían su alianza para optimizar de punta a punta la infraestructura de cómputo de asistentes de IA “capaces, eficientes y seguros”. Investing.com agregó que la aplicación del asistente Muse figuró entre las más descargadas en la semana de su lanzamiento.
Meta subió el tamaño de su emisión de acciones
El anuncio llegó un día después de que Meta informara que planea recaudar hasta USD 95.000 millones para financiar su expansión en IA, según CNBC. Nvidia, AMD y Broadcom habían manifestado interés en comprar hasta USD 5.000 millones en conjunto, con indicaciones no vinculantes.
El martes, Meta elevó su oferta de acciones comunes a USD 25.000 millones, desde USD 22.500 millones. Con la emisión de acciones de depósito, el total sube hasta USD 37.500 millones, según Investing.com. Las acciones comunes se fijaron en USD 625 cada una y las de depósito en USD 50.
Meta había dicho que no recibirá de inmediato el dinero de la emisión de acciones comunes, sino cuando liquide acuerdos de venta a futuro, algo que prevé hacer antes del 19 de noviembre del año próximo, según el resumen de Stocktwits publicado por Yahoo Finance.
Un cliente que gasta más de lo que genera
Meta calcula que su gasto de capital en 2026 será de USD 135.000 a 145.000 millones. En el tercer trimestre, sus ingresos subieron 26%, hasta USD 64.600 millones, pero el flujo de caja libre fue negativo en USD 2.120 millones, según Yahoo Finance.
Nvidia ya había acordado en febrero suministrar a Meta millones de chips Blackwell y Rubin, en un acuerdo de varios años cuyos términos financieros no se divulgaron, según el medio especializado Data Center Dynamics. AMD y Broadcom también son proveedores de Meta.
Con AMD el vínculo ya era de doble vía: en febrero, la empresa le otorgó a Meta derechos para comprar hasta 160 millones de acciones de AMD por un centavo cada una, sujetos a compras de chips y otras metas, según Yahoo Finance.
Los investigadores David McNay y Robin Marshall, de LSEG, advirtieron la semana pasada que estas “redes de propiedad” pueden convertir el rastreo de ingresos y ganancias en un ejercicio de contabilidad forense, según el mismo medio.
Meta planea además un programa separado de venta de acciones sin derecho a voto por USD 60.000 millones, que comenzaría a principios de 2027, aunque la empresa no lo da por garantizado.

articles.title: OpenAI busca ampliar su nuevo asistente dots: mantiene conversaciones con procesadores de pagos
articles.text:
Alexander Embiricos, responsable del equipo de producto para empresas de OpenAI, dijo que la compañía mantiene conversaciones avanzadas con procesadores de pagos para ampliar lo que puede hacer dots, su asistente de IA que trabaja en segundo plano. Lo afirmó en TechCrunch Disrupt, según informó TechCrunch.
“No puedo decir demasiado”, respondió Embiricos al ser consultado, pero explicó que la empresa está “muy metida” en esas conversaciones. El portal de noticias tecnológicas señaló que permitir que un asistente gaste dinero sería una fuente potencial de ingresos para OpenAI y una exigencia considerable para los consumidores.
Dots salió el 29 de septiembre, durante la conferencia de desarrolladores de OpenAI en San Francisco. Funciona con el modelo GPT-6 Astra, tiene su propia computadora en la nube y puede conectarse a más de 4.000 aplicaciones, según el anuncio oficial de la empresa.
Está disponible en ChatGPT para los suscriptores del plan Pro y del plan Business Premium en los mercados habilitados. Según Wired, el plan Pro cuesta USD 100 al mes. La primera instancia del asistente no tiene costo adicional dentro de esos planes.
Un asistente que propone antes de que se lo pidan
Embiricos explicó que el asistente incluye una función llamada “investigación proactiva”. A intervalos regulares, dots revisa lo que sabe del usuario, las conversaciones previas y los recursos a los que tiene acceso, y luego investiga cómo podría ser más útil y lo propone.
Esa lógica implica que use más capacidad de cálculo, lo que para OpenAI significa mayor consumo de tokens (las unidades de texto que procesa y cobra un modelo). El directivo la describió como un asistente que está “pensando en ti” y en cómo ayudarte.
TechCrunch probó el producto y encontró que anticipa conflictos de calendario y vencimientos, aunque no siempre a tiempo. El propio Embiricos contó que, en una etapa temprana de desarrollo, dots le avisó de una reunión con tres minutos de anticipación. Dijo esperar que el momento de los avisos mejore con el tiempo.
También relató el caso de un ingeniero de una empresa emergente de drones que le contó que su asistente detectó una caída del servicio, la analizó y le llevó información para resolverla antes de que él la notara.
Controles de privacidad todavía limitados
OpenAI sostiene que dots tiene los mismos controles de privacidad que ChatGPT: el usuario puede desactivar el uso de sus conversaciones para entrenar modelos y decidir a qué recursos de su computadora accede el asistente. Según TechCrunch, esos controles no son granulares y la aplicación insiste: no acepta acceso de solo lectura a unidades de almacenamiento en la nube.
Embiricos admitió que hace falta construir controles “súper granulares”. Dijo que la empresa recibió críticas por las configuraciones iniciales, muy conservadoras, con las que el asistente pedía permiso constantemente, y que las irán ajustando.
TechCrunch comparó el caso con Muse, el asistente de Meta, criticado por los perfiles que arma de familiares y amigos de los usuarios. El medio planteó que cuesta separar las necesidades de datos del agente de las de su empresa matriz. Hark, otra empresa emergente con un asistente personal, afirma que no recopila datos para publicidad.
Embiricos también dijo que no piensa reunirse nunca con el agente de otra persona. Tiene un asistente humano porque los socios corporativos de OpenAI prefieren tratar con una persona. El directivo no precisó con qué procesadores de pagos conversa OpenAI ni cuándo podría llegar la función a dots.
